name: Spring Boot

beginner.content:
Spring Framework Introduction

What Problem Was Spring Written to Solve?

Spring did not appear because someone wanted another framework. It appeared because the official way of building enterprise Java in 2002 had become unusable.

That official way was EJB 2 (Enterprise JavaBeans). To write one component that saved a customer to a database, you had to write a home interface, a remote interface, a bean class, and an XML deployment descriptor - four files before a single line of business logic. The bean class had to implement a container interface, so it could only run inside a full application server. You could not test it with a plain main method, and you could not test it with JUnit, because outside the server the class had no meaning.

In 2002 Rod Johnson published a book, Expert One-on-One J2EE Design and Development, arguing that most of this was unnecessary. He shipped 30,000 lines of working code with it to prove the point. Readers wanted the code more than the book. It became an open-source project, and in 2003 it was released as the Spring Framework - so named because it was meant to be the spring that followed the winter of J2EE.

The Central Claim: Your Class Should Stay a Plain Java Class

Spring's founding idea is small enough to state in one sentence: the framework should adapt to your objects, not force your objects to adapt to it.

A class managed by Spring is a POJO - a Plain Old Java Object. It extends nothing, it implements no framework interface, and it contains no reference to Spring at all. Spring finds it, builds it, hands it what it needs and manages it - but the class itself does not know that.

The practical consequence is the one that matters day to day: because the class is ordinary Java, you can create it with new in a unit test and it works. No server, no container, no deployment.

What Spring Actually Gives You

Four things, and they build on each other in that order.

WhatWhat it means in practice
An IoC containerSpring creates your objects and connects them together, instead of each object creating its own collaborators with new. This is the foundation everything else sits on - covered in the next two topics.
Templates over verbose APIsJdbcTemplate is the classic example. Raw JDBC makes you open a connection, create a statement, loop a ResultSet, catch SQLException and close three resources in a finally block. JdbcTemplate reduces the same work to the query and the row mapping; Spring does the rest and cannot forget to close anything.
Declarative servicesTransactions, security and caching are applied by declaring them - @Transactional on a method - rather than by writing begin/commit/rollback by hand. Spring wraps the object in a proxy that does the work around your method.
IntegrationSpring does not reimplement Hibernate, Jackson, Kafka or Tomcat. It provides a consistent way to configure and combine them, so the pieces of an application are wired the same way regardless of which library sits underneath.

Notice what is not on that list: Spring is not a web server, not an ORM and not a database driver. It is the thing that assembles those into an application.

Spring, Spring Framework, Spring Boot - the Names

These three names get used interchangeably in conversation and they are not the same thing.

NameWhat it is
Spring FrameworkThe core project: the IoC container, Spring MVC, transactions, AOP. This is what was released in 2003 and what this module is about.
Spring (the ecosystem)The whole family built on that core - Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Cloud, Spring Batch and around twenty more. Each is a separate project with its own version.
Spring BootNot a replacement for the framework and not a separate framework. It is a layer on top of it that removes the configuration work: sensible defaults, one dependency per feature, and an embedded server so the application runs as a plain java -jar. Every Spring Boot application is a Spring Framework application.

This matters when reading answers online. A 2011 Spring tutorial full of XML is not wrong - it is the same framework, configured the way people configured it before Boot existed. The concepts carry over unchanged; only the configuration style is dated.

The Timeline Worth Knowing

You will meet all of these in existing codebases, so the rough dates are useful.

VersionYearWhat changed
Spring 1.02003First release. Configuration is XML, and only XML.
Spring 2.52007Annotations arrive: @Component, @Autowired, component scanning. XML starts to shrink.
Spring 3.02009Java configuration (@Configuration, @Bean) and SpEL. XML becomes optional.
Spring 4.02013Java 8, lambdas, REST improvements.
Spring Boot 1.02014Auto-configuration and starters. This is the point at which most teams stopped writing configuration by hand.
Spring 5.02017Reactive stack (WebFlux) alongside the servlet stack.
Spring 6 / Boot 32022Java 17 minimum, and javax.* becomes jakarta.*. This rename breaks old code and is the single most common cause of "it compiled last year" errors.

The javax to jakarta change is worth remembering now rather than discovering later. On Boot 3, import javax.persistence.Entity; does not resolve - it is import jakarta.persistence.Entity;. Tutorials written before 2022 all use the old package.

Spring Architecture

Spring Is Not One Jar

The Spring Framework is a set of around twenty separate modules, each shipped as its own jar. You add only the ones you need. A batch job that never serves a web request does not carry Spring MVC; a REST service that never touches a database does not carry Spring ORM.

The modules are grouped into five areas, and they stack - the ones above depend on the ones below, never the other way round.

   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |                        TEST                                 |
   |            spring-test  (mock objects, TestContext)         |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+

   +----------------------------+  +-----------------------------+
   |   DATA ACCESS / INTEGRATION|  |            WEB              |
   |   spring-jdbc              |  |   spring-web                |
   |   spring-orm               |  |   spring-webmvc             |
   |   spring-oxm               |  |   spring-webflux            |
   |   spring-jms               |  |   spring-websocket          |
   |   spring-tx                |  |                             |
   +----------------------------+  +-----------------------------+

   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |            AOP  |  ASPECTS  |  INSTRUMENTATION              |
   |     spring-aop  |  spring-aspects  |  spring-instrument      |
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+

   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |                     CORE CONTAINER                          |
   |   spring-core | spring-beans | spring-context | spring-expression
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+

Read it bottom-up. Everything rests on the Core Container. Nothing in the Core Container knows that the web or data layers exist.

The Core Container - the Part That Is Always There

These four jars are Spring. Every other module is an addition to them.

ModuleWhat it does
spring-coreThe foundation: utility classes, the resource abstraction (Resource, ClassPathResource), and type conversion. Nothing above it works without it.
spring-beansThe bean factory itself - bean definitions, instantiation, and dependency injection. This is where BeanFactory lives.
spring-contextBuilds ApplicationContext on top of the bean factory and adds the enterprise services: events, internationalisation, resource loading, scheduling, and annotation configuration (@Component, @Configuration).
spring-expressionSpEL - the expression language used inside @Value("${...}"), @PreAuthorize and XML configuration.

The split between spring-beans and spring-context is the split between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext: the first is the container, the second is the container plus everything an application actually needs around it. In practice you always use ApplicationContext.

The Layers Above

AreaModulePurpose
AOPspring-aopProxy-based aspect support. This is what makes @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async work at all.
spring-aspectsIntegration with AspectJ, for the cases proxies cannot handle.
spring-instrumentClass instrumentation via a Java agent. Rare.
Data Accessspring-jdbcJdbcTemplate and the exception translation that turns vendor SQLException codes into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy.
spring-ormIntegration with JPA and Hibernate.
spring-txTransaction management - both programmatic and the declarative @Transactional.
spring-oxmObject/XML mapping (JAXB and friends).
spring-jmsJMS messaging.
Webspring-webThe shared web basics: multipart handling, HTTP clients, and the servlet integration both web stacks build on.
spring-webmvcThe servlet stack - DispatcherServlet, @Controller, view resolution. Thread-per-request, blocking.
spring-webfluxThe reactive stack - non-blocking, event-loop based. An alternative to webmvc, not an addition to it.
spring-websocketWebSocket and STOMP support.
Testspring-testLoads an application context inside JUnit, plus MockMvc and the mock servlet objects.

Note on the two web stacks: spring-webmvc and spring-webflux are alternatives. Putting both on the classpath is legal but Spring Boot will pick MVC and ignore WebFlux, which is a common source of confusion.

Where Spring Boot Fits

Spring Boot does not replace any of these modules. It sits above them and does two things: it chooses which of them you get, and it configures them.

That is what a starter is. spring-boot-starter-web contains no code of its own - it is a pom listing the modules a web application needs, so you declare one dependency instead of eight.
codeExamples:
<!-- WITHOUT Spring Boot: you name every module, and every version. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
    <version>6.1.4</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
    <version>6.1.4</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>2.16.1</version>   <!-- which version pairs with Spring 6.1.4? -->
</dependency>
<!-- ...plus a servlet container, plus validation, plus a logging binding. -->

<!-- WITH Spring Boot: one line, and no versions anywhere. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- It pulls in, transitively:
       spring-web, spring-webmvc     - the Web layer
       spring-core, spring-beans,
       spring-context, spring-aop    - the Core Container and AOP
       spring-boot-starter-json      - Jackson, at a version known to work
       spring-boot-starter-tomcat    - the embedded server
       spring-boot-starter-logging   - SLF4J + Logback

     The versions come from the parent pom, which pins a set that has been
     tested together. This is the actual value: not fewer lines, but the
     guarantee that the versions are compatible. -->

beginner.content:
Tracing One Request Through the Layers

The architecture is easier to hold on to when you follow a single HTTP call down and back.

  POST /api/customers
        |
        v
  [ Embedded Tomcat ]                        (spring-boot-starter-tomcat)
        |
        v
  [ DispatcherServlet ]                      (spring-webmvc)
        |  finds the handler, converts JSON to an object
        v
  [ @RestController ]                        (your code)
        |
        v
  [ @Service ]                               (your code)
        |  ...but the call goes through a proxy first:
        v
  [ transaction proxy ]                      (spring-aop + spring-tx)
        |  begin transaction
        v
  [ @Repository ]                            (your code)
        |
        v
  [ JPA / Hibernate ]                        (spring-orm)
        |
        v
  [ DataSource -> database ]                 (spring-jdbc)

  ...and the response returns up the same stack, the proxy committing
  the transaction on the way out.

Every box on that path belongs to a module in the diagram at the top, and the whole thing is assembled by the Core Container at startup.

expert.content:
Spring Framework Introduction (advanced)

Why "Inversion of Control" Is the Name

The term predates Spring and describes control of the flow, not just of object creation.

In an ordinary library, your code is in charge: you call list.add(x), the library returns, you carry on. In a framework, that relationship is inverted - the framework runs, and it calls your code at the points it decides. This is sometimes phrased as the Hollywood Principle: don't call us, we'll call you.

Spring applies that inversion to object assembly specifically. Without it, an object decides its own collaborators by calling new. With it, the object declares what it needs and something external decides what to supply. The decision moves out of the class - which is exactly what makes the class testable, because a test can supply something different.

Dependency Injection is not a synonym for IoC. IoC is the principle; DI is the specific technique Spring uses to implement it. Service Locator is a different implementation of the same principle - the object asks a registry for its collaborator instead of being handed it. Spring chose injection because it leaves the class with no reference to the framework at all; a Service Locator would put a lookup call inside your code.

What the Container Costs You

Every real framework has a bill, and being able to name Spring's is the difference between using it and being used by it.

CostWhat it looks like
Failures move to startupA wiring mistake is not a compile error. It surfaces as a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException or UnsatisfiedDependencyException when the context starts - which is still early, but later than the compiler.
Proxies make stack traces deep@Transactional and AOP work by wrapping your bean in a generated proxy. A stack trace then runs through a dozen frames of Spring internals before it reaches your method.
Self-invocation silently does nothingBecause those features live in the proxy, a method calling another method on the same object bypasses the proxy. An inner @Transactional or @Cacheable is simply not applied - no error, no warning.
Magic is hard to traceAuto-configuration decides a great deal on your behalf. When it decides wrongly, you need --debug and the auto-configuration report to find out why.

None of these are arguments against Spring. They are the specific places where "the container is doing it for you" turns into "the container did something I did not expect", and knowing them in advance saves hours.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Who created Spring and when?Rod Johnson; released in 2003, out of the code published with his 2002 book on J2EE design.
What problem was it solving?EJB 2 forced components to implement container interfaces, which made them impossible to run or test outside an application server, and required several files of boilerplate per component.
What is a POJO and why does Spring insist on it?A plain Java object that extends and implements nothing framework-specific. It keeps the class independent of Spring, so it can be instantiated and unit tested without a container.
Is Spring Boot a different framework from Spring?No. It is a layer on top of the Spring Framework that supplies auto-configuration, starter dependencies and an embedded server. Every Boot application is a Spring application.
Difference between IoC and DI?IoC is the principle - something other than the object decides its collaborators. DI is the technique Spring uses to apply it, by passing dependencies in. Service Locator is a different technique for the same principle.
Why is Spring called "lightweight" when the jars are large?Lightweight refers to how invasive it is on your code, not to its size on disk. Your classes carry no framework baggage.
What breaks when moving from Boot 2 to Boot 3?Java 17 becomes the minimum and every javax.* enterprise package becomes jakarta.* - persistence, servlet, validation. It is a rename, not a redesign, but nothing compiles until it is done.

Spring Architecture (advanced)

The Dependency Rule, and Why It Is Worth Knowing

The stacking is strict: a module may depend downward, never upward. spring-webmvc depends on spring-context; spring-context has no idea whether a web layer exists.

Two consequences follow, and both show up in real work.

ConsequenceWhy it matters
spring-context depends on spring-aopAOP sits below the context, not beside it. That is why @Transactional and @Async work in a plain non-web application with no extra dependency - the proxying machinery is already there.
The container is testable without a serverBecause nothing in the Core Container reaches up into the web layer, @SpringBootTest can start a full context with no servlet container at all. That is not a testing trick; it falls straight out of the dependency direction.

The rule is also why the framework survived the reactive shift in 2017. WebFlux was added as a sibling of WebMVC in the Web layer. Nothing below had to change, so adding an entire second web stack broke no existing application.

Version Alignment: the Problem the Parent Pom Solves

Spring's modules are released as a set and are only supported in matching versions. Mixing spring-core 6.1.4 with spring-webmvc 6.0.9 will often start, then fail at a random point with NoSuchMethodError or NoClassDefFoundError - the classic symptom of a split framework version.

Boot prevents this by managing versions centrally, and there are two ways to attach to that.
codeExamples:
<!-- Option 1: inherit from the Boot parent. Most projects do this. -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.3</version>
</parent>

<!-- Every Spring dependency below now omits <version>, and Boot supplies a
     set that was tested together - Spring, Hibernate, Jackson, SLF4J, Tomcat. -->

<!-- Option 2: import the BOM. Use this when the project already has a
     corporate parent pom and cannot inherit a second one. -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.3</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- Same version management, no parent required.

     To override one managed version - say a newer Jackson for a CVE fix -
     set the property rather than pinning the dependency, so every Jackson
     artifact moves together:

         <properties>
             <jackson-bom.version>2.17.0</jackson-bom.version>
         </properties>

     Pinning one artifact's <version> by hand upgrades that jar alone and
     leaves the rest of Jackson behind - which is how a version split gets
     introduced while trying to fix one. -->

expert.content:
Reading the Dependency Tree

When something unexpected is on the classpath - two logging bindings, an old Jackson, a servlet API you did not ask for - the tree tells you which starter dragged it in.
codeExamples:
# Which modules am I actually getting, and from where?
mvn dependency:tree

# OUTPUT (trimmed):
# [INFO] com.example:demo:jar:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
# [INFO] +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:jar:3.2.3:compile
# [INFO] |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter:jar:3.2.3:compile
# [INFO] |  |  +- org.springframework:spring-core:jar:6.1.4:compile
# [INFO] |  |  \- org.springframework:spring-context:jar:6.1.4:compile
# [INFO] |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-tomcat:jar:3.2.3:compile
# [INFO] |  +- org.springframework:spring-web:jar:6.1.4:compile
# [INFO] |  \- org.springframework:spring-webmvc:jar:6.1.4:compile

# Narrow it to one artifact when hunting a conflict:
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind

# Gradle equivalent:
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath

# Why is Spring Boot configuring something I never asked for?
java -jar app.jar --debug

# OUTPUT (the auto-configuration report, trimmed):
#
# Positive matches:
# -----------------
#    DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration matched:
#       - @ConditionalOnClass found required class DispatcherServlet
#       - found 'session' scope
#
# Negative matches:
# -----------------
#    DataSourceAutoConfiguration:
#       Did not match:
#          - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class DataSource
#
# Every decision Boot made, with the reason. The negative matches are the
# more useful half: they explain what is missing, not just what is present.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the layers of the Spring Framework?Core Container at the base; AOP/Aspects/Instrumentation above it; then Data Access-Integration and Web side by side; Test alongside. Dependencies point downward only.
Which modules make up the Core Container?spring-core, spring-beans, spring-context, spring-expression.
Difference between spring-beans and spring-context?spring-beans is the bean factory - definitions and injection. spring-context adds ApplicationContext with events, i18n, resource loading and annotation config.
Why does @Transactional work in a non-web application?It is implemented by spring-aop plus spring-tx, both below the web layer. spring-context already depends on spring-aop.
Is Spring MVC required to use Spring?No. It is one optional module in the Web layer. Batch jobs, CLI tools and message consumers use the container without it.
MVC and WebFlux together?They are alternatives. With both on the classpath Boot chooses MVC. Use one per application.
What does a starter contain?No code - a pom listing dependencies and their tested versions. spring-boot-starter-web pulls the web modules, Jackson, an embedded Tomcat and the logging binding.
How do you manage Spring versions without the Boot parent?Import spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM in dependencyManagement with <scope>import</scope>.
Symptom of mismatched Spring module versions?NoSuchMethodError or NoClassDefFoundError at runtime rather than at startup - the jars resolve but the classes disagree.

beginner.content:
Spring Core - IoC & Dependency Injection

What is Inversion of Control (IoC)?

Normally, in plain Java, YOU are in control of creating objects - you write new wherever you need something.
With Spring, that control is "inverted" - the Spring Container (IoC Container) creates the objects, wires them together, and hands them to you. You just declare what you need.

In short: "Don't call us, we'll call you." The framework calls your code and supplies the objects, instead of your code calling the framework to create objects.

Without Spring (You control everything):

Engine engine = new PetrolEngine();   // you create it
Car car = new Car(engine);            // you wire it
car.drive();

With Spring (Container controls it):

Car car = context.getBean(Car.class); // Spring already created
car.drive();                          // and wired Engine into Car
You never wrote new PetrolEngine() or new Car(engine) - Spring did it for you behind the scenes.

What is a Spring Bean?

A Bean is simply a Java object that is created, configured, and managed by the Spring IoC container (instead of being created manually with new).

Any class annotated with @Component (or a stereotype like @Service) becomes eligible to be turned into a bean.

Dependency Injection (DI) - The Mechanism Behind IoC

Dependency Injection is HOW Spring achieves Inversion of Control. Instead of a class creating the objects it depends on, those dependencies are "injected" (supplied) from outside.

There are 3 common ways to inject dependencies in Spring:
1. Constructor Injection (preferred)
2. Setter Injection
3. Field Injection

1. Constructor Injection

Dependencies are passed in through the class constructor. This is the recommended approach.

2. Setter Injection

Dependencies are supplied through a public setter method after the object is constructed.

3. Field Injection

Dependencies are injected directly into the field using @Autowired, with no constructor or setter needed. It's the shortest to write, but generally discouraged in real projects (explained in Expert Level).

Stereotype Annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository

These annotations all mark a class as a Spring-managed bean - they are functionally similar, but used to indicate the class's role, which makes the code more readable and lets Spring add role-specific behavior.

• @Component - generic, any Spring-managed class.
• @Service - marks a class holding business logic.
• @Repository - marks a class that talks to the database; Spring also auto-translates database exceptions here.

Dependency Injection

A Dependency Is Anything a Class Cannot Work Without

If OrderService cannot do its job without a PaymentGateway, then the gateway is a dependency of the service. Every class of any size has some.

The only real question is where that object comes from, and there are exactly two answers:

ApproachWhat happens
The class creates itprivate PaymentGateway gateway = new StripeGateway(); - the class chooses its own collaborator and is now welded to that choice.
The class is given itThe class declares that it needs a PaymentGateway and something outside decides which one to supply. This is dependency injection.

That is the whole idea. Dependency injection is not a Spring invention and needs no framework - handing an object into a constructor is dependency injection, whether Spring is present or not. What Spring adds is doing it for you, for every object in the application, automatically.

Why the First Approach Hurts

The problem with new is not that it is ugly. It is that it makes one specific thing impossible: substitution.

How Spring Does It

Spring's container performs the injection at startup, in three steps.

  1. FIND       Component scanning walks the packages and collects every
                class marked @Component / @Service / @Repository / @Controller,
                plus every @Bean method in a @Configuration class.
                Each becomes a "bean definition" - a recipe, not an object yet.

  2. ORDER      Spring reads what each definition needs. StripeGateway has
                no dependencies, so it can be built first. OrderService needs
                a PaymentGateway, so it must be built after.

  3. BUILD      Objects are created in that order and handed their
                collaborators as they go.

       StripeGateway  ---built first--->  passed into  --->  OrderService

The result lives in the ApplicationContext. By the time your application is up, every object exists and every reference is already filled in - there is no lazy wiring happening later while requests are being served.

Matching is by type, not by name. OrderService asks for a PaymentGateway; Spring looks for a bean assignable to that type and finds StripeGateway because it implements the interface. The variable name is irrelevant - until two candidates match, which is where @Qualifier and @Primary come in (topics 18 and 19).

The Three Forms of Injection

Spring can inject through a constructor, through a setter, or straight into the field. Each has its own topic next - this is the shape of all three side by side so the differences are visible in one place.

Which One to Use

FormField can be finalUnit-testable with newUse it when
ConstructorYesYesAlways, unless you have a specific reason not to. This is the form the Spring team recommends.
SetterNoYesThe dependency is genuinely optional, or must be swappable after construction.
FieldNoNoTest classes, and legacy code you are not rewriting today.

There is one more argument for the constructor that has nothing to do with Spring: a long parameter list is honest. When a constructor grows to eight dependencies, the class is visibly doing too much. Field injection hides that - eight @Autowired fields look no worse than two, so the class quietly keeps growing.

Constructor Injection

The Form to Use by Default

Constructor injection means the dependencies arrive as constructor parameters. Spring works out what the constructor needs, finds those beans, and calls it.

This is the form the Spring team recommends, and it is the only one of the three that gives you all four of these at once: final fields, an object that is never half-built, dependencies visible in the signature, and a class you can unit test without Spring.

Why final Matters More Than It Looks

Only constructor injection lets a dependency field be final, and that single keyword buys three separate guarantees.

GuaranteeWhat it prevents
Assigned exactly onceNothing - not a setter, not another method, not a later bug - can replace the gateway after construction.
Assigned before the constructor returnsThe compiler refuses to build the class otherwise. There is no window in which the field is null, so a method on a fully-constructed object can never NPE on a missing dependency.
Safe to publish across threadsThe Java Memory Model guarantees that a final field written in a constructor is visible to every thread that later sees the object. Non-final fields carry no such guarantee. Since Spring singletons are shared by every request thread, this is a real concurrency property, not a style preference.

That third point is the one people miss. A singleton service assembled by setter injection is technically publishing non-final state to dozens of threads; it works in practice because the context is fully built before the web server starts accepting requests, but the guarantee comes from that accident of ordering rather than from the language.

Several Constructors: Now You Must Choose

The "no annotation needed" rule applies to one constructor. With two or more, Spring will not guess.

Lombok: the Boilerplate Objection, Answered

The usual complaint about constructor injection is the typing - each dependency is named three times (field, parameter, assignment). Lombok removes that without giving up any of the guarantees.

Setter Injection

The Dependency Arrives After the Object Exists

Setter injection means Spring calls a normal JavaBean setter and passes the dependency in. The object is created first with its no-arg constructor, and the setters run afterwards.

That ordering is the entire difference from constructor injection, and everything else about setter injection - good and bad - follows from it.

What You Give Up

LostConsequence
final fieldsThe field is assigned after construction, so it cannot be final. Any code can reassign it later, and you lose the JMM safe-publication guarantee that makes a shared singleton's fields reliably visible to every request thread.
The guarantee of completenessAn object can exist with some dependencies set and others not. "Constructed" and "usable" become two different states.
A compile-checked test setupnew OrderService() compiles happily and produces a broken object. The test author must remember every setter; forgetting one is an NPE, not a compile error.
Startup-time cycle detectionA circular dependency resolves silently instead of failing. That is usually described as an advantage - see the Expert section for why it is not.

This is why the Spring reference documentation recommends constructors for mandatory dependencies and setters only for optional ones.

When Setter Injection Is the Right Answer

It is not obsolete - there are three cases where it is genuinely the better tool.

CaseWhy the setter fits
A dependency that must change at runtimeA JMX-exposed setter, or a component reconfigured by an admin endpoint. Constructor injection deliberately makes this impossible; if you need it, that is a reason to use a setter rather than to fight it.
Framework and base classesA subclass of a framework class you do not control cannot always dictate its own constructor signature. Spring's own JdbcDaoSupport works this way - setDataSource() exists precisely so subclasses need not redeclare it.
Legacy code you are not rewriting todayXML-configured Spring is built on setters, and a class already wired that way works. Migrating it is a choice, not a requirement.

Notice that "the dependency is optional" is not on this list. An optional dependency is better expressed as ObjectProvider<T> in the constructor with an explicit fallback, which keeps the field final and spares every caller a null check.
codeExamples:
// The XML form, for reading older projects. This is the same thing -
// <property> IS setter injection, and it is why the setter convention
// exists at all.

<bean id="orderService" class="com.shop.OrderService">
    <property name="gateway" ref="stripeGateway"/>
    <property name="retryLimit" value="3"/>
</bean>

<!-- Spring reads name="gateway" and calls setGateway(...).
     The name maps to the SETTER, not to the field: name="gateway"
     requires a method called setGateway. A field renamed without its
     setter still works; a setter renamed without the XML does not. -->

<!-- The constructor equivalent, for contrast: -->
<bean id="orderService" class="com.shop.OrderService">
    <constructor-arg ref="stripeGateway"/>
    <constructor-arg value="3"/>
</bean>

beginner.content:
Field Injection

The Shortest Form, and the One to Avoid

Field injection puts @Autowired directly on the field. There is no constructor and no setter - Spring reaches into the object and sets the field by reflection.

The Problem: There Is No Way In

Every other objection to field injection is a consequence of this one. A field-injected class has no seam. From outside, there is no legal way to supply a dependency.

The Full Comparison

ConstructorSetterField
Field can be finalYesNoNo
Object always fully builtYesNoNo
Testable with plain newYesYesNo
Dependencies visible in the APIYesYesNo
Missing dependency fails atStartupStartupStartup
Needs @AutowiredNo (single ctor)YesYes
Usable outside SpringYesYesNo

The last row is the one that decides it. A constructor-injected class is a normal Java class that Spring happens to build. A field-injected class only functions inside a dependency injection container - the framework has stopped being a convenience and become a runtime requirement.

This is why IntelliJ flags @Autowired on a field with "Field injection is not recommended", and why Spring's own reference documentation stopped showing it in examples.

Where It Is Actually Fine

Two places, and they share a property: the class is never instantiated by hand, so the missing seam costs nothing.

CaseWhy it is acceptable
Test classesJUnit constructs the test class, and Spring's test framework injects into it. You are never going to new a test class yourself, so there is nothing to lose. @Autowired fields in a @SpringBootTest are idiomatic, not a compromise.
@Configuration classesConfiguration classes exist only to be read by Spring. That said, prefer constructor parameters on @Bean methods, which are clearer and testable.

And one case that looks like an exception but is not: @Value on a field. It has all the same problems - the value cannot be supplied in a test without reflection - and constructor binding through @ConfigurationProperties is the modern answer.

expert.content:
Spring Core - IoC & Dependency Injection (advanced)

IoC Container Lifecycle - What Actually Happens Inside

When ApplicationContext starts up, it goes through a well-defined sequence before your application code ever runs.

1. Load & Parse Configuration
   (@Configuration classes / XML / @ComponentScan packages)
            |
            v
2. Scan for candidate classes
   (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @Bean methods)
            |
            v
3. Register BeanDefinitions
   (metadata only: class, scope, dependencies - NOT instantiated yet)
            |
            v
4. Instantiate Beans
   (constructor called - respects dependency order)
            |
            v
5. Populate Dependencies (Dependency Injection)
   (constructor args / setters / fields resolved & injected)
            |
            v
6. Apply BeanPostProcessors (before init)
            |
            v
7. Call Init callbacks
   (@PostConstruct -> InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() -> custom init-method)
            |
            v
8. Apply BeanPostProcessors (after init) -> Bean is now PROXIED if needed
   (AOP proxies, @Transactional wrapping etc. happen here)
            |
            v
9. Bean is READY and placed in the Singleton Cache
            |
            v
10. Application runs ... on shutdown -> @PreDestroy / destroy-method called
This is why a bean's constructor should NEVER assume other beans are fully initialized - dependencies are injected AFTER construction (for setter/field injection) but the container guarantees full graph resolution before you can call getBean() successfully.

Bean Scopes: singleton vs prototype

ScopeInstances CreatedDefault?Typical Use
singletonExactly ONE per Spring containerYes (default)Stateless services, repositories, controllers
prototypeA NEW instance every time it is requestedNoStateful, non-thread-safe objects
requestOne per HTTP request (web apps only)NoWeb request-scoped data
sessionOne per HTTP session (web apps only)NoUser session data

Why Constructor Injection Is Preferred Over Field Injection

AspectConstructor InjectionField Injection
ImmutabilityFields can be declared finalFields cannot be final (reflection sets them later)
Mandatory dependenciesObject cannot exist in a half-built state - compiler enforces itObject can exist with null dependency until Spring injects it
TestabilityEasy to unit test with plain new Car(mockEngine), no Spring neededNeeds reflection or a Spring context to set private fields in tests
Circular dependenciesFails FAST at startup (clear error)May silently succeed via early-reference proxies, hiding a design smell
ReadabilityAll required dependencies visible in one constructor signatureDependencies scattered as annotated fields, harder to see the full picture

Resolving Ambiguity: @Qualifier and @Primary

When two or more beans of the SAME type exist, Spring cannot decide which one to inject and throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException - unless you disambiguate with @Qualifier or @Primary.

• @Primary - marks ONE bean as the default choice when multiple candidates exist.
• @Qualifier("beanName") - explicitly picks a specific bean by name at the injection point (overrides @Primary if both are used together at the same site).

@Bean Methods in @Configuration - Wiring Third-Party Classes

You cannot put @Component on a class you don't own (e.g. a library class like ObjectMapper). For those, declare a method annotated with @Bean inside an @Configuration class - Spring calls the method once and registers its return value as a bean.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Inversion of Control?A design principle where object creation and wiring is handed over to a framework/container instead of being done manually in application code
What is Dependency Injection?The specific technique Spring uses to implement IoC - supplying a class's dependencies from outside rather than the class creating them itself
What is a Spring Bean?Any object whose lifecycle (creation, wiring, initialization, destruction) is managed by the Spring IoC container
Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?Enables immutability (final fields), guarantees mandatory dependencies at construction time, is easier to unit test without a container, and surfaces circular dependencies immediately at startup
What is the default bean scope in Spring?singleton - one shared instance per Spring container
Difference between @Component, @Service and @Repository?All register a class as a bean; @Service/@Repository are specializations of @Component used for semantic clarity, and @Repository additionally enables automatic persistence-exception translation
What happens if two beans of the same type exist and neither is qualified?Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup - resolve with @Primary or @Qualifier
Difference between @Primary and @Qualifier?@Primary sets a default candidate among multiple beans of a type; @Qualifier explicitly names the exact bean to inject at a given point, taking precedence when both are present
When would you use a @Bean method instead of @Component?When you need to create a bean from a class you don't own (third-party library) or when construction requires custom logic/parameters not expressible via class-level annotations
What is a circular dependency and how does Spring handle it?When Bean A needs Bean B and Bean B needs Bean A; with field/setter injection Spring can resolve it via early bean references, but with constructor injection it fails fast with a BeanCurrentlyInCreationException, forcing a redesign

Dependency Injection (advanced)

What Happens When the Match Is Not Exactly One

Injection by type has three outcomes, and only one of them is success.

Candidates foundResult
Exactly oneInjected.
NoneNoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup. Usually the class is outside the scanned packages, or the stereotype annotation is missing.
Two or moreNoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, unless one is @Primary, or the injection point carries @Qualifier, or the parameter name happens to match a bean name.

That last fallback is worth knowing because it fails silently in the other direction. If two PaymentGateway beans exist named stripeGateway and paypalGateway, then a parameter named stripeGateway resolves - and renaming that parameter during a tidy-up breaks startup. Never rely on it; use @Qualifier when there is a choice to make.

The full resolution order Spring applies at an injection point:

  1. Collect every bean assignable to the required type
  2. If a @Qualifier is present, keep only beans matching that qualifier
  3. If more than one remains, keep the one marked @Primary
  4. If still more than one, keep the one whose bean name equals the
     field or parameter name
  5. Exactly one left  -> inject it
     Zero left         -> NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
     More than one     -> NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException

Injecting More Than One, and Injecting Nothing

Two cases the by-type rule handles specially, and both are useful.

Why Not a Service Locator?

Both patterns implement Inversion of Control - the class stops calling new. The difference is which direction the knowledge flows.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is dependency injection?Supplying a class with the collaborators it needs from outside, rather than letting it create them. It is the technique Spring uses to implement Inversion of Control.
Is DI the same as IoC?No. IoC is the principle - something else decides. DI is one way to implement it; Service Locator is another.
How does Spring decide which bean to inject?By type. If several match, @Qualifier wins, then @Primary, then a bean name equal to the parameter or field name.
Which injection type is recommended and why?Constructor: the field can be final, the object is never half-built, dependencies are visible in the signature, and it needs no framework to unit test.
Is @Autowired required on a constructor?Not since Spring 4.3, when the class has a single constructor. With several constructors, one must be annotated.
What if no bean of the required type exists?NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup - typically a missing stereotype annotation or a package outside component scanning.
What if two beans match?NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, unless disambiguated by @Primary, @Qualifier or a matching bean name.
Can you inject every implementation of an interface?Yes - declare List<T> and Spring injects them all; Map<String, T> gives them keyed by bean name. Sequence is controlled with @Order.
How do you inject a prototype bean into a singleton?ObjectProvider<T> (or a lookup method). A plain field is resolved once at startup, so the singleton would keep the same instance forever.
Why is injecting ApplicationContext discouraged?It turns DI back into a Service Locator: dependencies become invisible, failures move from startup to request time, and the class gains a Spring import that stops it being unit-testable.

Constructor Injection (advanced)

Circular Dependencies Fail Loudly - and That Is the Feature

If A needs B and B needs A, constructor injection cannot resolve it. Neither object can be built first, because neither can be constructed without the other already existing.

Spring detects this at startup and refuses to start.

The Long Constructor Is a Message, Not a Nuisance

The most common complaint about constructor injection is that it produces constructors with eight parameters. That is not a flaw in the technique - it is the technique doing its job.

A class with eight collaborators has eight reasons to change, which is a Single Responsibility violation stated in code. Field injection does not remove that problem, it removes the signal: eight @Autowired fields scroll past as easily as two, so nobody notices the class growing.

DependenciesWhat it usually means
1-3Healthy.
4-5Worth a look. Often a controller doing service work, or a service doing mapping.
6+Almost always two or three classes wearing one name. Split along the lines the dependencies suggest - the groups that get used together are the classes trying to emerge.

Before splitting, check for the easy wins: a dependency used by exactly one method may belong in a parameter instead of the constructor, and three dependencies always used together are a collaborator waiting to be extracted.

Two Things the Constructor Cannot Do

Constructor injection has two genuine limits, and both have standard answers.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is constructor injection preferred?Fields can be final, the object is fully initialised the moment it exists, dependencies are visible in the signature, circular dependencies fail at startup, and the class is unit-testable with plain new.
Is @Autowired needed on the constructor?Not since Spring 4.3 when there is exactly one constructor. With several, exactly one must carry it.
What happens with two unannotated constructors?Spring looks for a no-arg constructor, does not find one, and fails with BeanInstantiationException: No default constructor found.
Why does final matter beyond immutability?The JMM guarantees a final field set in a constructor is visible to all threads that see the object - which matters because singletons are shared across request threads.
What happens on a circular dependency?Startup fails with a cycle diagram. Since Boot 2.6, spring.main.allow-circular-references is false by default, so field injection no longer hides it either.
How do you fix a cycle?Extract the shared responsibility into a third bean, or invert one direction with an application event. @Lazy breaks the cycle without fixing the design.
Does @RequiredArgsConstructor need @Autowired?No. It generates a single constructor at compile time, so the single-constructor rule applies. It cannot express @Qualifier - write that constructor by hand.
Constructor with ten dependencies - what do you do?Treat it as the SRP warning it is and split the class. Do not switch to field injection to hide the count.
How do you inject an optional dependency by constructor?ObjectProvider<T> with getIfAvailable(fallback). The field stays final and no caller null-checks.
Why can a bean not inject itself by constructor?It is a cycle. Use @Lazy or ObjectProvider when a bean genuinely needs its own proxy - though the method usually belongs on another bean.

Setter Injection (advanced)

Setters Tolerate Circular Dependencies - Which Hides the Problem

Setter injection resolves a cycle that constructor injection rejects, because the objects can be created empty first and wired afterwards. This is frequently listed as an advantage of setter injection. It is better understood as a deferred failure.

Ordering, and What Is Not Guaranteed

Two rules are worth knowing precisely, because code sometimes leans on assumptions that are not true.

GuaranteedNot guaranteed
All @Autowired setters run before any @PostConstruct method.The order in which the setters themselves run. Spring uses reflection order, which is not the source order and can differ between JVMs.
Constructor injection completes before any setter runs.That a setter runs at all if @Autowired is missing - the field silently stays null.

The practical rule: never let one setter depend on another having already run. If two dependencies must be combined into derived state, do that in @PostConstruct, which is the first point at which everything is guaranteed to be in place.

@Required, and How This Was Handled Historically

The obvious hole in setter injection - forgetting to wire something - had a dedicated annotation for it.

@Required on a setter made Spring fail at startup if that property was never set, converting a runtime NPE into a startup error. It was deprecated in Spring 5.1 and removed in Spring 6. You will meet it in older code; it has no replacement, because the replacement is constructor injection - a constructor parameter is required by construction, with no annotation and no framework involvement.

Two related notes for reading older or mixed codebases:

FormBehaviour
@Autowired on a setterRequired by default. No matching bean means NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup.
@Autowired(required = false)The setter is skipped entirely when no bean matches. The field keeps whatever the constructor left it as - which is how you give a setter-injected optional dependency a real default.
@Resource on a setterJSR-250. Matches by name first, then by type - the opposite of @Autowired. Mixing the two in one class is a common source of "why did it inject that one".

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is setter injection?Spring instantiates the bean with its no-arg constructor, then calls @Autowired setters to supply dependencies.
Is @Autowired optional on a setter?No. Without it the setter is never called and the field stays null - unlike the single-constructor rule, which needs no annotation.
Why can the field not be final?It is assigned after the constructor has returned, and final requires assignment during construction.
Setter vs constructor - when is each right?Constructor for mandatory dependencies; setter when the dependency must be replaceable at runtime, when a framework base class dictates it, or in legacy XML-wired code.
Why do setters tolerate circular dependencies?Spring can construct both beans empty and wire them afterwards using its early-reference cache. It resolves the cycle without fixing the design.
What breaks in a setter-resolved cycle?If one bean is later proxied (@Transactional, @Async), the other may hold the raw object. Spring 5.3+ throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; older versions silently skipped the proxy.
Are setters called in a defined order?No. Only the guarantee that all of them run before @PostConstruct. Combine dependencies there, never inside a setter.
What was @Required?An annotation failing startup if a setter was never called. Deprecated in 5.1, removed in Spring 6 - constructor injection gives the same guarantee for free.
@Autowired vs @Resource on a setter?@Autowired matches by type then name; @Resource (JSR-250) matches by name then type.
Best way to give an optional dependency a default?Initialise the field to a no-op and mark the setter @Autowired(required = false); better still, take ObjectProvider<T> in the constructor and keep the field final.

Field Injection (advanced)

The Objection That Is Usually Overstated

Field injection is often criticised for being slow, because it uses reflection. That argument is weak and it is worth knowing why, so you make the case on the grounds that actually hold.

ClaimReality
"Reflection makes it slow"It happens once per bean at startup. For a singleton that is one Field.set call in the entire life of the application - microseconds, and unmeasurable next to the class loading and proxying happening around it.
"It breaks encapsulation"Technically true - setAccessible(true) bypasses private. But Spring does the same for @PostConstruct methods and nobody objects to those. Encapsulation is not the real cost.
"It hides dependencies"This is the real argument. Not from the compiler - from the reader, and from any code that wants to construct the object without Spring.

Make the case on testability and on the SRP signal. A constructor that has grown to nine parameters is a class asking to be split; nine @Autowired fields scroll by unnoticed, so the class keeps growing and nobody is ever prompted to look.

The Failure Modes That Only Field Injection Has

Three bugs that constructor injection makes impossible to write.

Migrating a Codebase Off It

The change is mechanical and can be done class by class - no big-bang refactor, and each step leaves the code working.
codeExamples:
# Find every remaining field injection site in the project:
grep -rn --include=*.java -B1 "@Autowired" src/main/java \
  | grep -A1 "@Autowired" | grep "private "

# OUTPUT:
# src/main/java/com/shop/OrderService.java-15-    private PaymentGateway gateway;
# src/main/java/com/shop/CartService.java-22-     private CartRepository repository;
# ...

# To stop new ones appearing, ArchUnit can fail the build on it:
#
#   @ArchTest
#   static final ArchRule noFieldInjection =
#       noFields().should().beAnnotatedWith(Autowired.class)
#                 .because("use constructor injection");
#
# Run it over main only - test classes are the legitimate exception.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is field injection?@Autowired directly on a field. Spring sets it by reflection after construction, with no constructor or setter involved.
Why is it discouraged?The class cannot be constructed outside Spring, so it cannot be unit tested without reflection or a running context. Dependencies are invisible in the API, fields cannot be final, and an oversized class gives no signal.
Is the reflection a performance problem?No - one Field.set per bean at startup. Arguing performance is arguing the weak version of the case.
How does Spring set a private field?AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor finds the annotated fields and uses ReflectionUtils.makeAccessible / setAccessible(true) before Field.set.
How would you test a field-injected class?ReflectionTestUtils.setField, or start a context with @SpringBootTest and @MockBean. Both are heavier than a constructor call - which is the argument for changing the class.
Can an injected field be used in the constructor?No - it is still null. Use a constructor parameter, or @PostConstruct.
When is field injection acceptable?In test classes, which are constructed by JUnit and never by hand. Arguably in @Configuration classes, though constructor parameters on @Bean methods are better.
What about @Value on a field?Same trap - unsettable in a test without reflection. Prefer a @Value constructor parameter, or @ConfigurationProperties binding.
Does it hide circular dependencies?It did, until Spring Boot 2.6 made spring.main.allow-circular-references=false the default. Setting it back to true restores the old behaviour and the old bugs.
How do you migrate away from it?Make the fields final, drop the annotations and add one constructor - or @RequiredArgsConstructor. The IDE does it per class, and ArchUnit can stop new occurrences.

beginner.content:
Spring Beans

A Bean Is Just an Object the Container Owns

The word sounds like it implies something special about the class. It does not. A Spring bean is an ordinary Java object with one distinguishing property: Spring created it and Spring is holding on to it.

Two objects of the same class can differ on this. Only the first of these is a bean:

Definition First, Object Second

This is the distinction that makes everything else make sense. Spring works in two phases, and the thing it collects first is not an object at all.

  PHASE 1 - REGISTRATION            PHASE 2 - INSTANTIATION

  Scan classes, read @Bean          Walk the definitions and
  methods, parse XML.               actually build the objects.

  Produces BeanDefinitions:         Produces beans:

    name  : "orderService"            OrderService@4f3a2b
    class : com.shop.OrderService     (dependencies injected,
    scope : singleton                  wrapped in a proxy if
    lazy  : false                      it needs one)
    deps  : [paymentGateway]

  A recipe. No object exists yet.    The cake.

The BeanDefinition is the recipe: which class, which scope, which dependencies, lazy or eager. Every declaration style - annotations, @Bean methods, XML - is just a different way of producing one, which is why they can be mixed freely in a single application.

The gap between the two phases is what makes Spring extensible. Because every definition exists before any object does, code can run in between and change them - which is exactly how @ConditionalOnMissingBean, profiles and property placeholders work.

The Three Ways to Declare One

StyleUse it when
Stereotype annotation - @Component, @Service, @Repository, @ControllerYou own the class and can annotate it. This covers almost all of your own code.
@Bean method in a @Configuration classYou do not own the class - a library type like ObjectMapper or DataSource - or construction needs logic.
XML <bean>Legacy projects. Nothing new is written this way, but plenty of running code is.

Every Bean Has a Name

Names matter more than people expect, because they are the tie-breaker when two beans share a type, and they are what @Qualifier refers to.

Declared asDefault name
@Service class OrderServiceorderService - class name, first letter lowercased
@Bean public ObjectMapper objectMapper()objectMapper - the method name
@Service("orders") class OrderServiceorders - explicit wins
@Bean(name = "mapper")mapper

The exception worth memorising: if the first two letters of the class name are both uppercase, the name is left alone. URLBuilder becomes the bean URLBuilder, not uRLBuilder. This follows java.beans.Introspector.decapitalize, and it catches people out with classes like JWTService and APIClient.

Bean Lifecycle

Between new and Ready

Creating a bean is not one step. Between calling the constructor and handing the object out, Spring runs a fixed sequence - and the object is not usable until that sequence finishes.

  STARTUP
  =======

   1  Instantiate            the constructor runs
                             (constructor-injected deps arrive here)

   2  Populate properties    @Autowired fields and setters are filled

   3  Aware callbacks        setBeanName, setBeanFactory,
                             setApplicationContext

   4  BeanPostProcessor      postProcessBeforeInitialization(...)
         BEFORE

   5  Initialisation         @PostConstruct
                             then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()
                             then @Bean(initMethod = "...")

   6  BeanPostProcessor      postProcessAfterInitialization(...)
         AFTER               <-- PROXIES ARE CREATED HERE

   7  READY                  the bean is in the container and injectable


  SHUTDOWN
  ========

   8  @PreDestroy
   9  DisposableBean.destroy()
  10  @Bean(destroyMethod = "...")

Two things in that list explain most of the surprising behaviour you will meet later: step 2 happens after step 1 (so an injected field is null inside the constructor), and step 6 is where proxies are made (so what gets injected elsewhere is not the object your constructor built).

Seeing It Run

One class that implements every hook, so the order is not a claim but an output.

Which Initialisation Hook to Use

HookVerdict
@PostConstructUse this. A plain annotation - the class stays a POJO with no Spring import, and the method can be private. On Spring Boot 3 it is jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct; on Boot 2 it is javax.annotation.PostConstruct.
InitializingBeanAvoid. It forces your class to implement a Spring interface, which is the coupling the framework exists to prevent. Common in older code.
@Bean(initMethod = "...")For third-party classes you cannot annotate. The equivalent of @PostConstruct when you do not own the source.

What belongs in @PostConstruct: validation of injected configuration, building derived state from several dependencies, warming a cache, registering with something external. It is the first point at which every dependency is guaranteed to be set.

What does not: anything slow or unreliable. A @PostConstruct that calls a remote service means the application will not start when that service is down - and a startup failure is far harder to diagnose than a failed request. Use ApplicationRunner for work that should happen after the application is up.

Bean Scopes

Scope Answers One Question: How Many?

A bean definition is a recipe. Scope decides how many objects Spring makes from it, and how long each one lives.

ScopeOne instance perAvailable in
singletonContainer. This is the default.Everywhere
prototypeRequest for the bean - a new object every timeEverywhere
requestHTTP requestWeb applications only
sessionHTTP sessionWeb applications only
applicationServletContextWeb applications only
websocketWebSocket sessionWebSocket applications only

In practice you will use singleton for almost everything, prototype occasionally, and request/session rarely - and mostly in server-rendered applications rather than REST services.

"Singleton" Does Not Mean the Singleton Pattern

The name is borrowed and it misleads. A Spring singleton is one instance per container, not one per JVM.

GoF SingletonSpring singleton
One instance per class loader, enforced by a private constructor and a static field.One instance per ApplicationContext. The class has a public constructor and nothing stops you making more.
The class enforces it.The container manages it. The class does not know.

This has a practical consequence people meet in tests: two application contexts mean two instances of every singleton. A test suite that starts several differently-configured contexts is holding several copies of each service - which is fine, and is why static mutable state in a bean causes tests to interfere with one another.

The Consequence Nobody Mentions Until It Breaks

Singleton is the default, so one instance of every service is shared by every request thread at the same time. That makes instance fields shared mutable state.

Prototype: a New Object Every Time

A prototype bean is created fresh on every request for it, gets its dependencies injected, and is then forgotten - Spring does not keep a reference.

Two consequences follow from being forgotten, and the second is a real leak:

ConsequenceDetail
Created lazily, alwaysPrototypes are never instantiated at startup, even in an eager context - there is nothing to instantiate until someone asks.
Destroy callbacks never run@PreDestroy and DisposableBean are not called on a prototype, ever. Spring is not tracking it, so it cannot clean it up. If the bean holds a file handle, a socket or a thread, the caller must release it.

Use prototype for objects that carry per-use state - a builder, a parser, a report accumulator. Do not use it as a way to make a service thread-safe; that is the mistake the next section is about.

expert.content:
Spring Beans (advanced)

Inspecting What Is Actually in the Container

When a bean is missing, or the wrong one was injected, the fastest answer is to ask the context directly rather than reason about what should have happened.
codeExamples:
# Without writing code, if Actuator is on the classpath:
curl localhost:8080/actuator/beans | jq '.contexts.application.beans
                                          | to_entries[]
                                          | select(.key | test("Gateway"))'

# OUTPUT:
# {
#   "key": "stripeGateway",
#   "value": {
#     "scope": "singleton",
#     "type": "com.shop.StripeGateway",
#     "resource": "class path resource [com/shop/StripeGateway.class]",
#     "dependencies": ["shopProperties"]
#   }
# }
#
# "resource" is the field that answers the hardest version of the
# question: which class, config file or auto-configuration registered
# this. Enable it with:
#     management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=beans

expert.content:
@Bean Methods Are Not Ordinary Methods

Inside a @Configuration class, a call from one @Bean method to another does not do what the Java says.

Two Beans, One Name

Registering the same bean name twice used to be a silent override - the last definition won, and which was "last" depended on scanning order.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a Spring bean?An object instantiated, assembled and managed by the Spring IoC container. The same class created with new is not a bean - no injection, no proxy, no lifecycle callbacks.
BeanDefinition vs bean?The definition is the recipe - class, scope, dependencies, lazy flag - registered in phase one. The bean is the object built from it in phase two.
Why does that split matter?Because code can run between the phases and modify definitions. Conditional configuration, profiles and property resolution all depend on it.
Ways to declare a bean?Stereotype annotations plus component scanning, @Bean methods in a @Configuration class, and XML. They produce the same thing and can be mixed.
@Component vs @Bean?@Component goes on a class you own and Spring constructs it. @Bean is a method where you construct it - required for third-party types or conditional construction.
How is the default bean name derived?Class name or method name with the first letter lowercased - unless the first two letters are both uppercase, in which case it is left as-is (JWTService stays JWTService).
Why does calling one @Bean method from another return the singleton?Spring CGLIB-subclasses the @Configuration class and intercepts those calls - "full" mode. Under @Component or proxyBeanMethods = false it is a plain call that creates a second instance.
What happens on a duplicate bean name?Since Boot 2.1, startup fails. Overriding can be re-enabled with a property, but the fix is @Profile, @ConditionalOnMissingBean or distinct names.
How do you list the beans at runtime?context.getBeanDefinitionNames(), getBeanNamesForType(), or the /actuator/beans endpoint - whose resource field shows what registered each one.

Bean Lifecycle (advanced)

Step 6 Is Where @Transactional Comes From

This is the single most useful thing in the lifecycle, because it explains a family of bugs that otherwise look like magic failing at random.

A BeanPostProcessor runs around initialisation and may return a different object than the one it was given. That is how proxies are made: AbstractAutoProxyCreator takes your bean at step 6 and returns a proxy wrapping it. Everything downstream - every injection point, every getBean() - receives the proxy.

Shutdown: What Runs, and What Does Not

Destruction callbacks are less reliable than initialisation ones, in three specific ways.

SituationDo destroy callbacks run?
Normal shutdown - SIGTERM, context.close(), JVM exitYes. Spring Boot registers a shutdown hook automatically.
kill -9, power loss, OOM killNo. Nothing runs. Never depend on @PreDestroy for correctness - it is for tidiness, not for data integrity.
Prototype-scoped beansNo. Spring does not track prototype instances after handing them out, so their destroy callbacks are never called at all - even on a clean shutdown.

That prototype rule is a classic interview question and a real leak: a prototype bean holding a file handle or a connection has no framework-managed way to release it. The caller must do it, or the bean should not be a prototype.

@PostConstruct vs the Runners

Four hooks fire around startup and they are not interchangeable. The distinction is how much of the application exists when each one runs.

HookFires whenUse for
@PostConstructThat one bean is initialised. Other beans may not exist yet. No proxy on itself yet.Validating and preparing that bean's own state.
SmartInitializingSingletonEvery singleton is constructed - but the context is not refreshed.Work needing all beans of a type, without needing the web server.
ContextRefreshedEventThe context is fully refreshed. Fires again on a refresh.Whole-context work. Guard against running twice.
ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunnerLast. The application is fully started and the web server is accepting requests.Seeding data, warm-up calls, one-off jobs, anything slow or remote.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Walk through the bean lifecycle.Instantiate, populate properties, Aware callbacks, BeanPostProcessor before, initialisation (@PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → init-method), BeanPostProcessor after, ready. On shutdown: @PreDestroy → destroy() → destroy-method.
Order of the three init callbacks?@PostConstruct, then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet(), then @Bean(initMethod).
Why prefer @PostConstruct over InitializingBean?It keeps the class a POJO with no Spring interface, and the method can be private.
Why is an injected field null in the constructor?Field and setter injection happen at step 2, after the constructor has returned. Only constructor-injected dependencies are available at step 1.
Where are proxies created?In postProcessAfterInitialization - step 6, after @PostConstruct. This is why @Transactional does nothing inside @PostConstruct and nothing on a self-invoked method.
What is a BeanPostProcessor?An extension point running around every bean's initialisation, allowed to return a replacement object. AOP, @Autowired and @PostConstruct processing are all implemented as ones.
Do destroy callbacks run for prototype beans?No. Spring stops tracking a prototype once it hands it out, so cleanup is the caller's responsibility.
When do destroy callbacks not run at all?On kill -9, an OOM kill, or a JVM crash. Never rely on @PreDestroy for data integrity.
@PostConstruct vs CommandLineRunner?@PostConstruct runs when that bean is initialised; a runner runs after the whole application has started. Remote or slow work belongs in the runner, so a failure does not prevent startup.
Which package on Boot 3?jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct. It was javax.annotation on Boot 2.

Bean Scopes (advanced)

The Prototype-in-Singleton Trap

The most common scope bug. Injecting a prototype into a singleton does not give you a new instance per call - it gives you one instance, injected once, for the life of the singleton.

Request and Session Scope Need a Proxy

The same "injected once" problem applies to web scopes, but here it fails loudly, and the fix is standard.

Scope on a @Bean Method, and Custom Scopes

Two smaller points that come up in real configuration.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Name the scopes and the default.singleton (default), prototype, and the web scopes request, session, application, websocket.
Is a Spring singleton the Singleton pattern?No. One instance per ApplicationContext, not per JVM. The class has a public constructor and two contexts hold two instances.
Are singleton beans thread-safe?Spring makes no such guarantee. One instance serves all request threads, so any mutable instance field is shared state. Keep dependencies final and per-request data in parameters.
When is a prototype created?On every request for it - never at startup, even in an eager context.
Do prototypes get destroy callbacks?No. Spring does not retain a reference, so @PreDestroy never runs and cleanup is the caller's job.
Prototype injected into a singleton - what happens?It is resolved once at injection and the same instance is reused forever. Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup, or make it a plain object.
Why does a request-scoped bean need a scoped proxy?At startup no request exists, so there is nothing to inject. The proxy is injected once and resolves the current thread's instance on each call.
TARGET_CLASS vs INTERFACES?CGLIB subclass (class must not be final, needs a no-arg constructor) versus a JDK dynamic proxy over an implemented interface.
What breaks a request-scoped bean at runtime?Using it off the request thread - @Async, @Scheduled, a runner - throws "Scope 'request' is not active for the current thread".
How do you register a custom scope?Implement org.springframework.beans.factory.config.Scope and call registerScope from a BeanFactoryPostProcessor.

beginner.content:
@Component

One Annotation, One Job

@Component marks a class as a candidate for the container. It means: when you scan, register this class as a bean.

That is the whole contract. It takes no dependencies, changes no behaviour and adds no capability - it is a marker that component scanning looks for.

The Four Stereotypes Are the Same Annotation

@Service, @Repository and @Controller are not alternatives to @Component. Each one is a @Component - the annotation is stamped on their own declarations.

Which One to Put on a Class

AnnotationUse for
@Controller / @RestControllerClasses handling HTTP requests. Required - MVC will not map a plain @Component.
@ServiceBusiness logic. The layer that orchestrates repositories and enforces rules.
@RepositoryData access. Worth using for the exception translation, not only the label.
@ComponentEverything else: mappers, validators, event listeners, scheduled jobs, adapters, utility beans with dependencies.

The honest summary: reach for the specific one when it fits a layer, and @Component when it does not. Do not agonise - a mapper annotated @Service works exactly the same. The value of the convention is that a reader can tell what a class is for without opening it.

Where @Component Does Not Work

It only applies to a concrete class that Spring can construct. Four cases where it silently does nothing or fails.

@Service

The Annotation That Does Nothing

@Service is @Component with a different name. It registers a bean and adds no behaviour whatsoever - no transactions, no proxying, no validation. Swapping every @Service in an application for @Component would change nothing at runtime.

So the interesting question is not what it does. It is what belongs in a class you have decided to call a service.

  @RestController      HTTP.  Parse the request, call one service,
                       shape the response. No business rules.
        |
        v
  @Service             The decisions. Orchestrates repositories and
                       other services, enforces the rules, owns the
                       transaction boundary.
        |
        v
  @Repository          Persistence. Queries and writes. No rules.

The layer above and the layer below are both defined by what they must not contain. The service is where the actual application lives.

What a Service Method Looks Like

The shape is consistent: validate, decide, act, return. If a method is only forwarding to a repository, it is not carrying its weight.

The Transaction Boundary Lives Here

This is the one structural reason the service layer must exist, and it is not about tidiness.

A business operation is usually several writes that must all happen or none of them. That unit of work has to be defined somewhere, and the service method is the only layer where the whole operation is visible.

Services Are Singletons, So They Must Be Stateless

One instance serves every request thread. A service may hold its injected dependencies and nothing else.

Belongs as a fieldMust not be a field
Injected collaborators (final)The current user, order or request
Configuration bound at startupAnything accumulated during a call
Immutable lookup tables built in @PostConstructCounters, buffers, "last result" caches

Everything in the right column belongs in a method parameter or a local variable. The compiler will not stop you - this rule is enforced only by knowing it.

@Repository

The Stereotype That Earns Its Name

Unlike @Service, @Repository does something. It registers a bean like any @Component, and it additionally marks the class for persistence exception translation.

The problem it solves is specific. Every persistence technology throws its own exceptions, and they are not compatible with each other:

TechnologyThrows
Plain JDBCjava.sql.SQLException - checked, and carrying a vendor-specific error code
Hibernateorg.hibernate.HibernateException
JPAjakarta.persistence.PersistenceException

A service catching any of these is welded to that technology, and a SQLException tells you nothing useful without looking up what error code 1062 means in MySQL - which is not what it means in PostgreSQL.

Spring translates all of them into one hierarchy: DataAccessException, which is unchecked and vendor-neutral.
What Translation Looks Like

The DataAccessException Hierarchy

The value is in catching the branch that matches your intent, rather than everything.

  DataAccessException  (unchecked)
    |
    +-- DataIntegrityViolationException      constraint broken
    |     +-- DuplicateKeyException            unique key
    |
    +-- DataAccessResourceFailureException   cannot reach the database
    |
    +-- OptimisticLockingFailureException    @Version mismatch
    |     +-- ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException
    |
    +-- PessimisticLockingFailureException
    |     +-- CannotAcquireLockException       lock wait timeout
    |     +-- DeadlockLoserDataAccessException deadlock victim
    |
    +-- EmptyResultDataAccessException       queryForObject found none
    |
    +-- IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException  expected 1, got N
    |
    +-- QueryTimeoutException
    |
    +-- BadSqlGrammarException               malformed SQL

Two of these are worth acting on specifically. DuplicateKeyException is a business condition ("that email is taken") rather than a fault. CannotAcquireLockException and DeadlockLoserDataAccessException are transient - the same operation may succeed on retry, which distinguishes them from every other branch.

The Part That Surprises People

Spring Data JPA repositories do not need @Repository.

A repository declared as an interface extending JpaRepository gets its implementation generated by Spring Data at startup, and that generated proxy already applies exception translation. Adding the annotation is harmless and changes nothing.

@Controller

The Stereotype Spring MVC Looks For

@Controller registers a bean like any @Component, and it does one thing more: it tells Spring MVC that this class contains request handlers.

That second part is not optional. When the application starts, RequestMappingHandlerMapping walks the beans looking for classes annotated with @Controller and builds its URL-to-method table from their @GetMapping and @PostMapping methods. A class it does not recognise is never inspected.

@Controller vs @RestController

@RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody, applied to the whole class. That single difference changes what a returned value means.

@Controller@RestController
A returned String isa view name to renderthe response body
A returned object isa model attribute (needs a view)serialised to JSON
Used forServer-rendered pages - Thymeleaf, JSPREST APIs

The Bug Everyone Writes Once

Use @Controller where you meant @RestController, and a method returning a String compiles, starts, and then fails in a way that mentions nothing about controllers.

What Belongs in a Controller
