A controller translates between HTTP and the application. That is the whole job, and it is a narrow one.

BelongsDoes not
Binding the request - path variables, query parameters, bodyBusiness rules and validation logic
Triggering validation with @ValidRepository calls
Calling one service method@Transactional
Mapping the result to a response DTOTry/catch for business failures - @ControllerAdvice handles those centrally
Choosing the status code and headersAnything you would want to reuse from a scheduled job or a message consumer

The last row is the useful test. If logic sits in a controller and tomorrow the same operation must run from a Kafka consumer or a CLI command, that logic has to move. Writing it in the service to begin with saves the move.

expert.content:
@Component (advanced)

Writing Your Own Stereotype

Because @Component works as a meta-annotation, you can define project-specific stereotypes that behave as beans while carrying extra meaning - and extra configuration.

Registering Conditionally

A @Component is unconditional - if it is scanned, it is registered. Two annotations change that, and they are the mechanism behind most of Spring Boot's behaviour.

The Cost of Scanning, and How to Remove It

Component scanning reads the bytecode of every class under the scanned packages at startup. On a small service this is milliseconds; on a large one, or in a serverless function where every cold start pays it, it is measurable.
codeExamples:
<!-- The index: a build-time replacement for runtime scanning. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-context-indexer</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

<!-- It is an annotation processor. At COMPILE time it writes
     META-INF/spring.components listing every stereotype-annotated
     class. At RUNTIME Spring reads that file instead of walking
     the classpath.

     No code change is needed - adding the dependency is the whole
     setup, and the index is used automatically when present.

     Two conditions:
       * every module must be indexed; a jar without the file falls
         back to scanning, silently
       * @ComponentScan with include/exclude filters bypasses the
         index, because the filters need the bytecode anyway -->

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @Component do?Marks a class for registration as a bean during component scanning. Nothing else - no behaviour, no dependencies.
Difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller?Registration is identical - the last three are meta-annotated with @Component. @Repository adds exception translation, @Controller is required for MVC handler mapping, @Service adds nothing but intent.
Does @Service behave differently at runtime?No. It is documentation the container treats exactly like @Component.
Can @Component go on an interface or abstract class?No - it is ignored, because there is nothing to instantiate.
@Component vs @Bean?@Component is on a class you own and Spring constructs it by scanning. @Bean is a method where you construct it - needed for third-party types or conditional construction.
Class has @Component but the bean is missing - why?Its package is not scanned. @SpringBootApplication scans its own package and below, so a class outside that tree needs scanBasePackages or a relocated main class.
How do you create a custom stereotype?Annotate your own annotation with @Component, and use @AliasFor to forward the bean name. Other annotations added to it apply to every class that uses it.
How do you register a component conditionally?@Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty, or a custom @Conditional. @ConditionalOnMissingBean is scan-order dependent on user components and belongs in auto-configuration.
How do you avoid the cost of scanning?spring-context-indexer generates META-INF/spring.components at compile time. Narrowing scanBasePackages usually helps more.
"No qualifying bean" vs "Error creating bean" - what is the difference?The first means the class was never found (a scanning problem). The second means it was found but could not be constructed (a dependency problem).

@Service (advanced)

The Impl Question

Java codebases habitually pair every service with an interface: OrderService and OrderServiceImpl. It is worth knowing why that convention exists, because the original reasons have mostly expired.

Historical reasonStatus today
Spring AOP needed an interface to proxyGone. CGLIB subclass proxies have been the default since Spring Boot 2.0. A concrete class proxies fine.
Mocking frameworks needed an interfaceGone. Mockito mocks concrete classes.
There might be a second implementation one dayUsually false. A one-to-one interface adds a file and an indirection for a substitution that never happens.

When an interface still earns its place: there really are two implementations (StripeGateway / PayPalGateway); the interface is a port in a hexagonal architecture, owned by the domain and implemented outside it; or it is published in a shared module for other teams to depend on.

For a service with exactly one implementation and no architectural boundary, the concrete class alone is the better default. If a second implementation appears, extracting the interface is an IDE keystroke.

Two Bugs That Live in Service Classes

Both come from the proxy, and both are silent.

Services Calling Services

Legitimate and common - but it is where dependency cycles are born, and a cycle now fails startup by default.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @Service do that @Component does not?Nothing at runtime. It is meta-annotated with @Component and registers a bean identically; the value is intent and convention.
What belongs in a service?Business rules, orchestration of repositories and other services, and the transaction boundary. Not HTTP concerns, not queries.
Why does @Transactional belong on the service and not the repository?A business operation is several writes that must commit or roll back together. Only the service sees the whole unit of work; per-repository transactions commit each step separately.
Why not on the controller?The transaction would stay open through response serialisation, holding a connection for the duration of a slow client.
Are service beans thread-safe?Only if stateless. They are singletons shared by all request threads, so instance fields must be final dependencies and immutable configuration.
Do you need an interface for every service?No. AOP and Mockito both work on concrete classes. Use an interface when there are real alternative implementations or when it is an architectural port.
Why does @Transactional not apply on a self-invoked method?The annotation lives in the proxy; an internal call goes through this and never reaches it. Move the boundary, or split the beans.
Does a checked exception roll back?No - only RuntimeException and Error. Use rollbackFor, or make business exceptions unchecked.
Can services call each other?Yes, but cycles fail at startup since Boot 2.6. Pass data rather than collaborators, extract a third bean, or invert with an event.
@EventListener vs @TransactionalEventListener?The first fires immediately, inside the transaction; the second after commit. Use the second for work that must not happen if the transaction rolls back.

@Repository (advanced)

How the Translation Actually Happens

It is not the annotation doing the work. @Repository is only a marker; a BeanPostProcessor looks for it and wraps the bean.

  PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor
        |  at startup, finds every @Repository bean
        v
  wraps it in a proxy
        |
        v
  call arrives ---> your method ---> throws PersistenceException
        |                                     |
        |            proxy catches it <-------+
        v
  PersistenceExceptionTranslator.translateExceptionIfPossible(ex)
        |
        v
  DataAccessException  --->  propagates to the caller

Spring Boot registers that post-processor automatically. In a non-Boot application it must be declared, and its absence is the usual reason translation "does not work".

Two consequences follow from it being a proxy, and both catch people out:

ConsequenceDetail
Translation happens at the boundaryInside your own repository method, the exception is still the raw PersistenceException. It is translated on the way out. A catch (DataAccessException e) inside the repository itself never fires.
Self-invocation skips itSame rule as @Transactional - one repository method calling another on this does not cross the proxy, so nothing is translated.

How a Vendor Code Becomes a Spring Exception

For JDBC there are two translators, and knowing which is active explains the accuracy you get.

TranslatorBasis
SQLErrorCodeSQLExceptionTranslatorVendor error codes read from sql-error-codes.xml, shipped inside spring-jdbc. Precise, but only for the databases listed there. Deprecated in Spring 6.
SQLExceptionSubclassTranslator / SQLStateSQLExceptionTranslatorThe JDBC 4 SQLException subclasses and the standard SQLSTATE class codes. Works with any driver; slightly coarser. The Spring 6 default.

The practical effect of that change: on Spring 6 a database not covered by the old XML now translates correctly through SQLSTATE, but a few translations that used to be precise via vendor codes may land on a parent type instead. Code that catches DataIntegrityViolationException is unaffected; code that catches only DuplicateKeyException is worth re-checking after an upgrade.

What Belongs in a Repository

The boundary is easier to hold than the service one, because it is defined by exclusion.

BelongsDoes not
Queries and writesBusiness rules and validation
Mapping rows to entitiesTransaction boundaries (@Transactional belongs on the service)
Query-shaped projections and DTOsCalls to other services
Database-specific tuning - hints, batch size, fetch strategyHTTP concerns of any kind

One rule that catches people: a repository method should not decide what to do when a row is missing. Returning Optional<Order> is the repository's job; deciding whether an empty result is a 404, a default, or an exception is the service's.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @Repository do beyond @Component?Marks the bean for persistence exception translation - vendor exceptions become Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.
Why translate at all?SQLException is checked and carries vendor-specific codes. Translation gives one unchecked, vendor-neutral hierarchy so the service layer holds no database knowledge.
What performs the translation?PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor wraps every @Repository in a proxy that calls a PersistenceExceptionTranslator. Boot registers it automatically; a non-Boot application must declare it.
Do Spring Data JPA interfaces need the annotation?No. The generated proxy already translates. It is required only for repository classes you write yourself.
Why does catching DataAccessException inside the repository not work?Translation happens in the proxy as the exception leaves the bean, after any internal catch has run. Catch it in the service.
Name useful subtypes.DuplicateKeyException, DataIntegrityViolationException, EmptyResultDataAccessException, OptimisticLockingFailureException, DeadlockLoserDataAccessException, BadSqlGrammarException.
Which are worth retrying?Only TransientDataAccessException subtypes - deadlocks and lock timeouts. A constraint violation will fail identically on retry.
How does Spring map a vendor code?Historically SQLErrorCodeSQLExceptionTranslator using sql-error-codes.xml; from Spring 6 the default is SQLSTATE and JDBC 4 exception subclasses, with the error-code translator deprecated.
Should @Transactional go on the repository?No - the service owns the unit of work. Per-repository transactions commit each step separately and cannot roll back an operation as a whole.
Should a repository throw when a row is missing?No. Return Optional and let the service decide whether that is a 404, a default, or an error.

@Controller (advanced)

Returning an Entity Is a Bug Waiting for Load

Returning a JPA entity from a controller works in development and fails in production, for two separate reasons.

How a Handler Is Actually Found

Knowing the mapping rules removes most "why is this 404" and "ambiguous mapping" confusion.

RuleConsequence
The type must carry @Controller or @RequestMapping@Component plus @GetMapping is silently unmapped. A bare @RequestMapping on the class is enough, which is why some legacy controllers work without a stereotype.
Mappings are inherited from interfaces and superclassesA shared abstract base controller can declare the mappings. Convenient, and a common source of an unexpected duplicate.
Two methods matching the same request is a startup failureIllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping, naming both methods. Fails fast, which is right.
Handler methods are matched by type, not by nameParameters and return values can be almost anything Spring knows how to resolve - the method name is documentation only.

Controller Advice, and Where Errors Belong

Controllers should not contain try/catch for business failures. @ControllerAdvice handles them for every controller at once, which keeps the mapping consistent across the API.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @Controller add over @Component?It marks the class for RequestMappingHandlerMapping to scan for handler methods. Without it the mappings are never registered.
@Controller vs @RestController?@RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody. Return values become the response body instead of a view name.
What is "Circular view path"?A @Controller method returned a String that Spring treated as a view name, found no view, and forwarded back to the same URL. It means a missing @ResponseBody.
Endpoint returns 404 but the method exists - why?Usually the class carries @Component instead of @Controller, or its package is not scanned.
Should a controller return an entity?No. It couples the JSON contract to the schema, leaks internal fields, and serialises lazy proxies outside the transaction. Use a response DTO or record.
What is spring.jpa.open-in-view?Boot's default-on setting that keeps the persistence session open through view rendering. It hides lazy-loading errors by turning them into per-request extra queries; set it to false.
Should @Transactional go on a controller?No. The transaction would remain open during response serialisation, holding a connection for the duration of a slow client.
What causes "Ambiguous mapping"?Two handler methods matching the same path and method. Path variable names and parameter types do not disambiguate - routing happens before binding.
How do you inspect registered mappings?/actuator/mappings, or TRACE logging on RequestMappingHandlerMapping.
Where does exception handling belong?In @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods, so every controller maps the same failure the same way. ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) is the built-in response shape.

beginner.content:
@Configuration

A Class That Replaces an XML File

@Configuration marks a class as a source of bean definitions. It is the Java equivalent of a spring.xml file - same job, checked by the compiler.

It arrived in Spring 3.0 (2009) and is now the default way to configure everything. XML still works and you will meet it in older projects, but nothing new is written that way.
codeExamples:
<!-- The XML original -->
<beans>
    <bean id="dataSource" class="com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource">
        <property name="jdbcUrl" value="jdbc:mysql://localhost/shop"/>
        <property name="maximumPoolSize" value="20"/>
    </bean>

    <bean id="orderRepository" class="com.shop.OrderRepository">
        <constructor-arg ref="dataSource"/>
    </bean>
</beans>

beginner.content:
What Goes in a Configuration Class

Four things, and they are usually the reason the class exists rather than the beans themselves.

AnnotationPurpose
@BeanDeclare a bean by writing its construction. The main content.
@ComponentScanPoint scanning at packages. Implied by @SpringBootApplication for its own package downwards.
@PropertySourceLoad an extra properties file into the Environment. Not needed for application.properties, which Boot loads already.
@ImportPull in another configuration class explicitly, rather than relying on it being scanned.

@Configuration vs @Component for @Bean Methods

Both will register the beans. They differ in one specific way, and it is the reason to always use @Configuration.

@Configuration ("full")@Component ("lite")
Class is CGLIB-subclassedYesNo
One @Bean method calling anotherReturns the singletonRuns the method again - a second object
Startup costOne proxy class per configNone

The failure mode in the right column is quiet and expensive: a second DataSource means a second connection pool that nothing manages. Use @Configuration, and if you want the startup saving, use @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) deliberately - and then never call one @Bean method from another.

The habit that makes the distinction irrelevant: take dependencies as method parameters instead of calling methods. That behaves identically in every mode.

Conditional Configuration

A configuration class does not have to be unconditional, and this is how one codebase serves several environments without if statements.

@Bean

A Method Whose Return Value Becomes a Bean

@Bean goes on a method inside a @Configuration class. Spring calls the method once, takes what it returns, and puts that object in the container.

The distinction from @Component is who writes the construction. With @Component, Spring calls the constructor. With @Bean, you call it - which is what makes it work for classes you do not own and for construction that needs decisions.

Parameters Are Injection Points

A @Bean method's parameters are resolved from the container exactly like constructor parameters. This is how one bean is built from another, and it is the pattern to reach for by default.

The Attributes

AttributeEffect
name / valueOverrides the bean name, which defaults to the method name. Accepts several - the first is the name, the rest are aliases.
initMethodA method to call after construction. The @PostConstruct equivalent for a class you cannot annotate.
destroyMethodA method to call on shutdown. Inferred by default - see the Expert section.
autowireCandidatefalse keeps the bean out of by-type injection. It can still be reached by name.

Scope, and Conditional Beans

Everything that applies to a @Component class applies to a @Bean method - the annotation just moves onto the method.

expert.content:
@Configuration (advanced)

The Static @Bean Rule

The sharpest trap in configuration classes, and it produces a bug with no error message.

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor or BeanPostProcessor must be created very early - before ordinary beans exist. If it is declared as an instance @Bean method, Spring has to instantiate the configuration class to call it, which happens before that class can have its own @Value or @Autowired members resolved.

How @EnableXxx Works

@EnableWebSecurity, @EnableScheduling, @EnableCaching, @EnableJpaRepositories - all the same mechanism, and it is just @Import.

Processing Order, and When It Matters

Configuration classes are read by ConfigurationClassPostProcessor before any ordinary bean is instantiated. Understanding the sequence explains most "why did my bean lose" questions.

  1  Read @Configuration classes found by scanning
  2  Follow their @Import and @ComponentScan, recursively
  3  Register every @Bean method as a BeanDefinition
  4  Evaluate @Conditional / @Profile as each is read
  5  ---- user configuration is now complete ----
  6  Apply auto-configuration  (always LAST, by design)
  7  Instantiate the singletons

Step 6 being last is the whole reason @ConditionalOnMissingBean works in auto-configuration: by the time Boot asks "did the user define a DataSource?", every user definition already exists. The same annotation on your own scanned class is unreliable, because within steps 1-4 the answer depends on read order.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is @Configuration?A class that is a source of bean definitions - the Java replacement for an XML <beans> file, with compile-time checking and IDE refactoring.
@Configuration vs @Component holding @Bean methods?@Configuration is CGLIB-proxied, so one @Bean method calling another returns the singleton. Under @Component the call runs the method again and creates a second object.
What does proxyBeanMethods = false do?Skips the CGLIB subclass for faster startup. Safe only when no @Bean method calls another. Boot's own auto-configurations use it.
Why must some @Bean methods be static?BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor beans are created before the configuration class can be fully initialised. A non-static method forces early instantiation, leaving its own @Value and @Autowired members unresolved.
What does @Import do?Registers another configuration class explicitly, independent of component scanning - needed for configuration in a library jar.
How does @EnableScheduling work?It is a meta-annotation carrying @Import(SchedulingConfiguration.class). Every @EnableXxx is the same pattern.
ImportSelector vs ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar?The selector returns class names to import based on runtime conditions. The registrar registers BeanDefinitions directly - used by @EnableJpaRepositories, which has interfaces rather than classes to import.
When is auto-configuration processed?Last, after all user configuration. That ordering is what makes @ConditionalOnMissingBean reliable there.
How do you override an auto-configured bean?Define your own - the auto-configuration backs off. Exclude the auto-configuration only when it would fail at startup regardless.
When do you need @DependsOn?Only when one bean relies on another's side effect with no dependency between them - Flyway migrations before a cache warmer, for example. Otherwise a constructor parameter already orders them.

@Bean (advanced)

The Return Type Is the Contract

Spring resolves injection by type, and the type it records is the method's declared return type - not the class of the object you actually returned. Declaring it too narrowly hides capability; too widely, and nothing can find it.

destroyMethod Is Inferred, Which Surprises People

If you do not set destroyMethod, Spring does not do nothing - it looks for a public no-arg close() or shutdown() method and calls that on shutdown.
Three Mistakes Worth Recognising

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is @Bean?A method-level annotation in a @Configuration class whose return value Spring registers as a bean. You write the construction rather than Spring calling a constructor.
When do you need it over @Component?For third-party classes you cannot annotate, and when construction requires logic or configuration.
How are @Bean method parameters resolved?From the container, exactly like constructor parameters - including @Qualifier, @Value and ObjectProvider. Taking a parameter also fixes the creation order.
What is the bean's name?The method name by default. @Bean("x") overrides it; several values make the rest aliases. Renaming the method renames the bean.
Why does the declared return type matter?It is the type the container indexes the bean by. Declaring the interface makes injection by the concrete class fail, and it changes what @ConditionalOnMissingBean matches.
Interface or concrete return type?Concrete by default - it satisfies both. Use the interface only to deliberately hide the implementation.
What happens if you omit destroyMethod?Spring infers a public no-arg close() or shutdown() and calls it. Set destroyMethod = "" to disable that for objects you do not own.
Can you overload a @Bean method?You should not - matching is by method name, so both overloads claim one bean name and Spring silently uses one.
What if a @Bean method returns null?A null bean is registered and the failure surfaces far from the cause. Use @Conditional/@Profile so the bean either exists or does not.
Should a @Bean method do work?No - it runs during startup. Construct and configure only; move network calls and warm-up into an ApplicationRunner.

beginner.content:
@Autowired

"Find a Bean of This Type and Put It Here"

@Autowired marks an injection point. Spring looks for a bean assignable to the declared type and supplies it.

The important word is type. The field or parameter name is not what Spring matches on - it is only consulted as a tie-breaker when several beans of the same type exist.

The Four Places It Can Go

PositionNeeded?Notes
ConstructorOptional since Spring 4.3 when the class has one constructorThe recommended form. Most modern code omits the annotation entirely.
SetterRequiredWithout it the setter is never called and the field stays null.
FieldRequiredSet by reflection. Shortest and least testable.
Any methodRequiredLess known: any method can be an injection point, with every parameter resolved.

When the Match Is Not Exactly One

Three outcomes, and the second and third are the ones you will meet.

CandidatesResult
OneInjected.
NoneNoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup - unless required = false.
SeveralNoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, unless resolved by @Qualifier, @Primary, or a bean name equal to the field/parameter name.

Spring applies them in that last order: @Qualifier first, then @Primary, then the name match. That final fallback resolves silently and is worth avoiding deliberately - it makes a working application depend on a variable name, so a rename during cleanup breaks startup.

Injecting Several, and Injecting Maybe-None

Two cases the by-type rule handles specially.

@Qualifier

Choosing Between Beans of the Same Type

Injection is by type. When two beans satisfy the same type, Spring cannot choose, and startup fails. @Qualifier is how you make the choice at the injection point.

What the Value Actually Matches

This is the part that is usually half-understood. @Qualifier("x") matches a bean in two ways, and the second is the one people forget.

Matched againstExample
A @Qualifier on the bean declaration@Component @Qualifier("card") class StripeGateway - matched by @Qualifier("card")
The bean's name, as a fallback@Component class StripeGateway - matched by @Qualifier("stripeGateway")

Most code uses the fallback without realising, which is why @Qualifier is commonly described as "inject by name". It is not - the name is the second thing it tries. Declaring the qualifier on the bean is the better habit, because it decouples the injection point from the class name.

@Qualifier vs @Primary

They solve the same problem from opposite ends, and the choice is about where the knowledge belongs.

@Primary@Qualifier
Declared onThe beanThe injection point
Says"Use me unless told otherwise""I want that specific one"
Scope of effectEvery unqualified injection pointOne injection point
PrecedenceLowerHigher - a qualifier always beats a primary

The combination is the useful pattern: mark the common case @Primary so most code needs no annotation, and use @Qualifier at the few places that need the exception.

@Primary

"Use Me Unless Told Otherwise"

@Primary marks one bean as the default choice among several of the same type. It is declared on the bean, and it applies to every injection point that does not say otherwise.

The other beans are not removed or hidden. They still exist and can still be reached - by @Qualifier, by name, or in a List. @Primary only settles the question "which one when nobody said".

The Rule: Exactly One Per Type

Two @Primary beans of the same type is an error - but a delayed one. Spring only complains when an unqualified injection point actually forces the choice.

Precedence

@Qualifier always beats @Primary. The injection point is more specific than the bean, so it wins.

  Candidates of the required type
        |
        v
  @Qualifier at the injection point?   -> yes: that bean wins
        |  no
        v
  Exactly one bean marked @Primary?    -> yes: that bean wins
        |  no
        v
  @Priority(n) on the candidates?      -> yes: lowest n wins
        |  no
        v
  A bean whose NAME equals the field
  or parameter name?                   -> yes: that bean wins
        |  no
        v
  NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException

The intended pattern falls out of this: mark the common case @Primary so the majority of the codebase needs no annotation at all, and use @Qualifier at the handful of places that need the other one. The annotations then appear exactly where something unusual is happening.

The Case You Will Actually Meet: Two DataSources

The most common real use of @Primary, and the one where leaving it out produces a confusing failure.

expert.content:
@Autowired (advanced)

Generics Are Part of the Type

Spring matches the full generic type, not the raw one. This is more useful than it first appears, and it removes most of the need for qualifiers.

The Full Resolution Algorithm

Precisely what Spring does at an injection point, in order:

  1  Collect every bean assignable to the required type,
     including generic parameters

  2  Discard any bean marked autowireCandidate = false

  3  If a @Qualifier is present, keep only beans matching it
     (bean name, or a custom qualifier annotation)

  4  If several remain, keep those marked @Primary
        -> two @Primary beans of one type is itself an error:
           NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: more than one 'primary'

  5  If several remain, apply @Priority(n) - lowest number wins

  6  If several remain, keep the bean whose NAME equals the
     field or parameter name

  7  Exactly one   -> inject
     Zero          -> NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
                      (unless required=false / Optional / @Nullable)
     More than one -> NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException

One rule sits outside this list: a bean is never a candidate for injection into itself unless it is the only option. That is what allows a @Bean method taking a List<Validator> to live inside a configuration class that also declares a Validator.

@Autowired vs @Inject vs @Resource

Three annotations do overlapping jobs, and mixing them in one codebase produces "why did it inject that one" questions.

@Autowired@Inject@Resource
FromSpringJSR-330JSR-250
Packageorg.springframework...jakarta.injectjakarta.annotation
Matches byType, then nameType, then nameName, then type
required = falseYesNoNo
Qualifier@Qualifier@Namedname attribute

Practical advice: use constructor injection and none of them. Where an annotation is unavoidable, use @Autowired - it is the only one with required, and it is what the rest of Spring's documentation assumes. @Resource matching by name first is the surprise that catches people, since it behaves differently from the other two in exactly the ambiguous case where it matters.
Two Failures That Look Like @Autowired Problems

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does @Autowired resolve a dependency?By type, including generic parameters. Name is only a tie-breaker after @Qualifier and @Primary.
Where can it be placed?Constructor, setter, field, or any method - and on @Bean method parameters implicitly.
When is it optional on a constructor?Since Spring 4.3, when the class has exactly one constructor.
What happens with no matching bean?NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup, unless required = false, @Nullable, Optional or ObjectProvider is used.
What happens with several matches?NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, unless resolved by @Qualifier, then @Primary, then @Priority, then a matching bean name.
Can you inject every implementation of an interface?Yes - List<T> injects them all, Map<String, T> keys them by bean name, and @Order controls sequence. An empty list fails unless the injection point is optional.
Are generics respected?Yes. Converter<String, Money> resolves unambiguously among many Converter beans - provided the injection point declares the generics.
@Autowired vs @Resource?@Autowired matches by type then name; @Resource (JSR-250) by name then type. Only @Autowired supports required = false.
Why is an @Autowired field null?Almost always because the object was created with new rather than obtained from the container. Injection is done by Spring, not by the language.
Can @Autowired inject a property value?No - it resolves beans. Use @Value, or bind a group of settings with @ConfigurationProperties.

@Qualifier (advanced)

Custom Qualifier Annotations

A String qualifier is not checked by anything. A typo produces a startup failure at best, and at worst matches a bean you did not mean. Because @Qualifier works as a meta-annotation, you can make the compiler do the checking.

Qualifiers Filter Collections Too

Less known, and genuinely useful: putting a qualifier on a List injection point selects a subset of the implementations rather than one bean.
Where It Goes Wrong

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is @Qualifier for?Selecting one bean at an injection point when several match the required type.
What does its value match?A @Qualifier declared on the bean first; failing that, the bean name as a fallback.
Why prefer declaring a qualifier on the bean?It decouples the injection point from the class or method name, so renaming does not break wiring, and it states the bean's role rather than its identity.
@Qualifier vs @Primary?@Primary is on the bean and sets a default for every unqualified injection point. @Qualifier is on the injection point and wins over @Primary.
Can there be two @Primary beans of one type?No - any unqualified injection point then fails with "more than one 'primary' bean found".
How do you make a type-safe qualifier?Define an annotation meta-annotated with @Qualifier. Typos become compile errors and the IDE can find usages.
Can a custom qualifier carry attributes?Yes, and every attribute must match - including defaults - for a bean to be selected.
What does @Qualifier on a List do?Filters the collection to the beans carrying that qualifier, which is a clean way to declare groups or phases.
What happens on a misspelt qualifier?NoSuchBeanDefinitionException saying "expected at least 1 bean which qualifies" - it reads as a missing bean, so check the "Dependency annotations" line in the message.
Where does the qualifier annotation go on a constructor?On the parameter, not the constructor. On a field it accompanies @Autowired.

@Primary (advanced)

What @Primary Does Not Do

Three limits, each of which has surprised someone.

ExpectationReality
It filters collection injectionNo. List<PaymentGateway> still receives every implementation, primary or not. @Primary answers "which one", never "which ones".
It orders beansNo. Sequence in an injected List comes from @Order / Ordered. A primary bean is not placed first.
It affects getBeansOfType()No - that returns all of them. Only getBean(Type.class) honours primary.

@Primary vs @Priority

Both break a tie on the bean side, and they behave differently in one way that matters.

@Primary@Priority
FromSpringJSR-250 (jakarta.annotation)
ValueNone - it is a flagAn int; lower wins
Several allowed?No - two is an errorYes - they are ranked
PrecedenceBeats @PriorityOnly consulted if no primary
On @Bean methodsYesNo - class-level only

Use @Primary by default. @Priority earns its place when there are three or more candidates that need a genuine fallback order rather than one winner - a chain of resolvers, say, where the ranking is meaningful in itself.

Overriding an Auto-Configured Bean

A frequent misuse: reaching for @Primary to beat Spring Boot, when defining the bean is already enough.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @Primary do?Marks one bean as the default among several of its type, for every injection point that carries no qualifier.
Where is it declared?On the bean - a @Component class or a @Bean method - not at the injection point.
@Primary or @Qualifier?Qualifier wins; it is more specific. Use @Primary for the common case and @Qualifier for the exceptions.
Can two beans of a type be @Primary?No. The failure appears when an unqualified injection point exists: "more than one 'primary' bean found".
Does it filter List<T> injection?No - the list still gets every implementation. It answers "which one", not "which ones".
Does it control order in a list?No - that is @Order / Ordered.
Why is it required with two DataSource beans?Boot's auto-configuration injects a bare DataSource to build the entity manager factory and transaction manager. You cannot add a qualifier to Boot's code, so the choice must be made on the bean.
@Primary vs @Priority?@Primary is a flag and only one is allowed; @Priority(int) ranks several, lowest wins, and is only consulted if no primary exists. @Priority is ignored on @Bean methods.
Do you need @Primary to override an auto-configured bean?Usually not - Boot's bean is @ConditionalOnMissingBean and backs off. Only needed when the auto-configured bean is unconditional, so both exist.
Does @Primary remove the other beans?No. They are constructed and hold their resources; they are simply not the default. Use an auto-configuration exclusion to remove one.

beginner.content:
Component Scanning

How Spring Finds Your Classes

Annotating a class @Component does not register it. Something has to go looking. Component scanning is that search: at startup Spring walks a set of packages, reads every class it finds, and registers the ones carrying a stereotype annotation.

Two conditions must both hold for a class to become a bean:

   1. the class carries @Component
      (or @Service / @Repository / @Controller / a custom stereotype)

   2. the class sits inside a SCANNED package

   Miss either one and the class is invisible. There is no warning -
   the bean simply does not exist, and the failure appears wherever
   something tried to inject it.

The Default, and the Bug It Causes

@SpringBootApplication is itself annotated @ComponentScan, with no packages given. That means: scan the package this class is in, and everything below it.

So the location of your main class silently defines the scanned tree - which is the single most common cause of a missing bean.

Diagnosing a Missing Bean

Two questions, in this order, settle almost every case.

MessageMeaningLook at
"No qualifying bean of type X"X was never registeredIs X annotated? Is its package scanned?
"Error creating bean with name x"X was found; construction failedX's own dependencies

Those are different problems with different fixes, and telling them apart from the first line of the stack trace saves a lot of time.

Narrowing What Gets Scanned

Filters let you include classes that carry no stereotype, or exclude ones that do.

ApplicationContext

The Container Itself

Everything so far - scanning, bean definitions, injection, scopes, lifecycle - happens inside one object. The ApplicationContext is the Spring container. When people say "Spring starts", they mean this object is being built.

   ApplicationContext
   +-------------------------------------------------------+
   |  bean definitions   the recipes, from scanning,        |
   |                     @Bean methods and XML              |
   |                                                        |
   |  singleton beans    the objects, built at startup      |
   |                                                        |
   |  Environment        profiles + property sources        |
   |  MessageSource      i18n lookups                       |
   |  event publisher    ApplicationEvent delivery          |
   |  resource loader    classpath: / file: / http: access  |
   +-------------------------------------------------------+

In Spring Boot you rarely name it - SpringApplication.run() creates it, and returns it.

BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory. The factory is the bare container; the context is the factory plus everything a real application needs around it.

BeanFactoryApplicationContext
Bean creationLazy - on getBean()Eager - singletons at startup
Annotation configManual setupBuilt in
BeanPostProcessorsRegistered by handDetected automatically
EventsNoYes
i18n (MessageSource)NoYes
Environment / profilesNoYes

The eager/lazy difference is the one that matters in practice. Eager creation means a wiring mistake fails at startup rather than on the first request that needs the bean - a missing bean, a circular dependency or a bad property is on screen in seconds instead of surfacing in production at 2am.

You will never instantiate a BeanFactory yourself. It is worth knowing only because the distinction explains why spring.main.lazy-initialization=true is a worse trade than it looks: it buys startup time by giving up exactly that fail-fast property.

The Implementations

You choose one only outside Spring Boot; Boot picks based on the classpath.

ClassUsed for
AnnotationConfigApplicationContextPlain Java config, no web layer. Batch jobs, CLI tools, tests.
ClassPathXmlApplicationContextLegacy XML configuration.
AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContextWhat Boot creates for a servlet web application.
AnnotationConfigReactiveWebServerApplicationContextThe WebFlux equivalent.

Two Things It Gives You Beyond Beans

Environment and events are used constantly, and both come from the context rather than from any bean you wrote.

expert.content:
Component Scanning (advanced)

Scanning Reads Bytecode, Not Classes

The scanner does not load your classes to inspect them. It reads the .class files with ASM and examines the annotation metadata directly.

ConsequenceWhy it matters
No static initialisers runScanning a class with an expensive or failing static {} block is safe - the block only runs if the bean is actually created.
Missing dependencies do not break scanningA class referencing an absent optional library can be examined without a NoClassDefFoundError. This is what makes Boot's @ConditionalOnClass possible at all.
Cost is I/O, not class loadingThe expense is opening and parsing every .class file under the scanned packages - which is why a broad scan root costs more than a narrow one.

Scanning Stops at the Jar Boundary - by Design

A library's beans are not found by your component scan, because your scan root is your own package. Libraries therefore never rely on being scanned.

MechanismUsed by
@Import on an @EnableXxx annotationOpt-in libraries - the consumer writes @EnableAuditing
Auto-configuration registered in META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.importsSpring Boot starters - active with no annotation at all

The tempting shortcut - telling consumers to add @ComponentScan("com.mylib") - is a bad interface. It leaks your package structure into every consumer's configuration, and renaming an internal package becomes a breaking change.

Scanning in Tests

Test annotations control scanning too, and this is where startup time is won or lost.

AnnotationScans
@SpringBootTestEverything - the full application context. Slow, and shared between test classes only if the configuration matches exactly.
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)Controllers, advice and MVC infrastructure only. No services, no repositories - those are @MockBeans.
@DataJpaTestEntities and repositories only.
@SpringBootTest(classes = SomeConfig.class)Exactly that configuration - no scanning at all.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is component scanning?The startup search through configured packages for classes carrying a stereotype annotation, registering each as a bean definition.
What does @SpringBootApplication scan by default?Its own package and everything below it - which is why the main class belongs in the root package.
Why might an annotated class not become a bean?Its package is outside the scanned tree. The annotation alone does nothing.
How do you scan extra packages?scanBasePackages, or @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = ...) - the class form is refactor-safe where a string is not.
What filter types exist?ANNOTATION, ASSIGNABLE_TYPE, REGEX, ASPECTJ, CUSTOM. They affect scanning only, not beans registered by @Bean or @Import.
Does scanning load the classes?No - it reads bytecode with ASM. Static initialisers do not run, and a class referencing a missing optional library can still be examined, which is what makes @ConditionalOnClass work.
Are beans in a library jar scanned?No. Libraries use @Import behind an @EnableXxx, or auto-configuration registered in AutoConfiguration.imports.
How do you reduce scanning cost?Narrow the base packages first; spring-context-indexer replaces the classpath walk with a compile-time index. Measure before optimising.
How does scanning differ in tests?Slice annotations load only part of the context. @SpringBootTest(classes = ...) skips scanning entirely.
Why do some test suites start many contexts?Spring caches a context per unique configuration; any difference in profiles, mocks or properties creates another - each costing a full startup.

ApplicationContext (advanced)

What refresh() Does

Starting a context is one method - AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() - and its steps are the phases described across the previous topics, in order.

  refresh()
   1  prepareRefresh                 timestamp, validate required properties
   2  obtainFreshBeanFactory         create the BeanFactory
   3  prepareBeanFactory             register Environment, Aware processors
   4  postProcessBeanFactory         subclass hook (web contexts use it)

   5  invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors
        ConfigurationClassPostProcessor runs HERE - scanning, @Bean
        methods, @Import, auto-configuration. All definitions exist
        after this step, and definitions may still be MODIFIED.

   6  registerBeanPostProcessors     collect BPPs - not yet applied

   7  initMessageSource              i18n
   8  initApplicationEventMulticaster
   9  onRefresh                      START THE WEB SERVER (Boot)
  10  registerListeners

  11  finishBeanFactoryInitialization
        instantiate every non-lazy singleton: constructor, inject,
        @PostConstruct, then BPPs wrap it in proxies

  12  finishRefresh                  publish ContextRefreshedEvent
                                     then ApplicationReadyEvent (Boot)

Two things worth carrying away. Step 5 is why BeanFactoryPostProcessor beans must be static @Bean methods - they run before ordinary beans can exist. And step 9 comes before step 11, so the web server binds its port before your singletons are built; a failure at step 11 still fails startup, but the port was briefly open.

The Startup Events, and Which to Use

Boot publishes several events around refresh(), and picking the wrong one is a common cause of "it ran too early".

EventWhenUse for
ApplicationStartingEventBefore anything. No context, no environment.Logging system setup.
ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEventEnvironment ready, context not created.Adding property sources.
ContextRefreshedEventAll beans built. Fires again on a refresh.Whole-context work - guard against running twice.
ApplicationReadyEventLast. Server accepting requests.Warm-up, seeding, one-off jobs. The usual right answer.
ApplicationFailedEventStartup threw.Alerting on a failed boot.

Getting Hold of the Context - and Why to Avoid It

Three ways, in decreasing order of acceptability.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the ApplicationContext?The Spring IoC container - it holds bean definitions and singleton instances and provides the Environment, events, i18n and resource loading.
BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?ApplicationContext extends it and adds eager singleton creation, automatic post-processor detection, events, MessageSource and Environment.
Why does eager instantiation matter?Wiring errors fail at startup rather than on the first request. That is the property spring.main.lazy-initialization=true gives away.
Name some implementations.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext, ClassPathXmlApplicationContext, and Boot's servlet and reactive web variants.
What happens during refresh()?Prepare the bean factory, run BeanFactoryPostProcessors (which perform scanning and read @Bean methods), register post-processors, start the web server, instantiate non-lazy singletons, publish ContextRefreshedEvent.
Why must BeanFactoryPostProcessor @Bean methods be static?They run in an early refresh step, before the declaring configuration class can be fully initialised.
How do you publish an event?Inject ApplicationEventPublisher and call publishEvent. Listeners use @EventListener, or @TransactionalEventListener to run after commit.
Are events asynchronous?No - synchronous on the publishing thread by default. Add @Async if needed.
ContextRefreshedEvent vs ApplicationReadyEvent?The first can fire more than once and does not mean the server is up. ApplicationReadyEvent or ApplicationRunner fires once, after startup completes.
Why avoid injecting the context to call getBean()?It is Service Locator - dependencies become invisible, failures move from startup to request time, and the class needs a container to test. Inject a Map<String, T> when the choice is genuinely dynamic.

beginner.content:
Environment & Profiles

One Abstraction, Two Jobs

Environment is the part of the container that answers questions about where the application is running. It does exactly two things:

JobQuestion it answers
Property sources"What is the value of app.timeout?" - searching command line, environment variables, property files and defaults, in a defined order.
Profiles"Which environment is this?" - dev, test, prod - so that beans and configuration can differ.

The two work together: a profile decides which property files are loaded, and properties decide which profiles are active.

Property Sources Are Searched in Order

A property is not looked up in one place. Spring asks each source in turn and takes the first answer, so a source higher in the list overrides everything below it.

  HIGHEST PRECEDENCE - wins
    1  Command line arguments        --app.timeout=10s
    2  SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON       inline JSON in an env var
    3  OS environment variables      APP_TIMEOUT=10s
    4  Java system properties        -Dapp.timeout=10s
    5  application-{profile}.properties / .yml
    6  application.properties / .yml
    7  @PropertySource on a @Configuration class
    8  Defaults in code              @Value("${app.timeout:5s}")
  LOWEST PRECEDENCE

This ordering is what makes the same jar deployable everywhere: the file inside the artifact holds sensible defaults, and the environment overrides them without a rebuild.
codeExamples:
# application.properties - baked into the jar
app.timeout=5s
app.batch-size=100

# Overridden per environment, with no rebuild:
java -jar shop.jar --app.timeout=30s          # command line
APP_TIMEOUT=30s java -jar shop.jar            # environment variable
java -Dapp.timeout=30s -jar shop.jar          # system property

# Note the env var name. Spring's RELAXED BINDING maps
# APP_TIMEOUT -> app.timeout, because an environment variable cannot
# contain a dot. The rule: uppercase, and dots and dashes become
# underscores.
#
#   app.batch-size   ->  APP_BATCHSIZE  or  APP_BATCH_SIZE
#   spring.datasource.url -> SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL
#
# This is how every containerised deployment configures Spring.

beginner.content:
Profiles: Beans That Only Exist Sometimes

A profile is a named tag. @Profile on a bean or configuration class means "register this only when that tag is active".
codeExamples:
# Activating profiles - the same precedence list applies.

spring.profiles.active=dev                    # application.properties
java -jar shop.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod java -jar shop.jar

# Several at once - they are additive, not exclusive:
--spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics,eu-west

# A fallback when nothing is set:
spring.profiles.default=dev

# Profile-specific files are loaded ON TOP of the base file:
#
#   application.properties          always loaded
#   application-prod.properties     loaded too, and WINS on conflicts
#
# So the base file holds what is common and the profile file holds only
# the differences - not a full copy.

beginner.content:
In Tests

Profiles are how a test picks a configuration without touching production files.

Spring Expression Language (SpEL)

A Small Language Evaluated at Runtime

SpEL is an expression language built into spring-expression. It lets a string express a computation - reading a property, calling a method, comparing values - which Spring evaluates when it needs the answer.

You have already used it without naming it. It is what makes these work:

WhereExample
@Value@Value("#{systemProperties['user.region']}")
Spring Security@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') and #id == principal.id")
Caching@Cacheable(key = "#customerId + ':' + #year")
Conditional config@ConditionalOnExpression("${shop.enabled} and ${shop.region} == 'eu'")
Spring Data@Query("select o from Order o where o.tenant = :#{principal.tenant}")

#{ } and ${ } Are Not the Same Thing

This is the distinction that causes the most confusion, and they are frequently written side by side.

${ }#{ }
IsA property placeholderA SpEL expression
Resolved byPropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurerThe SpEL engine
ReadsEnvironment - files, env vars, CLIBeans, methods, operators, literals
Can computeNo - substitution onlyYes
Order${ } is resolved first, then the result is parsed as SpEL

The Syntax Worth Knowing

You will read far more SpEL than you write, so recognition matters more than fluency.

FeatureExampleResult
Literals#{'hello'}, #{42}, #{true}, #{null}as written
Arithmetic#{2 + 3 * 4}14
Comparison#{count > 5}, #{name == 'x'}boolean
Logical#{a and b}, #{!flag}, #{a or b}boolean
Ternary#{count > 0 ? 'some' : 'none'}either branch
Elvis#{name ?: 'unknown'}left, or right if null
Safe navigation#{customer?.address?.city}null instead of NPE
Bean reference#{@orderService.count()}calls the bean
Type reference#{T(java.lang.Math).PI}static access
Collection selection#{orders.?[total > 100]}matching subset
Collection projection#{orders.![reference]}list of one field

Where It Actually Earns Its Place

SpEL is a poor general-purpose tool - it is untyped, unrefactorable and only checked at runtime. It is worth using in the places where the alternative is worse.

UseWhy SpEL wins
Method security - @PreAuthorizeThe rule must reference method arguments and the current principal, neither of which exists at compile time.
Cache keys - @CacheableThe key is derived from arguments; a custom KeyGenerator for every method would be far more code.
Conditional beans - @ConditionalOnExpressionRegistration depends on a combination of properties that a single @ConditionalOnProperty cannot express.

expert.content:
Environment & Profiles (advanced)

Profile Expressions

@Profile accepts a small boolean language, not just a name.

ExpressionActive when
@Profile("prod")prod is active
@Profile("!prod")prod is not active
@Profile({"dev", "test"})either - the array is OR
@Profile("prod & eu")both
@Profile("(dev | test) & !ci")parenthesised combinations

A caution on & and |: they cannot be mixed at the same level without brackets. @Profile("a & b | c") throws IllegalArgumentException: Malformed profile expression at startup - write (a & b) | c.

Where Profiles Do Not Reach

Three limits, and each has produced a confusing bug.

LimitConsequence
Profiles are read before the context is builtSetting spring.profiles.active inside a profile-specific file has no effect - the decision was already made. Boot rejects this outright.
@Profile is evaluated at definition timeProfiles cannot change at runtime. Switching one means restarting the application.
Profiles do not filter properties already loadedA value in application.properties applies under every profile unless a profile file overrides it. There is no "unset in prod".
codeExamples:
# THE FIRST LIMIT, made concrete.
#
# application-prod.properties:
#   spring.profiles.active=metrics      # <-- illegal

# OUTPUT:
# InvalidConfigDataPropertyException: Property
# 'spring.profiles.active' imported from location
# 'class path resource [application-prod.properties]' is invalid in a
# profile specific resource
#
# Use a profile GROUP instead, declared in the base file:
#   spring.profiles.group.prod=metrics

expert.content: Two Failures Worth Recognising

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Environment?The container's abstraction over property sources and profiles - it resolves configuration values and reports which profiles are active.
What is the property precedence order?Command line, then SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, OS environment variables, system properties, profile-specific files, application.properties, @PropertySource, then in-code defaults.
How does an environment variable map to a property?Relaxed binding: uppercase with dots and dashes as underscores. spring.datasource.url is SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL.
What does @Profile do?Registers a bean or configuration class only when the given profile expression matches. Non-matching beans are never instantiated.
How do you activate profiles?spring.profiles.active as a property, command-line argument or SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE. Several are comma-separated and additive.
Can profile expressions use logic?Yes - !, &, | and brackets. Mixing & and | without brackets is a startup error.
What are profile groups?Boot 2.4+: spring.profiles.group.prod=metrics,tracing activates several profiles under one name. It replaced spring.profiles.include.
Can you change a profile at runtime?No. @Profile is evaluated when bean definitions are registered, so it requires a restart.
How do you add a custom property source?An EnvironmentPostProcessor registered in META-INF/spring.factories - it must run before the context exists, so it cannot be a bean.
@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?@Value fails loudly on a missing placeholder but is untyped and scattered. @ConfigurationProperties is typed and groups related settings, but silently ignores misspelt keys - pair it with @Validated.

Spring Expression Language (SpEL) (advanced)

Using the Parser Directly

Occasionally useful for a rules engine, a user-configurable filter, or a templating feature.

SpEL Injection Is Remote Code Execution

This is the most important thing on the page. SpEL can instantiate classes and call arbitrary static methods. An expression built from user input is an RCE vulnerability, not merely a bug.

Failure Modes and Their Messages

SpEL errors are runtime errors, and the codes are worth recognising because they say what went wrong precisely.

ErrorCause
EL1008E: Property or field 'x' cannot be foundThe name does not exist on the root object - or there is no public getter.
EL1007E: Property or field 'x' cannot be found on nullSomething earlier in the chain was null. Use safe navigation ?..
EL1041E: After parsing a valid expression, there is still more dataA substituted ${ } value produced invalid SpEL - usually a missing pair of quotes.
EL1005E: Type cannot be foundT() on an unknown class, or a restricted evaluation context.
Could not resolve placeholder 'x'Not SpEL at all - a ${ } placeholder with no value and no default.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is SpEL?Spring's runtime expression language, in spring-expression - used by @Value, method security, cache annotations and conditional configuration.
${ } vs #{ }?${ } is a property placeholder resolved from the Environment; #{ } is a SpEL expression that can compute. Placeholders resolve first, then the result is parsed as SpEL.
How do you give a default?${key:default} for a placeholder, the Elvis operator ?: in SpEL.
What is safe navigation??. returns null instead of throwing when part of the chain is null.
Selection and projection?.?[condition] filters a collection; .![expression] maps it.
How do you reference a bean?@beanName inside an expression - #{@orderService.count()}.
Why is SpEL injection dangerous?T() and constructors reach any class on the classpath, so an expression built from user input is remote code execution.
How do you evaluate untrusted expressions safely?SimpleEvaluationContext instead of StandardEvaluationContext - it removes type references, constructors and bean access. Better still, do not accept expressions.
How do you make SpEL fast?Parse once and reuse the Expression; optionally enable compiler mode, which requires stable types.
Why avoid SpEL that references beans in @Value?It is wiring expressed as an unchecked string, evaluated during bean creation - so ordering problems surface as confusing expression errors. Use constructor injection.

beginner.content:
Spring Boot is a framework that simplifies Spring application development with auto-configuration and embedded servers.

 Key Features:
 • Auto-configuration: Automatically configures beans
 • Starter dependencies: Pre-configured dependencies
 • Embedded server: Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow
 • Production-ready: Actuator for monitoring
 • No XML configuration: Annotation-based

 Advantages:
 • Rapid development
 • Microservices support
 • Easy testing
 • Reduced boilerplate code

expert.content:
What @SpringBootApplication Really Is

@SpringBootApplication is a convenience meta-annotation that bundles three separate annotations. Understanding what each one does is the single most-asked Spring Boot interview question.

AnnotationPurpose
@ConfigurationMarks the class as a source of bean definitions (can contain @Bean methods)
@EnableAutoConfigurationTells Spring Boot to auto-configure beans based on classpath jars, other beans, and property values
@ComponentScanScans the current package and sub-packages for @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.

SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args)
        |
        v
1. Create ApplicationContext (Servlet/Reactive/Default based on classpath)
        |
        v
2. Load @Configuration classes + run @ComponentScan
        |
        v
3. @EnableAutoConfiguration kicks in:
     - Reads META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports (Boot 3+)
       or spring.factories (Boot 2)
     - Each auto-config class is guarded by @Conditional* checks:
         @ConditionalOnClass      -> is the dependency on the classpath?
         @ConditionalOnMissingBean -> did the user NOT already define one?
         @ConditionalOnProperty   -> is a specific property set?
     - Only matching auto-configurations register their beans
        |
        v
4. Embedded server auto-configured (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow) if
   spring-boot-starter-web is on the classpath
        |
        v
5. ApplicationContext refreshed -> beans instantiated & wired
        |
        v
6. Embedded server started -> application ready to serve requests

This is why adding spring-boot-starter-data-jpa to the classpath is enough to get a working DataSource and EntityManager - DataSourceAutoConfiguration and HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration detect the JPA/JDBC classes and a spring.datasource.* property, then wire the beans automatically - no XML, no manual bean definitions.

Embedded Server Model vs Traditional WAR Deployment

Classic Spring MVC applications are packaged as a WAR file and deployed INTO an externally installed servlet container (Tomcat/JBoss/WebLogic). Spring Boot flips this: the servlet container is a library dependency that gets bundled INSIDE an executable JAR, so "the server" ships with the app.

AspectTraditional Spring MVC (WAR)Spring Boot (embedded, JAR)
Packaging.war.jar (executable, "fat jar")
ServerInstalled separately (Tomcat, etc.)Bundled inside the jar (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow)
DeploymentCopy WAR into server's webapps/ folderjava -jar app.jar - runs anywhere with a JVM
Multiple apps per serverCommon - one Tomcat, many WARsUncommon - one process, one embedded server (microservice style)
Server version controlOps team controls Tomcat versionDev controls server version via pom.xml/build.gradle
StartupDeploy descriptor / web.xml drivenmain() method calls SpringApplication.run()

Switching the embedded server is a one-line dependency change - exclude Tomcat and pull in Jetty or Undertow:
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml: swap embedded Tomcat for Jetty -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- Application now starts on embedded Jetty instead of Tomcat, -->
<!-- no other code changes required. -->

expert.content:
Spring Boot Starters - What a Starter POM Actually Does

A "starter" is NOT a magic feature - it is simply a curated dependency descriptor with no code of its own, whose pom.xml pulls in a compatible, version-tested set of libraries via transitive dependencies.

For example, spring-boot-starter-web transitively brings in: spring-webmvc, spring-boot-starter-tomcat (embedded server), spring-boot-starter-json (Jackson for JSON binding), and spring-boot-starter (core auto-config + logging). You declare ONE dependency and get a whole working stack whose versions are guaranteed compatible with each other - that compatibility matrix is the real value of the "Spring Boot BOM" (Bill of Materials).
codeExamples:
<!-- Without starters: managing every library + version yourself -->
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework</groupId><artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId><version>6.1.2</version></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>org.apache.tomcat.embed</groupId><artifactId>tomcat-embed-core</artifactId><version>10.1.17</version></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId><artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId><version>2.16.0</version></dependency>
<!-- ... and you must manually keep all versions compatible -->

<!-- With a starter: one line, versions managed by Spring Boot's parent BOM -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- OUTPUT: -->
<!-- mvn dependency:tree shows spring-webmvc, embedded Tomcat, Jackson -->
<!-- and spring-boot-starter (logging + core) all pulled in transitively -->

expert.content:
Common Starters Reference

StarterBrings In
spring-boot-starter-webSpring MVC + embedded Tomcat + Jackson (REST APIs, MVC)
spring-boot-starter-data-jpaHibernate + Spring Data JPA + JDBC (database access)
spring-boot-starter-securitySpring Security (authentication/authorization)
spring-boot-starter-testJUnit, Mockito, AssertJ, Spring Test (testing)
spring-boot-starter-actuatorProduction-ready monitoring endpoints
spring-boot-starter-validationHibernate Validator (Bean Validation / @Valid)

Externalized Configuration: application.properties / application.yml

Spring Boot lets you pull hard-coded values OUT of Java code into a config file, so behavior changes per environment without recompiling. Both formats configure the exact same underlying properties - YAML is just a more structured/nested syntax.
codeExamples:
# application.properties
server.port=9090
app.greeting=Hello from properties file
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=secret

# application.yml (equivalent to the properties above)
server:
  port: 9090
app:
  greeting: Hello from properties file
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb
    username: root
    password: secret

expert.content:
Profiles - Environment-Specific Beans and Configuration

Profiles let the SAME codebase behave differently in dev, test, and prod by activating different beans and property files. A bean annotated @Profile("dev") is registered ONLY when that profile is active.
codeExamples:
# application-dev.yml   (loaded only when profile "dev" is active)
app:
  mode: development

# application-prod.yml  (loaded only when profile "prod" is active)
app:
  mode: production

# Activating a profile - any ONE of:
# 1) application.properties:      spring.profiles.active=dev
# 2) command line:                java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
# 3) environment variable:        SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
# OUTPUT (spring.profiles.active=dev):
# ConsoleNotificationService bean is injected wherever NotificationService is used
// [DEV LOG] Order placed successfully

expert.content:
Spring Boot Actuator - Production Monitoring

Adding spring-boot-starter-actuator exposes ready-made HTTP endpoints for health checks, metrics, and environment inspection - no custom code needed. Essential for production observability (load balancer health checks, Prometheus scraping, etc.).
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

# application.properties - expose the endpoints you need
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics

# GET /actuator/health
# OUTPUT:
# { "status": "UP" }

# GET /actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used
# OUTPUT:
# { "name": "jvm.memory.used", "measurements": [{"statistic":"VALUE","value":5.8E7}] }

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What three annotations does @SpringBootApplication combine?@Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan
How does auto-configuration decide which beans to create?Via @Conditional* checks (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty) evaluated against the classpath, existing beans, and properties
What is a Spring Boot starter?A dependency-only POM with no code that transitively pulls in a version-compatible set of libraries for a feature (e.g. web, JPA)
Difference between WAR deployment and Spring Boot's embedded server model?WAR is deployed into an externally installed container; Spring Boot bundles the server (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow) inside an executable JAR so "java -jar" is enough
How do you override an auto-configured bean?Define your own bean of the same type - most auto-configurations are annotated @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so yours wins
properties vs yml - functionally different?No, both configure the same underlying property keys; YAML just supports hierarchical nesting more concisely
How do you activate a Spring profile?spring.profiles.active property, --spring.profiles.active= CLI arg, or SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE env var
What does Spring Boot Actuator provide?Production-ready HTTP endpoints (health, metrics, info, env, etc.) for monitoring a running application
Can you switch the embedded server from Tomcat to Jetty?Yes - exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from spring-boot-starter-web and add spring-boot-starter-jetty (or undertow)
What debug flag reveals why an auto-configuration did or didn't apply?Run with --debug (or debug=true) to print the Conditions Evaluation Report

beginner.content:
Not a Choice Between Two Things

The question is usually asked as though these were alternatives. They are not. Spring Boot is a layer on top of the Spring Framework - every Spring Boot application is a Spring application, using the same container, the same @Component, the same @Transactional.

   +-----------------------------------------------------+
   |  SPRING BOOT                                        |
   |    auto-configuration   starters   embedded server  |
   |    Actuator             sensible defaults           |
   +-----------------------------------------------------+
   |  SPRING FRAMEWORK                                   |
   |    IoC container   Spring MVC   AOP   transactions  |
   +-----------------------------------------------------+

Boot writes no new container and replaces no Spring feature. It answers a different question: not "how do I wire objects together" but "why must I configure the same twenty things in every project".

The Same Application, Both Ways

The clearest way to see what Boot does is to build one web endpoint twice.

The Four Things Boot Adds

FeatureWhat it replaces
StartersHand-picking compatible dependency versions. spring-boot-starter-web is a pom listing modules and versions known to work together.
Auto-configurationThe configuration classes above. Boot inspects the classpath and configures what it finds - and backs off wherever you define your own bean.
Embedded serverInstalling and managing Tomcat. The server is a library inside the jar, so the artifact runs itself.
Production featuresBespoke health and metrics endpoints. Actuator supplies /health, /metrics, /prometheus and more with one dependency.

Notice what is not in that list: no new dependency injection, no new web framework, no new persistence API. Boot is entirely about the setup around Spring.

WAR to JAR - the Deployment Change

The change with the widest practical effect, and the one that made Boot fit modern deployment.

Traditional SpringSpring Boot
Artifactshop.warshop.jar
NeedsA Tomcat installed on the hostA JVM
Run withCopy to webapps/, start Tomcatjava -jar shop.jar
Server configserver.xml, outside the artifactapplication.properties, inside it
Server versionWhatever the host hasPinned in pom.xml

The consequence: the thing you tested is the thing that runs. There is no host-provided container whose version or configuration can differ between staging and production - which is precisely what containers and orchestration need.
codeExamples:
# The Dockerfile this makes possible - no application server to install.
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
COPY target/shop.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]

# Compare the WAR equivalent: a Tomcat base image, a matching Tomcat
# version, server.xml, context.xml, and a JNDI DataSource defined
# outside the application.

# Boot can still produce a WAR when a platform requires it:
#   <packaging>war</packaging>
#   + extend SpringBootServletInitializer
#   + mark spring-boot-starter-tomcat as <scope>provided</scope>
#
# Needed for legacy application servers - WebSphere, WebLogic, or a
# shared Tomcat estate.

expert.content:
"Opinionated" Means Defaults, Not Restrictions

Boot is described as opinionated, which is sometimes read as inflexible. Every opinion is a default that yields to yours.

Boot's defaultOverridden by
Tomcat as the servlet containerExcluding spring-boot-starter-tomcat and adding -jetty or -undertow
HikariCP as the connection poolDefining your own DataSource bean
Jackson for JSONDefining your own ObjectMapper
Logback for loggingExcluding spring-boot-starter-logging, adding -log4j2
Port 8080server.port

The mechanism is uniform: nearly every auto-configured bean is declared @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and auto-configuration is processed after all your configuration. So defining a bean is all it takes - no @Primary, no exclusion.
codeExamples:
<!-- Swapping the embedded server - the shape of every such change. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- No code changes. Auto-configuration selects the server by what is
     on the classpath - @ConditionalOnClass(Undertow.class) matches
     now, and the Tomcat one no longer does. -->

expert.content:
What Boot Costs

Being able to state the downsides is the difference between using it and being used by it.

CostDetail
Configuration is implicitNothing in your source says a DataSource exists. Understanding the running system means reading auto-configuration classes or the --debug report.
Surprise beansAdding a dependency can register beans and endpoints you did not ask for - a real concern when the endpoint is publicly reachable.
Artifact sizeA fat jar carries its server and every transitive dependency - typically 30-60MB against a few MB of WAR.
Version couplingThe parent pom pins everything. Upgrading one library often means upgrading Boot, and a Boot major upgrade moves Spring, Hibernate and Jackson at once.
Startup timeClasspath scanning plus condition evaluation. Fine for a long-running service; a real cost for short-lived functions.
codeExamples:
# Reducing startup time, in order of effect - measure first.

# 1. See where the time actually goes.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=startup
# then: curl localhost:8080/actuator/startup | jq '.timeline.events
#         | sort_by(-.duration) | .[0:10]'

# 2. Narrow component scanning to the packages you own.
@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "com.shop")

# 3. Exclude auto-configurations you provably do not use.
spring.autoconfigure.exclude=  org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration

# 4. Only for short-lived workloads, and knowing the trade:
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true
#    Faster start, but wiring errors now surface on the first request
#    instead of at startup - usually the wrong trade for a service.

# 5. For genuinely fast cold starts, a GraalVM native image:
#    mvn -Pnative native:compile   -> ~50ms startup, ~40MB binary
#    Costs: long build times, reflection needs registration, and some
#    libraries do not work.

expert.content:
When Plain Spring Is Still Right

Rare, but not never - and knowing the cases is how you avoid arguing the wrong side.

SituationWhy
Deploying into a shared application server estateWebSphere or WebLogic with a governed container version. Boot can build a WAR, but its main advantages go with the embedded server.
Adding Spring to an existing non-Boot applicationRetrofitting Boot to a large legacy WAR is a project in itself; adding spring-context is a dependency.
A library rather than an applicationA library should depend on the Spring modules it needs, not drag a starter and its opinions into every consumer.
Extreme startup or size constraintsEven here, Boot with a native image usually beats hand-configured Spring.

For a new standalone application in 2026, there is effectively no argument for configuring Spring by hand. The reason to understand the manual form is diagnostic: when auto-configuration does something unexpected, knowing what it is doing instead of you is what lets you fix it.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is Spring Boot a replacement for Spring?No - it is a layer on top. Every Boot application is a Spring application using the same container and annotations.
What does Boot add?Starters, auto-configuration, an embedded server, and production features such as Actuator.
What is a starter?A pom with no code that lists a feature's dependencies at versions tested together.
What does "opinionated" mean here?Sensible defaults, not restrictions. Nearly every auto-configured bean is @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so defining your own replaces it.
JAR or WAR?An executable JAR with an embedded server by default, so the tested artifact is the deployed artifact. A WAR is still possible via SpringBootServletInitializer and a provided-scope server.
How do you change the embedded server?Exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat and add Jetty or Undertow. No code changes - selection is by classpath condition.
How do you find out what Boot configured?--debug prints the auto-configuration report; the negative matches explain what was skipped and why.
What are Boot's downsides?Implicit configuration, beans appearing from added dependencies, large artifacts, tight version coupling through the parent pom, and startup cost.
