Name a real risk from a starter.Actuator with exposure.include=* publishes /env and /heapdump. Expose a named list and use a separate management port.
When would you not use Boot?Deploying into a governed application-server estate, retrofitting a large legacy application, or writing a library that should not impose starters on consumers.

beginner.content:
What is Spring Boot?

Spring Boot is a module of the Spring framework that brings RAD - Rapid Application Development - to Spring. It was developed by the Pivotal team in 2014.

The framework itself did not change: Spring Boot is Spring, plus opinionated defaults, plus an embedded server, minus the XML.

Features of Spring Boot - Part 1

FeatureWhat it gives you
1. Spring ApplicationA class whose run() method starts or launches the Spring Boot application. It creates the ApplicationContext object internally.
2. Lazy InitializationOnce enabled, beans are created as they are needed rather than during application startup.
3. Admin FeaturesMonitor one or many Spring Boot application endpoints through the Actuator - beans, health, dumps, logger, info, metrics, mappings and more.
4. SecuritySeveral kinds of authentication for endpoint URLs and REST endpoints, including OAuth and JWT, so unauthorised users cannot reach them. Also supports encrypting and decrypting passwords.
5. LoggingKeeps track of everything the application does. The log file carries exception details with date and time, so you can find where an error occurred.
6. CachingReduces the number of executions by serving results already held in the cache, which makes data access much faster.
7. ValidationAnnotations on the bean class check a field at field level - not null, not empty, minimum and maximum values.
8. JSONRead and write data in JSON, the key-and-value format used by web APIs.
9. TestingTest the application with JUnit; Spring Boot supplies annotations dedicated to this.
10. Task SchedulingSchedule and execute a task on a fixed period, so manual effort is removed and jobs are automated.
11. Email SendingLibraries such as SMTP support let the application send mail, with or without attachments.
12. Multiple Database HandlingSeveral database configurations in one application.properties file - MySQL, Oracle, MongoDB and others together.

Features of Spring Boot - Part 2

FeatureWhat it gives you
13. Profile SupportMultiple profiles for different environments - dev, test, prod.
14. Properties fileSettings live in application.properties, e.g. server.port = 8082.
15. Deploy on CloudDeploy the application to AWS, Heroku and other cloud providers.
16. Avoid XML FileA plain Spring application needs XML configuration to run, which is a difficult process. Spring Boot does not use heavy XML configuration files.
17. Embedded Tomcat ServerNo external server is needed to run the application - Apache Tomcat is built in.
18. Third Party IntegrationSupports payment gateways, Kafka, Docker, Kubernetes, Jenkins and more.
19. Error HandlingSend a custom error message to the client so the failure is easy to understand.
20. Rest TemplateConsume one RESTful web service from inside another.
21. Metrics and Health CheckThrough the Actuator, inspect application health and many other runtime details.
22. Externalized ConfigurationMove configuration outside the code so the same application runs in different environments. Use properties files, YAML files, environment variables or command-line arguments.
23. Starter DependenciesA special dependency for one particular feature. Building a web application? Add spring-boot-starter-web. Need REST endpoints? The same starter covers it.
24. Automatic ConfigurationCreates Spring beans for you and scans the packages and their classes.
25. Rapid Application DevelopmentThe sum of all the above - applications get built fast.

Spring Boot Dependencies and Their Purpose

StarterPurpose
spring-boot-starterThe base starter, used by every Spring-based application.
spring-boot-starter-webUsed to write REST endpoints.
spring-boot-starter-actuatorUsed to monitor and manage the application.
spring-boot-starter-securityUsed for Spring Security.
spring-boot-starter-testUsed for writing test cases.

Spring Boot Annotations

AnnotationPurpose
@SpringBootApplicationMarks the class that holds the main method used to run the Spring Boot application.
@ComponentScanScans all the beans - Spring bean classes and model classes - and the package declarations under the base package.
@EnableAutoConfigurationScans the sub-packages and all the classes available in the Spring Boot application, and configures beans to match.

Note: @SpringBootApplication is equivalent to @Configuration + @ComponentScan + @EnableAutoConfiguration written together.

Spring Boot Architecture

A Spring Boot application is organised into five layers. Each one has a single responsibility, and a request travels down through them and back up.

        +-------------------------------+
        |  1. CLIENT LAYER              |   JSP / HTML / Angular / React
        |     Presentation logic        |
        +-------------------------------+
                    |  HTTP request
                    v
        +-------------------------------+
        |  2. API / CONTROLLER LAYER    |   @RestController
        |     RESTful web services      |
        +-------------------------------+
                    |
                    v
        +-------------------------------+
        |  3. SERVICE LAYER             |   @Service
        |     Business logic            |   interfaces + implementations
        +-------------------------------+
                    |
                    v
        +-------------------------------+
        |  4. DAO / REPOSITORY LAYER    |   @Repository
        |     Persistence logic         |
        +-------------------------------+
                    |
                    v
        +-------------------------------+
        |  5. DATABASE LAYER            |   MySQL / Oracle
        |     insert, update, delete, get|
        +-------------------------------+
LayerResponsibility
1. Client LayerPresentation logic - the UI, built with JSP, HTML or Angular.
2. API LayerThe RESTful web services that receive requests and return responses.
3. Service LayerAll the business logic. Contains interfaces and their implementations.
4. DAO LayerAll the storage logic; translates business objects to and from database rows.
5. Database LayerWhere insert, update, delete and get operations actually run.

expert.content:
Why the Layers Exist - the Rule That Makes Them Worth It

Splitting a project into four packages is not architecture on its own. The value comes from one rule: a layer may call the layer directly below it and nothing else. Break that rule and you get the two most common failures in Spring Boot codebases.

Anti-patternWhy it hurts
Controller calls the repository directlyBusiness rules end up in the controller, where they cannot be reused by a scheduled job or a message listener, and cannot be unit-tested without MockMvc.
JPA entity returned straight from the controllerThe database schema becomes your public API contract. Renaming a column breaks every client, and lazy associations blow up during JSON serialisation.
Service layer imports HttpServletRequestBusiness logic is now tied to HTTP and cannot run from a Kafka consumer or a CLI runner.
@Transactional on the controllerThe transaction spans JSON serialisation and view rendering, holding a database connection far longer than needed.

The fix for the second row is a DTO: a separate class shaped for the API, so the entity never leaves the service layer.

Lazy Initialization Is a Trade, Not a Free Win

Feature 2 in the list is easy to switch on and easy to regret. Turning it on globally makes startup measurably faster - useful for a large application in local development - and moves every configuration error from startup to the first request that touches the broken bean.

SettingEffect
spring.main.lazy-initialization=trueEvery bean becomes lazy. Fast boot, late failures.
@Lazy on one beanOnly that bean waits. This is the version worth using in production - typically for an expensive client that most requests never touch.
@Lazy(false)Forces one bean to stay eager even under global lazy init - the escape hatch for a bean whose configuration you want validated at boot.

The usual advice: enable it in a dev profile, never in the profile you deploy. A misconfigured datasource should break the deployment, not the first customer.
codeExamples:
# application-dev.properties -- fast local restarts
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true

# application-prod.properties -- fail fast, in front of the pipeline
spring.main.lazy-initialization=false

expert.content:
What "Avoid XML File" Really Replaced

Feature 16 undersells itself. Spring Boot did not just delete XML - it replaced three separate things that a classic Spring MVC project had to set up by hand.

Classic Spring MVCSpring Boot equivalent
web.xml registering DispatcherServletAuto-configured by spring-boot-starter-web
applicationContext.xml declaring every bean@ComponentScan from @SpringBootApplication
dispatcher-servlet.xml for view resolvers, converters, static resourcesWebMvcAutoConfiguration, overridable via WebMvcConfigurer
A Tomcat install, and a WAR copied into webapps/Embedded Tomcat inside an executable jar; java -jar app.jar
Matching jar versions by handThe starter BOM pins a tested, compatible set

Auto-configuration is not magic. Each auto-configuration class is guarded by @Conditional* checks - @ConditionalOnClass asks whether a library is on the classpath, @ConditionalOnMissingBean asks whether you already defined one yourself. That second condition is why defining your own bean of a type always wins over the auto-configured one. Run with --debug to print the Conditions Evaluation Report and see exactly which auto-configurations matched and why.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Spring Boot and who created it?A Spring framework module that adds Rapid Application Development to Spring, built by the Pivotal team in 2014.
Spring vs Spring Boot?Spring Boot is not a replacement - it is Spring with opinionated auto-configuration, starter dependencies and an embedded server, so no XML and no external Tomcat.
What are the five layers of the architecture?Client (presentation), API/Controller (REST), Service (business logic), DAO (persistence), Database.
What three annotations does @SpringBootApplication combine?@Configuration, @ComponentScan and @EnableAutoConfiguration.
What is a starter dependency?A dependency-only POM with no code of its own that transitively pulls in a version-compatible set of libraries for one feature.
Which starter for REST endpoints, and which for monitoring?spring-boot-starter-web for endpoints; spring-boot-starter-actuator for monitoring and management.
What does externalized configuration mean?The same code runs in every environment because settings live outside it - properties files, YAML files, environment variables, command-line arguments.
What does lazy initialization change?Beans are created on first use rather than at startup. Boot is faster; configuration errors surface on the first request instead of at deployment.
Why should a controller not return a JPA entity?It makes the database schema the public API contract, leaks fields such as password hashes, and lazy associations fail during JSON serialisation. Return a DTO instead.
How do you override an auto-configured bean?Define your own bean of that type. Most auto-configurations carry @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so yours takes precedence.
How do you find out why an auto-configuration did or did not apply?Run with --debug (or debug=true) and read the Conditions Evaluation Report.
What does RestTemplate give you?The ability to consume one RESTful web service from inside another. In new code, WebClient or the Spring 6 RestClient is preferred.

beginner.content:
Beyond the Big Four

Starters, auto-configuration, the embedded server and Actuator are the headline features, and the previous topics cover them. Boot also ships a second tier that rarely appears on a feature list but shapes daily work more than any of them.

FeatureWhat it is for
DevToolsAutomatic restart on a code change, so you stop stopping and starting the application.
Configuration metadataAutocomplete and validation for your own properties in the IDE.
RunnersCode that runs once, after startup completes.
Graceful shutdownFinish in-flight requests before the process exits.
Test support@SpringBootTest, slice annotations, and auto-configured test utilities.
Image buildingA container image from Maven, with no Dockerfile.

DevTools

One dependency. When a class file changes, Boot restarts the application context in about a second rather than the usual several.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>          <!-- keeps it out of consumers -->
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

// How it is fast: TWO classloaders. Your classes are loaded by a
// throwaway "restart" loader; the jars, which do not change, stay in
// the base loader. A restart discards only the first, so nothing is
// re-read from disk.
//
// It also switches development-hostile defaults off automatically:
//   template caching       off   (edit a template, refresh)
//   static resource cache  off
//   H2 console             on
//   debug logging for web  on

// Safe by design in production - DevTools disables itself when it
// detects it is running from a fully packaged jar, and <optional>true
// stops it leaking to anything that depends on your artifact.

// The trigger is a change to the CLASSPATH, not to the source file.
// In IntelliJ, enable "Build project automatically" or restarts never
// happen; Eclipse compiles on save already.

# Restarting on demand rather than on every save - useful when a
# save mid-edit leaves the code uncompilable.
spring.devtools.restart.trigger-file=.reloadtrigger
# then: touch .reloadtrigger

# Exclude paths that should not cause a restart:
spring.devtools.restart.exclude=static/**,public/**,templates/**

# Turn it off entirely for one run:
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=false

# LiveReload is also included - a browser extension refreshes the page
# when a resource changes:
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=true

beginner.content:
Configuration Metadata

The annotation processor that makes your own properties behave like Spring's in the IDE.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

// With a @ConfigurationProperties class:
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "shop")
public record ShopProperties(
    /** How long to wait for the payment provider. */
    Duration timeout,
    /** Orders processed per batch. Must be at least 1. */
    int batchSize) { }

// The processor writes META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json at
// COMPILE time. The IDE then offers:
//
//   shop.timeout      autocomplete in application.properties
//   shop.batch-size   with the Javadoc as the description
//   shop.btach-size   flagged as an unknown property
//
// That last line is the real value. Without metadata a misspelt
// property binds to nothing and reports nothing - the application
// starts and quietly uses the default. This is the cheapest defence
// against that whole class of bug.
//
// Note the naming: batchSize in Java is batch-size in properties.
// Relaxed binding accepts batchSize, batch_size and BATCH_SIZE too,
// but kebab-case is the documented convention.

beginner.content:
Runners and Graceful Shutdown

The two ends of the application's life.
codeExamples:
# Graceful shutdown - not on by default, and worth turning on.
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s

# On SIGTERM the sequence becomes:
#   1. stop accepting new connections
#   2. let in-flight requests finish, up to the timeout
#   3. run @PreDestroy / close the context
#   4. exit
#
# Without it, step 1 and 2 do not happen: the context closes while
# requests are still running, and a connection pool is torn down under
# active threads.

# In Kubernetes, keep this BELOW terminationGracePeriodSeconds
# (default 30) or the pod is SIGKILLed mid-shutdown:
#
#   spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s
#   terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
#
# And pair it with a readiness probe on
#   /actuator/health/readiness
# so traffic stops arriving before the shutdown begins.

expert.content:
Building Images Without a Dockerfile

Boot builds an OCI image directly from Maven or Gradle using Cloud Native Buildpacks.
codeExamples:
# One command. No Dockerfile.
mvn spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=shop:1.0

# It selects a JDK, applies memory settings from the container limits,
# and produces a layered image.

# What it does that a naive Dockerfile does not: LAYERED JARS.
#
# A fat jar is one big file, so changing one class invalidates the
# whole layer. Boot splits the jar into layers ordered by how often
# they change:
#
#   dependencies            changes rarely      <- cached
#   spring-boot-loader      almost never        <- cached
#   snapshot-dependencies   sometimes
#   application             every build         <- only this is re-pushed
#
# A code-only change then pushes a few hundred KB instead of 50MB.

# The same layering by hand, when you need your own base image
# (a corporate base, or a distroless one):

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/shop.jar shop.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar shop.jar extract

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/application/ ./
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

# The COPY order matters - least-changing first, so Docker's layer
# cache survives a code change.
#
# Note the launcher class moved in Boot 3.2:
#   Boot 3.2+  org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher
#   earlier    org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher

expert.content:
Test Support Is a Feature, Not an Afterthought

spring-boot-starter-test pulls JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Hamcrest, JSONassert and JsonPath, and Boot adds slice annotations on top.

AnnotationLoadsTypical cost
@SpringBootTestThe whole contextSeconds
@WebMvcTestControllers + MVC onlyFast
@DataJpaTestEntities + repositories, with a rolled-back transaction per testFast
@JsonTestJackson configuration onlyVery fast
@RestClientTestA client plus MockRestServiceServerVery fast
NoneNothing - plain JUnitMilliseconds

The last row is the one people forget. A service class with constructor injection needs no Spring at all to test - new OrderService(fake) is a complete unit test, and it runs a thousand times faster than the fastest slice.
Smaller Features Worth Knowing
codeExamples:
# THE FAILURE ANALYZER. Boot translates common startup exceptions
# into an explanation and an action, instead of a stack trace.

***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:
Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in use.

Action:
Identify and stop the process that's listening on port 8080 or
configure this application to listen on another port.

# There are analyzers for port conflicts, missing DataSource URLs,
# bean cycles, duplicate bean names and more. When you see this shape
# of message, the Action line is usually correct - read it before
# reading the stack trace.

# You can add your own for a domain-specific failure:
#   implement AbstractFailureAnalyzer<YourException>
#   register it in META-INF/spring.factories under
#     org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalyzer

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does DevTools do and how is it fast?Restarts the context when classes change, using two classloaders - only the throwaway loader holding your classes is discarded. It also disables template and resource caching.
Is DevTools a production risk?No - it disables itself when running from a packaged jar, and <optional>true</optional> keeps it out of dependent artifacts.
What is the configuration processor for?It generates property metadata at compile time so the IDE autocompletes your own properties and flags misspelt ones - which otherwise bind silently to nothing.
ApplicationRunner vs CommandLineRunner?Both run once after startup; ApplicationRunner receives parsed ApplicationArguments rather than a raw String[].
Why put startup work in a runner rather than @PostConstruct?@PostConstruct runs during bean creation, so a failure prevents the application starting. A runner executes after the server is up.
What does graceful shutdown do?With server.shutdown=graceful, the server stops accepting connections and lets in-flight requests finish before the context closes. Keep the timeout below Kubernetes' grace period.
How do you build a container image?mvn spring-boot:build-image using buildpacks, or extract a layered jar with -Djarmode=layertools in a multi-stage Dockerfile.
Why do layered jars matter?Dependencies and application code become separate image layers, so a code change re-pushes kilobytes instead of the whole fat jar.
What replaced @MockBean?@MockitoBean, from Boot 3.4. Each distinct mock configuration still creates a separate cached test context.
What is @ServiceConnection?Boot 3.1+ - wires a Testcontainers container straight into the matching Spring configuration, replacing manual @DynamicPropertySource plumbing.
What is a failure analyzer?A component that turns a known startup exception into a Description and an Action. You can add your own via AbstractFailureAnalyzer.

beginner.content:
The Standard Way to Start a Project

start.spring.io generates a working, correctly-versioned Spring Boot project as a zip. It is the official starting point, and every Spring Boot tutorial that begins "create a new project" means this.

It exists because the two things that go wrong at the start of a project are both version problems: picking a Boot version that does not match your Java version, and picking library versions that were never tested together. Initializr cannot get either wrong - it only offers combinations that exist.

The same generator is built into IntelliJ IDEA (New Project → Spring Boot), VS Code (Spring Initializr: Create a Project) and Eclipse with STS, so most people never open the website.

The Fields, and What Each One Sets

FieldSetsGuidance
ProjectMaven or GradleMaven unless your team already uses Gradle.
LanguageJava / Kotlin / Groovy—
Spring BootParent pom versionTake the highest plain number. SNAPSHOT, M1 and RC1 are pre-releases.
Group<groupId>Reverse domain - com.dhipan.
Artifact<artifactId>, and the jar nameLowercase with hyphens - order-service.
NameThe main class nameFollows Artifact by default.
Package nameThe root packageGroup + artifact. This decides what gets component-scanned.
PackagingJar or WarJar, unless deploying to an external application server.
JavaSource/target releaseThe highest LTS your Boot version supports - 17 or 21 for Boot 3.
DependenciesStarters in the pomAdd only what you need now; adding one later is one line.

The field that matters most later is Package name. The generated main class goes there, and @SpringBootApplication scans its own package downwards - so that value silently defines the scanned tree for the life of the project.
What You Get

Picking the Versions

The two version choices are linked, and getting them wrong is the most common first-day failure.

Spring BootJava requiredNamespace
2.x8+javax.*
3.0 - 3.117+jakarta.*
3.2+17+, 21 supportedjakarta.*

Two consequences worth knowing before you generate:

Boot 3 requires Java 17. Choosing Boot 3 with Java 8 selected is not offered, and a project generated for Boot 3 will not build on a JDK 11 machine - the error is a cryptic class-file version message, not a helpful one.

Boot 3 renamed the enterprise packages. javax.persistence.Entity is now jakarta.persistence.Entity. This is why a pre-2022 tutorial's imports will not resolve in a project you generate today - the code is right, the package moved.

expert.content:
Initializr Is an API

The website is a front end over a REST service, which means project generation can be scripted - useful for templates, workshops and CI.
codeExamples:
# Generate and unpack in one line.
curl https://start.spring.io/starter.tgz \
  -d type=maven-project \
  -d language=java \
  -d bootVersion=3.2.3 \
  -d groupId=com.dhipan \
  -d artifactId=order-service \
  -d name=OrderService \
  -d packageName=com.dhipan.orderservice \
  -d javaVersion=21 \
  -d dependencies=web,data-jpa,validation,actuator,postgresql \
  | tar -xzvf -

# starter.zip works the same way for a zip.

# Ask what is available rather than guessing an id:
curl https://start.spring.io/metadata/client | jq '.dependencies.values[]
                                                   | .values[]
                                                   | {id, name}'
# OUTPUT:
# { "id": "web",       "name": "Spring Web" }
# { "id": "data-jpa",  "name": "Spring Data JPA" }
# { "id": "lombok",    "name": "Lombok" }
# ...

# The plain-text help, readable in a terminal:
curl https://start.spring.io

# The Spring Boot CLI does the same without curl:
#   sdk install springboot
#   spring init --build=maven --java-version=21 \
#               --dependencies=web,data-jpa \
#               --package-name=com.dhipan.orderservice \
#               order-service
#
# and lists what it can offer:
#   spring init --list

expert.content:
Running Your Own Initializr

Initializr is open source and designed to be self-hosted, which is how organisations standardise new services.

The First Ten Minutes After Generating

Initializr gives a project that runs, not a project that is set up. Five things are worth doing immediately.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Spring Initializr?The official project generator at start.spring.io, also built into IntelliJ, VS Code and STS. It produces a runnable Boot project with compatible versions.
What problem does it solve?Version compatibility - it only offers Boot, Java and starter combinations that are known to work together.
Which field has the longest-lived effect?Package name - the main class goes there and @SpringBootApplication scans that package downwards, so it defines the scan root for the project's life.
Jar or War?Jar with an embedded server by default; War only for deployment to an external application server.
What is mvnw and should it be committed?The Maven Wrapper - it downloads and uses the exact Maven version the project pins. Commit mvnw, mvnw.cmd and .mvn/.
What Java version does Boot 3 need?17 minimum, with 21 supported from 3.2. Boot 3 also moved javax.* to jakarta.*.
What does the generated test do?contextLoads() starts the whole application context - it catches missing beans, wiring errors and bad configuration in one empty method.
Can projects be generated without the website?Yes - curl https://start.spring.io/starter.tgz -d ..., or spring init with the Boot CLI.
Why would a company self-host Initializr?To offer internal starters and conventions by default, so new services begin identically and template changes propagate through a dropdown rather than word of mouth.
Why not add every dependency you might need?Each starter brings auto-configuration. Adding Security "just in case" locks every endpoint behind Basic auth with a generated password.

beginner.content:
Two Jobs the Build Tool Does for Boot

Spring Boot needs its build tool for two things beyond compiling, and both are provided by a plugin you get from Initializr.

JobProvided by
Dependency management - so you never write a version numberThe parent pom (Maven) or the dependency-management plugin (Gradle)
Packaging - turning a normal jar into one that runs with java -jarspring-boot-maven-plugin / the org.springframework.boot Gradle plugin

Neither is optional. Without the first you are back to matching Spring, Hibernate and Jackson versions by hand; without the second, java -jar fails with no main manifest attribute.
The Maven Setup
codeExamples:
<project>
    <!-- 1. The parent supplies versions for ~350 libraries and sets
            sensible compiler and resource defaults. -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.2.3</version>
        <relativePath/>            <!-- look it up in the repository -->
    </parent>

    <groupId>com.dhipan</groupId>
    <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
    </properties>

    <!-- 2. Dependencies with NO version - the parent decides. -->
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <!-- 3. The plugin that makes the jar executable. -->
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

# The commands you will actually use.

./mvnw spring-boot:run             # run without packaging
./mvnw clean package               # build target/order-service-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
./mvnw test                        # tests only
./mvnw clean package -DskipTests   # skip them (CI already ran them)
./mvnw dependency:tree             # what is really on the classpath
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image     # an OCI image, no Dockerfile

# Passing arguments and profiles to a run:
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev
./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments="--server.port=9090"

# Note -DskipTests vs -Dmaven.test.skip=true:
#   -DskipTests             compiles tests, does not run them
#   -Dmaven.test.skip=true  does not even compile them - so a broken
#                           test compiles nowhere and is found later

beginner.content:
The Gradle Setup

The same two jobs, split across two plugins.
codeExamples:
# The command equivalents:

./gradlew bootRun                  # spring-boot:run
./gradlew build                    # clean package (runs tests)
./gradlew bootJar                  # the executable jar only
./gradlew test
./gradlew build -x test            # skip tests
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath
./gradlew bootBuildImage

./gradlew bootRun --args='--spring.profiles.active=dev --server.port=9090'

# Maven vs Gradle, honestly:
#
#   Maven   XML, rigid, predictable. Everyone can read it. The default
#           choice, and what most Spring documentation assumes.
#   Gradle  Groovy/Kotlin DSL, flexible, incremental builds with a
#           daemon - noticeably faster on large multi-module projects.
#
# For a single Spring Boot service the difference is small. Pick what
# your team already uses; do not mix within one organisation.

beginner.content:
Overriding a Managed Version

The parent pins everything, so upgrading one library is not done by adding a <version>.
codeExamples:
<!-- CORRECT - set the property the parent uses. Every artifact in
     that family moves together. -->
<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
    <jackson-bom.version>2.17.0</jackson-bom.version>
    <postgresql.version>42.7.2</postgresql.version>
    <testcontainers.version>1.19.7</testcontainers.version>
</properties>

<!-- WRONG - pinning one artifact by hand. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>2.17.0</version>          <!-- moves ONLY this one -->
</dependency>

<!-- jackson-databind is now 2.17.0 while jackson-core and
     jackson-annotations remain at the managed 2.16.1. Mixed Jackson
     versions produce NoSuchMethodError at runtime, not at build time -
     which is how a CVE fix introduces a worse bug than the CVE.

     Find the right property name in the parent:
       ./mvnw help:effective-pom | grep -i jackson  -->

expert.content:
What repackage Actually Produces

The plugin's main goal runs in the package phase. It takes the ordinary jar Maven just built, renames it .jar.original, and writes a new one with a different internal layout.
codeExamples:
<!-- Why the .jar.original file exists, and when it matters. -->

target/
 |- order-service-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar            executable, ~45MB
 |- order-service-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar.original   the plain jar, ~80KB

<!-- If this module is a LIBRARY that other modules depend on, the
     executable jar is the wrong artifact - a nested-jar layout cannot
     be a dependency. Turn repackaging into a classifier so both are
     published: -->

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <classifier>exec</classifier>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

<!-- Now you get order-service.jar (a normal, dependable jar) and
     order-service-exec.jar (the runnable one).

     The symptom of getting this wrong in a multi-module build:
       package com.dhipan.common does not exist
     when a sibling module depends on a Boot-repackaged jar. -->

expert.content:
Multi-Module Projects

The rule is simple once stated: only the deployable module is repackaged.
codeExamples:
order-platform/
 |- pom.xml                    <parent>, <modules>, dependencyManagement
 |- common/pom.xml             library  - plugin NOT applied
 |- domain/pom.xml             library  - plugin NOT applied
 |- api/pom.xml                the app  - plugin applied

<!-- order-platform/pom.xml -->
<packaging>pom</packaging>
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.3</version>
</parent>
<modules>
    <module>common</module>
    <module>domain</module>
    <module>api</module>
</modules>

<!-- common/pom.xml - a plain library. No build plugin section at all. -->
<parent>
    <groupId>com.dhipan</groupId>
    <artifactId>order-platform</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
</parent>
<artifactId>common</artifactId>

<!-- api/pom.xml - the only module that produces a runnable artifact. -->
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

<!-- Because the parent pom inherits from spring-boot-starter-parent,
     every module gets version management without applying the
     packaging plugin. That separation is the whole trick. -->

expert.content:
Build Reproducibility and CI

Three settings that prevent the "works on my machine" class of build failure.
codeExamples:
# 1. THE WRAPPER pins the build tool version. Always invoke it.
./mvnw clean verify          # not: mvn clean verify

# In CI, the same:
- run: ./mvnw --batch-mode --no-transfer-progress clean verify
#   --batch-mode           no interactive prompts, cleaner logs
#   --no-transfer-progress hides the download spam

# 2. THE TOOLCHAIN pins the JDK, so the build does not silently use
#    whatever the agent has installed.
<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
</properties>
# Gradle's toolchain block goes further and DOWNLOADS the JDK:
#   java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }

# 3. NO SNAPSHOT DEPENDENCIES in a released build. A SNAPSHOT is
#    re-resolved and can change between two builds of the same commit,
#    which makes the build non-reproducible.
#    Enforce it rather than trusting review:
<plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-enforcer-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions><execution>
        <goals><goal>enforce</goal></goals>
        <configuration><rules>
            <requireReleaseDeps/>
            <requireMavenVersion><version>[3.9,)</version></requireMavenVersion>
        </rules></configuration>
    </execution></executions>
</plugin>

# Which phase runs what - the distinction that matters in CI.
#
#   ./mvnw test       unit tests        (*Test.java)      surefire
#   ./mvnw verify     unit + INTEGRATION (*IT.java)       + failsafe
#   ./mvnw package    builds the jar; runs test, not verify
#
# 'mvn verify' is the correct CI command. 'mvn package' silently skips
# integration tests, so a pipeline using it reports green while never
# running them.

# Failsafe is not configured by the Boot parent - add it if you use
# the *IT.java convention:
<plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions><execution>
        <goals><goal>integration-test</goal><goal>verify</goal></goals>
    </execution></executions>
</plugin>

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does spring-boot-starter-parent provide?Managed versions for hundreds of libraries, plus compiler, resource-filtering and plugin defaults - so dependencies need no <version>.
What if you cannot use the parent?Import spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM in dependencyManagement with <scope>import</scope>.
What does spring-boot-maven-plugin do?Its repackage goal rewrites the jar into the Boot layout with a launcher, and it provides the run and build-image goals.
Describe the executable jar layout.BOOT-INF/classes for your code, BOOT-INF/lib for dependencies as nested jars, the loader classes at the root, and a manifest whose Main-Class is JarLauncher with your class as Start-Class.
Why is a custom classloader needed?Standard Java cannot load a jar nested inside a jar, so Boot's launcher builds a classloader over BOOT-INF/lib before invoking your main class.
How do you upgrade one managed library?Override the parent's version property - not by adding a <version> to one artifact, which splits a library family and causes NoSuchMethodError at runtime.
Which module gets the plugin in a multi-module build?Only the deployable one. Library modules must stay plain jars, or use <classifier> so both artifacts are produced.
Why are library-module beans not found?Component scanning follows packages, not jars. Share a root package, or have the library ship an auto-configuration.
-DskipTests vs -Dmaven.test.skip=true?The first compiles tests but does not run them; the second does not compile them, so breakage is hidden until later.
mvn package or mvn verify in CI?verify - package runs unit tests only and silently skips Failsafe integration tests.

beginner.content:
A Starter Contains No Code

This surprises people the first time they look inside one. spring-boot-starter-web has no classes at all - it is a pom.xml listing other dependencies.

That is the entire mechanism. A starter is a curated list: one name standing in for the set of libraries a feature needs, at versions that have been tested together.
codeExamples:
<!-- The actual contents of spring-boot-starter-web, trimmed. -->
<project>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>          <!-- pom, not jar - no code -->

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-json</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>

<!-- Starters compose: this one pulls three other starters, each of
     which pulls more. One line in your pom becomes ~35 jars. -->

# Seeing what a starter actually brought in:
./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.springframework*

# OUTPUT (trimmed):
# +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web:jar:3.2.3
# |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter:jar:3.2.3
# |  |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot:jar:3.2.3
# |  |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-autoconfigure:jar:3.2.3
# |  |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-logging:jar:3.2.3
# |  |  - org.springframework:spring-core:jar:6.1.4
# |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-json:jar:3.2.3
# |  |  - com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:jar:2.15.4
# |  +- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-tomcat:jar:3.2.3
# |  - org.springframework:spring-webmvc:jar:6.1.4

# This is the command to reach for whenever you wonder "where did this
# jar come from" or "why is there a second logging binding".

beginner.content:
Starters and Auto-Configuration Are a Pair

A starter puts jars on the classpath. Auto-configuration reacts to what it finds there. Neither does much alone - together they are why adding one line makes a feature work.

   add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
             |
             v
   Hibernate, spring-orm, HikariCP land on the classpath
             |
             v
   at startup, auto-configuration asks:
       @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)          -> matches
       @ConditionalOnClass(EntityManagerFactory.class) -> matches
       @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)     -> matches
             |
             v
   registers DataSource, EntityManagerFactory,
   JpaTransactionManager, and enables repositories

This explains the behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary: removing a starter can silently remove beans and endpoints, because the conditions stop matching. It also explains why an unused starter is not harmless - it configures things.

The Ones You Will Use

StarterBrings
spring-boot-starterThe core - context, auto-configuration, logging, YAML. Every other starter includes it.
spring-boot-starter-webSpring MVC, Jackson, embedded Tomcat, validation API.
spring-boot-starter-webfluxThe reactive alternative to -web, with Netty. Not an addition.
spring-boot-starter-data-jpaSpring Data JPA, Hibernate, HikariCP, transactions.
spring-boot-starter-data-jdbcSpring Data JDBC - lighter, no ORM.
spring-boot-starter-validationHibernate Validator. Not included in -web since Boot 2.3.
spring-boot-starter-securitySpring Security. Locks every endpoint the moment it is added.
spring-boot-starter-testJUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, JSONassert, JsonPath, Spring Test.
spring-boot-starter-actuatorHealth, metrics and management endpoints.
spring-boot-starter-data-redisLettuce and Redis templates.
spring-boot-starter-mailJavaMail and JavaMailSender.
spring-boot-starter-thymeleafServer-side templating.
spring-boot-starter-aopSpring AOP and AspectJ weaving support.

The validation row catches people regularly. Before Boot 2.3, -web included Hibernate Validator; it was removed to slim the default web application. @Valid then compiles - the annotation is in -web - but silently does nothing, because no validator implementation exists to run it.

The Naming Rule

There is a convention, and it tells you at a glance who maintains a starter.

PatternOwnerExample
spring-boot-starter-*The Spring Boot team - reservedspring-boot-starter-web
*-spring-boot-starterEveryone elsemybatis-spring-boot-starter

The prefix is reserved deliberately. If you write a starter for your organisation, it is dhipan-security-spring-boot-starter, not spring-boot-starter-dhipan-security - the suffix form makes it immediately clear the artifact is not from the Spring team.

expert.content:
Writing a Starter: the Two-Module Split

The convention is two artifacts, and the reason is worth understanding rather than copying.

ModuleContains
xyz-spring-boot-autoconfigureThe auto-configuration classes, properties and conditions. The code.
xyz-spring-boot-starterA pom with no code, depending on the autoconfigure module plus the libraries it needs.

The split lets a consumer take the auto-configuration without the opinionated dependency set - useful when they already manage those libraries themselves, or need a different version. For an internal starter used by one organisation, a single module is a reasonable simplification.
codeExamples:
# Registration - and this is the file people get wrong.

# Boot 3.x:
# src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/
#     org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
com.dhipan.audit.AuditAutoConfiguration

# Boot 2.7 and earlier:
# src/main/resources/META-INF/spring.factories
org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=  com.dhipan.audit.AuditAutoConfiguration

# A starter supporting both ships both files - they are ignored
# harmlessly by the version that does not use them.
#
# Symptom of a missing/misplaced file: the jar is on the classpath, the
# class is right, and NOTHING happens. No error, no bean. Check the
# path character by character - a typo in that filename is silent.

# Verify it is being picked up:
#   java -jar app.jar --debug | grep AuditAutoConfiguration

expert.content:
Testing a Starter Without Starting an Application

ApplicationContextRunner builds a throwaway context in milliseconds, which is how conditions get tested properly.

Starter Hygiene

Four rules that separate a starter people are glad to depend on from one they work around.

RuleWhy
Every bean @ConditionalOnMissingBeanAn application that wants its own must not have to exclude your auto-configuration to get it.
Ship configuration metadataAdd spring-boot-configuration-processor so consumers get autocomplete and typo detection on your properties.
Depend narrowlyDepend on the specific Spring modules you use, not spring-boot-starter-web. Dragging a web server into a consumer that has none is a real and common mistake.
Never inherit spring-boot-starter-parentImport spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM instead - a library must not force its parent onto consumers.
codeExamples:
<!-- A library's pom: BOM import, not parent inheritance. -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.3</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <!-- narrow: exactly what the code uses -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-jdbc</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-autoconfigure</artifactId>
    </dependency>

    <!-- optional: available if the consumer already has it, not forced -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-webmvc</artifactId>
        <optional>true</optional>
    </dependency>

    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
        <optional>true</optional>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- <optional>true</optional> paired with @ConditionalOnClass is the
     standard pattern: the feature activates if the consumer happens to
     have the library, and stays silent otherwise. -->

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a starter?A dependency descriptor - a pom with no code - listing the libraries a feature needs at versions tested together.
Does a starter contain classes?No. Its packaging is pom. The behaviour comes from auto-configuration in the jars it pulls.
How do starters and auto-configuration relate?The starter puts classes on the classpath; auto-configuration's @ConditionalOnClass conditions then match and register beans.
What is in spring-boot-starter?Core context, auto-configuration, logging and YAML support - included by every other starter.
Why does @Valid sometimes do nothing?spring-boot-starter-validation was removed from -web in Boot 2.3. The annotation compiles but no validator implementation is present.
What is the naming convention?spring-boot-starter-* is reserved for the Spring team; third parties use *-spring-boot-starter.
Why is a custom starter split into two modules?So consumers can take the auto-configuration without the opinionated dependency list, when they manage those libraries themselves.
How is auto-configuration registered?META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports on Boot 3; META-INF/spring.factories on 2.7 and earlier.
How do you test a starter?ApplicationContextRunner - with withPropertyValues, withUserConfiguration and FilteredClassLoader to exercise each condition in milliseconds.
Why should a starter never inherit the Boot parent?A library must not impose a parent pom on consumers. Import spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM instead.

beginner.content:
The One Every Other Starter Contains

spring-boot-starter is the core. You rarely declare it yourself, because every other starter depends on it - adding spring-boot-starter-web brings it along.

It contains six things, and knowing what each is for explains a lot of behaviour that otherwise looks like magic.

DependencyProvides
spring-bootSpringApplication, the runners, the embedded-server abstraction, @ConfigurationProperties binding.
spring-boot-autoconfigureEvery @AutoConfiguration class Boot ships - around 150 of them.
spring-boot-starter-loggingSLF4J, Logback, and the bridges from other logging APIs.
spring-coreThe container foundation, pulled transitively with spring-context.
jakarta.annotation-api@PostConstruct, @PreDestroy, @Resource.
snakeyamlYAML parsing, so application.yml works.

Note what is not here: no web server, no JSON library, no database support. This starter gives you a Spring application that starts, configures itself and logs - nothing more.
codeExamples:
<!-- Declaring it directly is right for a non-web application:
     a batch job, a CLI tool, a message consumer. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>

// A complete application with just this:
@SpringBootApplication
public class ImportJob implements ApplicationRunner {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ImportJob.class);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ImportJob.class, args);
    }

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        log.info("Importing {}", args.getOptionValues("file"));
    }
}

// OUTPUT:
//   ... : Starting ImportJob using Java 21
//   ... : No active profile set, falling back to 1 default profile
//   ... : Started ImportJob in 0.84 seconds
//   ... : Importing [orders.csv]
//
// Note "Started ... in 0.84 seconds" and then EXIT. With no web server
// on the classpath there is no non-daemon thread keeping the JVM
// alive, so the process ends when the runners finish. That is correct
// behaviour for a job, and a surprise if you expected a server.

beginner.content:
The Logging Bridges

The most useful thing in this starter, and the least understood. spring-boot-starter-logging contains five artifacts, and three of them exist purely to redirect other logging frameworks.

   Your code            log.info(...)         SLF4J API
   An old library       Log4j 1.x calls   --\
   Another library      java.util.logging --+--> BRIDGES
   Apache Commons       JCL calls         --/       |
                                                    v
                                              SLF4J API
                                                    |
                                                    v
                                              Logback  ->  console / file

   log4j-to-slf4j       reroutes Log4j 2 API calls
   jul-to-slf4j         reroutes java.util.logging
   jcl-over-slf4j       reroutes Commons Logging
        (via spring-jcl, which Spring uses internally)

Without these, a dependency logging through Log4j would write to its own destination with its own format, ignoring your configuration entirely. The bridges mean one configuration controls every log line in the process, whatever API produced it.
codeExamples:
# Because everything funnels into Logback, one file configures all of
# it - and application.properties is enough for most needs:

logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.dhipan=DEBUG
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG

logging.file.name=logs/order-service.log
logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-file-size=10MB
logging.logback.rollingpolicy.max-history=30

logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss} %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n

# That third line works even though Hibernate does not use SLF4J
# directly - the bridge puts it under the same control.

beginner.content:
Switching to Log4j2

The one common reason to touch this starter. The exclusion must be complete or you get two competing implementations.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-log4j2</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- The exclusion must go on EVERY starter that pulls
     spring-boot-starter-logging, which is all of them. Missing one
     leaves Logback on the classpath and produces:

  SLF4J: Class path contains multiple SLF4J bindings.
  SLF4J: Found binding in [.../logback-classic-1.4.14.jar!/org/slf4j/...]
  SLF4J: Found binding in [.../log4j-slf4j2-impl-2.21.1.jar!/org/slf4j/...]
  SLF4J: Actual binding is of type [ch.qos.logback.classic.util...]

     One is picked non-deterministically, so log configuration may work
     on one machine and not another.

     The global alternative, cleaner in a multi-module build: -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.3</version>
            <scope>provided</scope>          <!-- never packaged -->
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- Verify afterwards, do not assume:
       ./mvnw dependency:tree | grep -i logback     -> should be empty -->

expert.content:
Why spring-jcl Exists

A piece of history that explains an artifact you will see in every dependency tree and may be tempted to exclude.

Spring's own internals log through Jakarta Commons Logging - a decision made in 2003, long before SLF4J existed. JCL had a genuine problem: its runtime discovery mechanism broke in containers with complex classloader hierarchies, producing the well-known "commons-logging classloader hell".

Rather than rewrite every logging call across the framework, Spring 5 shipped spring-jcl: a drop-in replacement exposing the JCL API but delegating to SLF4J, Log4j2 or java.util.logging - whichever it finds - with no runtime discovery.

ConsequenceDetail
commons-logging must not be on the classpathBoth provide org.apache.commons.logging.Log. Two copies of one class is undefined behaviour. Boot's starters exclude it, but a third-party library can drag it back in.
Do not exclude spring-jclIt is how Spring itself logs. Removing it silences the framework's own output, including startup diagnostics.
codeExamples:
# Finding a rogue commons-logging - worth checking when framework
# log lines vanish or appear in the wrong format.
./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=commons-logging:commons-logging

# OUTPUT:
# [INFO] com.dhipan:order-service:jar:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
# [INFO] - com.example:legacy-soap-client:jar:2.1.0:compile
# [INFO]    - commons-logging:commons-logging:jar:1.2:compile   <-- here

# Exclude it at the source:
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>legacy-soap-client</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>commons-logging</groupId>
            <artifactId>commons-logging</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

# The symptom this fixes: Spring's own INFO lines stop appearing, or
# appear with a different format than your application's, because two
# implementations of the same API are on the classpath and the one
# picked depends on jar order.

expert.content:
SnakeYAML, and Why the Version Matters

snakeyaml is here so application.yml parses. It has a security history worth knowing, because it is one of the more common CVE flags on a Spring Boot dependency scan.

The issue is that YAML supports type tags - !!com.example.SomeClass - which instruct the parser to instantiate a class. A parser reading untrusted YAML with unrestricted type resolution can therefore be driven to construct arbitrary objects, which has produced remote code execution (CVE-2022-1471 being the widely-cited one).

SituationRisk
Boot parsing your own application.ymlNone in practice - Boot uses a restricted constructor, and the file is part of your artifact, not user input.
Your code calling new Yaml().load(userInput)Serious. This is the vulnerable pattern.

So the practical advice is not "remove snakeyaml" - it is: keep Boot current so the managed version is patched, and never hand user-supplied YAML to a default Yaml instance.

What You Get Without a Web Server

Declaring only spring-boot-starter produces a specific and useful application shape.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is in spring-boot-starter?spring-boot, spring-boot-autoconfigure, spring-boot-starter-logging, spring-core, jakarta.annotation-api and snakeyaml.
Do you usually declare it?No - every other starter includes it. Declare it directly only for a non-web application such as a batch job or CLI tool.
What does the logging starter contain?SLF4J and Logback plus bridges - log4j-to-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j - so libraries using other logging APIs are routed through one configuration.
Why do the bridges matter?Without them a dependency's log output ignores your configuration and format entirely.
How do you switch to Log4j2?Exclude spring-boot-starter-logging from every starter that pulls it and add spring-boot-starter-log4j2. Missing one exclusion gives multiple SLF4J bindings and non-deterministic behaviour.
What is spring-jcl?Spring's drop-in replacement for Commons Logging that delegates to SLF4J without JCL's runtime discovery. Do not exclude it; do ensure real commons-logging is absent.
Why is SnakeYAML flagged by scanners?YAML type tags can instantiate arbitrary classes, so parsing untrusted YAML with a default Yaml is an RCE risk. Boot's own use is restricted and safe; keep the version current and use SafeConstructor for user input.
What happens if you exclude SnakeYAML?application.yml is ignored silently - no error, just unapplied configuration.
Why does a non-web Boot application exit immediately?Nothing holds a non-daemon thread once the runners finish. Set the application type explicitly and block if it must stay alive.
Does @Transactional work without a web starter?Yes - AOP and transaction support live in the core, below the web layer.

Spring Boot uses annotations everywhere - they are just special markers placed above a class, method, or field that tell Spring "treat this piece of code in a special way".

You don't write the plumbing yourself (no XML config, no manual object wiring) - the annotation tells Spring Boot what to do, and Spring Boot does the rest at startup.

In this topic we will look at the most common annotations you will see in almost every Spring Boot project, one at a time, with a tiny example each.

1. @SpringBootApplication

This goes on top of your main class - the class that has the main() method.
It simply tells Spring Boot "this is the starting point of my application, start scanning and configuring everything from here."

At the beginner level, just remember: every Spring Boot app has exactly one class with this annotation, and it is the class you run to start the app. We will look at what it actually does internally later (Expert Level).

2. @RestController and @Controller

These annotations mark a class as one that handles incoming web requests (like when someone opens a URL in the browser or calls your API).

• @Controller - used for classes that return a webpage (a view, like an HTML page).
• @RestController - used for classes that return data directly (usually JSON) instead of a webpage. This is the one you will use for almost every REST API you build.

3. @RequestMapping / @GetMapping / @PostMapping

These annotations connect a URL to a Java method - this is called "mapping" a request.

• @RequestMapping("/path") - the general-purpose one, can handle any HTTP method.
• @GetMapping("/path") - shortcut for handling GET requests (reading/fetching data).
• @PostMapping("/path") - shortcut for handling POST requests (creating new data).

4. @Autowired

This annotation tells Spring "please give me an object of this type - I don't want to create it myself with new." Spring finds (or creates) the right object and injects it for you. This is called Dependency Injection.

Below, StudentService is automatically injected into StudentController - we never wrote new StudentService() anywhere.

5. @Component / @Service / @Repository

These three annotations all do the same basic thing - they tell Spring "create an object (a bean) of this class and manage it for me, so it can later be @Autowired anywhere."

They only differ in the message they give to other developers reading the code:
• @Component - a generic, general-purpose Spring-managed class.
• @Service - a class that holds business logic.
• @Repository - a class that talks to the database.

expert.content:
Annotation Categories - The Big Picture

Spring Boot has dozens of annotations, but almost all of them fall into one of five categories. Knowing the category tells you what the annotation is really for:

Category Annotations Purpose
Stereotype @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller Marks a class to be auto-detected and registered as a bean in the Spring container
Configuration @Configuration, @Bean Manually declares beans, usually for third-party classes you cannot annotate directly
Web @RequestMapping family, @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, @ResponseBody Maps HTTP requests to methods and extracts/returns data
Data @Entity, @Id, @Column, @Transactional Maps Java objects to database tables/rows and manages DB transactions
Validation @Valid, @NotNull, @Size Validates incoming data before it reaches your business logic 

@SpringBootApplication
    +-- @SpringBootConfiguration  (a specialised @Configuration)
    +-- @EnableAutoConfiguration  (auto-configures beans based on classpath jars)
    +-- @ComponentScan           (scans the package + sub-packages for @Component,
                                   @Service, @Repository, @Controller/@RestController
                                   and registers them as beans)
This is why @SpringBootApplication is really "3 annotations glued into 1" - it starts component scanning, enables auto-configuration, and marks the class itself as a configuration source.

@Component vs @Service vs @Repository - Functionally Similar, Semantically Different

All three are meta-annotated with @Component, so Spring's component scan treats them identically for bean-registration purposes - any of them would technically work anywhere.

The real, functional difference is only with @Repository: it additionally enables persistence exception translation - Spring wraps low-level, database-specific exceptions (like SQLException, driver-specific errors) into Spring's own consistent unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy, so your service/controller code does not need to know which database driver is underneath.

@RequestBody vs @ResponseBody, and @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody

• @RequestBody - takes the incoming HTTP request's JSON/XML body and converts ("deserializes") it into a Java object as a method parameter.
• @ResponseBody - takes the Java object a method returns and converts ("serializes") it into JSON/XML to send back as the HTTP response body, instead of resolving it as a view name.

@RestController is simply @Controller + @ResponseBody applied automatically to every method in the class - that is exactly why you never need to write @ResponseBody yourself when using @RestController.

@Transactional - Propagation and Rollback Basics

@Transactional wraps a method in a database transaction - either everything inside it commits together, or everything rolls back together if something fails.

Two things matter most for interviews:
• Rollback rule: by default, Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses), NOT on checked exceptions - unless you tell it to with rollbackFor.
• Propagation: controls how a transactional method behaves when it is called from another transactional method - the default, REQUIRED, means "join the existing transaction if one is already running, otherwise start a new one."

Writing a Custom Annotation

You are not limited to Spring's built-in annotations - you can define your own using @interface, then control its behaviour with two meta-annotations:
• @Target - where the annotation is allowed to be placed (method, field, type, etc).
• @Retention - how long the annotation is kept: SOURCE (discarded by compiler), CLASS (kept in .class file, not visible at runtime), or RUNTIME (kept and readable via reflection at runtime - required if a framework like Spring AOP needs to detect it while the app is running).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @SpringBootApplication actually combine?@SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan
Is @RestController a completely different annotation from @Controller?No - @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody applied to every method
Functionally, what is the real difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository?They register beans the same way; only @Repository additionally enables persistence exception translation into DataAccessException
Why use @Configuration + @Bean instead of @Component?To register beans for classes you don't own/can't annotate (e.g. third-party library classes)
Does @Transactional roll back on checked exceptions by default?No - only on unchecked (RuntimeException) exceptions unless rollbackFor is specified
What does propagation = REQUIRES_NEW do?Suspends any existing transaction and starts a brand-new independent one
Difference between @RequestParam and @PathVariable?@RequestParam reads a query string parameter (?name=x); @PathVariable reads a value embedded in the URL path (/students/{id})
Why must a custom annotation have @Retention(RUNTIME) to be used by Spring AOP?Spring reads annotations via reflection at runtime; CLASS/SOURCE retention discards the annotation before the app runs, so it would be invisible to reflection
What does @Autowired actually do under the hood?Spring's IoC container looks up (or creates) a matching bean by type from the ApplicationContext and injects the reference - no "new" is written by the developer
Can @Valid be used without any constraint annotations like @NotNull?It has no effect alone - @Valid only triggers validation of whatever constraint annotations (@NotNull, @Size, etc.) are present on the target object's fields

How Spring Boot Works Internally

One line starts a Spring Boot application:

SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);

Behind that line is a fixed sequence of eight steps. Knowing the order is what lets you place your own code correctly - and what makes startup log messages readable.

1.  Main method
        |
        v
2.  SpringApplication.run()
        |
        v
3.  Stop watch started
        |
        v
4.  Prepare environment      (profiles + property sources)
        |
        v
5.  Print banner
        |
        v
6.  Create Spring IoC container   (ApplicationContext)
        |
        v
7.  Refresh context          (beans created and wired, server started)
        |
        v
8.  Trigger runners          (your code, after startup)
        |
        v
    APPLICATION READY

The Eight Steps in Detail

StepWhat happens
1. Main methodThe starting point of Spring Boot application execution.
2. run() methodContains the run() implementation, which calls a further run() internally.
3. Stop watchCaptures the total time required to run the application or complete the task - this is the number you see in "Started DemoApplication in 1.923 seconds".
4. Prepare EnvironmentThe configuration interface implemented by all Environment types. Provides facilities for setting active and default profiles and for manipulating the underlying property sources - java home, user home, JVM version and so on. Test, Dev and Production environments are prepared here from application.properties.
5. Print BannerSpring Boot shows text as a banner when the application starts up. The banner can be customised.
6. Spring IoC Containerrun() creates the ApplicationContext object.
7. Refresh ContextrefreshContext(context) inside run() triggers a refresh of the application context: it is initialised and configured with all the beans and components the application needs.
8. Trigger RunnerUsed to execute code after the Spring Boot application has started.

Step 5 - Customising the Banner

Drop a banner.txt into src/main/resources and Spring Boot prints it instead of the default. It is the simplest visible proof that the startup sequence is doing exactly what the list says.
codeExamples:
# To switch the banner off entirely:
spring.main.banner-mode=off

# Or send it to the log file instead of the console:
spring.main.banner-mode=log

beginner.content:
Step 8 - Trigger Runner

The runner is where you put code that must run once, after the context is fully built and the server is listening. Spring Boot offers two interfaces for it.

InterfaceDifference
CommandLineRunnerrun(String... args) - receives the raw command-line arguments as an array.
ApplicationRunnerrun(ApplicationArguments args) - receives them already parsed into option and non-option arguments.

Both run after the context refresh, so every bean is available. Use @Order if several runners must go in a fixed sequence.

expert.content:
What refreshContext() Actually Does

Step 7 is one line in the summary and the bulk of the work in reality. AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() is a fixed twelve-step template method, and every Spring Boot startup error you will ever read comes from one of these steps.

refresh()
  1  prepareRefresh()                  mark active, validate required properties
  2  obtainFreshBeanFactory()          load bean DEFINITIONS (nothing built yet)
  3  prepareBeanFactory()              register built-in beans, expression resolver
  4  postProcessBeanFactory()          subclass hook -- creates the web server factory
  5  invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors() @ComponentScan + auto-configuration run HERE
  6  registerBeanPostProcessors()      register @Autowired / @Transactional processors
  7  initMessageSource()               i18n
  8  initApplicationEventMulticaster() event publishing
  9  onRefresh()                       CREATE AND START THE EMBEDDED TOMCAT
 10  registerListeners()               @EventListener beans
 11  finishBeanFactoryInitialization() INSTANTIATE ALL NON-LAZY SINGLETONS
 12  finishRefresh()                   publish ContextRefreshedEvent

Three of those repay close reading:

StepWhy it matters
5 - BeanFactoryPostProcessorsComponent scanning and every auto-configuration class execute here, adding bean definitions. Nothing is instantiated yet, which is why a bean can be defined conditionally on another bean's existence.
9 - onRefresh()Tomcat is created and started before your singletons exist. It does not accept traffic yet - the connector is bound at step 12 - but the ordering explains "Tomcat initialized" appearing early in the log.
11 - finishBeanFactoryInitialization()Every non-lazy singleton is constructed and wired here. A missing dependency, an ambiguous @Autowired or a failing @PostConstruct throws at this step - which is why those stack traces all mention finishBeanFactoryInitialization.

Step 4 - Where a Property Value Actually Comes From

"Prepare environment" builds an ordered list of property sources. When something asks for server.port, the Environment walks that list and the first source holding the key wins. This ordering is the answer to "why is my application.properties being ignored?".

PriorityProperty source
1 (highest)Devtools global settings in ~/.config/spring-boot
2@TestPropertySource and test properties
3Command-line arguments - --server.port=9090
4SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON
5ServletConfig / ServletContext init parameters
6JNDI attributes
7Java System properties - -Dserver.port=9090
8OS environment variables - SERVER_PORT=9090
9Profile-specific files outside the jar - application-prod.properties
10Profile-specific files inside the jar
11application.properties outside the jar
12application.properties inside the jar
13 (lowest)@PropertySource on a @Configuration class

The practical shape of it: command line beats environment variable beats packaged file, and a profile-specific file always beats the plain one. That is what makes the same jar deployable to dev, test and prod unchanged.

Hooking Into Startup - Which Callback, and When

Runners are step 8, and they are not the only hook. Choosing the wrong one is a common source of "my initialisation code ran too early".

HookFires when
ConstructorDuring bean creation. Setter- and field-injected dependencies are still null.
@PostConstructAfter that bean's own dependencies are injected. Other beans may still be unbuilt.
InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()Same point as @PostConstruct, just after it. Ties the class to a Spring interface, so prefer the annotation.
ApplicationListener<ContextRefreshedEvent>Step 12 - every singleton exists. Careful: fires again for a child context, e.g. in some test setups.
CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunnerStep 8 of the outer sequence - after the context is refreshed AND the server is up. The right place for one-off startup work.
ApplicationListener<ApplicationReadyEvent>After the runners. The last hook before the application is declared ready.

An exception thrown from a runner stops the application - the context closes and the process exits non-zero. That is usually the behaviour you want for a failed startup migration, and a surprise if you were only warming a cache.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the main steps of the Spring Boot startup sequence?main method, SpringApplication.run(), start the stop watch, prepare the environment, print the banner, create the IoC container, refresh the context, trigger the runners.
What is the stop watch for?It measures total startup time - the number reported in "Started DemoApplication in 1.923 seconds".
What does "prepare environment" do?Sets the active and default profiles and assembles the ordered list of property sources the application will read configuration from.
What does refreshContext() do?Runs ApplicationContext.refresh(): loads bean definitions, runs component scanning and auto-configuration, starts the embedded server, and instantiates every non-lazy singleton.
At which refresh step does auto-configuration run?invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors - step 5. It registers bean definitions; nothing is instantiated until step 11.
When is the embedded Tomcat created?In onRefresh(), before the application's own singletons are built. It begins accepting requests only at finishRefresh().
What object does SpringApplication.run() return?The ConfigurableApplicationContext - the fully built IoC container.
CommandLineRunner vs ApplicationRunner?Same timing; CommandLineRunner receives raw String... arguments, ApplicationRunner receives them parsed as ApplicationArguments.
What happens if a runner throws an exception?Startup fails - the context closes and the JVM exits with a non-zero status.
Which wins: application.properties or a command-line argument?The command-line argument. Command line beats system properties, which beat environment variables, which beat the packaged properties file.
How do you customise or disable the banner?Add banner.txt to src/main/resources, or set spring.main.banner-mode to off or log.
Why does initialisation code belong in @PostConstruct, not the constructor?Setter- and field-injected dependencies are not yet set when the constructor runs; @PostConstruct fires after injection is complete.

Spring Boot Profiles

Using Spring Boot we can set different profiles for the dev, test and prod environments.

Why do we use them?

In a company you work across several environments, and each has its own configuration - driver name, URL, username, password. Editing one application.properties file every time you move between them is not workable.

The answer is to create one properties file per environment and let Spring pick the right one at startup.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot Maven project
2. Add the Maven dependency to pom.xml
3. Write the database connection code in the main properties file
4. Create an application.properties file for each environment
5. Go to the main application.properties and set the active profile
6. Run the Spring Boot application
7. Check the console for the environment
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
    <version>8.0.33</version>
</dependency>

# Step 3 - application.properties  (the COMMON file)
server.port=8081

spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/27augustjavabatch?autoReconnect=true&useSSL=false
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.MySQL8Dialect

beginner.content:
Step 4 - One File Per Environment

The naming pattern is fixed: application-{profile}.properties. The part between the hyphen and .properties is the profile name.

FileProfilePort
application-dev.propertiesdev8082
application-test.propertiestest8083
application-prod.propertiesprod8084

All three live in src/main/resources alongside the common file.
