beginner.content:
Steps 5 to 7 - Activate a Profile and Run

One line in the main application.properties selects which environment file is loaded on top of it.

The key is lowercase: spring.profiles.active, not Spring.profiles.active. Property keys are case-sensitive, so the capitalised version is silently ignored and no profile is activated at all.
codeExamples:
# application.properties - add this line
spring.profiles.active=dev

beginner.content:
How to Read Values From application.properties

Two ways, both useful.

Way 1 - @Value

Inject a single property straight into a field.

Way 2 - the Environment Object

Inject Spring's Environment and look properties up by name at runtime. Useful when you need several values, or when the key is not known at compile time.

expert.content:
Do Not Hard-Code the Active Profile Into the Jar

Putting spring.profiles.active=dev in application.properties works for a demo and defeats the purpose of profiles: the profile is now baked into the artefact. Deploying to production means editing a file and rebuilding, so the jar you tested is not the jar you ship.

The profile should come from outside the jar - which is exactly what the property-source ordering allows.

How to set itWhen
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prodCommand line - the highest priority, and the clearest.
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prodEnvironment variable - the standard for Docker and Kubernetes.
-Dspring.profiles.active=prodA JVM system property.
@ActiveProfiles("test")On a test class.
In application.propertiesOnly as a safe default - typically dev.

Note the environment-variable spelling: Spring maps SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE to spring.profiles.active automatically via relaxed binding, so uppercase and underscores are correct there and wrong everywhere else.
codeExamples:
# The same artefact, three deployments
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=test
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# Docker
docker run -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod myapp:1.0

# Kubernetes
env:
  - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
    value: "prod"

# Several profiles can be active at once - they layer left to right,
# with later files overriding earlier ones.
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics,eu-west

# Loading order:
#   application.properties            (always)
#   application-prod.properties
#   application-metrics.properties
#   application-eu-west.properties    (wins on conflicts)

# spring.profiles.group bundles them (Boot 2.4+):
spring.profiles.group.production=prod,metrics,eu-west
# then simply: --spring.profiles.active=production

expert.content:
Secrets Must Not Live in Properties Files

Every file above contains spring.datasource.password=root. Those files are committed to git, packaged into the jar, and readable by anyone who can unzip it.

Where the password leaksWhy
Git historyDeleting it later does not remove it from earlier commits.
The built jarunzip -p app.jar BOOT-INF/classes/application-prod.properties
CI build logsAnything that echoes the config.
Docker image layersPresent in the image even if a later layer deletes the file.
/actuator/envExposed over HTTP if the endpoint is open.

Keep the shape of the config in the file and inject the value from the environment. Spring Boot's ${VAR:default} syntax makes that a one-line change.

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties

Both read configuration. @ConfigurationProperties is what you want once there is more than a handful of keys.

Aspect@Value@ConfigurationProperties
ScopeOne key per fieldA whole prefix bound to an object
Type safetyString expression; a typo is a runtime failureReal types, bound and validated at startup
ValidationNone@Validated plus Bean Validation annotations
Nested / list valuesAwkwardNatural
Relaxed bindingExact key onlyapp.max-size, APP_MAXSIZE, app.maxSize all bind
IDE autocompleteNoYes, with the configuration-processor

A missing key with @Value fails at startup with an unhelpful message; with a default (${key:fallback}) it silently uses the fallback, which is worse when the key was meant to be set.
codeExamples:
# A group of related settings
app.report.title=Employee Report
app.report.max-rows=5000
app.report.formats=pdf,xlsx,csv
app.report.retention-days=30

<!-- Enables IDE autocomplete for your own properties -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

expert.content:
Profiles Select Beans, Not Just Properties

The examples switch database URLs. @Profile goes further: it decides which beans exist at all - so an entire implementation can differ per environment.
codeExamples:
// Profile-specific YAML in ONE file, using document separators
// application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: employee-service
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: dev
server:
  port: 8082
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
server:
  port: 8084
// Boot 2.4+ syntax. Older versions used "spring.profiles: dev".

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem do profiles solve?The same codebase and the same artefact run in dev, test and prod with different configuration, instead of editing files per environment.
What is the file-naming convention?application-{profile}.properties - the name between the hyphen and the extension is the profile.
How does the profile file relate to the main one?application.properties always loads; the profile file loads on top and overrides matching keys.
How do you activate a profile?spring.profiles.active in the properties file, --spring.profiles.active=prod on the command line, or the SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE environment variable.
Why is Spring.profiles.active ignored?Property keys are case-sensitive; the capitalised form is not the key Spring looks for, so nothing is activated.
Why should the active profile not be hard-coded in the jar?It bakes the environment into the artefact, so shipping to production requires a rebuild and the tested jar is not the deployed one.
Can several profiles be active at once?Yes - comma-separated. They layer left to right, with later ones winning.
What does @Profile on a bean do?Registers that bean only when the named profile is active, so whole implementations can differ per environment.
What does @Profile("!prod") mean?Active in every profile except prod.
@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?@Value injects one key per field with no validation; @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole prefix to a typed, validated object and supports relaxed binding.
How do you keep secrets out of properties files?Use ${DB_PASSWORD} placeholders and supply the value from an environment variable or a secrets manager - never commit the value.
Two ways to read a property in code?@Value("${key}") for a single value, or inject Environment and call getProperty("key") for dynamic lookups.

What is Internationalization?

• Internationalization, or I18N, is the process that makes your application adaptable to different languages.
• For example, you can display messages, currencies, dates and times according to a specific region or language.
• Many web applications on the market support several languages - Spanish, Russian, Japanese and so on.

Why "i18n"? It is a numeronym: i + 18 letters + n, because "internationalization" is a long word to keep typing. The related term L10n (localization) is the act of supplying the translations themselves.

Business requirement

Display the "Hello" message in different languages.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot Maven project
2. Add the Maven dependency to pom.xml
3. Create a properties file per country/language
4. Create the REST controller
5. Create InternationalizationConfiguration.java
6. Run the application
7. Open Postman (request and response)
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml : only the web starter is needed.
     MessageSource is part of spring-context, which comes with it. -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Step 3 - One Properties File Per Language

The naming pattern is a basename followed by the locale code. The basename is what you configure; the suffix is what Spring matches against the requested locale.

FileLocaleLanguage
welcome.properties(default)The fallback when nothing else matches
welcome_en.propertiesenEnglish
welcome_fr.propertiesfrFrench
welcome_ja.propertiesjaJapanese

All of them live directly in src/main/resources, and every file uses the same keys - only the values differ. That is the whole idea: the code refers to a key, never to a piece of text.
codeExamples:
# src/main/resources/welcome.properties   (default fallback)
welcome.to.country=Hello

# src/main/resources/welcome_en.properties
welcome.to.country=Hello

# src/main/resources/welcome_fr.properties
welcome.to.country=Bonjour

# src/main/resources/welcome_ja.properties
welcome.to.country=Konnichiwa

# Do NOT wrap the values in quotes. In a .properties file the quotes
# are part of the value, so "Hello" is returned literally including
# the quote characters.

beginner.content:
Step 5 - The Configuration Class

Two beans are needed, and they do different jobs.

BeanJob
LocaleResolverDecides which locale this request is for.
MessageSourceLooks the key up in the file for that locale.

AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver reads the standard Accept-Language HTTP header, which is what browsers send automatically. setDefaultLocale gives it a fallback when the header is absent.

Step 4 - The REST Controller

Inject the MessageSource and ask it for the key, passing the locale.

The header name is Accept-Language, with the hyphen. Writing AcceptLanguage means the header never matches, locale is always null, and every request silently falls back to the default language.

Steps 6 and 7 - Run and Test

In Postman, add a Header with key Accept-Language and value en, fr or ja.

Accept-LanguageFile usedResponse
enwelcome_en.propertiesHello
frwelcome_fr.propertiesBonjour
jawelcome_ja.propertiesKonnichiwa
de (no file)welcome.propertiesHello (the fallback)
(header absent)welcome.propertiesHello

expert.content:
Encoding Is the Failure Everyone Hits

Java .properties files are read as ISO-8859-1 by default. Any character outside Latin-1 - Japanese, Hindi, Chinese, even a French accent in some setups - is mangled into question marks or mojibake, silently.

Notice that the walkthrough uses "Konnichiwa" rather than こんにちは. That romanised spelling sidesteps the problem instead of solving it.

FixEffect
setDefaultEncoding("UTF-8")Required. Without it, non-Latin text is garbage.
spring.messages.encoding=UTF-8The same thing via properties, if you use Boot's auto-configured MessageSource.
Save the files as UTF-8The IDE must agree with the code - check the editor's encoding setting.
\uXXXX escapesThe old workaround; unreadable and now unnecessary.
codeExamples:
# welcome_ja.properties, saved as UTF-8, read as ISO-8859-1:
welcome.to.country=こんにちは
# OUTPUT: ã\u0081\u0093ã\u0082\u0093ã\u0081«ã\u0081¡ã\u0081¯

# With setDefaultEncoding("UTF-8"):
# OUTPUT: こんにちは

# The pre-Java-9 workaround, still seen in old codebases:
welcome.to.country=\u3053\u3093\u306B\u3061\u306F
# Correct, and nobody can proofread it.

expert.content:
How the Locale Is Chosen: the Fallback Chain

Accept-Language is richer than a two-letter code. Browsers send a weighted list, and Spring resolves it against your available bundles in a defined order.

Accept-Language: fr-CA,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8

    q = quality weight, 1.0 when omitted.
    Preference order:  fr-CA  >  fr  >  en

For fr-CA, Spring looks for:
    welcome_fr_CA.properties     most specific
    welcome_fr.properties        language only
    welcome.properties           the default bundle
    -> NoSuchMessageException if none exist
LocaleResolverDecides the locale from
AcceptHeaderLocaleResolverThe Accept-Language header. Stateless - ideal for a REST API.
SessionLocaleResolverAn attribute in the HTTP session. The user's choice persists for the session.
CookieLocaleResolverA cookie, so the choice survives across sessions.
FixedLocaleResolverAlways the same locale. Useful in tests.

AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver cannot be changed at runtime - setLocale() throws UnsupportedOperationException. If users need a language switcher, use the session or cookie resolver.

Placeholders, Plurals and Formatting

Real messages are rarely a bare word. MessageSource takes an argument array and formats it with MessageFormat, which handles number, date and currency formatting per locale.

Never build a sentence by concatenating translated fragments - word order differs between languages, so the fragments cannot be reassembled correctly. Put the whole sentence in the bundle with placeholders.
codeExamples:
# welcome_en.properties
greeting.user=Hello {0}, you have {1} new messages.
policy.premium=Your premium of {0,number,currency} is due on {1,date,long}.

# welcome_fr.properties
greeting.user=Bonjour {0}, vous avez {1} nouveaux messages.
policy.premium=Votre prime de {0,number,currency} est due le {1,date,long}.

expert.content:
ResourceBundleMessageSource vs ReloadableResourceBundleMessageSource

The example uses the first. The difference matters in development and in deployment.

ResourceBundleMessageSourceReloadableResourceBundleMessageSource
Reads fromThe classpath, via java.util.ResourceBundleAny Spring Resource - classpath, file system, URL
CachingPermanent - a change needs a restartsetCacheSeconds(n) re-reads without a restart
Files outside the jarNoYes - file:/opt/app/messages
Best forProduction defaultsDevelopment, and translations updated without redeploying

The reloadable version is what lets a translation team fix wording on a running system.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does i18n mean?Internationalization - i, 18 letters, n. Making an application adaptable to different languages and regions.
Difference between i18n and L10n?i18n is building the capability; L10n (localization) is supplying the actual translations and regional formats.
What is the properties file naming convention?basename_language_COUNTRY.properties - e.g. welcome_fr_CA.properties, falling back to welcome_fr then welcome.
Which two beans are required?A LocaleResolver to decide the locale, and a MessageSource to look the key up.
What does AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver use?The Accept-Language HTTP header. It is stateless, which suits a REST API.
Why can't you change the locale with AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver?setLocale() throws UnsupportedOperationException - the header is the source of truth. Use Session or Cookie resolvers for a language switcher.
Why does non-Latin text come out as mojibake?.properties files default to ISO-8859-1. Call setDefaultEncoding("UTF-8") or set spring.messages.encoding=UTF-8.
What is the basename?The file name without the locale suffix or extension - welcome, not welcome.properties.
What happens when a key is missing?NoSuchMessageException. Pass a default message, or set useCodeAsDefaultMessage.
How do you insert values into a message?getMessage(code, args, locale) with {0}, {1} placeholders; MessageFormat also formats numbers, currencies and dates per locale.
Why not concatenate translated fragments?Word order differs between languages, so fragments cannot be reassembled correctly. Put the whole sentence in the bundle.
Difference between ResourceBundleMessageSource and the Reloadable one?The first caches permanently and reads only from the classpath; the second can read from the file system and re-read on a timer, so translations can change without a restart.
Why set fallback-to-system-locale=false?Otherwise a missing translation falls back to the server machine's locale, making behaviour depend on where the app runs.

beginner.content:
What is REST?

• REST is an architectural style that defines a set of rules for creating RESTful web services.
• It stands for REpresentational State Transfer.

Why do we need it?

Suppose you run a job site, freshersworlds.com, and you want to show tour packages from different countries on it. What are your options?

   www.freshersworlds.com                      www.makemytrip.com
   (Job site)                                  (Tours and travel)

        |                                              |
        |------------  GET /api/tours  --------------->|
        |                                              |
        |<---------  list of tour packages  -----------|
        |                                              |

There is exactly one sensible option: call the tour company's API from your site. That is why REST APIs exist. Put more generally: if your application needs to work with a third-party application, a REST API is how they talk.

In client-server communication, REST says: build an object holding the data the client asked for, and send the values of that object back in the response.

The Four Main HTTP Methods

MethodPurpose
GETRead a resource.
POSTCreate a new resource.
PUTUpdate an existing resource.
DELETEDelete a resource.

REST API Annotations

AnnotationPurpose
@RestControllerMarks the class as a RESTful web service.
@RequestMappingA REST controller holds several handler methods for different HTTP requests; this is how Spring maps a particular request to a particular handler method.
@PathVariableRetrieves data from the URL and binds it to a method argument.
@RequestBodyConverts inbound HTTP data into the Java object passed into the handler method.
@ResponseBodyBinds a method's return value to the web response body.
@ResponseStatusOverrides the HTTP response code for a response. Useful for error handling in a web application or RESTful web service.

Setting Up: STS (Spring Tool Suite)

Spring Tool Suite is an IDE for developing Spring applications.

1. Download Spring Tool Suite from https://spring.io/tools and click the platform you use.
2. Select the Windows 64-bit option.
3. Go to the download folder, then right-click the file and unzip it.
4. Open the extracted sts-4.x.x.RELEASE folder.
5. Double-click SpringToolSuite4.exe.
6. The launcher box appears on screen.
7. Set the workspace location - keep the default or change it.
8. Click Launch. It takes a moment on first run.

Note: create the workspace on any drive except C:. If a system problem or a virus forces you to format C:, your work is somewhere else.

Steps to Create RESTful Web Services

1. Create the Spring Boot project
2. Add the Maven dependencies to pom.xml
3. Create the REST controller
4. Run the Spring Boot application
5. Test with the Postman tool (request and response)

Step 1 - Create the Spring Boot Maven Project

FieldValue
WizardFile -> New -> Spring Starter Project
Project NameSpringBootRestApiDemo
TypeMaven
Java Version8
PackagingJar
LanguageJava

Then click Next.

Step 2 - Add the Maven Dependency

Either add it to pom.xml directly, or - simpler - search for Spring Web in the dependency screen of the wizard, select it, then Next and Finish.
codeExamples:

    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

beginner.content:
Step 3 - Create the REST Controller

@RestController tells Spring this class serves REST endpoints; @GetMapping("/getTest") maps a GET request for /getTest to the method below it.

Step 5 - Testing with Postman

Download and install Postman

1. Go to https://www.postman.com/downloads/ and choose your platform - Mac, Windows or Linux. Click Download.
2. Click Windows 32-bit or 64-bit to match your operating system. The download takes a moment.
3. Go to the download folder and double-click the exe file.
4. The Postman window appears.
5. Click the + icon to open a new request tab.
6. Enter the request details.

The request

FieldValue
MethodGET
URLhttp://localhost:8080/getTest
ActionClick Send

Response: Spring Boot Rest API Example with status 200 OK.

The same endpoint also works straight from a browser, because it is a GET request. Postman becomes necessary once you need POST, PUT, DELETE, headers or a request body.

Example 2 - Return a List

Business requirement: design a RESTful web service that returns a list of students as the response.

The method returns List<String> and nothing else changes - Spring Boot converts the list into a JSON array automatically.

Example 3 - Return an Object

Business requirement: design a RESTful web service that returns a student object.

First create the model class, then return it from the controller. The object becomes a JSON object in the response - each getter supplies one key.

expert.content:
The Six REST Constraints

"An architectural style that defines a set of rules" - these are the rules. An API that breaks them is often still called REST, but the properties REST promises come from following them.

ConstraintWhat it requires
Client-ServerThe UI and the data store evolve independently, connected only by the API contract.
StatelessEvery request carries everything needed to serve it. The server holds no client session between requests - which is what lets you run twenty instances behind a load balancer.
CacheableA response says whether it may be cached, so repeat reads need not reach the server.
Uniform InterfaceResources are identified by URI, manipulated through representations, and responses are self-descriptive.
Layered SystemA client cannot tell whether it is talking to the origin server or to a proxy, gateway or cache in front of it.
Code on Demand (optional)The server may ship executable code to the client. Rarely used.

Stateless is the one that gets broken in practice - typically by storing user state in an HttpSession. The moment you do, a second instance of the application cannot serve that user, and the API stops scaling horizontally. This is exactly why token-based schemes such as JWT are used with REST APIs: the token travels with each request rather than living on the server.

Designing the URL and Choosing the Status Code

The example endpoints - /getTest, /getlist, /getStudent - are fine for a first run and are not how a real API is shaped. REST puts the noun in the URL and the verb in the HTTP method.

Instead ofUse
GET /getStudent?id=10GET /api/students/10
GET /getlistGET /api/students
POST /createStudentPOST /api/students
POST /updateStudentPUT /api/students/10
GET /deleteStudent?id=10DELETE /api/students/10

The status code is half the response, and returning 200 OK for everything throws that half away.

CodeWhen to return it
200 OKSuccessful GET, PUT or DELETE.
201 CreatedSuccessful POST. Include a Location header pointing at the new resource.
204 No ContentSuccess with nothing to return - typically DELETE.
400 Bad RequestThe payload failed validation.
401 / 403Not authenticated / authenticated but not allowed.
404 Not FoundNo resource with that id.
409 ConflictDuplicate key, or a version conflict on update.
500 Internal Server ErrorAn unhandled failure on the server. Never return this for a client mistake.

Binding Request Data - Which Annotation, and When

@PathVariable, @RequestParam and @RequestBody read three different parts of the request. Choosing between them is not a style question.

AnnotationReads from
@PathVariableA segment of the URI path - /students/10. Use it to identify which resource.
@RequestParamThe query string - ?city=pune&page=2. Use it to filter, sort or paginate.
@RequestBodyThe HTTP body. Use it for the resource itself on POST and PUT.
@RequestHeaderOne HTTP header - Authorization, Accept-Language.

@RestController vs @Controller: @RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody applied to every method. That is why the examples above never write @ResponseBody - it is already there. A plain @Controller returns a view name for a template engine to render.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does REST stand for, and what kind of thing is it?REpresentational State Transfer. It is an architectural style - a set of constraints - not a protocol or a library.
What are the four main HTTP methods and their purposes?GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes.
What does "stateless" mean, and why does it matter?The server keeps no client session between requests, so any instance can serve any request. Break it with HttpSession and the API stops scaling horizontally.
@RestController vs @Controller?@RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody on every method, so return values are written to the response body instead of resolved as a view name.
@PathVariable vs @RequestParam?@PathVariable reads a URI path segment and identifies which resource; @RequestParam reads the query string and is used for filtering, sorting and paging.
What does @RequestBody do?Converts the inbound HTTP body - usually JSON - into the Java object passed to the handler method, via Jackson.
How does a Java object become JSON without any conversion code?Jackson arrives with spring-boot-starter-web, and an HttpMessageConverter serialises the return value automatically.
Which status code for a successful POST?201 Created, with a Location header naming the new resource.
How do you return 404 instead of 500 for a missing record?Annotate the exception with @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND), or handle it in a @RestControllerAdvice.
PUT vs PATCH?PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent; PATCH applies a partial update.
Which methods are idempotent?GET, PUT and DELETE - repeating them leaves the same end state. POST is not.
Why is GET /deleteStudent?id=10 wrong?GET must be safe and must not change state. A crawler or a browser prefetch would start deleting records.
REST vs SOAP?REST is a style over HTTP, usually with JSON, lightweight and cacheable. SOAP is a protocol with a strict XML envelope, WSDL contracts and built-in WS-* standards.

topics.name: Building REST APIs with Spring Boot

beginner.content:
What is REST?

REST (REpresentational State Transfer) is an architectural style for building web APIs. It is built around two simple ideas:

• Resources - everything is a "thing" identified by a URL, e.g. /employees, /employees/1.
• HTTP Verbs - the action you want to perform on that resource is expressed using the HTTP method.

HTTP VerbMeaningExample
GETRead a resourceGET /employees/1
POSTCreate a new resourcePOST /employees
PUTUpdate/replace a resourcePUT /employees/1
DELETERemove a resourceDELETE /employees/1

Spring Boot makes it very easy to expose Java methods as REST endpoints using the @RestController annotation.

A Minimal @RestController

@RestController is a combination of @Controller + @ResponseBody. It tells Spring that every method's return value should be written directly into the HTTP response body (instead of being resolved to a view/HTML page).

Returning JSON Automatically from a POJO

You don't have to build JSON strings by hand. If a controller method returns a plain Java object (POJO), Spring Boot uses the Jackson library (included by default) to automatically convert it into a JSON response.

Path Variables - @PathVariable

@PathVariable is used to capture a value directly from the URL path, e.g. the "1" in /employees/1.

Query Parameters - @RequestParam

@RequestParam reads values that appear after the "?" in the URL, e.g. ?department=IT.

Receiving JSON Input - @RequestBody

@RequestBody tells Spring to take the JSON sent in the request body (e.g. from a POST call) and automatically convert it into a Java object, the exact reverse of what happens on the way out.

expert.content:
Full CRUD REST Controller with ResponseEntity

Real REST APIs don't just return raw objects/strings - they return the correct HTTP status code along with the body, using ResponseEntity<T>. This gives full control over status code, headers, and body in a single response.

OperationHTTP VerbSuccess Status
Read one / allGET200 OK
CreatePOST201 Created
UpdatePUT200 OK
DeleteDELETE204 No Content

HTTP Status Codes in a REST API

Choosing the right status code is what separates a "toy" API from a well-designed one. Consumers of your API rely on the status code, not just the body, to decide how to react.

CodeMeaningWhen to use in a REST API
200 OKSuccessSuccessful GET, PUT, or PATCH
201 CreatedResource createdSuccessful POST that creates a new resource (include Location header)
204 No ContentSuccess, nothing to returnSuccessful DELETE, or PUT with no response body
400 Bad RequestClient sent invalid dataValidation failure, malformed JSON, missing required field
401 UnauthorizedNot authenticatedMissing/invalid credentials or token
403 ForbiddenAuthenticated but not allowedUser is known but lacks permission for this action
404 Not FoundResource does not existGET/PUT/DELETE on an id that isn't in the system
409 ConflictState conflictDuplicate resource, version/concurrency conflict
500 Internal Server ErrorUnexpected server failureUncaught exception - should be rare and always logged

Global Exception Handling with @ControllerAdvice

Instead of wrapping every controller method in try/catch, Spring lets you centralize error handling in one class annotated with @ControllerAdvice (or @RestControllerAdvice). Each @ExceptionHandler method intercepts a specific exception type thrown from ANY controller and converts it into a clean, structured JSON error response.

API Versioning Strategies

As an API evolves, you need a way to change it without breaking existing clients. The two most common strategies: 

1) URI Versioning (most common, easiest to understand)
   GET /api/v1/employees
   GET /api/v2/employees
   -> version is baked into the path itself

2) Header Versioning (keeps URLs clean)
   GET /api/employees
   Header: X-API-VERSION: 2
   -> same URL, server branches based on the header value

StrategyProsCons
URI VersioningSimple, visible, easy to test/cache"Pollutes" the URL, resource identity changes across versions
Header VersioningClean/stable URLs, resource identity stays the sameLess discoverable, harder to test directly in a browser

Content Negotiation - Accept, produces, consumes

Content negotiation is how a client and server agree on the data format (JSON, XML, etc.) to exchange. The client sends an Accept header saying what it can understand; the server declares what it can output using produces, and what request bodies it accepts using consumes.

A Note on HATEOAS

HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) is the most advanced level of REST maturity (Level 3 of the Richardson Maturity Model). Instead of the client having to know every URL in advance, each response includes hyperlinks describing what the client can do next - similar to how a website has clickable links.

// Plain REST response
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Pankaj"
}

// HATEOAS-enriched response
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Pankaj",
  "_links": {
    "self":   { "href": "/api/employees/1" },
    "update": { "href": "/api/employees/1", "method": "PUT" },
    "delete": { "href": "/api/employees/1", "method": "DELETE" },
    "all":    { "href": "/api/employees" }
  }
}

Spring provides the spring-hateoas library (EntityModel, WebMvcLinkBuilder) to add these links without hand-building JSON. Most everyday REST APIs stop at Level 2 (proper verbs + status codes) since HATEOAS adds complexity that is only worth it for large, evolving public APIs.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does @RestController do that @Controller doesn't?@RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody, so every method's return value is written straight into the HTTP response body instead of being resolved as a view name
How does Spring Boot convert a Java object to JSON automatically?Via the Jackson library (HttpMessageConverter), included by default in spring-boot-starter-web, using the object's getters
Difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?@PathVariable extracts a value from the URI path (/employees/{id}); @RequestParam extracts a value from query string parameters (?key=value)
What is ResponseEntity used for?To control the full HTTP response - status code, headers, and body - rather than just returning a raw object with an implicit 200 OK
What status code should a successful POST that creates a resource return?201 Created, ideally with a Location header pointing to the new resource's URL
How do you centralize exception handling across all controllers?@RestControllerAdvice (or @ControllerAdvice) combined with @ExceptionHandler methods for specific exception types
What is the difference between produces and consumes in @RequestMapping?consumes restricts the Content-Type of the incoming request body the endpoint accepts; produces restricts the Content-Type/format of the response, matched against the client's Accept header
Name two common API versioning strategies.URI versioning (/api/v1/..., /api/v2/...) and header versioning (a custom header like X-API-VERSION)
What is HATEOAS?A REST maturity concept where responses include hyperlinks describing available next actions/related resources, so clients don't need to hardcode every URL
What status code means "the resource doesn't exist" vs "you're not allowed to see it"?404 Not Found for a missing resource; 403 Forbidden when the resource exists but the caller lacks permission (401 Unauthorized means the caller isn't authenticated at all)

Business Requirement

An orders service exposes GET /api/orders. It returns every order in the table. On the developer's machine the table holds ten rows and the endpoint answers in four milliseconds. In production the table holds two million rows.

Problem Statement

That endpoint is a production incident waiting to happen, and it fails in three places at once.

The database - a full table scan reads and sorts two million rows.
The application - Hibernate builds two million entity objects, then Jackson serialises them into a single string. The heap holds the whole result twice. This is where OutOfMemoryError arrives, and it takes the process down for every other user, not only for the one who made the call.
The client - a 900 MB JSON document over a mobile connection. The request times out at the load balancer long before the last byte is written.

An unpaginated collection endpoint is therefore not a small inefficiency. It is an unbounded resource request that any caller can make, and it fails only in production, because only production has the data.

The rule is simple: any endpoint that returns a collection must return a bounded page of that collection. There are no exceptions for "small" tables - small tables grow.

Pageable and Page

Spring Data does the work. Declare a Pageable parameter on the controller method and hand it to the repository; Spring MVC populates it from the query string automatically through PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver, which is registered by Boot's web auto-configuration.

TypeMeaning
PageableThe request for a page - page number (zero-based), page size and sort order.
PageRequest.of(0, 20)How you build a Pageable in code rather than from the request.
Page<T>The result - the rows plus totalElements and totalPages. Costs a second COUNT query.
Slice<T>The rows plus a hasNext flag, with no COUNT. Use it for infinite scroll, where nobody displays a total.
@PageableDefaultSets the page size and sort used when the caller supplies none.

Note the two queries a Page issues. On a large table the COUNT is often slower than the page itself, which is why Slice exists.

Sorting

sort is a repeatable query parameter of the form field,direction. Repeat it for a multi-column sort; the order of the parameters is the order of the ORDER BY clause.

Two things bite here. First, the value is a property name on the entity, not a column name - createdAt, not created_at. Second, an unrecognised property produces a PropertyReferenceException and a 500, so a caller can crash the endpoint with a typo. Validate the field against an allow-list if the API is public.

Always include a tie-breaker in the sort. If you sort by status alone and a thousand rows share a status, the database is free to return them in any order it likes, and it will not return the same order twice. Rows then appear on two pages, or on none. Appending a unique column - the primary key - makes the ordering total and the paging deterministic.

Filtering and Search

Filters are optional query parameters. Two or three of them can be handled with derived query methods; beyond that the combinations explode - four optional filters mean sixteen repository methods - and you need a query built at run time.

Specifications (the JPA Criteria API wrapped by Spring Data) let you compose one predicate per supplied filter and ignore the rest. Extend JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> on the repository and the findAll(Specification, Pageable) overload appears.

Keep filtering and searching in the query string, never in the path. /api/orders?status=SHIPPED is a filtered view of the orders collection; /api/orders/shipped invents a resource that does not exist and forces a new endpoint for every filter you ever add.

DTO versus Entity

The entity is the shape of your database. The DTO is the shape of your API. Returning the entity welds them together, and the consequences show up quickly.

ProblemWhat happens
Data leaksAdd a passwordHash, internalNotes or costPrice column and Jackson publishes it. Nobody changed the API; the API changed anyway.
Accidental breaking changeRenaming a column renames a JSON field and breaks every client.
Lazy loadingSerialising a detached entity with a LAZY association throws LazyInitializationException, or, if the session is still open, triggers a cascade of extra queries.
CyclesOrder holds Customer, Customer holds List<Order>. Jackson recurses until the stack overflows.
Mass assignmentBinding @RequestBody Order lets a caller post {"id":5,"role":"ADMIN"} and set fields you never intended to expose for writing.

A Java record makes the DTO a three-line class, so the usual objection - boilerplate - has mostly gone. Use a separate request DTO from the response DTO where they genuinely differ: the request has no id and no createdAt, and the response has no password.

ResponseEntity, @RequestHeader and @CookieValue

Returning a plain object gives you 200 and the default headers. ResponseEntity<T> is the escape hatch: it lets the handler set the status code, the headers and the body explicitly.

Use it where the status varies (200 or 404), where a header is part of the contract (Location on a create, ETag on a read), or where the body may legitimately be empty. Where the status is always the same, a plain return type plus @ResponseStatus reads better - ResponseEntity on every method is noise.

@RequestHeader binds one header, @CookieValue binds one cookie. Both take required and defaultValue; a missing header with required=true - the default - produces 400, not 500.

A Consistent Response Envelope

Many teams wrap every response in a fixed structure so that clients always parse the same shape.

  RAW                             ENVELOPED
  {                               {
    "id": 4711,                     "success": true,
    "customer": "ajay"              "data": { "id": 4711, ... },
  }                                 "message": "OK",
                                    "timestamp": "2024-05-14T09:12:04Z",
                                    "errors": []
                                  }
PositionThe argument
ForOne parse path in the client. Metadata - paging, request id, warnings - has a home. Error bodies and success bodies look alike, so generated client code is uniform.
AgainstHTTP already carries status, and "success": true alongside a 200 duplicates it - worse, teams then return 200 with "success": false, which hides failures from every proxy, monitor and retry policy in the path. It also breaks caching and content negotiation, adds a nesting level to every client, and is not what RFC 9457 application/problem+json standardised for errors.

A defensible middle position: do not wrap successful responses - return the resource, and let the status code and headers carry the metadata. Do standardise error responses, using ProblemDetail, which Spring Framework 6 provides out of the box. If your organisation mandates an envelope, apply it once in a ResponseBodyAdvice rather than by hand in every controller.

Naming Standards

Naming is the part of an API a client sees before anything else, and the part you cannot change afterwards without breaking them.

RuleReason
Plural nouns for collections - /orders, not /order/orders is the collection; /orders/4711 is one member of it. Reads naturally at both levels.
No verbs in the pathThe HTTP method is the verb. POST /orders, not POST /createOrder.
Lower case, hyphens between words/purchase-orders. Paths are case-sensitive; mixed case invites bug reports. Underscores are hard to see under a link underline.
camelCase in the JSON bodyMatches Java field names and what JavaScript clients expect. Pick one convention and enforce it globally rather than per class.
Nest only to show ownership/customers/7/orders is right when an order belongs to a customer. Stop at two levels - /a/1/b/2/c/3 is unreadable and forces the client to know your whole schema.
Filters in the query string/orders?status=SHIPPED, not /orders/shipped. Filters combine; paths do not.
No file extensions/orders/4711, not /orders/4711.json. Format is negotiated with the Accept header.
No trailing slashPick one form. Spring Boot 3 no longer matches both by default, so /orders/ now returns 404 where Boot 2 accepted it.
codeExamples:
# Poor                                Better
POST   /api/createNewOrder            POST   /api/orders
GET    /api/getOrderById?id=4711      GET    /api/orders/4711
POST   /api/updateOrder               PUT    /api/orders/4711
GET    /api/deleteOrder?id=4711       DELETE /api/orders/4711
GET    /api/orderList                 GET    /api/orders
GET    /api/orders/shipped            GET    /api/orders?status=SHIPPED
GET    /api/Orders/4711.json          GET    /api/orders/4711
GET    /api/customer/7/order/list     GET    /api/customers/7/orders

# Actions that are genuinely not CRUD do exist. Model them as a
# sub-resource rather than pretending:
POST   /api/orders/4711/cancellation
POST   /api/orders/4711/refunds
# ...which stays a noun, and gives the action its own history and id.

expert.content:
The Four Versioning Strategies

Versioning exists because you cannot change a published contract and you cannot stop changing your product. Every strategy is a way of running the old contract and the new one at the same time.

StrategyFormAdvantagesDisadvantages
URI path/api/v1/ordersVisible in every log, browser bar, curl command and bug report. Trivially routable at the gateway - v1 and v2 can be different deployments. Easy to cache and to document. Works with any client.Violates the idea that a URI names a resource: /v1/orders/1 and /v2/orders/1 are the same order under two names. Version leaks into every hyperlink. Bumping the version rewrites every path.
Query parameter/api/orders?version=1Keeps one URI per resource. Easy to default - no parameter means the oldest supported version.Easy to drop by accident. Muddles filtering parameters with routing metadata. Some caches ignore query strings when building the cache key. Gateway routing on a query param is awkward.
Custom headerX-API-Version: 1URI stays clean and stable. Version is metadata, and metadata belongs in headers.Invisible in a browser - you cannot paste a URL to a colleague and have them see v2. Harder to test by hand. Caches must be told to vary on it. Non-standard header names proliferate.
Accept headerAccept: application/vnd.company.order.v2+jsonThe most correct by the letter of HTTP - this is exactly what content negotiation is for. One URI, many representations, and per-resource versioning rather than a whole-API bump.Verbose and easy to get wrong. Poor tooling support. Impossible to explore in a browser. Most client libraries make it awkward. Confuses newcomers badly.

URI path versioning is the least elegant and by far the most widely used - Stripe, GitHub, Twilio and almost every internal API you will meet. The reason is not ignorance of the alternatives. It is that a version you can see beats a version that is theoretically pure: it appears in access logs, so you can prove which clients are still on v1 before you switch it off; it routes at the load balancer with a path prefix rule and no application awareness at all; and any engineer can reproduce a bug with a curl command copied out of a ticket. The purity argument loses to the operational one, and it should.

Whichever you pick: version the whole API, not individual endpoints, unless you have the discipline for per-resource media types; support at most two versions at once; and publish a deprecation date with the Deprecation and Sunset response headers rather than announcing it in a changelog nobody reads.

What Actually Counts as a Breaking Change

You need a version only for a breaking change, so the definition decides how often you version. The test is: would an existing client, written against the old contract and not recompiled, still work? Judge it from the client's position, not from the diff.

ChangeBreaking?
Adding a new optional field to a responseNo - a tolerant reader ignores unknown fields. This is the single most important reason to configure clients with FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false.
Adding a new optional request parameter or body fieldNo, provided the old behaviour is preserved when it is absent.
Adding a new endpointNo.
Adding a value to an enumYes, in practice. Clients that switch on the enum, or deserialise into a Java enum, fail on the unknown value. Treat enums in a response as strings on the client side.
Removing or renaming a fieldYes.
Changing a field's type - "total": 249 to "total": "249.00"Yes. Number to string breaks strict parsers, and so does the reverse.
Making an optional request field requiredYes.
Making a response field nullable when it never wasYes - the client's non-null assumption is part of the contract it was written against.
Adding a validation rule to an existing fieldYes. Payloads that used to be accepted are now rejected with 400.
Changing the status code for an existing outcomeYes - 200 to 204 breaks any client that parses the body.
Changing default sort order or default page sizeYes in effect, even though no field changed. Behaviour the client depended on has moved under it.
Tightening a rate limit, or changing pagination defaultsNot a schema change; still breaks clients. Announce it like one.

The practical consequence is that most changes are additive, and a well-designed API versions rarely. Reaching v4 in eighteen months is not evidence of rapid iteration - it is evidence the first design was guessed at.

Offset Pagination Is Not Correct on a Changing Dataset

This is the bug that survives code review because it is invisible in a test with static data.

LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20 means "sort the whole result, discard the first twenty rows, return the next twenty". Between the request for page 0 and the request for page 1, other users insert and delete rows. The result set is re-sorted from scratch for the second query, so rows shift across the page boundary.

 t0: newest-first list        client requests page 0 (LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0)
     [ E D C B A ]            gets  E D C

 t1: a new row F is inserted
     [ F E D C B A ]

 t2: client requests page 1 (LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3)
     offset 3 now lands on C, not B
     gets  C B A
                              ^ C is delivered TWICE.
                                Nothing tells the client.

 The mirror image: delete a row between the two requests and
 the row that shifts up across the boundary is NEVER delivered.
 A nightly export job silently misses records.
The dropped row is worse than the duplicate, because a duplicate is visible in the UI and a missing row is not. Any job that walks an entire table page by page while writes continue - an export, a reindex, a migration - will silently lose records.

Cursor (keyset) pagination fixes it. Instead of "skip N rows", say "give me the rows after this exact position". The position is the sort key of the last row of the previous page, and it does not move when rows are inserted elsewhere.

The cursor must be unique and stable. Sorting by created_at alone is not enough - two rows can share a timestamp, and a row at the boundary is duplicated or skipped again. Use a compound key of the sort column plus the primary key, and compare it as a tuple.
codeExamples:
-- OFFSET pagination: correct only if nothing is writing
SELECT id, customer, created_at
  FROM orders
 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;
-- The database must produce, sort and then THROW AWAY 20 rows.

-- KEYSET pagination: "after this row", not "skip this many rows"
-- Page 1 (no cursor):
SELECT id, customer, created_at
  FROM orders
 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20;

-- Page 2: pass the LAST row of page 1 back as the cursor
--   last_created_at = '2024-05-14 09:12:04', last_id = 4692
SELECT id, customer, created_at
  FROM orders
 WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2024-05-14 09:12:04', 4692)   -- row-value comparison
 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20;

-- Portable form for databases without row-value comparison:
 WHERE (created_at < '2024-05-14 09:12:04')
    OR (created_at = '2024-05-14 09:12:04' AND id < 4692)

-- With an index on (created_at DESC, id DESC) the database SEEKS
-- straight to the cursor position. Page 50,000 costs the same as page 1.

expert.content:
Why Deep Offset Pagination Gets Slower the Further You Go

OFFSET 1000000 does not mean "start at row one million". SQL has no such operation. The database evaluates the query, produces rows in sort order, counts off a million of them, discards them, and then returns twenty. The work is proportional to the offset, so page one million costs fifty thousand times what page one costs, for exactly the same twenty rows.

  latency
    ^
    |                                                    ,-'  OFFSET
    |                                            ,--''
    |                                    ,--''
    |                            ,--''
    |                    ,--''
    |            ,--''
    |    ,--''
    |__--_______________________________________________  KEYSET
    +----------------------------------------------------> page number
     1      100     1k      10k     100k    1M
There is a second cost people miss: if the sort column is not indexed, or the index cannot supply the required order, the database sorts the entire table for every single page request. Twenty pages means twenty full sorts of two million rows.

It is also a denial-of-service vector on a public API. GET /api/orders?page=999999&size=100 is one cheap HTTP request that costs the database a great deal, and an attacker can send thousands of them in parallel. Cap the reachable depth, or use cursors and remove the ability to express deep offsets at all.
codeExamples:
-- Measure it. MySQL, 2 million rows, index on (created_at, id):
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;
-- actual time=0.041..0.132 rows=20 loops=1        (0.1 ms)

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000;
-- actual time=1893.4..1893.7 rows=20 loops=1      (1.9 SECONDS)
-- The index was scanned for 1,000,020 entries and 1,000,000 rows
-- were fetched and thrown away.

-- The deferred-join trick: keep OFFSET, but pay it on the narrow index only
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
  JOIN (SELECT id FROM orders
         ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
         LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000) AS page ON page.id = o.id
 ORDER BY o.created_at DESC, o.id DESC;
-- actual time=284.1..284.4 rows=20    (0.28 s - 6x better, still linear)
-- It avoids fetching a million WIDE rows, but still walks a million
-- index entries. It is a mitigation, not a fix. Keyset is the fix.

expert.content:
PATCH, and the Difference Between JSON Merge Patch and JSON Patch

PUT replaces a resource in full: whatever you send is what the resource becomes, and any field you leave out is set to null or reset to its default. That is why "PUT with only the fields I want to change" is a bug - it silently wipes the rest.

PATCH applies a partial modification, and the awkward truth is that the PATCH method does not define how. The body is a patch document whose format is given by its content type, and there are two standard ones.

FormatDetail
JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386), application/merge-patch+jsonThe body looks like the resource, with only the changed fields present. null means "delete this field". Simple and readable - and unable to express "set this field to null", or to modify one element of an array without resending the whole array.
JSON Patch (RFC 6902), application/json-patch+jsonAn ordered array of operations - add, remove, replace, move, copy, test - each addressing a location with a JSON Pointer. Verbose, but expresses null explicitly, edits array elements precisely, and test gives optimistic concurrency inside the patch itself.

Most APIs use merge patch, often without naming it and with Content-Type: application/json. That is acceptable if you document it. What is not acceptable is the common Spring implementation that binds the body to a DTO and copies every non-null field onto the entity: it cannot distinguish "field absent" from "field explicitly null", so a caller can never clear an optional value. Bind to a JsonNode or Map, or use Optional-typed DTO fields, or use ObjectMapper.readerForUpdating, which handles absence correctly by construction.

PATCH is not idempotent in general. A merge patch happens to be, since applying the same field values twice gives the same result; a JSON Patch containing {"op":"add","path":"/lines/-"} appends a line every time it is applied. Pair PATCH with If-Match and an ETag when concurrent edits are possible.

HATEOAS, Honestly

HATEOAS - Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State - is the fourth and strictest part of REST's uniform-interface constraint. A response carries not only data but the links describing what can be done next, so the client navigates the API by following links from a single entry point rather than by constructing URLs from documentation. In Fielding's original formulation, an API without it is not REST at all; it is HTTP with JSON. Spring HATEOAS builds the representations, and spring-boot-starter-hateoas renders HAL.

Almost nobody uses it, and the reasons are worth understanding rather than dismissing.

The promised benefit does not materialise. The point of links is that the server can move a URL and clients follow along. In practice the client is written by a team that reads the documentation, hardcodes the paths, and ships a mobile binary you cannot update. The coupling the links were meant to remove is still there, in the client's source.
No client actually navigates. Writing a generic hypermedia-driven client is genuinely hard, and no mainstream front-end framework does it. What clients do is read _embedded.orders[0].id and build the next URL themselves.
It inflates every payload. A twenty-field order can carry more link metadata than data. Over mobile networks, and multiplied across a page of results, that is real cost for no delivered benefit.
It complicates the server. Every response needs assembler code, and the links must reflect authorisation - showing a cancel link to a user who may not cancel is worse than showing none.
OpenAPI won the discoverability argument. Teams wanted a machine-readable contract they could generate clients and documentation from. That is what a Swagger/OpenAPI spec gives them, at design time, where it is more useful than at run time.

Where it does earn its place: long-lived public APIs with many independent clients and workflow-driven resources where the available actions genuinely depend on state - a payment that may be captured only while authorised, an order that may be cancelled only before dispatch. Encoding those transitions as links stops every client reimplementing the state machine. Be able to explain it in an interview, expect to be asked why your API does not use it, and give the answer above.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must a collection endpoint be paginated?An unpaginated endpoint is an unbounded resource request. Ten rows in development becomes two million in production, and the full result is materialised as entities and again as a JSON string, producing an OutOfMemoryError that takes down the process for every user, not only the caller.
Page versus Slice?Page carries totalElements and totalPages and therefore issues a second COUNT query, which on a large table can cost more than the page itself. Slice reports only whether a next page exists and issues no count - the right choice for infinite scroll.
Why does a sort need a tie-breaker?Without a unique final sort column, rows sharing the sort value have no defined order, and the database will not repeat the same order between queries. Rows then appear on two pages or on none. Append the primary key to make the ordering total.
What is the correctness bug in offset pagination?Each page is a fresh query against the current data. Rows inserted or deleted before the offset shift the boundary, so a row can be returned on two consecutive pages or skipped entirely. The skip is the dangerous case - an export job silently loses records.
How does keyset/cursor pagination fix it?It asks for rows after a specific position rather than skipping a count of rows. The cursor is the sort key of the last row seen - a compound of the sort column and the primary key - so inserts elsewhere in the table cannot move the boundary.
Why does deep offset pagination get slower?OFFSET n makes the database produce and discard n rows before returning any, so cost grows linearly with depth. Page one million costs fifty thousand times page one for the same twenty rows. Keyset seeks the index directly and costs the same at any depth.
When would you still choose offset pagination?Admin screens over modest, quiet tables where users click page numbers and expect a total page count. Keyset gives no page numbers and usually no total.
Why enforce a maximum page size??size=2000000 reproduces the unpaginated failure through a supported parameter, and it is a cheap denial-of-service request. Set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size, and cap page depth separately, since max page size does not limit the page number.
Name the four versioning strategies and the one used most.URI path, query parameter, custom header and Accept-header content negotiation. URI path versioning is the least elegant - the same resource has two URIs - and by far the most used, because it is visible in logs, routable at the gateway with a path prefix, and reproducible with a copied curl command.
Which changes are breaking?Removing or renaming a field, changing a field's type, making an optional request field required, adding validation, changing a status code, adding an enum value, and changing default paging or sort behaviour. Adding an optional response field or a new endpoint is additive, provided clients ignore unknown properties.
Why not return the entity from the controller?It couples the API contract to the database schema. New columns leak automatically, renames break clients, lazy associations throw LazyInitializationException or trigger extra queries, bidirectional relations recurse in Jackson, and binding an entity from the request body allows mass assignment.
When should a handler return ResponseEntity?When the status varies with the outcome, when a header is part of the contract such as Location or ETag, or when the body may be absent. Where the status is fixed, a plain return type with @ResponseStatus is clearer.
Is a response envelope a good idea?It gives clients one parse path and a home for metadata, but it duplicates the status line and tempts teams into returning 200 with "success": false, which hides failures from proxies, monitoring and retry policies. The defensible position is: do not wrap success responses; standardise errors with ProblemDetail (RFC 9457).
PUT versus PATCH, and merge patch versus JSON Patch?PUT replaces the whole resource, so omitted fields are cleared. PATCH is a partial update whose format comes from the content type: JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) looks like the resource with null meaning delete, and JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is an ordered list of operations addressed by JSON Pointer, able to express null, edit array elements and test preconditions.
Why is HATEOAS rarely used?Clients hardcode URLs from documentation rather than following links, so the decoupling never arrives; links inflate every payload; the server needs assembler code that must also respect authorisation; and OpenAPI answered the discoverability need at design time. It still earns its place for workflow resources where available actions depend on state.

What is JSON?

PointDetail
Stands forJavaScript Object Notation
Used forStoring and exchanging data
File extension.json
Internet media typeapplication/json

Usage of JSON

• Transfer data from the server - when you send a request to a server, the data comes back in JSON form.
• Transfer data between the server and a web application using JSON.
• Web services and APIs use the JSON format to deliver data.

JSON Data Types

There are six data types used in JSON.

TypeRule and example
StringMust be written in double quotes only. {"name": "ajay"} - name is the key, ajay is the value.
NumberMust be an integer or a floating-point number. {"age": 30}
ObjectA value can itself be an object. {"employee": {"name": "ajay", "age": 30}}
ArrayA value can be an array. {"employee": ["ram", "ajay", "ashok"]}
BooleanA value can be true or false. {"sale": true}
NullA value can be null. {"middlename": null}

JSON Syntax Rules

• Data should be in key and value pairs.
• Data should be separated by commas.
• Curly braces { } hold objects.
• Square brackets [ ] hold arrays.

JSON Objects

A JSON object holds key and value pairs. Each key is a String; the value can be any of the six types.

• The key and the value are separated by a colon.
• One key/value pair is separated from the next by a comma.
• The curly brace { starts a JSON object.

In the example below, employee is the object; name and salary are its keys, and ajay and 50000 are the matching values.

JSON Arrays

• A JSON array represents an ordered list of values.
• It can store multiple values: strings, numbers, booleans or objects.
• Values must be separated by commas.
• Square brackets [ ] represent a JSON array.
codeExamples:
// Reading the braces of a nested document

{                                    <-- outer object starts
  "firstName": "ajay",
  "lastName": "patil",
  "age": 30,
  "address": {                       <-- inner object starts
    "streetNo": "M G Road",              <-- value is a string
    "city": "pune",
    "state": "maharashtra",
    "country": "india"
  }                                  <-- inner object ends
}                                    <-- outer object ends

expert.content:
Five Things That Are Not Valid JSON

JSON looks like a JavaScript object literal and is stricter than one. Every item below is legal JavaScript and rejected by a JSON parser - and each is a real cause of "Unexpected token" at 2am.

Not allowedWhy, and the fix
{'name': 'ajay'}Single quotes. Strings and keys must use double quotes: {"name": "ajay"}.
{name: "ajay"}Unquoted key. Every key must be a quoted String.
[1, 2, 3,]Trailing comma before the closing bracket or brace. Remove it.
{"x": .5} or {"x": 05}A number needs a leading digit and no leading zero: 0.5, 5.
// a commentJSON has no comments at all. Use a "_comment" key, or a format that supports them (YAML, JSON5).

Also worth knowing: NaN, Infinity and undefined are not JSON values, and the smart/curly quotes that a word processor substitutes for " break every parser. If a JSON file was copied out of a PDF or a Word document, that is the first thing to check.

json-simple vs Jackson - Use Jackson

json-simple 1.1.1 is the library the example uses, and it is worth knowing why you will not use it in a Spring Boot project. It was last released in 2012, has no generics (JSONObject is a raw Map, hence every cast in that example), and cannot bind JSON to your own classes.

Jackson is what spring-boot-starter-web already puts on the classpath, so in a Spring Boot application you add no dependency at all.

Aspectjson-simpleJackson
Reading a field(String) obj.get("city") - unchecked castBound to a typed field, checked by the compiler
Nested arraysManual loop with a cast per elementList<Address> filled automatically
Writing JSONBuild a Map by handwriteValueAsString(object)
In Spring BootExtra dependencyAlready present via spring-boot-starter-web
MaintainedNo - last release 2012Yes

JSON in a Spring Boot REST Controller

In a Spring Boot application you almost never touch a parser. Jackson sits behind @RequestBody and the return value of a @RestController method, converting in both directions through an HttpMessageConverter.

AnnotationDirection
@RequestBodyIncoming JSON -> Java object (deserialisation)
Return value of a @RestController methodJava object -> outgoing JSON (serialisation)

The annotations most worth knowing on the model class:

AnnotationEffect
@JsonProperty("first_name")Maps a Java field to a differently-named JSON key.
@JsonIgnoreKeeps a field out of the JSON entirely - the standard guard for password hashes.
@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)Omits null fields instead of emitting "x": null.
@JsonFormat(pattern = "dd-MM-yyyy")Controls date and time rendering.
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)Accepts JSON containing keys the class does not have, instead of failing.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does JSON stand for, and what is its media type?JavaScript Object Notation; application/json.
What are the six JSON data types?String, Number, Object, Array, Boolean, Null.
What are the four syntax rules?Data in key/value pairs; pairs separated by commas; curly braces hold objects; square brackets hold arrays.
Can JSON keys use single quotes?No. Keys and string values must use double quotes - single quotes are a parse error.
Is a trailing comma allowed?No. [1, 2, 3,] is valid JavaScript and invalid JSON.
Can JSON contain comments?No. Use a "_comment" key or a different format.
Difference between a JSON object and a JSON array?An object is an unordered set of key/value pairs in { }; an array is an ordered list of values in [ ].
JSON vs XML?JSON is lighter, has no closing tags, maps directly to language data structures, and parses faster. XML supports attributes, namespaces, comments and schema validation.
Which JSON library does Spring Boot use by default?Jackson, pulled in transitively by spring-boot-starter-web.
Which annotation converts an incoming JSON body into a Java object?@RequestBody. The return value of a @RestController method goes the other way automatically.
How do you keep a field out of the JSON response?@JsonIgnore on the field, or leave it off the DTO entirely.
Incoming JSON has a key your class does not declare - what happens?Jackson throws UnrecognizedPropertyException by default. @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) makes it tolerant.

Business Requirement - Save

Suppose you want to save employee data - id, name, city - into the database.

Problem statement: design the REST API (RESTful web service) to store or save the employee data into the database.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project    2. Add Maven dependencies to pom.xml    3. Create the model class
4. Create the service    5. Create the service implementation    6. Create the repository
7. Create the REST controller    8. application.properties    9. Run the application
10. Open Postman (request and response)    11. Check the database    12. Trace the application flow

The layers a request travels through

Postman  POST http://localhost:8181/save
      |
      v
  Employee  (model / entity)
      |
      v
  EmployeeController      @RestController      -- receives JSON
      |
      v
  EmployeeService         (interface)
      |
      v
  EmployeeServiceImpl     @Service             -- business logic
      |
      v
  EmployeeRepository      @Repository          -- extends JpaRepository
      |
      v
  DATABASE (MySQL)

Step 2 - Maven Dependencies

Three dependencies do all the work: the MySQL driver, Spring Data JPA (which brings Hibernate), and spring-boot-starter-web for the REST endpoint.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
    <version>8.0.12</version>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Step 3 - Model Class (Entity)

AnnotationPurpose
@EntityMarks the class as a JPA entity - one instance maps to one table row.
@Table(name = "employee")Names the table this entity maps to.
@IdMarks the primary key field.
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)The database generates the id (MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT); the application does not supply it.

Steps 4, 5 and 6 - Service, Implementation, Repository

The service interface declares what the application can do; the implementation says how; the repository talks to the database. Note how little the repository contains - JpaRepository supplies save() already.

Step 7 - REST Controller (Save)

@PostMapping because we are creating a resource, and @RequestBody converts the incoming JSON into the Employee object.

server.port=8181

FieldValue
MethodPOST
URLhttp://localhost:8181/save
Bodyraw -> JSON (see below)
ActionClick Send

Notice that the request body carries no id - the database generates it - and the response comes back with one.

Business Requirement - Update

Suppose you have an employee with id, name and city, and you have to update the name in the database.

Problem statement: design the REST API to update or edit the employee data in the database.

Everything is identical to the save flow except three things:

ElementSaveUpdate
HTTP method@PostMapping("/save")@PutMapping("/update")
Service methodsaveEmployee(...)updateEmployee(...)
Request bodyNo idMust include the id

Note: while updating, passing the id in the JSON request is mandatory. Without it, JPA treats the object as new and inserts a second row instead of updating the existing one.

expert.content:
save() Does a Full Replace - and That Loses Data

The update above works because the JSON happened to carry every field. Real entities have ten or twenty, and a client that sends only the field it wants to change wipes the rest.

save() takes the object you hand it and makes the row look exactly like that object. A field that is null in your object becomes NULL in the row. Jackson sets every field the JSON does not mention to null. Put those two facts together:

ddl-auto - the Setting That Deletes Your Data

The save example used spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create. That value drops every table and recreates it on each startup. In development it is convenient; anywhere else it is a data-loss bug waiting for a restart.

ValueWhat Hibernate does at startup
noneNothing. The correct production value.
validateChecks the schema matches the entities and fails startup if not. Safe, and the best production choice when you want the check.
updateAdds missing tables and columns. Never drops or alters existing ones - so a renamed field leaves the old column behind forever.
createDrops all tables and recreates them at every startup.
create-dropSame as create, and drops them again on shutdown. Used for tests.

Even update is not a migration tool: it cannot rename a column, change a type, add an index, or backfill data, and it will happily leave your schema half-right. Real projects use Flyway or Liquibase and set ddl-auto=validate.
codeExamples:
# Development
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update

# Production - schema owned by Flyway, Hibernate only checks it
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.flyway.enabled=true

# src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_employee.sql
CREATE TABLE employee (
    id   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255),
    city VARCHAR(255)
);
# OUTPUT at startup:
# Flyway: Successfully applied 1 migration to schema `test`
# Hibernate: schema validation passed

expert.content:
Why the Controller Should Not Take the Entity

@RequestBody Employee works and is what almost every tutorial shows. It also means the client can set any field on your table, including ones you never intended to expose.

RiskWhat happens
Mass assignmentThe JSON {"id": 1, "role": "ADMIN"} is bound straight onto the entity. If the field exists, the client just set it.
Leaked columnsThe response serialises every field - password hashes, internal flags, audit columns.
Schema as contractRenaming a column renames a JSON key, breaking every client.
Lazy associationsSerialising an entity with a lazy @OneToMany throws during JSON writing.

The fix is a DTO - a small class shaped for the API, with only the fields the endpoint should accept and return.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which annotations turn a class into a JPA entity?@Entity on the class, @Id on the key field, usually @Table to name the table and @GeneratedValue for key generation.
What does GenerationType.IDENTITY mean?The database generates the key - MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT. The insert happens immediately so the id can be read back.
How does save() know whether to INSERT or UPDATE?By whether the entity is new - typically a null or zero id. New means insert; an existing id means Hibernate loads the row and updates it.
Why must the id be sent when updating?Without it the entity looks new, so save() inserts a second row instead of updating the first.
What is wrong with using save() for a partial update?It replaces the whole row, so any field missing from the JSON is written as NULL. Load the entity first and copy only the fields that were sent.
PUT vs PATCH?PUT replaces the entire resource and is idempotent; PATCH applies a partial change.
What does the second type parameter of JpaRepository mean?The type of the entity's @Id field. It must match, or lookups fail at runtime.
What does ddl-auto=create do?Drops and recreates every table at each startup - all data is lost. Use validate in production with Flyway or Liquibase owning the schema.
Is ddl-auto=update safe for production?No. It only adds; it cannot rename, retype, index or backfill, and it silently leaves stale columns behind.
Why not accept the entity directly in @RequestBody?Mass assignment - a client can set any field that exists. It also leaks columns in the response and makes the DB schema the public API contract. Use DTOs.
What does spring.jpa.show-sql=true do?Logs the SQL Hibernate generates - the fastest way to see whether an insert or an update actually ran.

beginner.content:
Business Requirement - Get

Suppose you want to get the employee data from the database based on the employee id.

Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch (retrieve / get / select) the employee data by employee id from the database.

The project layout, entity and dependencies are the same as the save example. Only the service method, the repository method and the controller mapping change.

PieceWhat it becomes for a GET by id
Controller@GetMapping("/get/{id}") with @PathVariable
ServicegetEmployeeById(Integer id)
RepositoryNothing new - findById() is inherited
Request bodyNone. Nothing is sent; the id travels in the URL.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Steps 4, 5 and 6 - Service, Implementation, Repository

JpaRepository already declares Optional<Employee> findById(Integer id), so the repository body stays empty. The service unwraps the Optional and decides what "not found" means.

Important: do not declare public Employee findById(Integer id) in the repository. The inherited method returns Optional<Employee>, and redeclaring it with a different return type is a compile error:

findById(Integer) in EmployeeRepository cannot override
findById(ID) in CrudRepository
  return type Employee is not compatible with Optional<Employee>

If you want a method that returns the entity directly, give it a different name - findEmployeeById - or just use the inherited Optional, which is the better habit.

Step 7 - REST Controller (Get)
