expert.content:
Returning null Is the Bug in This Example

orElse(null) hands a null back to the controller, and Spring serialises that as 200 OK with an empty body. To the client, "this employee does not exist" and "everything is fine" look identical - and a client that does response.name gets a null-pointer of its own.

A missing resource is a 404. Three ways to get one, in increasing order of quality:

Delete: Three Methods, Three Different Behaviours

deleteById() looks like one obvious choice. There are actually several, and they behave differently when the row is not there or when there are many rows.

MethodBehaviour
deleteById(id)Spring Data 2.x: throws EmptyResultDataAccessException if the row is missing. Spring Data 3.x (Boot 3): silently does nothing.
delete(entity)Needs the entity, so you have already loaded it and know it exists.
deleteAllById(ids)Deletes a batch - but issues one SELECT and one DELETE per id.
deleteAllByIdInBatch(ids)A single delete ... where id in (?, ?, ?). Far faster, but skips cascades and lifecycle callbacks.
Derived deleteByCity(city)Needs @Transactional or it fails with TransactionRequiredException.

Deleting a row that other tables reference by foreign key fails at the database level, not in Java:

java.sql.SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException:
  Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails
  (`test`.`policy`, CONSTRAINT `FK_policy_user`
   FOREIGN KEY (`user_id`) REFERENCES `user` (`id`))

The fix is a deliberate decision, not a workaround: cascade the delete, null the child's foreign key, or refuse the delete with a clear 409 Conflict.

Why findById() Returns Optional

Spring Data 2.0 changed findById() from returning T to returning Optional<T>, and that change is the reason redeclaring it in your repository does not compile.

The point is that the compiler now forces you to say what happens when the row is missing. With a plain return type you can forget, and the forgetting shows up as a NullPointerException three layers away.

CallMeaning
.orElseThrow(() -> new NotFound(id))Missing is an error. The usual choice for a GET by id.
.orElse(defaultEmployee)Missing has a sensible default.
.map(this::toDto)Transform if present, stay empty if not.
.isPresent() / .ifPresent(...)Branch explicitly.
.get()Throws NoSuchElementException if empty - you have re-created the NPE. Avoid.

There is also getReferenceById() (formerly getOne()), which returns a lazy proxy without hitting the database. It is useful for setting a foreign key you already know, and it throws EntityNotFoundException on first property access rather than at lookup time - so it is the wrong tool for a "fetch and return" endpoint.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which annotation maps a URL segment to a method argument?@PathVariable. @RequestParam reads the query string instead.
Why does findById() return Optional?Since Spring Data 2.0, so the compiler forces you to handle the missing-row case instead of leaking a null.
Why can't you declare Employee findById(Integer id) in your repository?It clashes with the inherited Optional<T> findById(ID) - same signature, incompatible return type, so it will not compile. Use a different method name.
What is wrong with returning null from a GET-by-id endpoint?Spring serialises it as 200 OK with an empty body, so the client cannot tell success from not-found. Return 404.
Which status code should a successful DELETE return?204 No Content when there is no body; 200 OK if you return something.
What happens if you deleteById() a row that does not exist?Spring Data 2.x throws EmptyResultDataAccessException; Spring Data 3.x does nothing. Check with existsById() first if you need a 404.
Why might a delete fail with a constraint violation?Another table references the row by foreign key. Cascade, null the child key, or reject with 409 Conflict.
Difference between deleteAllById and deleteAllByIdInBatch?The first issues a select and delete per id; the second issues one delete ... where id in (...) but skips cascades and lifecycle callbacks.
What is a soft delete and why use one?Flag the row as deleted instead of removing it, so audit history survives and foreign keys stay valid. Implemented with a boolean column and a filtered query.
findById vs getReferenceById?findById hits the database and returns an Optional; getReferenceById returns a lazy proxy with no query, and throws on first property access if the row is missing.
Why does a derived deleteByCity() need @Transactional?Derived delete methods are modifying queries, and JPA refuses to run one outside a transaction - TransactionRequiredException.

beginner.content:
What is an Interceptor?

• When a request is delivered to a Spring controller, it must travel through one or more Interceptors before the controller handles it.
• The concept is similar to a Servlet Filter. The difference: a Spring Interceptor intercepts only requests that are going to a Controller.
• Before the request reaches the controller you can use an Interceptor to perform tasks such as user authentication, writing logs, and adding or modifying configuration.

When do we use it?

Use an interceptor when you need to act before the request reaches the controller and before the response is sent back to the client.

   CLIENT
     |
     |  request
     v
+------------------+
|  preHandle()     |  ---- returns false ----> request stops here
+------------------+
     |  returns true
     v
+------------------+
|  REST CONTROLLER |
+------------------+
     |
     v
+------------------+
|  postHandle()    |   before the response goes to the client
+------------------+
     |
     v
+------------------+
| afterCompletion()|   after request AND response are complete
+------------------+
     |
     v
   CLIENT

Interceptor Methods

MethodPurpose
preHandle()Performs an operation before the request is sent to the controller.
postHandle()Performs an operation before the response is sent to the client - that is, it executes after the REST controller.
afterCompletion()Performs operations after the request and the response are both complete.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot Maven project
2. Add the Maven dependency to pom.xml
3. Create the REST controller
4. Create ExampleInterceptor
5. Create ExampleInterceptorConfig
6. Run the Spring Boot application
7. Open Postman (request and response)
8. Check the console

Step 5 - Create ExampleInterceptorConfig

expert.content:
preHandle() Returning false - What Actually Happens

The boolean return value is the reason interceptors are used for authentication. Return false and the chain stops: the controller is never invoked, postHandle() never runs, and afterCompletion() does not run for this interceptor either.

The trap: stopping the chain is not the same as sending a response. If you return false without writing a status or body, the client gets an empty 200 OK - which looks like success. You must write the response yourself.

The Three Methods Are Not Symmetric

It is natural to assume the three methods always fire together. They do not, and each exception is worth knowing.

MethodWhen it runs, and when it does not
preHandle()Always, before the handler. If it returns false, nothing after it runs for this interceptor.
postHandle()Only if the handler completed without throwing. An exception in the controller skips it entirely.
afterCompletion()Always, provided preHandle() returned true - even when the handler threw. The exception is passed in as the last parameter.

That makes afterCompletion() the correct place for cleanup - clearing an MDC, closing a resource, stopping a timer - because it is the only one guaranteed to run after a failure.

A second asymmetry that surprises people: in a @RestController, postHandle() runs before the response body is written by the message converter, and its ModelAndView parameter is always null. Modifying the response body there is too early to be useful - use a ResponseBodyAdvice or a filter instead.

With multiple interceptors, preHandle runs in registration order and afterCompletion runs in reverse order, like nested try/finally blocks.

Interceptor vs Filter vs @ControllerAdvice

All three sit "around" a request, and they sit at different depths. Choosing wrongly means you either cannot see the information you need, or you see it too late.

        HTTP request
             |
             v
   +---------------------+
   |   SERVLET FILTER    |   servlet spec, sees EVERY request
   |                     |   (static files, errors, /actuator too)
   |  +---------------+  |
   |  | DispatcherServlet |
   |  |  +-----------+  |  |
   |  |  |INTERCEPTOR|  |  |   Spring MVC, only mapped handlers
   |  |  | +-------+ |  |  |   knows WHICH controller method
   |  |  | |@Contro| |  |  |
   |  |  | |llerAdv| |  |  |   wraps the handler call itself
   |  |  | +-------+ |  |  |
   |  |  +-----------+  |  |
   |  +---------------+  |
   +---------------------+
AspectFilterInterceptor
Defined byServlet specificationSpring MVC
SeesEvery request, including static resources and errorsOnly requests mapped to a handler
Knows the handler?NoYes - the Object handler parameter is the controller method
Can modify the raw bodyYes, by wrapping request/responseNo, not practically
Spring beans availableYes, if registered as a beanYes, always
Typical useCORS, compression, security filter chain, request wrappingAuth checks per handler, logging, timing, MDC, tenant resolution

Rule of thumb: if you need to see the controller method or its annotations, use an interceptor. If you need to touch the raw bytes or catch requests that never reach a controller, use a filter. If you are handling exceptions or reshaping the response body, use @RestControllerAdvice.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a Spring interceptor?A Spring MVC component that a request passes through before and after the controller handles it - used for authentication, logging, timing and configuration changes.
What are its three methods?preHandle() before the controller, postHandle() after the controller but before the response is sent, afterCompletion() after the request and response are complete.
Which interface do you implement?HandlerInterceptor.
How is an interceptor registered?In a @Configuration class implementing WebMvcConfigurer, by overriding addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry).
When does addInterceptors() run?Once, at application startup - not per request.
What does returning false from preHandle() do?Stops the chain: the controller and postHandle() never run. You must write the status and body yourself, or the client receives an empty 200.
Does postHandle() run if the controller throws?No. afterCompletion() still does, and receives the exception as its last parameter.
Where do you put cleanup code?afterCompletion() - the only method guaranteed to run after a failure.
Interceptor vs Filter?A filter is servlet-level and sees every request but not the handler; an interceptor is Spring MVC-level, sees only mapped handlers, and knows which controller method will run.
Can an interceptor read the controller method's annotations?Yes - cast the handler parameter to HandlerMethod. This is the main thing a filter cannot do.
In what order do multiple interceptors run?preHandle in registration order; afterCompletion in reverse order, like nested try/finally blocks.
Why is ModelAndView null in a REST controller's postHandle()?There is no view - the return value is serialised by a message converter. To alter a REST response body, use ResponseBodyAdvice instead.
How do you apply an interceptor to only some URLs?addPathPatterns("/api/**") and excludePathPatterns("/api/login") on the registration.

topics.name: Exception Handling in Spring Boot REST APIs

beginner.content:
When you build a REST API with Spring Boot, clients call your endpoints over HTTP and expect a clean, predictable JSON response - even when something goes wrong.

If you let a normal Java exception (like NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, or a custom exception) bubble up without handling it, Spring Boot does not crash silently - it falls back to its default error handling mechanism, called the Whitelabel Error Page (for browsers) or a generic JSON error body (for REST clients / Postman).

This default response is ugly and unsafe for a real API because:
• It exposes internal details like the exception class name and sometimes stack trace info.
• It does not tell the client anything meaningful about what went wrong or how to fix it.
• The HTTP status code returned is almost always a generic 500 Internal Server Error, even for things that are really the client's fault (like passing a bad ID) which should be a 404 or 400.

Below is what a typical unhandled exception looks like when hit through a REST client:

Step 1: Catch a specific exception with @ExceptionHandler

The simplest fix is to add a method annotated with @ExceptionHandler directly inside the same controller. Spring Boot automatically routes any exception of that type (thrown by any handler method in that controller) to this method instead of letting it bubble up to the default handler.

This gives you full control over the response body - no more leaked stack traces.

Step 2: Control the HTTP status with ResponseEntity

Returning a plain String fixed the message, but the HTTP status is still 200 OK by default - which is wrong, because "user not found" should really be a 404 Not Found.

ResponseEntity<T> lets your exception handler set both the response body AND the exact HTTP status code to send back, so REST clients can correctly branch on status (404 vs 400 vs 500 etc).

Limitation of this approach: the @ExceptionHandler method above only protects this one controller. If you have 10 controllers in your project, you would have to copy-paste the same handler into every one of them - which does not scale and is easy to forget.

The Expert section covers @RestControllerAdvice, which solves this by handling exceptions globally, across every controller in the application, from a single place.

expert.content:
Global Exception Handling with @ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice

Instead of writing an @ExceptionHandler in every single controller, Spring lets you centralize exception handling in one class using @ControllerAdvice (returns views, older MVC style) or @RestControllerAdvice (combination of @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody, the standard choice for REST APIs - every handler method's return value is automatically serialized to JSON).

Spring scans this class at startup and registers it as a cross-cutting "advice" that intercepts exceptions thrown from any @RestController in the application, not just one. 

                     ┌─────────────────────────┐
                     │   UserController        │──┐
                     └─────────────────────────┘  │  throws
                     ┌─────────────────────────┐  │  exception
                     │   OrderController        │──┼──────────►  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                     └─────────────────────────┘  │              │  @RestControllerAdvice        │
                     ┌─────────────────────────┐  │              │  GlobalExceptionHandler       │
                     │   ProductController      │──┘              │  (single centralized class)   │
                     └─────────────────────────┘                 └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                                                                  │
                                                                  picks best-matching
                                                                  @ExceptionHandler method
                                                                                  │
                                                                                  ▼
                                                                    Clean JSON error response
Below is a full working example: a custom ResourceNotFoundException mapped to 404, a validation failure mapped to 400, and a catch-all fallback mapped to 500.

Designing a Structured Error Response DTO

Returning a plain String as the error body (as above) is fine for a demo, but real APIs return a consistent JSON shape for every error, so client applications can parse it reliably instead of guessing the format each time. A typical structured error DTO includes:
• timestamp - when the error occurred
• status - numeric HTTP status code (e.g. 404)
• error - the HTTP status reason phrase (e.g. "Not Found")
• message - human-readable, safe-to-expose description
• path - the request URI that triggered the error

@Valid + Bean Validation: Field-Level Validation Errors

Real APIs receive request bodies (e.g. creating a new user) that must satisfy rules before hitting business logic - fields must not be null, strings must be within a size range, emails must be well-formed, etc. Spring integrates with the Bean Validation spec (jakarta.validation) so you annotate the DTO fields directly, add @Valid on the controller parameter, and Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException automatically if any rule fails - before your controller method body even runs. You then catch that exception globally and return field-level messages.

Precedence: Which @ExceptionHandler Wins?

A single @RestControllerAdvice class often has multiple @ExceptionHandler methods mapped to different exception types in the same class hierarchy (e.g. ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException extends Exception). Spring resolves which handler to call using the same rule as Java's own catch-block matching: the most specific matching exception type always wins, regardless of the order the methods are declared in the class.

Exception Thrown Handlers Available Handler That Actually Runs Why
ResourceNotFoundException handles(ResourceNotFoundException), handles(RuntimeException), handles(Exception) handles(ResourceNotFoundException) Exact type match - most specific always wins
IllegalStateException handles(RuntimeException), handles(Exception) handles(RuntimeException) No exact match, so the nearest ancestor in the hierarchy wins
IOException (checked) handles(RuntimeException), handles(Exception) handles(Exception) IOException is not a RuntimeException, only Exception matches
Any exception with no dedicated handler at all handles(Exception) only handles(Exception) Acts as the global catch-all / fallback (should always be present)

Key rule: declaration order in the class does NOT matter - Spring always walks up the exception's class hierarchy and picks the handler whose declared type is the closest ancestor (or exact match). This is why it is safe (and recommended) to always keep a generic @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) as a fallback - it will only be invoked when nothing more specific matches.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What happens by default if you don't handle an exception in a Spring Boot REST API?Spring Boot's default error handler (Whitelabel) returns a generic JSON body with status 500, and it can leak internal details like the exception message/trace.
Difference between @ControllerAdvice and @RestControllerAdvice?@RestControllerAdvice = @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody; it automatically serializes handler return values to JSON, which is what REST APIs need. @ControllerAdvice alone is meant for MVC apps returning views.
Does @ExceptionHandler inside a controller work only for that controller?Yes - a handler defined inside a specific @RestController only catches exceptions thrown within that controller. A handler inside a @RestControllerAdvice class applies globally to all controllers.
How does Spring decide which @ExceptionHandler method to call when several match?It picks the handler whose declared exception type is the closest match in the thrown exception's class hierarchy (most specific wins), regardless of method declaration order.
What triggers MethodArgumentNotValidException?It's thrown automatically when a @RequestBody parameter annotated with @Valid fails one or more Bean Validation constraints (like @NotNull, @Size, @Email) on its fields.
Why use ResponseEntity in an exception handler instead of just returning an object?ResponseEntity lets you explicitly control the HTTP status code returned to the client (404, 400, 500, etc.), not just the response body.
Why is a consistent error response DTO (timestamp/status/error/message/path) considered a best practice?It gives every error the same predictable JSON shape so client applications can parse and handle errors uniformly instead of writing custom parsing logic per endpoint.
Should you always include a catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)?Yes - it acts as a safety net for any exception type without a dedicated handler, ensuring the client never sees the raw Whitelabel error page/stack trace.
Can you have multiple exception types mapped to the same handler method?Yes - @ExceptionHandler({TypeA.class, TypeB.class}) lets one method handle multiple unrelated exception types.
Where does @ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice fit in the request lifecycle?It acts as a cross-cutting concern (similar to AOP) - it doesn't run on every request, only when an exception propagates out of a controller method, at which point Spring routes it to the best-matching handler.

Spring Data JPA is a part of the larger Spring Data family that makes it easy to work with relational databases in a Spring application.

It sits on top of JPA (Java Persistence API) and Hibernate (the most common JPA implementation) and removes almost all of the boilerplate code (DAO classes, SQL statements, ResultSet mapping) that we normally have to write when talking to a database.

The two building blocks we start with are:
• @Entity - a plain Java class that represents a database table.
• Repository interface - an interface that gives us ready-made methods to save, read, update and delete rows for that table, without writing any implementation ourselves.

1. What is an @Entity class?

An @Entity class is a normal Java (POJO) class annotated with @Entity so that JPA knows this class should be mapped to a database table.

• Each object (instance) of the entity class represents one row of the table.
• Each field of the class represents one column of the table.
• @Id marks the field that is the primary key.
• @GeneratedValue tells JPA/Hibernate to auto-generate the primary key value (like an auto-increment column).

Below is a simple Employee entity that maps to an employee table:

2. What does JpaRepository give you for free?

Instead of writing a DAO class with hand-written SQL for every operation, we simply create an interface that extends JpaRepository<T, ID>, where T is the entity type and ID is the type of its primary key.

Spring Data JPA automatically generates the implementation at runtime (we never write a class body), and we instantly get methods like:
• save(entity) - insert or update a row
• findById(id) - fetch a single row by primary key
• findAll() - fetch all rows
• deleteById(id) / delete(entity) - remove a row
• count() - count total rows

No implementation class is needed - Spring creates a proxy for this interface behind the scenes.

3. Derived Query Methods

Spring Data JPA can generate the SQL/JPQL query automatically just by reading the name of a method we declare in the repository interface - this is called a "derived query method".

For example, a method named findByEmailAddress(String email) is parsed by Spring Data as:
"find" + "By" + "EmailAddress" -> generate a query that filters the Employee table where the emailAddress column equals the given parameter.

We only declare the method signature - Spring Data writes the query for us behind the scenes (roughly equivalent to SELECT * FROM employee WHERE email_address = ?).

4. Saving and Retrieving an Entity - Full Demo

Putting it together: we create an Employee object, save it using the repository, and then read it back using findById - all without writing a single line of SQL.

expert.content:
Entity Relationship Mapping - @OneToMany / @ManyToOne

Real applications rarely have a single isolated table - entities relate to each other. The most common relationship is one-to-many (one Department has many Employees) which, from the other side, is a many-to-one (many Employees belong to one Department). 

   DEPARTMENT (1)                 EMPLOYEE (N)
   +----+----------+        +----+--------+---------------+
   | id | name     |        | id | name   | department_id |  (FK)
   +----+----------+        +----+--------+---------------+
   | 1  | Engg     |  <----  | 1  | Jiva   |      1        |
   |    |          |  <----  | 2  | Anaji  |      1        |
   +----+----------+         +----+--------+---------------+

   Department.employees  ------ @OneToMany (mappedBy = "department") ------>
   Employee.department   <----- @ManyToOne (owning side, has FK column) -----
The @ManyToOne side is always the "owning" side because it physically holds the foreign key column (department_id). The @OneToMany side uses mappedBy to say "I don't own the foreign key, look at the field named 'department' on the Employee entity for it".

Lazy vs Eager Fetching

Every association (@OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @OneToOne) has a fetch type that decides WHEN the related data is loaded from the database.

Fetch TypeBehaviorDefault for
FetchType.EAGERRelated data is loaded immediately, in the same query/session, whether you need it or not@ManyToOne, @OneToOne
FetchType.LAZYRelated data is loaded only when you actually access it (a proxy is returned initially)@OneToMany, @ManyToMany

The Classic LazyInitializationException Trap

When a field is LAZY, Hibernate returns a proxy object instead of the real data. The proxy can only be "filled in" while the original Hibernate Session (JPA persistence context) is still open. If you try to access a lazy field after the session has closed (for example, after the @Transactional service method has already returned and the entity is being serialized to JSON in the controller), Hibernate throws LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session.

Custom Queries: @Query (JPQL) vs Native SQL

Derived query methods work well for simple filters, but for anything complex (joins, aggregations, subqueries) we write the query explicitly using @Query.

AspectJPQL (@Query, default)Native SQL (@Query(nativeQuery = true))
Operates onEntity names & fields (Employee, name)Actual table & column names (employee, name)
Database portabilityPortable across databasesTied to the specific database's SQL dialect
Can use DB-specific functionsNoYes
Return type mappingAutomatically maps to entityMay need manual mapping for complex results

Pagination and Sorting with Pageable

Fetching an entire table into memory does not scale. Spring Data JPA lets any repository method accept a Pageable parameter to fetch results page by page, optionally sorted.

The N+1 Select Problem

The N+1 problem happens when you fetch a list of N parent entities (1 query), and then, for each parent, a lazy association is accessed separately (N more queries) - resulting in N+1 total queries instead of 1. 

BEFORE (N+1 problem):
  1 query  -> SELECT * FROM department                     (returns 3 rows)
  +3 query -> SELECT * FROM employee WHERE department_id=1
  +3 query -> SELECT * FROM employee WHERE department_id=2
  +3 query -> SELECT * FROM employee WHERE department_id=3
  ---------------------------------------------------------
  TOTAL: 1 + 3 = 4 queries just to print 3 departments and their employees

AFTER (JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph):
  1 query  -> SELECT d.*, e.* FROM department d
              JOIN employee e ON e.department_id = d.id
  ---------------------------------------------------------
  TOTAL: 1 query, employees loaded together with departments
Cause: iterating over a list of parents and, inside the loop, touching a LAZY collection/association that was never fetched up front - each access triggers its own SELECT.

Fix option 1 - JOIN FETCH in JPQL:
Fix option 2 - @EntityGraph which tells Spring Data JPA to eagerly fetch specific associations for that particular query, without changing the entity's default fetch type globally.

@Transactional and Spring Data JPA

@Transactional wraps a method in a database transaction and keeps the JPA persistence context (the "session") open for the duration of that method.

ScenarioNeed @Transactional?Why
Single save() / findById() callNot requiredEach repository method already runs in its own short transaction by default
Multiple repository calls that must all succeed or all fail togetherRequiredEnsures atomicity - a failure rolls back every change made so far in that method
Accessing a LAZY association after the initial fetchRequiredKeeps the persistence context/session open so the lazy proxy can still be initialized
Read-only reporting queriesRecommended: @Transactional(readOnly = true)Lets Hibernate skip dirty-checking, improving performance

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between JpaRepository, CrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository?CrudRepository has basic CRUD methods; PagingAndSortingRepository adds pagination/sorting on top of it; JpaRepository extends both and adds JPA-specific batch operations like flush(), saveAndFlush(), and deleteAllInBatch()
How does Spring Data JPA generate SQL from a method like findByNameAndSalaryGreaterThan?It parses the method name into a keyword tree (find/By/And/GreaterThan etc.), maps each token to an entity field or operator, and builds the equivalent JPQL/SQL query at application startup, not at runtime per call
What causes a LazyInitializationException and how do you fix it?Accessing a LAZY-fetched field/collection after the persistence context (Hibernate session) has already closed; fix by accessing it inside a @Transactional method, using JOIN FETCH/@EntityGraph, or mapping to a DTO before the session closes
Why is @ManyToOne the "owning side" of a relationship?Because it holds the physical foreign key column in its table; the @OneToMany side uses mappedBy to point to that owning field and does not itself create a column
What is the N+1 select problem and how do you solve it?Fetching a list of parent entities (1 query) and then lazily loading a related collection/entity separately for each parent (N queries); solved with JOIN FETCH in JPQL or @EntityGraph to load associations in a single query
What is the difference between JPQL and native queries in @Query?JPQL operates on entity names/fields and is database-portable, translated to SQL by Hibernate; native queries are written in the actual database's SQL dialect using real table/column names and can use DB-specific functions
How does Pageable/PageRequest avoid loading the whole table?Spring Data JPA translates it into a SQL query using LIMIT/OFFSET (or the equivalent) plus ORDER BY, so only the requested page of rows is ever fetched from the database
When is @Transactional actually required with Spring Data JPA?When multiple repository operations must succeed or fail together (atomicity), or when a LAZY association needs to be accessed after the initial query, keeping the persistence context open
What does cascade = CascadeType.ALL do on a @OneToMany mapping?It propagates persist/merge/remove/refresh/detach operations performed on the parent entity to its related child entities automatically, e.g. saving a Department also saves its new Employees
Why is EAGER fetching risky as a default on associations?It loads related data on every query whether needed or not, which can silently cause large joins, extra queries, and performance problems as the object graph grows - LAZY plus explicit JOIN FETCH/@EntityGraph is generally the safer default

topics.name: Derived Query Methods - Fetch by Single & Multiple Fields

beginner.content:
Spring Data JPA

• It is part of the Spring framework.
• It reduces the amount of boilerplate code in the repository / DAO layer.
• It generates the JPA query on your behalf from the method name - you write the name, Spring writes the query.

The Naming Rules

• Create a method starting with the prefix findBy followed by the field name.
• For several fields, join them with the logical operators And / Or:
  findByFieldName1AndFieldName2, findByFieldName1OrFieldName2

Suppose Employee has id, name, city and status, and you want to fetch by city. Several method names work:

Method nameValid?
findByCity()Yes - and the preferred form by Java naming convention.
findBycity()Works. Spring is tolerant of the first letter's case.
getByCity() / readByCity() / queryByCity()Work. get, read, query, search, stream are all recognised prefixes.
fetchByCity()Does not work. fetch is not a recognised prefix - startup fails.
findBycities()Does not work. There is no cities field, so the property cannot be resolved.

The part after By must name a real field on the entity. Get it wrong and the application refuses to start:

org.springframework.data.mapping.PropertyReferenceException:
  No property 'cities' found for type 'Employee'
  Did you mean 'city'?

That failure at startup is the feature: a typo in a query method is caught before a single request arrives.

Business Requirement 1 - Single Field

Fetch user details based on the email id from the database.

Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch user details by email id.

The User entity carries the fields the rest of this topic uses.

Business Requirement 2 - Multiple Fields

Display the list of users based on city and status:

• If city is pune and status is active, display active users in Pune only.
• If city is mumbai and status is inactive, display inactive users in Mumbai only.

Two fields, joined by And. Nothing else changes - the return type becomes a List because several rows can match.

Business Requirement 3 - Update the Password

Update the user password based on the user id.

This combines a read and a write: fetch the user, change one field, save it back.

expert.content:
Never Use GET to Change Data

The original walkthrough maps the password update to @GetMapping("/update/{id}"). It works in Postman, and it is one of the more dangerous habits in web development.

HTTP defines GET as safe: it must not change server state. Everything on the network assumes that.

Who assumes GET is safeWhat goes wrong
Browsers & link prefetchersSpeculatively fetch links, changing passwords nobody asked to change.
Search-engine crawlersFollow every URL they find, executing every update.
Proxies and CDNsCache the response, so the second call never reaches you - or serves someone else's result.
Retry logicReplays a failed GET automatically, because retrying a read is harmless.
Server access logsThe new password sits in plain text in the query string, in every log and in browser history.

That last row matters most here: ?password=12341234 is recorded by the browser, every proxy, and the server's access log. A password belongs in the request body of a POST, PUT or PATCH, over HTTPS.

The Derived-Query Vocabulary

And and Or are the start of it. The full grammar covers most day-to-day queries without a line of SQL.

KeywordGenerated condition
findByCityAndStatuswhere city = ? and status = ?
findByCityOrStatuswhere city = ? or status = ?
findByAgeBetweenwhere age between ? and ?
findByAgeGreaterThanEqualwhere age >= ?
findByNameLike / Containingwhere name like ? (Containing wraps the value in %)
findByNameStartingWith / EndingWithlike ?% / like %?
findByStatusIn(List)where status in (?, ?, ?)
findByEmailIsNull / IsNotNullwhere email is null
findByCityIgnoreCasewhere upper(city) = upper(?)
findByCityOrderByNameDescwhere city = ? order by name desc
findTop5ByCity / findFirstByCityAdds a row limit
findDistinctByCityselect distinct ...
countByCity / existsByEmailReturns long / boolean instead of entities
deleteByStatusDeletes matching rows - requires @Transactional

Return types are just as expressive: List<User> for many, Optional<User> for at most one, User for exactly one (which throws IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException if two rows match), long for a count, boolean for existence.

When the Method Name Stops Being Readable

Derived queries are excellent up to about three conditions. Past that, the name becomes unreadable and un-editable:

List<User> findByCityAndStatusAndAgeGreaterThanEqualAndEmailIsNotNullOrderByLastNameAsc(
        String city, String status, int age);

Three ways out, in order of how often you will reach for them:

ApproachUse when
@Query with JPQLThe condition is fixed but complex. Readable, and validated at startup.
Specification (Criteria API)Filters are optional - a search screen where the user may fill in any subset of fields.
Query by ExampleSimple "match this populated probe object" searches.

The optional-filter case is the one derived queries genuinely cannot handle: with four optional filters you would need sixteen method names.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a derived query method?A repository method whose name Spring Data parses to generate the query - no implementation or SQL is written.
What prefixes can a query method start with?find, get, read, query, search, stream, count, exists, delete. fetch is not one of them.
What happens if the property name is wrong?Startup fails with PropertyReferenceException, usually suggesting the correct field - the error arrives before any request does.
How do you query on two fields?Join them with And or Or: findByCityAndStatus(String city, String status). Arguments follow the order in the name.
What does a list-returning query return when nothing matches?An empty list - never null. The endpoint returns [] with 200 OK, which is correct.
What if a single-result query matches two rows?IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException. Add a UNIQUE constraint or return a List.
Why is existsByEmail better than findByEmail() != null?It issues a COUNT and never loads the entity - cheaper, and it states the intent.
Why must you never use GET for an update?GET is defined as safe. Prefetchers, crawlers, caches and retries all assume no state changes, and query-string data lands in logs and browser history.
Where should a password travel?In the request body of a POST/PUT/PATCH over HTTPS - never in the URL - and it must be stored hashed with BCrypt or Argon2.
When do you outgrow derived queries?Past about three conditions, or as soon as filters are optional. Move to @Query for fixed complex queries, or Specification for dynamic ones.
Why do Specification filters handle optional criteria so well?A specification that returns null is skipped, so one findAll call covers every combination of present and absent filters.
Which derived methods need @Transactional?Modifying ones - deleteBy... and any @Query marked @Modifying.

JPQL

Native Query

This topic is being written and will be published shortly.

In the meantime, the surrounding module already covers the ground it sits on - work through the topics either side of it and come back once this one is live.

How to Write a Native Query

• Use the @Query annotation to specify a query inside a repository.
• Always write the SQL query in the repository layer only - never in the service or the controller.
• You can refer to the table name or the POJO class name while fetching the data, depending on which kind of query you write.

The one attribute that changes everything

SettingWhat the query string must be
nativeQuery = trueReal SQL against real table and column names. Passed straight to the database.
nativeQuery = false (the default)JPQL against entity class and field names. Hibernate translates it into SQL.

Correction worth noting: writing nativeQuery = false with SQL in the string does not produce a compile-time error - @Query takes a plain String, so the compiler has nothing to check. It fails when Hibernate tries to parse it as JPQL, and that happens at application startup:

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Validation failed for query
  for method public abstract java.util.List
  com.velocity.repository.EmployeeRepository.findByCity(java.lang.String)!
Caused by: QuerySyntaxException: unexpected token: * near line 1, column 8
  [select * from employee c where city=?1]

JPQL has no select * and knows no table called employee - only the entity Employee.

Business Requirement 1 - List Users by City

Display the list of users according to city. Using the native-query approach:

Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch the list of users based on city.

Business Requirement 2 - City and Status

• Display the list of users based on city and status.
• If city is pune and status is active, display active users in Pune only.
• If city is mumbai and status is inactive, display inactive users in Mumbai only.

Two parameters means ?1 and ?2, bound by position.

Changing the Port

Every example here runs on 8181 rather than the default 8080. That is one line:

Step 1 - open application.properties and add:
    server.port=8082

Step 2 - run the Spring Boot application.

The console confirms it: Tomcat started on port(s): 8082 (http). Setting server.port=0 picks a random free port, which is what integration tests use.

Application Flow

Postman  GET /getcity/pune
     |
     v
 EmployeeController  ->  EmployeeService  ->  EmployeeServiceImpl
     |
     v
 EmployeeRepository  ->  @Query(nativeQuery = true)
     |
     v
 DATABASE

expert.content:
Native SQL vs JPQL - Choosing Between Them

The tutorial reaches for nativeQuery = true immediately, and for a simple where city = ? that is the less good choice. Both options have a real place.

AspectJPQL (default)Native SQL
Refers toEntity classes and field namesTable and column names
Validated at startupYes - a bad field name fails the bootNo - errors surface at query time
Rename a fieldCompiler and startup catch itQuery silently breaks at runtime
Portable across databasesYes - Hibernate emits dialect-specific SQLNo - MySQL syntax will not run on Oracle
PaginationPageable works out of the boxNeeds a separate countQuery
Vendor featuresNot availableFull access - window functions, hints, CTEs, JSON operators
Returns entitiesAlways managed and dirty-checkedManaged only if every column is selected

The rule: use JPQL by default; drop to native SQL when you need something JPQL cannot express - a database-specific function, a complex analytic query, or a bulk statement you have tuned by hand.

Named Parameters Beat Positional Ones

?1 and ?2 work until someone adds a third parameter in the middle, or reorders the method signature. Then the query still compiles, still runs, and returns the wrong rows.

:city and :status bind by name, so the order of the arguments stops mattering and the query reads like a sentence.

String Concatenation Is SQL Injection

Both parameter styles are safe because they become bind parameters - the value never becomes part of the SQL text. Building the query with + removes that protection completely.

Modifying Native Queries and Pagination

Two things trip people up the first time they go beyond a SELECT.

1. A native UPDATE or DELETE needs two extra annotations. Without @Modifying Spring Data tries to run it as a query; without @Transactional JPA refuses to execute it at all.

2. A paginated native query needs its own count query. Spring Data can derive a count from JPQL, but not from arbitrary SQL.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does the @Query annotation do?Attaches an explicit JPQL or SQL query to a repository method, replacing the derived-from-the-name behaviour.
What does nativeQuery = true change?The string is treated as real SQL against table and column names and sent to the database unchanged, instead of JPQL against entities.
Is nativeQuery = false with SQL a compile error?No - @Query takes a plain String. It fails at startup when Hibernate cannot parse it as JPQL: QuerySyntaxException: unexpected token: *.
JPQL vs native SQL - which should you default to?JPQL: it is validated at startup, survives field renames, is database-portable, and paginates without extra work. Go native only for vendor-specific features.
Difference between ?1 and :city?Positional binds to argument order; named binds by name. Named is safer - reordering parameters cannot silently break it.
Are @Query parameters safe from SQL injection?Yes - they become bind parameters, so the value is never parsed as SQL. Concatenating the value into the string with + is not safe.
What can you not pass as a bind parameter?Identifiers - table names, column names, sort direction. Use Sort/Pageable, or validate against an allow-list.
What do you need for a native UPDATE or DELETE?@Modifying and @Transactional. Missing either gives InvalidDataAccessApiUsageException or TransactionRequiredException.
Why can a bulk update leave stale entities in memory?It runs directly in the database and bypasses the persistence context. Use @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushBeforeExecution = true).
How do you paginate a native query?Add a Pageable parameter and supply countQuery - Spring Data cannot derive a count from arbitrary SQL.
Where should queries live?The repository layer only. A SQL string in a service or controller mixes persistence with business logic and cannot be reused or tested in isolation.
What happens with an empty list in an IN clause?It renders as in (), a SQL syntax error on MySQL. Guard for the empty case before calling.

Scenario 1 - One User Has Many Policies and Many Nominees

Two one-to-many relationships hanging off the same parent. This is where the individual mappings start combining into something that looks like a real application.

Business requirement: save one user's details with multiple policies and multiple nominees.
Problem statement: design the REST API to save one user with multiple policies and multiple nominees.

Table structure

     POLICY TABLE                              NOMINEE TABLE
   +----------------+                        +----------------+
   | id        (PK) |                        | id        (PK) |
   | policy_id      |                        | first_name     |
   | policy_name    |                        | last_name      |
   | status         |                        | relationship   |
   | user_id   (FK) |                        | user_id   (FK) |
   +----------------+                        +----------------+
           ^  M                                   M  ^
           |                                         |
           +--------------+     +--------------------+
                        1 |     | 1
                    +--------------+
                    |  USER TABLE  |
                    | id     (PK)  |
                    | name         |
                    | email        |
                    +--------------+

Both children carry user_id. The user carries neither - it holds two collections instead.

Scenario 1 - Saving the Whole Graph

The walkthrough saves the user, then loops over each list calling a separate service. With cascade = CascadeType.ALL on both collections, one save() does all of it - and one @Transactional makes it atomic.

Scenario 3 - One User Has Policies, Payment Modes, Premiums and Claims

The same pattern extended to four child collections, and this time we are reading rather than writing.

Business requirement: get one user's details together with their policies, payment modes, premiums and claims.

Table structure

  POLICY TABLE          M   1                1   M    PAYMENT_MODE TABLE
 +----------------+  <-----+                +----->  +------------------+
 | id        (PK) |        |                |        | id          (PK) |
 | policy_id      |        |                |        | payment_type     |
 | policy_name    |        |                |        | user_id     (FK) |
 | status         |     +--------------+    |        +------------------+
 | user_id   (FK) |     |  USER TABLE  |    |
 +----------------+     | id     (PK)  |----+
                        | name         |
  PREMIUM TABLE         | email        |         CLAIM TABLE
 +----------------+     +--------------+        +------------------+
 | id        (PK) |  <-----+        +----->     | id          (PK) |
 | premium_id     |     M  1        1   M       | claim_id         |
 | amount         |                             | claim_status     |
 | user_id   (FK) |                             | claim_amount     |
 +----------------+                             | user_id     (FK) |
                                                +------------------+

Scenario 3 - Assembling the Response

The original controller takes five path variables - a user id plus a policy id, premium id, claim id and payment-mode id - and then uses each of them to look up lists. That is one id too many for the job: everything already hangs off the user, so the user id alone is enough.

Original:  GET /user/getUser/{id}/{policyId}/{premiumId}/{claimId}/{paymentModeId}
           - five path variables, but the example calls it with four
             -> 404, because the pattern does not match the URL
           - each child list is fetched by its own id, then assigned
             to the user, and users.setId(...) overwrites the user's
             own id inside every loop

Corrected: GET /user/{id}/summary
           - one id, four lookups, one assembled response

expert.content:
Do Not Fetch Four Collections in One Query

Scenario 3 is the classic setup for a MultipleBagFetchException. The instinct is to replace five queries with one big join fetch. JPA refuses:

org.hibernate.loader.MultipleBagFetchException:
  cannot simultaneously fetch multiple bags:
  [com.velocity.model.User.policyList, com.velocity.model.User.premiumList]

And the refusal is doing you a favour. Joining two collections produces a cartesian product: 3 policies and 4 premiums return 12 rows, not 7. Add claims and payment modes and one user with a handful of children becomes hundreds of duplicated rows that Hibernate then has to de-duplicate in memory.

ApproachVerdict
One query with four join fetchThrows MultipleBagFetchException.
Change every List to SetCompiles and runs - and silently builds the cartesian product. Worse.
One query per collection (as above)Correct. Five small, indexed queries beat one enormous join.
@BatchSize on each collectionGood when loading many users - batches the child queries.

"Five queries" sounds worse than "one query" and is not. Each is a simple indexed lookup on user_id; the single join would transfer the user's row four times over.

Returning the Entity Is Wrong Here for Three Separate Reasons

Scenario 3's endpoint returns a User entity with four populated collections. Each problem below is independent, and a DTO fixes all three at once.

ProblemSymptom
Infinite recursionEach child has a user back-reference. Without @JsonIgnore: StackOverflowError during serialisation.
Lazy proxiesSerialising outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException - which is exactly what @JsonIgnoreProperties({"hibernateLazyInitializer","handler"}) is papering over in the original.
Mutating a managed entityuser.setPolicyList(...) on an entity inside a transaction makes Hibernate think the collection changed and can trigger unwanted DELETE/INSERT statements on flush.

That last one is the subtle one: assigning a new list to a managed entity's collection replaces the Hibernate-managed collection wrapper, and Hibernate treats that as "all old children removed, all new children added".

Designing the Endpoint: One Fat Response or Several?

Scenario 3 returns everything about a user in one call. Whether that is right depends on what the screen actually needs.

ShapeUse when
GET /users/{id}/summary - everythingOne screen shows all of it at once. Saves four round trips.
GET /users/{id}/policies - sub-resourcesEach list has its own screen, paging, or filters. Also lets the client cache each independently.
GET /users/{id}?include=policies,claimsClient picks what it needs. Flexible, more work to implement.

The one thing a fat endpoint must not do is return unbounded collections. A user with 5,000 claims makes this endpoint slow, memory-hungry, and eventually the cause of an outage. Either page the sub-resources, or cap what the summary returns.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you model one parent with two different child collections?Two @OneToMany(mappedBy = "...") fields on the parent, and a @ManyToOne back-reference on each child holding its own foreign key.
What must mappedBy name?The association field on the child - not the foreign-key column. Pointing it at an Integer userId field fails at startup.
Why is the foreign key NULL after a cascaded save?Only the parent's collection was populated. The child's @ManyToOne field is the owning side and must be set too.
What is MultipleBagFetchException?Hibernate refusing to join fetch two List collections at once, because the result would be a cartesian product.
Does changing List to Set fix it?It stops the exception and not the problem - the cartesian product is still built and de-duplicated in memory. Use one query per collection instead.
Is fetching four collections in four queries bad?No. Four indexed lookups on user_id are cheaper than one join that repeats the parent row for every combination.
What does @BatchSize do?Loads lazy collections for many parents in batches - where user_id in (?, ?, ...) - turning N+1 into roughly N/size + 1.
Why does @JsonIgnoreProperties({"hibernateLazyInitializer","handler"}) appear on these entities?It hides the synthetic fields Hibernate adds to a lazy proxy so Jackson does not try to serialise them. Returning a DTO removes the need for it.
Why is assigning a new list to a managed entity's collection risky?It replaces Hibernate's managed collection wrapper, so on flush Hibernate can delete all the old children and re-insert the new ones.
What is wrong with an endpoint returning every child collection?The response is unbounded - a parent with thousands of children makes it slow and memory-hungry. Page the sub-resources or cap the summary.
How does findByUserId work when the child maps a User object?Spring Data traverses the association - user then id - and generates where user_id = ?.

beginner.content:
Spring Boot JPA Mapping

• Spring Boot JPA is a Java specification for managing relational data in Java applications.
• It lets us access and persist data between a Java object/class and a relational database.
• JPA follows ORM - Object-Relational Mapping.

There are four types of mapping:

MappingMeaning
One to OneThe primary key of one table becomes the foreign key of another. Example: one user has one cart.
One to ManyOne row in a table maps to multiple rows in another. Example: one user has many policies.
Many to OneMultiple rows map to a single row in another table. Example: many employees have one address.
Many to ManyMultiple rows map to multiple rows in another table. Example: many users have many nominees.

1. One-to-One Mapping

The primary key of one table becomes the foreign key of another table.

Business requirement: save one user's details with one cart's details into the database.
Problem statement: design the REST API to save one user with one cart into the database.

Table structure

   USER TABLE                1        1        CART TABLE
 +--------------+          <-------->       +--------------+
 | id      (PK) |                           | cart_id (PK) |
 | name         |                           | cart_name    |
 | email        |                           +--------------+
 | cart_id (FK) |
 +--------------+
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
    <version>8.0.33</version>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Steps 4 to 7 - Service, Repository, Controller

Only User is saved. cascade = CascadeType.ALL means saving the user also saves the cart - there is no CartRepository call anywhere.
codeExamples:

beginner.content:
2. One-to-Many Mapping

One row in a table can be mapped to multiple rows in another table. Example: one user has multiple policies.

Business requirement: save one user's details with multiple policy details.
Problem statement: design the REST API to save one user with multiple policies.

Table structure

   USER TABLE                1        M        POLICY TABLE
 +--------------+          <-------->       +----------------+
 | id     (PK)  |                           | id        (PK) |
 | name         |                           | policy_id      |
 | email        |                           | policy_name    |
 +--------------+                           | status         |
                                            | user_id   (FK) |
                                            +----------------+

The foreign key always lives on the "many" side. A user cannot hold many policy ids in one column, so each policy row stores the id of its user.

One-to-Many - Service, Repository, Controller

Because the association cascades, one save() writes the user and every policy. The only thing you must remember is to set the back-reference so the foreign key is not null.

expert.content:
Owning Side vs Inverse Side - the Idea Behind mappedBy

A relational foreign key lives in exactly one column, on one table. A Java object graph has references on both sides. mappedBy is how you tell JPA which Java side corresponds to that single database column.

SideMarked byMeaning
Owning@JoinColumn, no mappedByHolds the foreign key. Changes to this side are what get written.
InversemappedBy = "fieldOnOwner"A read-only view of the same relationship. Changing it alone writes nothing.

This is why setting only the collection is the classic bug: the collection is the inverse side, so JPA ignores it when deciding what to write.

The Infinite JSON Loop

Map both directions and serialise an entity, and Jackson walks the graph forever: user -> policies -> user -> policies...

com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonMappingException:
  Infinite recursion (StackOverflowError)
  (through reference chain:
   com.velocity.model.User["policyList"]
     ->java.util.ArrayList[0]
       ->com.velocity.model.Policy["user"]
         ->com.velocity.model.User["policyList"]  ->  ...)
FixEffect
@JsonManagedReference / @JsonBackReferenceForward side is serialised; back side is skipped. The pair must match.
@JsonIgnore on the child's parent fieldSimplest. The child's user never appears in JSON.
@JsonIdentityInfoSerialises the repeat as an id instead of a nested object.
Return a DTOThe real fix - the loop cannot exist because the DTO has no back-reference.

The other annotation you will see in this material is @JsonIgnoreProperties({"hibernateLazyInitializer", "handler"}). That is a different problem: it hides the two synthetic fields Hibernate adds to a lazy proxy, which Jackson would otherwise try to serialise. A DTO removes the need for it as well.

Fetch Types - and the N+1 Problem

Each mapping annotation has a default fetch type, and the defaults are not consistent.

AnnotationDefault fetch
@OneToOneEAGER
@ManyToOneEAGER
@OneToManyLAZY
@ManyToManyLAZY

The "to-one" defaults are the dangerous ones. Every findAll() on Policy silently loads the User for each row - the N+1 select problem: one query for the list, then one more per row.

One-to-One: Which Table Gets the Foreign Key?

A one-to-one has a genuine choice, and the walkthrough's version puts cart_id on the user table. Three options exist.

StrategyHow
FK on the owner (used above)@JoinColumn(name = "cart_id") on User. Simple; add a UNIQUE constraint or it is really a many-to-one.
Shared primary key@MapsId - the cart's PK is the user's PK. No extra column, and genuinely one-to-one by construction.
Join table@JoinTable. Useful when the relationship is optional on both sides.

Without a UNIQUE constraint on cart_id, nothing stops two users pointing at the same cart - the database will happily allow it, and the mapping only claims to be one-to-one.

There is also a well-known wrinkle: an optional lazy @OneToOne on the inverse side cannot be made lazy. Hibernate must query to know whether to give you a proxy or null, so it queries every time. The shared-primary-key form avoids it.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the four JPA relationship types?@OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne and @ManyToMany.
In a one-to-many, which table holds the foreign key?The "many" table - a single column cannot hold many ids.
What does mappedBy do?Marks the side as inverse (read-only) and names the field on the owning entity that holds the foreign key.
What must mappedBy point at?An association field on the other entity, not a plain column. Pointing it at an Integer userid fails at startup.
Why is the foreign key null after saving a parent with children?Only the inverse collection was set. Set the owning side too - child.setParent(parent).
What does cascade = CascadeType.ALL do?Propagates persist, merge, remove, refresh and detach from the parent to the children, so one save() writes the whole graph.
What is orphanRemoval?Removing a child from the parent's collection deletes its row. Different from cascade REMOVE, which only fires when the parent is deleted.
Default fetch types?@OneToOne and @ManyToOne are EAGER; @OneToMany and @ManyToMany are LAZY.
What is the N+1 select problem?One query for a list, then one extra query per row for an eager association. Fix with join fetch or @EntityGraph.
What causes LazyInitializationException?Touching a lazy association after the persistence context has closed. Fetch it inside the transaction.
Why does a bidirectional mapping break JSON serialisation?Jackson follows both directions forever - infinite recursion. Fix with @JsonIgnore or, properly, by returning a DTO.
How do you guarantee a @OneToOne really is one-to-one?Add a UNIQUE constraint on the FK column, or use a shared primary key with @MapsId.

1. Many-to-One Mapping

Many-to-one means that multiple rows in a table can be mapped to a single row in another table.

Example: many employees have one address.

Business requirement: save many employee details with one address into the database.
Problem statement: design the REST API to save multiple employees with one address.

Table structure

  EMPLOYEE TABLE            M        1        ADDRESS TABLE
 +-----------------+       <-------->       +----------------+
 | id         (PK) |                        | id        (PK) |
 | first_name      |                        | address_line   |
 | last_name       |                        | city           |
 | city            |                        | state          |
 | address_id (FK) |                        | country        |
 +-----------------+                        +----------------+

Many-to-one is simply the other end of a one-to-many. The same foreign key column, address_id, serves both views: @ManyToOne on Employee owns it, @OneToMany(mappedBy = "address") on Address reads it.

Many-to-One - Service, Repository, Controller

Two entities, so two repositories and two services. The controller receives an Address carrying its employees, saves the address, then links each employee to it.

2. Many-to-Many Mapping

Many-to-many means multiple rows in a table can be mapped to multiple rows in another table.

Example: one user has many nominees, and many nominees belong to one user.

Business requirement: save multiple user details with multiple nominee details.
Problem statement: design the REST API to save users with their nominees.

Table structure - note the third table

   USER TABLE          USER_NOMINEE (join table)      NOMINEE TABLE
 +------------+        +--------------------+        +------------+
 | id   (PK)  | <----- | user_id     (FK)   |        | id   (PK)  |
 | name       |        | nominee_id  (FK)   | -----> | name       |
 | email      |        +--------------------+        +------------+
 +------------+

A many-to-many cannot be stored with a single foreign key on either side, so it always needs a join table holding one row per pairing.

Many-to-Many - Repository, Service, Controller

Both ids are declared long, so both repositories take Long.

expert.content:
Why Set and Not List for Many-to-Many

The example declares Set<Nominee>, and that is not a style preference.

With a List, removing one element from a many-to-many collection makes Hibernate delete every join-table row for that owner and re-insert the survivors. With 50 nominees, removing one produces 50 deletes and 49 inserts.

A Set has no ordering to maintain, so Hibernate issues a single targeted delete.

CollectionRemoving one element from 50
List1 bulk DELETE + 49 INSERTs
Set1 DELETE

Using a Set means the entity needs sane equals() and hashCode(). The rule: never use the generated id - it is null before the entity is saved, so the object's hash changes after insertion and it is lost inside the HashSet. Use a business key, or the pattern below.

CascadeType.ALL on a Many-to-Many Is Almost Always Wrong

ALL includes REMOVE. On a many-to-many that means deleting a user deletes the nominee rows themselves - including nominees shared with other users.

When to Replace @ManyToMany With Two @OneToMany

A plain @ManyToMany gives you a join table with exactly two columns. The moment the relationship needs an attribute of its own - a date, a status, a percentage - that shape stops working.

Question about the pairingVerdict
Does it need any extra column?Replace with an explicit join entity.
Does it need its own id or audit fields?Replace.
Do you ever query the pairings directly?Replace.
Purely "which of these link to which"?@ManyToMany is fine.

Nominees are a good example of the first case: real insurance nominees carry a relationship type and a share percentage, neither of which fits in a two-column join table.

Reading the Four Mappings Off the Schema

Once the foreign keys are drawn, the annotations follow mechanically.

ONE-TO-ONE          FK on either table, with a UNIQUE constraint
  user.cart_id -> cart.id  UNIQUE
      User:  @OneToOne @JoinColumn(name="cart_id")
      Cart:  @OneToOne(mappedBy="cart")

ONE-TO-MANY / MANY-TO-ONE     FK on the MANY table
  policy.user_id -> user.id
      Policy: @ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name="user_id")     <- owner
      User:   @OneToMany(mappedBy="user")                <- inverse

MANY-TO-MANY        a JOIN TABLE with two FKs
  user_nominee(user_id, nominee_id)
      User:    @ManyToMany @JoinTable(...)               <- owner
      Nominee: @ManyToMany(mappedBy="nominees")          <- inverse
MappingOwning sideWhere the FK lives
@OneToOneWhichever declares @JoinColumnThat entity's table
@OneToMany / @ManyToOneAlways the @ManyToOne sideThe "many" table
@ManyToManyWhichever declares @JoinTableA separate join table

A unidirectional @OneToMany without mappedBy is a trap: with no @ManyToOne on the child, JPA creates a join table even though a plain foreign key would do, and updates it with extra statements. Add @JoinColumn to force the foreign-key form, or make the association bidirectional.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Difference between @OneToMany and @ManyToOne?Two views of the same foreign key. @ManyToOne sits on the child and owns the FK column; @OneToMany sits on the parent with mappedBy and is the inverse view.
Why does a many-to-many need a join table?Neither table can hold many foreign keys in one column, so the pairings live in a separate two-column table.
What do joinColumns and inverseJoinColumns mean?In @JoinTable, joinColumns is the FK back to the owning entity; inverseJoinColumns is the FK to the other entity.
Which side should declare @JoinTable?Only the owning side. Declaring it on both creates two join tables.
Why use Set rather than List for @ManyToMany?With a List, removing one element makes Hibernate delete and re-insert every join row for that owner. A Set issues one targeted delete.
What is the rule for equals/hashCode on a JPA entity?Never base hashCode on a generated id - it is null before insert, so the object is lost inside a HashSet. Use a business key or a constant hashCode.
Why is CascadeType.ALL dangerous on @ManyToMany?It includes REMOVE, so deleting one owner deletes shared rows on the other side. Cascade only PERSIST and MERGE.
How do you remove just the association?Remove the element from both collections. Only the join-table row is deleted; the entity rows survive.
When should @ManyToMany become two @OneToMany?As soon as the relationship needs its own attributes - a date, status, or percentage - or you need to query the pairings directly.
What happens with a unidirectional @OneToMany and no @JoinColumn?JPA silently creates a join table instead of using a foreign key. Add @JoinColumn, or make it bidirectional.
Default fetch type for @ManyToOne?EAGER - the usual source of N+1 selects. Set it to LAZY and fetch deliberately.

Two-Table Join Operation

Business requirement: you have two tables and want to fetch data from both. In that case we go with the join approach.

Problem statement: design the REST API to return this response, built from two tables:

empDept  •  empDeptDesc  •  empName  •  empEmail  •  empAddress

Table structure

  EMPLOYEE TABLE            M        1        DEPARTMENT TABLE
 +---------------+        <-------->        +-----------------+
 | id       (PK) |                          | id         (PK) |
 | name          |                          | name            |
 | email         |                          | description     |
 | address       |                          +-----------------+
 | dept_id  (FK) |
 +---------------+

Notice that the five fields we want come from both tables and match neither entity. That is what a DTO is for: a class shaped like the answer rather than like a table.

beginner.content:
Step 4 - The DTO Class

The DTO holds exactly the five fields the response needs. Its constructor is what the query calls, so the parameter order must match the SELECT list exactly.

Step 7 - The Repository: select new

This is the key line of the whole topic. JPQL's select new constructs a DTO per result row, so the query returns List<DeptEmpDto> directly - no manual mapping, and only the five needed columns are fetched.

PartMeaning
select new com.velocity.dto.DeptEmpDto(...)The fully qualified class name. A short name will not resolve.
FROM Department d INNER JOIN d.employees eJoins through the mapped association, so no ON clause is needed - JPA already knows the foreign key.
d.name, d.description, e.name, e.email, e.addressFive values, matching the five constructor parameters in order.

Three-Table Join Operation

Business requirement: fetch data from three tables.

Problem statement: return empDept, empDeptDesc, empName, empEmail, empAddress and courseName.

Table structure

  EMPLOYEE TABLE       M   1   DEPARTMENT TABLE   1   M    COURSE TABLE
 +---------------+   <------  +----------------+  ------>  +---------------+
 | id       (PK) |            | id        (PK) |           | id       (PK) |
 | name          |            | name           |           | course_name   |
 | email         |            | description    |           | dept_id  (FK) |
 | address       |            +----------------+           +---------------+
 | dept_id  (FK) |
 +---------------+

Department sits in the middle: employees hang off it on one side, courses on the other. Both joins go through Department.

expert.content:
The Three-Table Join Multiplies Rows

Look again at that response. One employee appeared twice, because the department has two courses. That is not a bug in the query - it is what a join does.

Department "Engineering"
    3 employees  x  2 courses  =  6 result rows

Every employee is repeated once per course, and every course
is repeated once per employee. The two collections have nothing
to do with each other - joining them produces a CARTESIAN PRODUCT.

With 10 employees and 5 courses you get 50 rows to convey 15 facts. The join is only meaningful when the two child sets are genuinely related - and here they are not.

What you actually wantHow to get it
Employees, each with their department nameOne join. Employee -> Department is many-to-one, so no multiplication.
Departments, each with its employees and its coursesTwo separate queries, assembled into a nested DTO.
Every valid (employee, course) pairingThe cartesian join is correct - if that is the question.

INNER JOIN Silently Drops Rows

Both examples use INNER JOIN, which returns only rows that have a match on both sides. A department with no employees vanishes from the result entirely - and nothing tells you it happened.

Join typeReturns
INNER JOINOnly rows matching on both sides.
LEFT JOINEvery row from the left side; nulls where the right has no match.
RIGHT JOINEvery row from the right side. Rare in JPQL.

"List all departments and their employee count" needs a LEFT JOIN, or every empty department disappears from the report.

JOIN vs JOIN FETCH - Two Different Jobs

Both put a join in the SQL. They differ in what comes back, and mixing them up is a common source of confusion.

JOINJOIN FETCH
PurposeFilter or project across tablesLoad an association eagerly, for this query only
ReturnsWhatever the SELECT names - scalars or a DTOFully-populated entities
Works with select newYesNo - fetch and projection are incompatible
Works with PageableYesWarns and paginates in memory for collections
Typical useBuilding a report DTOAvoiding N+1 when you need the entities

That fourth row is worth remembering. join fetch on a collection plus Pageable produces:

HHH000104: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch;
           applying in memory!

Hibernate loads every matching row and pages the list in Java. On a large table this is exactly the outage you were trying to avoid.

Three Ways to Project, and When to Use Each

select new is one option. Spring Data offers two more, and each has a case where it is clearly the best fit.

ApproachStrengthWeakness
Constructor expression (select new)Explicit, works with any JPA provider, immutable resultFully-qualified class name in a string; refactoring can break it silently
Interface projectionNo class name in the query, no constructor to keep in syncSpring Data only; getter names must match the aliases
Native query + interfaceFull SQL power with typed resultsNot portable across databases

Interface projections are the lightest to maintain: declare an interface of getters, and Spring Data builds the proxy. Renaming the DTO cannot break a query string, because there is no class name in it.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a DTO projection and why use one?A class shaped like the response rather than like a table. It fetches only the needed columns and keeps the entity out of the API.
What does select new do in JPQL?Calls a constructor once per result row, so the query returns a list of DTOs directly.
What must you get right in a constructor expression?The fully qualified class name, and the parameter order and types matching the SELECT list exactly.
Why does INNER JOIN d.employees e need no ON clause?It joins through a mapped association, so JPA already knows the foreign key and writes the ON clause itself.
What is wrong with INNER JOIN Course c ON c.id = d.id?It joins two unrelated primary keys. The relationship is course.dept_id -> department.id; join through the association instead.
Why does joining two collections duplicate rows?It builds a cartesian product - every employee is repeated once per course. Use separate queries and a nested DTO.
INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN?INNER returns only matched rows, so a department with no employees disappears. LEFT keeps it, with nulls on the right.
Difference between JOIN and JOIN FETCH?JOIN is for filtering and projection; JOIN FETCH eagerly loads an association and returns entities. They cannot be combined with select new.
What happens when you paginate a collection JOIN FETCH?Hibernate warns HHH000104 and paginates in memory - every row is loaded first. Paginate a projection instead.
What is an interface projection?An interface of getters that Spring Data implements as a proxy. The query aliases must match the getter names.
How do you fix N+1 on a many-to-one?Make it LAZY and use join fetch or @EntityGraph where the association is actually needed.
Can mappedBy point at an id field?No - it must name an association field. mappedBy = "id" fails at startup.
