Beyond Mapping: What This Topic Adds

By now an entity maps to a table, a repository writes queries from method names, and a join pulls two tables together. This topic covers the parts of JPA that appear once an application is actually in production: fields that must not be persisted, enums stored safely, hooks that run around a save, columns that fill themselves in, and queries built at runtime rather than declared at compile time.

FeaturePurpose
@TransientKeep a field in the Java object but out of the table.
@EnumeratedDecide HOW an enum is written to its column - and the default is the wrong choice.
Lifecycle callbacksRun code at defined moments: before insert, after load, before delete.
JPA auditingFill createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy automatically.
PagingAndSortingRepositoryThe layer of the repository hierarchy that supplies Pageable and Sort.
SpecificationBuild a WHERE clause at runtime from whichever filters the caller actually supplied.

1. @Transient - A Field That Is Not a Column

By default JPA maps every non-static, non-final field of an entity to a column. A field that is derived, cached in memory, or holds a value that has no business being in the database must be marked @Transient, otherwise Hibernate tries to create a column for it and the application fails at startup against a fixed schema.

Two annotations share that name and they are not interchangeable:

AnnotationMeaning
jakarta.persistence.TransientThe JPA one. "Do not map this field to a column." This is the one you almost always want.
Java's transient keywordExcludes a field from Java serialization. JPA also honours it, which is why the two get confused - but it changes serialization behaviour as a side effect.

A transient field is not repopulated when an entity is loaded from the database, so anything derived from persistent state has to be computed - typically in a @PostLoad callback.

2. @Enumerated - and Why ORDINAL Corrupts Data

An enum has to be turned into something a column can hold. JPA offers two strategies, and the default is ORDINAL, which stores the enum constant's position as an integer: 0, 1, 2.

That position is not part of the enum's meaning. It is an accident of the order somebody typed the constants in. The day a developer inserts a new constant in the middle - a completely reasonable edit that compiles, passes review, and passes every test - every existing row in the database silently changes meaning.

VERSION 1 of the enum          Rows written by version 1
  ACTIVE    -> 0                  id=1  status=0   (ACTIVE)
  SUSPENDED -> 1                  id=2  status=1   (SUSPENDED)
  CLOSED    -> 2                  id=3  status=2   (CLOSED)

Someone adds PENDING in alphabetical-ish order:

VERSION 2 of the enum          The SAME rows, re-read by version 2
  ACTIVE    -> 0                  id=1  status=0   ACTIVE     (still right)
  PENDING   -> 1                  id=2  status=1   PENDING    <-- was SUSPENDED
  SUSPENDED -> 2                  id=3  status=2   SUSPENDED  <-- was CLOSED
  CLOSED    -> 3

No exception. No error log. No failing test. Closed accounts are now
suspended, and suspended accounts are now pending approval.

There is no migration that can repair this afterwards, because nothing in the database records which version of the enum wrote which row. Always write @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING). The column then holds 'SUSPENDED', which means the same thing regardless of declaration order, and is readable to anyone querying the table directly.

The cost is a few bytes per row and a slightly wider index. That is not a trade worth having.

3. Entity Lifecycle Callbacks

JPA lets a method run at defined points in an entity's life. The method must return void, take no arguments, and live either on the entity itself or on a separate listener class registered with @EntityListeners.

CallbackWhen it fires
@PrePersistBefore the INSERT, when the entity becomes managed. The id is usually still null here.
@PostPersistAfter the INSERT. The generated id is now populated.
@PreUpdateBefore an UPDATE - and only if dirty checking found something actually changed.
@PostUpdateAfter the UPDATE statement is issued.
@PreRemoveBefore the DELETE. The last chance to read the row's state.
@PostRemoveAfter the DELETE.
@PostLoadAfter the entity is loaded or refreshed from the database.

The rule callbacks come with: never call a repository, an EntityManager, or anything that touches the database from inside a callback. You are running in the middle of a flush; issuing another query there produces undefined behaviour and, in Hibernate, often a ConcurrentModificationException or a silent lost write. Keep callbacks to setting fields on this.

@PreUpdate is worth a second look: it does not run because you called save(). It runs because the flush found a changed field. If nothing changed, no UPDATE is issued and no callback fires.

4. JPA Auditing - Stop Writing the Same Four Fields

Almost every table wants to know when a row was created, when it last changed, and who did it. Writing that by hand in every entity is repetitive and easy to forget on the one entity that later matters. Spring Data supplies it declaratively.

Four pieces have to be in place:

PieceResponsibility
@EnableJpaAuditingOn a configuration class. Without it the annotations are inert and the columns stay null - by far the most common auditing bug.
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)On the entity (or its mapped superclass). This is the listener that does the work.
@CreatedDate / @LastModifiedDate / @CreatedBy / @LastModifiedByOn the fields to populate.
AuditorAware<T> beanAnswers "who is the current user?" Required only for the @CreatedBy / @LastModifiedBy pair.

Put the four fields in a @MappedSuperclass and every entity inherits them by extending one class. A @MappedSuperclass is not an entity and gets no table of its own - its fields simply become columns on each subclass's table.

AuditorAware returns an Optional deliberately: during startup data loading, a scheduled job, or a health check there is no logged-in user, and the correct answer is "nobody" rather than a crash.

5. The Repository Hierarchy and PagingAndSortingRepository

JpaRepository is the one everybody extends, but it is the bottom of a chain, and each level exists so you can expose less when you want to.

Repository<T, ID>                    marker interface, no methods
      |
CrudRepository<T, ID>                save, findById, findAll, delete, count, existsById
      |
ListCrudRepository<T, ID>            same, but returns List instead of Iterable
      |
PagingAndSortingRepository<T, ID>    findAll(Pageable), findAll(Sort)
      |
JpaRepository<T, ID>                 + flush(), saveAndFlush(), deleteAllInBatch(),
                                       getReferenceById()

  ... and orthogonal to the chain:
JpaSpecificationExecutor<T>          findAll(Specification), count(Specification)

Note the shape change in Spring Data 3.x: PagingAndSortingRepository no longer extends CrudRepository. It is a standalone interface, so a repository that needs both now extends both. Code written against Spring Boot 2.x that extends only PagingAndSortingRepository and calls save() stops compiling on the upgrade.

Page versus Slice is the other choice worth making deliberately: Page issues a second COUNT query to report the total, Slice does not and only knows whether a next page exists. On a large table that COUNT is often the slower half of the request.

6. Specifications - a WHERE Clause Built at Runtime

A search screen with five optional filters cannot be served by derived query methods: five optional filters is thirty-two possible WHERE clauses. A Specification is a small object representing one predicate, and predicates compose with and / or. Null ones are skipped, which is what makes optional filters work.

The repository has to extend JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> alongside JpaRepository; that is what supplies findAll(Specification), findAll(Specification, Pageable) and count(Specification).

A specification is a lambda with three parameters:

ParameterWhat it is
rootThe entity being queried. root.get("city") names a field; root.join("department") walks an association.
queryThe whole query, for distinct(), orderBy(), or subqueries. Frequently unused.
cb (CriteriaBuilder)The factory for predicates: equal, like, greaterThan, between, in, isNull.

Field names inside root.get("...") are strings, so a rename refactor will not update them. They fail at runtime, not at compile time - the JPA metamodel (Employee_.city) exists to fix exactly that and is worth generating on any project that leans on specifications heavily.

expert.content:
Dirty Checking - Why an Update Happens Without save()

This is the single most surprising thing JPA does, and the source of both the "I never saved it and it saved" bug and the "I called save() and nothing happened" bug.

Inside a transaction, every entity loaded through the EntityManager is managed. The persistence context keeps two things for each one: the object you hold a reference to, and a snapshot of the field values as they were when it was loaded. At flush - triggered before a query that could be affected, and always at commit - Hibernate compares every managed entity against its snapshot and issues an UPDATE for each field that differs.

@Transactional
public void raise(Long id) {
    Employee e = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();   // MANAGED + snapshot taken
    e.setSalary(e.getSalary() * 1.10);              // only the Java object changes
}                                                   // COMMIT -> flush -> compare

  persistence context
  +-----------------------------------------------+
  | Employee#7  -> object   { salary = 66000 }     |
  |             -> snapshot { salary = 60000 }     |
  +-----------------------------------------------+
                     |
              differ? yes
                     v
  Hibernate: update employee set salary=? where id=?

There is no save() in that method. There does not need to be one.

The corollary matters just as much: an entity outside a transaction, or one you constructed with new, is detached. Nothing tracks it, and no amount of setter calls will write anything. save() on a detached entity with an id performs a merge: it loads the current row, copies your fields onto the managed copy, and returns that - which is why save()'s return value, not the argument, is the object you should keep using.

Optimistic Locking - the Lost Update, Concretely

Two users open the same record, both edit it, both save. Without locking, one of those edits vanishes and nobody is told. This is the lost update problem, and it is not prevented by a transaction - both transactions are perfectly serialisable on their own.

           STOCK ROW: product 42, quantity = 10

  Session A (warehouse)              Session B (returns desk)
  ---------------------              ------------------------
  t1  select quantity -> 10
  t2                                 select quantity -> 10
  t3  ships 3 -> sets 7
  t4  update stock set qty=7
  t5  COMMIT                         (row is now 7)
  t6                                 receives 2 -> sets 12
  t7                                 update stock set qty=12
  t8                                 COMMIT

           FINAL: quantity = 12.  Correct answer: 9.
  Session A's shipment was silently overwritten. No error anywhere.

Optimistic locking fixes this with one extra column. Add @Version to an integer or timestamp field; Hibernate then appends the version to every UPDATE's WHERE clause and increments it:

update stock set quantity=?, version=version+1
 where id=? and version=?      <-- the version READ at the start

Session A: where id=42 and version=0  -> 1 row updated  -> version becomes 1
Session B: where id=42 and version=0  -> 0 rows updated
                                          |
                    Hibernate sees rowCount 0 and throws
                    ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException

Nothing is locked. The check is deferred to the moment of writing, which is why it costs nothing when there is no contention - and that is the normal case. The application's job is to catch the failure and decide: retry, or show the user "this record changed while you were editing it".

Never expose @Version only server-side in a stateless API. If the client does not send back the version it read, you have reintroduced the lost update through the back door.

Pessimistic Locking - and the Price It Charges

Optimistic locking detects a conflict after the fact. Pessimistic locking prevents one by taking a database lock on the row at read time, so the second reader waits. It is the right answer when conflicts are frequent enough that retrying is wasteful, or when the work between read and write cannot be repeated.

ModeEffect
PESSIMISTIC_READA shared lock. Others may read, nobody may write. SQL: for share / lock in share mode.
PESSIMISTIC_WRITEAn exclusive lock. Nobody else may read-for-update or write. SQL: for update. This is the one you normally want.
PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENTExclusive lock and bumps the @Version, so optimistic readers elsewhere also notice.
OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENTBumps the version even if nothing on the entity changed - used to mark a parent as modified when only a child changed.

Two risks come with it, and both bite in production rather than in testing:

Deadlock. Transaction 1 locks row A then wants B; transaction 2 locks B then wants A. Neither can proceed. The database detects the cycle and kills one of them - a real error the application must handle. Prevention is discipline: always acquire locks in a deterministic order, typically ascending primary key.
Timeout and queueing. A lock held across a slow operation serialises every request behind it. The default wait in MySQL InnoDB is 50 seconds; long before that, the connection pool is exhausted and the whole application stops responding, not merely the one endpoint.

Rules of thumb: hold the lock for as short a time as possible, never across a remote call, and always set an explicit timeout so a stuck transaction fails fast instead of parking a connection.

Choosing Between the Two

Optimistic (@Version)Pessimistic (@Lock)
When the check happensAt write time, by row countAt read time, by database lock
Cost with no contentionEffectively zeroA real lock, held to commit
Cost with contentionWasted work, then a retryWaiting, then correct work
Scales across nodesYes - the version is in the rowYes, but the database becomes the bottleneck
Survives a user thinkingYes - the version travels in the DTONo - you cannot hold a lock across an HTTP round trip
Failure modeOptimisticLockException / 409Lock timeout, deadlock, pool exhaustion
Right forWeb edits, rare collisions, anything user-facingInventory decrements, ledger postings, job claiming

The default should be optimistic. Reach for pessimistic when the read-modify-write must be atomic and conflicts are common - decrementing stock under flash-sale traffic is the textbook case, where an optimistic approach would fail and retry so often it becomes a livelock.

There is a third answer that beats both when it applies: don't read at all. update stock set quantity = quantity - ? where product_id = ? and quantity >= ? is a single atomic statement; a row count of 0 means insufficient stock. No locking strategy needed - the database already serialises the write.

Criteria API vs Specifications - the Same Engine, Different Ergonomics

A Specification is not an alternative to the Criteria API; it is a thin, composable wrapper over it. Its toPredicate method receives exactly the Criteria objects you would otherwise build yourself. The difference is entirely in how much ceremony you write and whether the pieces can be reused.

AspectRaw Criteria APISpecification
Lines for a 3-filter searchRoughly 25, plus a separate count queryRoughly 5, count handled for you
ComposabilityManual list of predicates, joined by hand.and() / .or() / .not(), nulls skipped
PaginationWrite the COUNT query separately and keep it in syncfindAll(spec, pageable)
Type safetySame string-or-metamodel choiceSame string-or-metamodel choice
Reuse across queriesNone - it is one method bodyEach predicate is a named, testable static method
Reach for it whenBuilding the query structure itself is dynamic - dynamic SELECT, dynamic grouping, subqueriesThe structure is fixed and only the WHERE varies

The honest summary: raw Criteria is verbose enough that teams avoid it, then reach for string concatenation into JPQL - which is how SQL injection gets into an ORM-based application. Specifications keep the safety and remove most of the verbosity. Where the query structure genuinely varies, jOOQ or QueryDSL are more pleasant than either.

@EntityGraph vs join fetch

Both solve N+1 by loading associations in the same query. They differ in where the decision lives and in what they can express.

join fetch@EntityGraph
Expressed inThe JPQL stringAn annotation, or a named graph on the entity
Works on derived query methodsNo - requires @QueryYes - annotate findAll() or any derived method
Join typeWhatever you write - inner or leftAlways a LEFT OUTER JOIN
Can add a WHERE on the fetched sideYes (with care - it filters the collection)No
Reusable across methodsNoYes, via @NamedEntityGraph
Same collection-pagination problemYesYes - identical HHH000104 behaviour

The FETCH vs LOAD distinction is the part usually missed. EntityGraphType.FETCH (the default) treats every attribute not in the graph as LAZY, overriding the entity's mapping. EntityGraphType.LOAD loads the graph's attributes eagerly and leaves everything else at its declared fetch type. If a mapping is EAGER and a FETCH graph omits it, that association becomes lazy for that query - which surprises people.

The rule that avoids all of this: map every association LAZY, then declare eagerness per query with join fetch or @EntityGraph. Fetch strategy is a property of the use case, never of the entity.

Neither fixes the multi-collection problem: fetching two collections in one query is a cartesian product, and Hibernate 6 will reject it with MultipleBagFetchException if both are List. Use Set, or split into two queries and let the persistence context stitch them together.

Persistence Context Mechanics Worth Knowing

BehaviourWhat it means in practice
First-level cacheTwo findById(1L) calls in one transaction issue ONE select and return the identical object reference. == is true. This cache is not optional and cannot be disabled.
Repeatable reads within the contextIf another transaction changed the row after your first read, your second findById still returns the OLD state - it never reaches the database. em.refresh() is the only way back.
Write-behindStatements are queued and issued at flush, not at the setter. This lets Hibernate batch and reorder them, and is why the SQL log order rarely matches the code order.
Bulk updates bypass itA @Modifying JPQL update goes straight to the database. Entities already loaded are now stale. Always use clearAutomatically = true.
getReferenceById returns a proxyNo SELECT is issued. Ideal for setting a foreign key without loading the parent - but touching any field outside a transaction gives LazyInitializationException, and a missing id gives EntityNotFoundException later, not immediately.
Size mattersEvery managed entity is dirty-checked at every flush. Loading 200,000 rows in one transaction makes each flush O(200,000). Batch jobs must clear() periodically.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is @Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL) dangerous?It stores the enum's declaration position. Inserting or reordering a constant silently changes the meaning of every existing row - no exception, no failing test, and no way to repair it afterwards. Always use STRING.
What does @Transient do, and how is it different from Java's transient?@Transient excludes a field from the database mapping only. The keyword excludes it from Java serialization and, as a side effect, from JPA too. Use the annotation.
Why must a lifecycle callback never call a repository?It runs in the middle of a flush. Issuing another query there gives undefined behaviour - typically ConcurrentModificationException or a silently lost write. Publish a domain event and act after commit.
My @CreatedDate columns are all null. Why?@EnableJpaAuditing is missing, or the entity lacks @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class). The annotations compile happily and do nothing without both.
Why does AuditorAware return an Optional?Because there is often no current user - startup seeding, scheduled jobs, async threads. Empty means "leave the column null" rather than throwing.
An entity is loaded in a @Transactional method and a setter is called, with no save(). Is it written?Yes. The entity is managed, and at flush Hibernate compares it to the snapshot taken at load and issues an UPDATE for the changed fields. This is dirty checking.
The same code without @Transactional?Nothing is written. The entity is detached the moment the repository's own short transaction ends, so nothing tracks the change.
What is the lost-update problem?Two transactions read the same row, both compute a new value from it, and both write. The second overwrites the first, no error is raised, and one user's change is gone.
How does @Version prevent it?The version is appended to the UPDATE's WHERE clause and incremented. The second writer's UPDATE matches zero rows; Hibernate sees the row count and throws OptimisticLockException / ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.
What HTTP status suits an optimistic lock failure?409 Conflict, with a message telling the user to reload. The version must round-trip through the DTO or an ETag, or the check is bypassed entirely.
When is pessimistic locking the right choice?When the read-modify-write must be atomic and conflicts are frequent enough that optimistic retries become livelock - stock decrements under heavy traffic, ledger postings, job claiming.
What are the two risks of PESSIMISTIC_WRITE?Deadlock, when two transactions take the same locks in opposite orders - prevented by always locking in ascending id order; and lock queueing, which exhausts the connection pool and takes down the whole application, not just one endpoint.
How is a Specification related to the Criteria API?It is a composable wrapper over it. toPredicate receives the same Root, CriteriaQuery and CriteriaBuilder; the gain is reusable named predicates, null-skipping composition, and a count query you do not have to write twice.
@EntityGraph versus join fetch?Same SQL goal. @EntityGraph works on derived methods, is reusable as a named graph, and is always a LEFT OUTER JOIN; join fetch lets you choose the join type and add conditions. Both paginate collections in memory.

Spring Boot - Multiple Data Source Working

A Spring Boot application is not limited to one database. It can hold a separate connection to each schema, each with its own pool, its own Hibernate session factory and its own transactions.

Business Requirement

Suppose you want to store the user data and the policy data in different schemas. One application, two databases. That is what the multiple data source configuration is for.

Problem Statement

1.1 Design the RESTful web service to store the user data into the datasource1 schema
1.2 Design the RESTful web service to store the policy data into the datasource2 schema

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot Starter project
2. Add the Maven dependencies to pom.xml
3. Create the model classes - one package per database
4. Create the service interfaces
5. Create the service implementations
6. Create the repositories - one package per database
7. Create the REST controllers
8. Create the database configuration classes
9. Write the application.properties file
10. Run the Spring Boot application
11. Open Postman and send the requests
12. Go to the database and check the rows

The one thing that makes this different from every earlier example: the moment you define your own DataSource bean, Spring Boot's auto-configuration steps aside and you become responsible for the whole chain of beans behind it.
codeExamples:
Package Structure

com.velocity
 |
 +-- SpringBootMultipleDataSourceApplication.java
 |
 +-- config
 |    +-- UserDBConfig.java          <- datasource1  (@Primary)
 |    +-- PolicyDBConfig.java        <- datasource2
 |
 +-- model
 |    +-- user
 |    |    +-- User.java             <- scanned by the USER entity manager
 |    +-- policy
 |         +-- Policy.java           <- scanned by the POLICY entity manager
 |
 +-- user
 |    +-- repository
 |         +-- UserRepository.java   <- scanned by @EnableJpaRepositories (user)
 |
 +-- policy
 |    +-- repository
 |         +-- PolicyRepository.java <- scanned by @EnableJpaRepositories (policy)
 |
 +-- service
 |    +-- userservice
 |    |    +-- UserService.java / UserServiceImpl.java
 |    +-- policyservice
 |         +-- PolicyService.java / PolicyServiceImpl.java
 |
 +-- controller
      +-- usercontroller/UserController.java
      +-- policycontroller/PolicyController.java

// The package split is NOT cosmetic. Each configuration class points at
// exactly one entity package and one repository package. If two databases
// share a package, the configuration cannot tell them apart.

beginner.content:
Steps 1 and 2 - Project and Dependencies

Create the project with File -> New -> Spring Starter Project, enter the name and artifact, then accept the defaults.

Nothing here is special to multiple databases - spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, spring-boot-starter-web and the MySQL driver are the same dependencies a single-database project uses. The difference is entirely in the configuration classes.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
    <version>8.0.33</version>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

<!-- The PDF also lists spring-boot-starter-tomcat with <scope>provided</scope>.
     That scope is for building a WAR to deploy on an external Tomcat. If you
     run this as an executable jar, "provided" removes the embedded server and
     the application starts and exits immediately with no port open. Leave the
     tomcat dependency out entirely - spring-boot-starter-web already brings it. -->

beginner.content:
Step 3 - Model Classes

Two entities, and - this is the part that matters - two different packages. User lives in com.velocity.model.user, Policy in com.velocity.model.policy. Each entity manager is told to scan exactly one of those packages.

The entities themselves are ordinary JPA classes. There is no annotation on an entity that says which database it belongs to; the mapping is made by the package it sits in.

Steps 4 and 5 - Services

Two interfaces and two implementations. Neither one knows anything about data sources - they call a repository and the repository has already been bound to the right database by the configuration class.

That is the point of the whole exercise: the multi-database wiring stays in the configuration layer and the business code stays unaware of it.

Step 6 - Repositories

Two JpaRepository interfaces in two separate packages. Note the ID type: both entities declare private int id, so the repository parameter is Integer - the boxed form of the field's type. Getting this wrong (JpaRepository<User, Long> against an int id) produces a startup failure rather than a compile error, which makes it harder to spot.

Step 7 - REST Controllers

One POST endpoint per database. /saveUser ends up in datasource1, /savePolicy in datasource2, and neither controller contains a single line that says so.

Step 8 - The Database Configuration Classes

This is the heart of the topic. Each database needs three beans, and one of the two sets must be marked @Primary.

BeanPurpose
DataSourceThe connection pool - URL, credentials, driver, pool size.
LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBeanThe Hibernate session factory. It is told which entity packages to scan and which dialect and DDL mode to use.
PlatformTransactionManagerBegins, commits and rolls back transactions on that one entity manager.

@EnableJpaRepositories then ties a repository package to that entity manager and that transaction manager. Read it as: "the repositories in this package are backed by that entity manager".

Step 9 - application.properties

Two prefixes, spring.user.datasource and spring.policy.datasource, each bound to its own DataSource by @ConfigurationProperties.

Two details bite everybody the first time.

DetailWhy
jdbcUrl, not urlDataSourceBuilder produces a HikariDataSource, and Hikari's setter is setJdbcUrl. Writing spring.user.datasource.url leaves the URL null and startup fails with jdbcUrl is required with driverClassName.
spring.jpa.* is ignoredThose keys are read by Spring Boot's auto-configured entity manager. You built yours by hand, so only the HashMap in the config class is applied.
codeExamples:
# Step 9 - application.properties

#MYSQL - user schema (primary)
spring.user.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/datasource1?useSSL=false&serverTimezone=UTC
spring.user.datasource.username=root
spring.user.datasource.password=root
spring.user.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver

#MYSQL - policy schema (secondary)
spring.policy.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/datasource2?useSSL=false&serverTimezone=UTC
spring.policy.datasource.username=root
spring.policy.datasource.password=root
spring.policy.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver

# These three are inert in this project - kept only because the PDF has them.
# A hand-built LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean does not read spring.jpa.*
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# Corrections against the PDF:
#   com.mysql.jdbc.Driver  ->  com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
#   The old class is deprecated in Connector/J 8 and logs:
#     "Loading class 'com.mysql.jdbc.Driver'. This is deprecated. The new
#      driver class is 'com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver'."
#
#   The PDF also sets:
#     spring.autoconfigure.exclude=...jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
#   That line is unnecessary. DataSourceAutoConfiguration is @ConditionalOnMissingBean
#   already, so defining your own DataSource disables it. Excluding it by hand
#   also switches off DataSourceTransactionManager and the /actuator/health
#   database indicator, which you may still want.

beginner.content:
Steps 10 to 12 - Run, Test, Verify

Right-click the project, Run As -> Spring Boot App. The console tells you straight away whether both data sources came up: you get two HikariPool startups and two persistence units.

Then send one POST to each endpoint from Postman and confirm the rows landed in different schemas.
codeExamples:
-- Step 12 - verify in MySQL

USE datasource1;
SELECT * FROM USER_TB;
-- +----+----------+
-- | id | userName |
-- +----+----------+
-- |  1 | ajay     |
-- +----+----------+

USE datasource2;
SELECT * FROM POLICY_TB;
-- +----+----------------+
-- | id | name           |
-- +----+----------------+
-- |  1 | Life Insurance |
-- +----+----------------+

-- Both ids are 1. They are independent sequences in independent schemas -
-- there is no shared identity space across data sources.

Application Flow

Follow one request end to end and the role of each bean becomes obvious.
codeExamples:
POST /savePolicy   {"name":"Life Insurance"}
        |
        v
  PolicyController
        |
        v
  PolicyServiceImpl  ---->  PolicyRepository
                                  |
                                  |  which repositories live in
                                  |  com.velocity.policy.repository?
                                  v
                    @EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = "com.velocity.policy.repository",
                                           entityManagerFactoryRef = "policyEntityManagerFactory",
                                           transactionManagerRef  = "policyTransactionManager")
                                  |
                +-----------------+------------------+
                v                                    v
   policyEntityManagerFactory              policyTransactionManager
   (scans com.velocity.model.policy)       (begin / commit / rollback)
                |
                v
        policyDataSource  (HikariPool-2)
                |
                v
        jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/datasource2
                |
                v
           POLICY_TB

// The SAME diagram with "user" substituted for "policy" describes /saveUser,
// ending at HikariPool-1 and datasource1. Two parallel stacks, sharing nothing
// below the service layer.

expert.content:
Exactly One DataSource Must Be @Primary

The instant a second DataSource bean exists, every injection point that asks for "a DataSource" becomes ambiguous. Spring will not guess. @Primary is the tie-breaker: it marks the bean to use when a request is by type and nothing narrows it further.

Leave it off and the container fails at startup with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Put it on both and you get the same class of failure with a different message - more than one 'primary' bean found.

The rule is per type, and it applies three times over: one DataSource, one EntityManagerFactory and one PlatformTransactionManager must be primary, and they should all be the same side. Marking the user data source primary but the policy transaction manager primary produces an application that starts cleanly and then commits the wrong transactions.

SituationResult
No @PrimaryNoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup for anything injecting by type.
@Primary on bothNoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: more than one 'primary' bean found.
@Primary on one, mixed sidesStarts. Silently wrong at runtime.
@Qualifier everywhere insteadWorks, but every third-party library that injects a bare DataSource - Flyway, Liquibase, Batch, Actuator - breaks.

That last row is the real argument for @Primary: you do not control every injection point. Framework and library code asks for a DataSource by type and has no way to pass your qualifier.

The Three Beans, and Why Nothing Less Works

The single-database case hides all of this. Boot's auto-configuration builds a DataSource, an EntityManagerFactory over it, and a JpaTransactionManager over that, and hands you repositories. Define one DataSource bean yourself and DataSourceAutoConfiguration backs off - it is @ConditionalOnMissingBean - and the whole chain becomes yours.

BeanResponsibility
DataSourcePooled JDBC connections. Knows the URL and credentials. Knows nothing about entities.
LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBeanBuilds the Hibernate SessionFactory: which entity classes exist, which dialect, which DDL strategy, which second-level cache. Bound to exactly one DataSource.
PlatformTransactionManagerOwns the transaction boundary on one entity manager. @Transactional resolves to one of these.
@EnableJpaRepositoriesNot a bean - a scanner. It generates repository proxies for one package and injects the named entity manager and transaction manager into them.

Omit any one of the three and the failure is not subtle, but it also is not obviously about the missing bean. A missing second PlatformTransactionManager, for instance, does not fail at startup - the second set of repositories quietly enlists in the first database's transaction manager, so a rollback on the policy side rolls back nothing.

Why the Packages Must Be Split - and What Happens When They Are Not

Neither User nor UserRepository carries any marker saying "datasource1". The only thing that binds them to a database is the package they sit in, because .packages(...) and basePackages = ... both address packages.

That makes the package structure load-bearing. A developer who drops a new repository into the nearest convenient package has changed which database it talks to, without changing a line of configuration.

Rule 1: no package may be scanned by two configurations. Overlapping basePackages means two sets of proxies for the same interface.
Rule 2: a repository outside every basePackages is never created at all.
Rule 3: an entity outside every .packages(...) is not a known entity, whatever @Entity says.

Rule 2 produces the single most confusing error in this whole topic, because the message names the entity and says nothing about packages.

@Transactional Binds to ONE Transaction Manager

This is the limitation that surprises people, and it is the question an interviewer asks after you have described the configuration.

@Transactional selects a single PlatformTransactionManager. Not two. A method that writes to both databases inside one @Transactional block is not atomic - one manager commits its connection, the other commits its own, and there is nothing coordinating them. If the second write fails, the first has already committed and stays committed.

With no explicit name, @Transactional resolves to the @Primary transaction manager. That is why a write to the secondary database inside a plain @Transactional method appears to work: it runs on the secondary connection, but the transaction boundary is the primary manager's, which means the secondary is running in auto-commit and cannot be rolled back.

Name the manager explicitly whenever the method touches the non-primary database: @Transactional("policyTransactionManager").

Connection Pools: Total Size Is What Matters

Two data sources means two independent HikariCP pools. Each has its own maximum-pool-size, its own idle connections, its own leak detection. Nothing shares.

The mistake is sizing each pool as if it were the only one. Copy the single-database default of 10 into both and the application now opens up to 20 connections per instance. Run eight instances behind a load balancer and that is 160 connections against a MySQL server whose max_connections is typically 151.

QuantityHow to reason about it
Per-pool sizeSize to the concurrency that that database actually sees, not to a copied default. A rarely-used reporting schema does not need ten connections.
Total per instanceThe sum across all pools. This is what a thread-starved instance actually holds.
Total per clusterinstances x pools x max-pool-size, plus migration tools, plus admin sessions. Compare against the server's max_connections.
Connections are not freeEach is a server-side thread and its buffers. Oversized pools make a database slower, not faster - past the point where all cores are busy, more concurrency only adds context switching and lock contention.

The counter-intuitive part: a smaller pool is usually faster. Hikari's own guidance is that a pool of ten serving requests quickly beats a pool of a hundred where every query waits behind lock contention.
codeExamples:
# Per-source pool tuning. @ConfigurationProperties binds these to
# the HikariDataSource that DataSourceBuilder produced.

# user schema - the hot path
spring.user.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/datasource1
spring.user.datasource.username=root
spring.user.datasource.password=root
spring.user.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.user.datasource.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.user.datasource.minimum-idle=5
spring.user.datasource.connection-timeout=3000
spring.user.datasource.leak-detection-threshold=20000
spring.user.datasource.pool-name=user-pool

# policy schema - low traffic, sized accordingly
spring.policy.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/datasource2
spring.policy.datasource.username=root
spring.policy.datasource.password=root
spring.policy.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.policy.datasource.maximum-pool-size=4
spring.policy.datasource.minimum-idle=1
spring.policy.datasource.connection-timeout=3000
spring.policy.datasource.pool-name=policy-pool

# Total per instance: 14, not 2 x "whatever the default was".
# pool-name is worth setting - the logs then say "user-pool - Connection
# is not available" instead of the unhelpful "HikariPool-2".

# Actuator reports every pool separately once you enable the metrics.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

# GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active
# {
#   "name": "hikaricp.connections.active",
#   "measurements": [ { "statistic": "VALUE", "value": 7.0 } ],
#   "availableTags": [
#     { "tag": "pool", "values": [ "user-pool", "policy-pool" ] }
#   ]
# }
#
# GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active?tag=pool:policy-pool
# -> the policy pool alone. Alert on
#    hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 per pool: that is the metric that
#    goes non-zero BEFORE the timeouts start.

expert.content:
AbstractRoutingDataSource - the Common Real-World Case

Two genuinely different schemas, as in this walkthrough, is the textbook example. In production, the far more frequent reason for more than one DataSource is read-replica routing: one writable primary, one or more read-only replicas, the same schema on both.

The configuration above is the wrong shape for that, because it splits by package - and a replica has the same entities and the same repositories as the primary. What you want instead is one logical DataSource that picks its physical target per transaction. That is exactly what AbstractRoutingDataSource does.

AspectSeparate configsAbstractRoutingDataSource
Use caseDifferent schemasSame schema, different servers
EntitiesDifferent per sourceIdentical
RepositoriesSplit by packageOne set
Entity managersOne per sourceOne, over the router
Routing decisionAt compile time, by packageAt runtime, per transaction

determineCurrentLookupKey() is called when the connection is first acquired, which is at transaction start. That timing is the whole trick, and also the whole trap: the decision cannot change mid-transaction, and it must be made before the first statement runs.
codeExamples:
# Related routing patterns, same mechanism:
#
#   Multi-tenancy - the lookup key is the tenant id taken from the JWT or a
#     header, and setTargetDataSources holds one DataSource per tenant. This
#     is the schema-per-tenant model.
#
#   Sharding - the key is derived from the entity id (customerId % shardCount).
#
#   Both share the ThreadLocal-leak problem above. Clear the context in a
#   servlet Filter's finally block, not only in the aspect, so an exception
#   thrown before the aspect runs still cleans up.

expert.content:
Operational Consequences Worth Knowing Before the Design Review

Adding a second data source changes more than the persistence layer.

AreaWhat changes
Health checksBoot auto-configures a DataSourceHealthIndicator per DataSource bean, so /actuator/health reports db entries for both. If one schema is optional, a replica outage now marks the whole instance DOWN and Kubernetes restarts a healthy pod.
MigrationsFlyway and Liquibase auto-configure against the primary data source only. The second schema is not migrated unless you declare a second Flyway bean pointing at it.
Startup timeTwo entity managers means two Hibernate metadata scans and two pool warm-ups, run sequentially. Noticeable on a large model.
Testing@DataJpaTest configures a single embedded data source and will not reproduce this wiring. Use @SpringBootTest with Testcontainers, or the slice test asserts against the wrong database.
Failure isolationThe upside: one database down means one feature degraded, not the whole application - provided the code does not call both in one request path.
ddl-autoupdate in this walkthrough is fine for a classroom. create or create-drop drops every table on restart, and with two schemas it does so to both. Production uses validate and a migration tool.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
When does Spring Boot's data source auto-configuration stop applying?As soon as you define your own DataSource bean. DataSourceAutoConfiguration is @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so it backs off and you must supply the entity manager factory and transaction manager yourself.
Which beans does each data source need?Three: a DataSource, a LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean over it, and a PlatformTransactionManager over that - plus an @EnableJpaRepositories pointing a repository package at the last two by bean name.
Why must exactly one data source be @Primary?Injection by type is ambiguous with two candidates. Without a primary you get NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException; with two primaries you get "more than one 'primary' bean found". Library code that injects a bare DataSource cannot pass a qualifier, so the primary is what it receives.
Could you use @Qualifier everywhere instead of @Primary?For your own code, yes. It breaks anything you do not control - Flyway, Actuator, Spring Batch - which injects DataSource by type.
What do the three @EnableJpaRepositories attributes do?basePackages selects which repository interfaces to proxy; entityManagerFactoryRef and transactionManagerRef name the beans those proxies use. Both refs are Strings, so a typo fails at runtime, not compile time.
Why must entities and repositories be in separate packages per database?Nothing on the class says which database it belongs to. The package is the only binding - .packages(...) for entities, basePackages for repositories. Overlapping packages means one config silently wins.
A repository is in a package no config scans - what happens?Startup fails with "required a bean of type ... that could not be found" naming the repository interface. The message suggests defining the bean, which is impossible; the real fix is to add the package to a basePackages.
What does IllegalArgumentException: Not a managed type mean here?The entity is not in any package scanned by the entity manager that this repository is wired to. @Entity alone does not register it with a specific persistence unit.
Can one @Transactional method atomically write to both databases?No. @Transactional binds to one transaction manager. The other database commits independently, so a failure after the first write leaves a partial result.
How do you target the non-primary transaction manager?@Transactional("policyTransactionManager"), or the equivalent transactionManager = "..." attribute. Unqualified @Transactional resolves to the primary manager.
What if you genuinely need atomicity across both?JTA/XA two-phase commit with an JtaTransactionManager and XA data sources, at a significant throughput cost and with in-doubt transactions to resolve after a crash; or a saga with compensating actions, accepting eventual consistency. Most systems choose the saga.
How should the connection pools be sized?Per source, to that source's real concurrency - then check the total: instances x pools x max-pool-size against the server's max_connections. Copying a single-database default into both pools doubles the footprint per instance.
Why jdbcUrl rather than url in the properties?DataSourceBuilder builds a HikariDataSource, whose setter is setJdbcUrl. With url the property does not bind and startup fails with "jdbcUrl is required with driverClassName".
What is AbstractRoutingDataSource for?One logical DataSource that selects a physical target at runtime via determineCurrentLookupKey(), called when the connection is acquired. It is the standard answer for read-replica routing, multi-tenancy and sharding - cases where the schema is identical so the package-splitting approach does not apply.
What breaks first in a routing setup?A ThreadLocal route left uncleared: a pooled Tomcat thread carries the previous request's key and sends a write to a read-only replica. Always clear it in a finally block. Second is forgetting LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy, which makes everything route to the primary silently.

Why Validate at All?

Every request that arrives from outside your application is untrusted. A browser form can be bypassed, a mobile client can be out of date, and a script can send anything at all. If the controller passes bad data straight into the service layer, the failure surfaces somewhere deep and unhelpful - a database constraint violation, a NullPointerException, or worse, a row of nonsense saved successfully.

Without validation:

Bean Validation - the Standard

Java has a specification for this - Bean Validation (JSR 380, now Jakarta Validation). You declare the rules as annotations on the fields, and the framework enforces them.

PiecePurpose
Jakarta Validation APIThe specification - the annotations themselves.
Hibernate ValidatorThe reference implementation that actually does the checking.
spring-boot-starter-validationBrings both in and auto-configures them.

Important: since Spring Boot 2.3 validation is not included in spring-boot-starter-web. If you add @NotBlank and nothing happens, this missing dependency is almost always why.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Without it, the annotations compile (they come in transitively
     via JPA in some setups) but NOTHING enforces them. Invalid data
     passes straight through with no error - the most confusing
     possible failure mode, because the code looks correct. -->

beginner.content:
The Core Constraint Annotations

AnnotationWhat it requires
@NotNullThe value is not null. An empty string passes.
@NotEmptyNot null and not empty. A string of spaces passes.
@NotBlankNot null, and contains at least one non-whitespace character. For Strings, this is usually what you want.
@Size(min, max)Length of a String, or size of a collection or map.
@Min / @MaxNumeric bounds, inclusive.
@Positive / @PositiveOrZeroGreater than zero / not negative.
@EmailA syntactically well-formed email address.
@Pattern(regexp)Matches a regular expression.
@Past / @FutureA date before / after now.
@DecimalMin / @DecimalMaxBounds for BigDecimal, where precision matters.
@Digits(integer, fraction)Limits digits before and after the decimal point.

The distinction between the first three catches people constantly:

Applying Them: @Valid on the Request Body

Two things are needed, and forgetting either means no validation happens:

1. Constraint annotations on the DTO fields.
2. @Valid on the controller parameter - this is what triggers the check.

The annotations alone do nothing. @Valid is the switch.

Returning Useful Error Messages

A bare 400 tells the client something was wrong but not what. Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, and a @RestControllerAdvice can turn it into a response the client can act on - ideally field by field, so a form can highlight the offending inputs.

Validating Path Variables and Request Parameters

@Valid works on objects. To constrain a bare @PathVariable or @RequestParam, put the annotation directly on the parameter and add @Validated to the class.

Without the class-level @Validated, parameter constraints are silently ignored - the same quiet failure as the missing starter dependency.

expert.content:
Two Exceptions, Not One

This is the detail that makes validation error handling look inconsistent until you know it. Where the constraint sits decides which exception is thrown, and they need separate handlers.

TriggerExceptionDefault status
@Valid on @RequestBodyMethodArgumentNotValidException400
@Valid on @ModelAttribute (form binding)BindException400
@Validated class + constrained paramsConstraintViolationException500
@Valid on a service method argumentConstraintViolationException500

That third row is a real bug in a lot of applications: a client sends ?size=500, breaks a @Max(100), and receives 500 Internal Server Error - telling them the server is broken when they made the mistake. It defaults to 500 because ConstraintViolationException is a generic Jakarta exception with no HTTP meaning attached.

Nested Objects Need @Valid Too

Constraints do not cascade automatically. A DTO containing another DTO, or a list of them, is validated only at the top level unless the nested field is itself annotated @Valid.

This is a silent gap: the outer object passes, the inner rubbish goes through.

Custom Constraints

The built-in annotations cover shape, not meaning. "Must be a valid PAN number", "must not be a disposable email domain", "delivery date must be a working day" - those need a custom constraint.

A custom constraint is two pieces: the annotation, and a ConstraintValidator that implements the check.

Validation Groups - Different Rules for Different Operations

Create and update rarely have the same rules. On create the id must be absent; on update it is mandatory. One DTO cannot express both with plain annotations - which is why people duplicate the DTO.

Groups solve it: tag each constraint with a marker interface, then activate a group per endpoint with @Validated (note: @Valid cannot select a group - this is the one place you must use @Validated on the parameter).

Where Validation Belongs - and What It Cannot Do

Bean Validation checks the shape of data. It cannot check anything requiring context, state, or a decision.

Bean Validation handlesBusiness logic handles
Is the email well-formed?Is this user allowed to change that email?
Is the amount positive?Does the account have sufficient balance?
Is the date in the future?Is the venue free on that date?
Is the SKU 8 characters?Is that product still in stock?

Validation belongs at the boundary - reject malformed input before it reaches the service. Business rules belong in the service and throw domain exceptions. Putting a balance check in a ConstraintValidator hides an important rule inside an annotation where nobody looks for it.

Layered defence. None of these replaces the others:

LayerProtects against
Client-side (browser)Nothing - it is UX only. Trivially bypassed.
Bean Validation at the controllerMalformed input from any client.
Service-layer business rulesOperations that are well-formed but not allowed.
Database constraintsEverything else, including bugs and races. The last line, and the only one that cannot be bypassed.

Localised Messages

Hard-coded English strings in message = "..." cannot be translated. Bean Validation supports message keys in braces, resolved from a resource bundle - so validation errors come back in the caller's language.
codeExamples:
# messages_en.properties
employee.name.required=Name is required
employee.age.min=Employee must be at least {value} years old

# messages_fr.properties
employee.name.required=Le nom est obligatoire
employee.age.min=L'employe doit avoir au moins {value} ans

# {value} interpolates the constraint's own attribute, so the
# message stays correct if you change @Min(18) to @Min(21).

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Bean Validation?The Jakarta specification (JSR 380) for declaring constraints as annotations, implemented by Hibernate Validator.
Why do the annotations sometimes do nothing?spring-boot-starter-validation is missing - it was removed from the web starter in Boot 2.3 - or @Valid is not on the parameter.
Difference between @NotNull, @NotEmpty and @NotBlank?@NotNull rejects only null; @NotEmpty also rejects empty; @NotBlank also rejects whitespace-only. For Strings, @NotBlank is usually correct.
@Valid vs @Validated?@Valid is the Jakarta annotation and triggers validation; @Validated is Spring's, and additionally selects validation groups and enables method-parameter validation at class level.
Which exception does body validation throw?MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring maps to 400.
Which exception does parameter validation throw, and why does it matter?ConstraintViolationException, which defaults to 500. You must handle it, or clients get a server error for their own bad input.
Why is a nested object not validated?Constraints do not cascade. The nested field itself needs @Valid.
How do you write a custom constraint?An annotation meta-annotated @Constraint(validatedBy = ...) with message, groups and payload attributes, plus a ConstraintValidator implementation.
Should a custom validator return true or false for null?True - let @NotNull own null so constraints compose.
What are validation groups for?Applying different rules to the same DTO per operation, e.g. id forbidden on create and required on update.
What is the trap with groups?Naming a group deactivates Default, so every untagged constraint is skipped. Tag them all, or include Default.class.
Can validation check a database uniqueness rule?Technically yes via an injected validator, but it is racy - keep the database UNIQUE constraint as the real guarantee.
Where does validation end and business logic begin?Validation checks the shape of the input; anything needing state or context - balance, availability, permission - is a business rule that belongs in the service.
Is client-side validation a security control?No. It is purely UX and is trivially bypassed; the server must revalidate everything.
