Spring Security is the standard way to add authentication and authorization to a Spring Boot application.

Just adding the spring-boot-starter-security dependency to your project is enough to secure every endpoint by default - no configuration required.

Add the dependency (Maven):
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
What happens the moment you add the starter

As soon as the app starts up, Spring Boot auto-configures a default security setup:
• Every HTTP endpoint now requires authentication.
• A default login form (HTML page) is generated automatically.
• A default user named user is created.
• A random password for that user is generated fresh on every startup and printed to the console log.

Below is what you will see printed in the console when the application boots up with only the security starter added and nothing else configured:

Authentication vs Authorization

These two words sound similar but answer completely different questions - almost every interview question in security starts here:

Authentication - "Who are you?"
• Verifying identity - checking a username/password, a token, etc.
• Happens first. If it fails, the request is rejected before authorization is even considered.

Authorization - "What are you allowed to do?"
• Once identity is confirmed, checking whether that identity has permission to access a particular resource or perform a particular action (e.g. only an ADMIN can delete a user).
• Happens after authentication succeeds.

Simple analogy: showing your ID card at the office gate is authentication. Whether your ID card lets you enter the server room is authorization.

A minimal in-memory user configuration

Instead of relying on the auto-generated random password, you can define your own users directly in configuration - useful for learning, demos, or very small applications (never for production, where users should come from a database).

403 Forbidden vs 401 Unauthorized

Both are error responses Spring Security can return, and mixing them up is a very common beginner mistake:

401 Unauthorized - "I don't know who you are."
• Returned when authentication itself failed or was never provided (missing/invalid credentials or token).
• The server is saying: prove your identity first.

403 Forbidden - "I know who you are, but you're not allowed here."
• Returned when authentication succeeded, but the authenticated user lacks the required role/permission for that specific resource.
• The server is saying: your identity is fine, your permissions are not enough.

expert.content:
The Security Filter Chain

Every incoming HTTP request to a Spring Boot application secured with Spring Security passes through a chain of servlet filters before it ever reaches your controller. Each filter has one job (parse a token, check a session, enforce CSRF, etc.) and either lets the request continue to the next filter or rejects it outright. 

HTTP Request
   |
   v
+--------------------------------------------------+
|           DelegatingFilterProxy                  |
|         (bridges servlet container -> Spring)     |
+--------------------------------------------------+
   |
   v
+--------------------------------------------------+
|           FilterChainProxy                       |
|   +--------------------------------------------+ |
|   | SecurityContextPersistenceFilter            | |  restores/saves SecurityContext
|   +--------------------------------------------+ |
|   | CsrfFilter                                   | |  blocks unsafe cross-site requests
|   +--------------------------------------------+ |
|   | UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter /       | |  handles login form submit
|   | JwtAuthenticationFilter (custom)              | |  or validates bearer token
|   +--------------------------------------------+ |
|   | ExceptionTranslationFilter                    | |  converts security errors to
|   |                                                | |  401 / 403 HTTP responses
|   +--------------------------------------------+ |
|   | FilterSecurityInterceptor /                   | |  final authorization decision -
|   | AuthorizationFilter                           | |  checks role/permission rules
|   +--------------------------------------------+ |
+--------------------------------------------------+
   |
   v
DispatcherServlet -> Controller -> Your Business Logic
If any filter in the chain rejects the request, it never reaches the controller at all - the response is short-circuited straight back to the client (typically with 401 or 403).

Configuring a Custom SecurityFilterChain (Spring Security 6+)

The old WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter class-based approach is deprecated. Modern Spring Security (5.7+ / 6.x, the version shipped with current Spring Boot) configures security declaratively by exposing a SecurityFilterChain bean instead.

Password Encoding with BCryptPasswordEncoder

Storing plain-text passwords is never acceptable, even for internal tools or "just a demo." If the database is ever leaked (breach, misconfigured backup, insider access), plain-text passwords hand attackers every user's real password instantly - and because people reuse passwords across sites, the damage spreads far beyond your own application.

BCryptPasswordEncoder is the standard choice: it is a one-way, adaptive hashing algorithm that automatically salts each password and can be configured to run slower as hardware gets faster, making brute-force attacks impractical.

JWT-Based Stateless Authentication

Traditional session-based login stores authentication state on the server (an HTTP session). This does not scale well across multiple server instances. JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication instead makes the server stateless - the token itself carries the proof of identity, so no session needs to be stored anywhere on the server. 

Client                                   Server
  |                                          |
  |---- POST /login (username, password) --->|
  |                                          | validate credentials
  |                                          | generate signed JWT
  |<----------- 200 OK { token: "xyz..." } --|
  |                                          |
  |  (client stores token - memory/storage)  |
  |                                          |
  |--- GET /api/orders --------------------->|
  |    Header: Authorization: Bearer xyz...  |
  |                                          | JwtAuthenticationFilter:
  |                                          |   1. extract token from header
  |                                          |   2. verify signature + expiry
  |                                          |   3. load user identity from token
  |                                          |   4. set SecurityContext (per-request,
  |                                          |      NOT stored server-side)
  |<------------- 200 OK { orders: [...] } --|
  |                                          |
  | No session lookup needed on any request. |
  | Each request is self-contained.          |
Because there is no server-side session, any server instance behind a load balancer can validate the token independently - this is what makes JWT auth naturally horizontally scalable.

Method-Level Security with @PreAuthorize

Besides URL-based rules in the SecurityFilterChain, Spring Security can enforce authorization directly on individual service/controller methods. This keeps the permission check right next to the business logic it protects, which is often clearer than a giant list of URL patterns.

Requires @EnableMethodSecurity on a configuration class.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does adding spring-boot-starter-security do by default?Secures every endpoint, generates a default login form, creates a "user" account with a random password printed to the console on startup
Authentication vs Authorization?Authentication verifies identity ("who are you"); authorization checks permissions ("what are you allowed to do") and always happens after authentication
401 vs 403 - what's the difference?401 means the request was never authenticated (missing/invalid credentials); 403 means authentication succeeded but the user lacks permission for that resource
Why is WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter deprecated?Spring Security 5.7+/6 moved to a component-based model - you expose a SecurityFilterChain @Bean instead of extending a base class, which is more testable and composable
Why must passwords always be hashed, never stored in plain text?A database leak would expose every user's real password directly; hashing (e.g. BCrypt) is one-way, so even a leaked hash can't be reversed to the original password
Why is BCrypt preferred over plain MD5/SHA-256 for passwords?BCrypt automatically salts each hash and is deliberately slow/adaptive (configurable work factor), which makes brute-force and rainbow-table attacks impractical - fast general-purpose hashes do not
What makes JWT authentication "stateless"?The server stores no session; the signed token itself carries the user's identity and claims, so any server instance can validate it independently on every request
Where does the JWT travel on each request?In the Authorization HTTP header as "Bearer <token>", read and validated by a custom filter early in the security filter chain
What does @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") do?Blocks the annotated method from executing at all unless the currently authenticated user has ROLE_ADMIN - the check runs before the method body, requires @EnableMethodSecurity
What happens if a filter rejects a request early in the chain?The request never reaches the controller - it is short-circuited immediately with an error response (typically 401 or 403)

beginner.content:
Authentication

This topic is being written and will be published shortly.

In the meantime, the surrounding module already covers the ground it sits on - work through the topics either side of it and come back once this one is live.

Authorization

This topic is being written and will be published shortly.

In the meantime, the surrounding module already covers the ground it sits on - work through the topics either side of it and come back once this one is live.

Business Requirement

• A REST endpoint is currently reachable by anyone who knows the URL.
• The data it returns is confidential, so the caller must prove who they are before the controller runs.
• Build the security up in two passes: first HTTP Basic authentication backed by a custom UserDetailsService, then a stateless JWT flow where the client trades credentials for a signed token and sends that token on every later request.

Problem Statement

Without security, GET http://localhost:8080/getBasicExample returns 200 OK to any caller. We want the same URL to return 401 Unauthorized to an anonymous caller and 200 OK only once valid credentials are supplied.

Package structure for Part A

src/main/java
 └── com.velocity
      ├── SpringBootSecurityApplication.java   (@SpringBootApplication)
      ├── restcontroller
      │     └── TestController.java            (@RestController)
      └── configuration
            ├── MyUserDetailsService.java      (implements UserDetailsService)
            └── SecurityConfig.java            (the SecurityFilterChain bean)
This topic is the laboratory walkthrough - project setup, the configuration class, users held in memory and then in a database, password encoders, and testing each stage in Postman. The concepts themselves (what a filter chain is, 401 against 403, method security) are covered separately.

Step 1 - Create the project and add the web starter

File -> New -> Spring Starter Project, enter the project name, click Next, then Finish. Add the web starter first and get an unsecured endpoint working before you add any security at all - that way, when the 401 appears later, you know exactly which change caused it.

Note the dependency has no version tag. The spring-boot-starter-parent supplies the version through its dependency management. The source material pins <version>3.1.0</version> on the security starter, which is a good way to end up with a security jar that does not match the rest of Boot.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.5</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>

    <!-- optional: restarts the app when classes change -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
        <optional>true</optional>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- COMMON MISTAKE in the handout: the artifactId is written as
     "spring-boot-startersecurity" (the hyphen is lost by the PDF line break).
     Maven then fails the build with:
     [ERROR] Could not resolve dependencies ... spring-boot-startersecurity:jar:3.1.0 was not found
     The correct artifactId is spring-boot-starter-security. -->

beginner.content:
Step 2 - The REST controller

One trivial GET endpoint. Nothing here knows anything about security; that is the point. Security in Spring is applied by servlet filters that run before the DispatcherServlet, so the controller stays clean.

Step 3 - Add the security starter and observe the default

Add spring-boot-starter-security and restart without writing a single line of configuration. Boot's auto-configuration secures every endpoint, generates a login form and creates one user called user with a random password printed to the console.

Read that console line before you go any further - a surprising number of "my app is broken" reports are a developer who added the starter and did not notice the endpoint is now protected.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

// CONSOLE OUTPUT on startup:
//
// Using generated security password: 3f6a1c88-9c0e-4d3b-b0f7-1a25f0e9d4c2
//
// This generated password is for development use only. Your security configuration
// must be updated before running your application in production.
//
// Postman, same request as before, still "No Auth":
// OUTPUT:
// Status: 401 Unauthorized
// Header: WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm"
// Body  : {"timestamp":"...","status":401,"error":"Unauthorized","path":"/getBasicExample"}

beginner.content:
Step 4 - Supply your own users with a UserDetailsService

The generated password is regenerated on every restart, so it is useless for a real lab. Replace it with a UserDetailsService: a single-method interface whose job is to answer the question "given this username, what is the stored password and what authorities does this account hold?" It does not compare passwords - that comparison is the PasswordEncoder's job, and keeping the two separate is what lets you swap a database, LDAP or a REST call in behind the same interface.

Two corrections to the handout's version are marked in the code and both are compile- or startup-time failures, not style points.

Step 5 - The security configuration class

This is where the source material is most out of date. It extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and overrides configure(...) methods. That class was deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 and deleted in Spring Security 6, so on any current Spring Boot the handout's class does not compile - the import itself cannot be resolved.

The modern form declares a SecurityFilterChain bean and configures it with the lambda DSL. Same behaviour, no inheritance, and every rule is an ordinary bean you can test.

Note also the encoder. The handout returns NoOpPasswordEncoder.getInstance(), which stores and compares passwords in plain text. Never do this, not even in a lab - BCryptPasswordEncoder costs one line and behaves identically from the student's point of view.

Step 6 - Wiring the UserDetailsService in

There is no configure(AuthenticationManagerBuilder) to override any more, and none is needed. Spring Boot builds a DaoAuthenticationProvider automatically as soon as it finds exactly one UserDetailsService bean and one PasswordEncoder bean in the context. Declaring the beans is the wiring.

If you ever need it explicit - two user stores, say, or a custom provider - build the AuthenticationManager yourself as shown below.

Step 7 - Test Part A in Postman

Run the application, then send the same request three ways. The three outcomes below are the whole lesson of Part A: no credentials and wrong credentials are indistinguishable to the client (both 401), and that is deliberate - telling an attacker "the username exists but the password is wrong" hands them half the answer.

Application flow, Part A

main()  ->  SecurityConfig  ->  filterChain(HttpSecurity) bean built once at startup
                              ->  passwordEncoder() bean built once at startup

Postman GET /getBasicExample
   |
   v
BasicAuthenticationFilter        reads the Authorization header, decodes base64
   |
   v
AuthenticationManager
   |
   v
DaoAuthenticationProvider
   |
   v
MyUserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername("javaindustry")
   |                                        |
   |                          not found ----+--> UsernameNotFoundException -> 401
   v
PasswordEncoder.matches(raw, storedHash)
   |
   |  false --> BadCredentialsException -> 401
   v
  true
   |
   v
SecurityContextHolder gets the Authentication
   |
   v
AuthorizationFilter    checks the authorizeHttpRequests rules
   |
   v
DispatcherServlet -> TestController.getBasicExample() -> 200 OK
Notice how far the request travels before your controller is reached, and that every rejection point short-circuits back to the client without the controller ever running.

Part B - Moving the users into a database

Hard-coded users are fine for one lesson and wrong for everything after it. The only class that has to change is the UserDetailsService: the filter chain, the encoder and the controller are untouched. That is the payoff of the interface split described in Step 4.

Add the JPA and MySQL dependencies, an entity, a repository and one query method.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml additions -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>


# src/main/resources/application.properties

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/securitydb
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root

# NOTE: the property is driver-class-name, with a hyphen before "name".
# The handouts repeatedly write "spring.datasource.driver-classname", which
# Boot does not recognise; it is ignored, and you get a confusing
# "Failed to determine a suitable driver class" only in some setups.
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
# ddl-auto=create DROPS AND RECREATES every table on each restart -
# your users vanish between runs. Use "update" while learning, and
# a migration tool (Flyway/Liquibase) for anything real.

spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.MySQL8Dialect
# (the handout prints this as "org.hibernate.dial ect.MySQL8Dialect" -
#  a PDF line-break artefact, not a real package)

beginner.content:
Part B - Entity, repository and the DB-backed UserDetailsService

The entity is an ordinary JPA class. The one detail that matters is that the password column stores the bcrypt hash, never the raw password, and it needs to be at least 60 characters wide or the hash is silently truncated and no one can ever log in again.

Part C - Stateless JWT authentication

Basic Auth resends the password on every request. The JWT flow replaces that: the client posts its credentials once to /token, receives a signed token, and sends that token in the Authorization header thereafter. The server keeps no session.

ClassResponsibility
JwtUtilGenerates, parses, and validates the signed token. Holds the signing key and the expiry policy.
JWTRequestRequest body of POST /token - username and password.
JWTResponseResponse body of POST /token - the token string.
JWTControllerAuthenticates the credentials through the AuthenticationManager, then asks JwtUtil for a token.
JWTAuthenticationFilterRuns on every request, reads the Bearer token, validates it, and populates the SecurityContext.

The handout uses io.jsonwebtoken:jjwt:0.9.0. That release is from 2018, needs a jaxb-api patch on Java 11 and above, and its API is deprecated. Use the split 0.12.x artifacts instead - the extra dependency lines below are the whole cost of the upgrade.
codeExamples:
<!-- What the handout asks for, and the failure it causes -->
<!--
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId><artifactId>jjwt</artifactId><version>0.9.0</version>
</dependency>

Running on Java 11+ this throws at the first token generation:
  java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/DatatypeConverter
        at io.jsonwebtoken.impl.Base64Codec.encode(...)

The handout then patches it by adding javax.xml.bind:jaxb-api:2.3.1. That works,
but it is a workaround for a library that should be replaced.

Also note: spring-security-jwt:1.1.1.RELEASE is listed too. It is an unrelated,
long-retired Spring artifact and is not used by any code in the exercise. Remove it.
-->

<!-- Use these instead -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId>
    <artifactId>jjwt-api</artifactId>
    <version>0.12.5</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId>
    <artifactId>jjwt-impl</artifactId>
    <version>0.12.5</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId>
    <artifactId>jjwt-jackson</artifactId>
    <version>0.12.5</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Part C - JwtUtil

Two problems in the handout's version are worth stopping on.

The signing key. It uses the literal string "secret". HS256 requires a key of at least 256 bits; jjwt 0.11 and later reject anything shorter with a WeakKeyException. Even where it is accepted, a six-character key is guessable offline in seconds, and anyone who guesses it can mint tokens for any user, including an administrator.

The unused constant. JWT_TOKEN_VALIDITY is declared as 5 hours and then never referenced - createToken hardcodes ten hours instead. Both numbers are far too long for an access token that cannot be revoked.

Part C - The token endpoint

POST /token must be reachable without a token - otherwise there is no way to obtain one. It authenticates the submitted credentials through the AuthenticationManager and only then issues a token.

The handout catches UsernameNotFoundException. That is the wrong exception: the manager throws BadCredentialsException when the password does not match, so a wrong password escapes the catch and surfaces as a 500. Catch AuthenticationException, the common supertype.

Part C - The JWT filter

This filter reads the token on every request and, if it is valid, places an Authentication into the SecurityContextHolder so the rest of the chain treats the caller as logged in.

The handout's version contains a bug that stops the whole application, and it is worth understanding rather than just copying the fix: filterChain.doFilter(request, response) sits inside the if (requestTokenHeader != null) block. A request that carries no Authorization header therefore never continues down the chain - the response is never written and the client hangs until it times out. POST /token itself has no header, so token generation breaks the moment the filter is added.

A second bug: loadUserByUsername(username) is called before username is checked for null, so a malformed token produces a UsernameNotFoundException or an NPE instead of a clean 401.

Part C - Registering the filter and going stateless

Three settings turn the application into a stateless API. Each one has a reason, and csrf.disable() in particular is safe only because of the other two.

Part C - Testing the JWT flow

Run the application and work through the four requests below in order. Request 3 is the one students usually hit first and misread as a bug in their code - it is not, it is the expected result of asking for a protected resource with no token.

Application flow, Part C

FLOW 1 - obtaining the token (runs once)

POST /token  { username, password }
   |
   v
JWTAuthenticationFilter.doFilterInternal()
   |   no Authorization header -> context stays empty -> chain continues
   v
AuthorizationFilter   /token is permitAll -> allowed through
   |
   v
JWTController.generateToken()
   |
   v
AuthenticationManager.authenticate()
   |
   v
DaoAuthenticationProvider -> UserDetailsService -> PasswordEncoder.matches()
   |
   |  no match --> BadCredentialsException --> 401 { "error": "Bad credentials" }
   v
JwtUtil.generateToken() -> signWith(key) -> compact()
   |
   v
200 OK  { "token": "eyJ..." }


FLOW 2 - using the token (runs on every subsequent request)

GET /getDemo   Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
   |
   v
JWTAuthenticationFilter.doFilterInternal()
   |
   +-- header missing / not "Bearer " --> context empty --> ... --> 401
   |
   v
JwtUtil.getUsername(token)      verifies signature, reads "sub"
   |
   +-- bad signature or expired --> JwtException --> context empty --> 401
   v
UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername()
   |
   v
JwtUtil.validateToken()   subject matches AND not expired
   |
   v
SecurityContextHolder.setAuthentication(...)
   |
   v
filterChain.doFilter()   <-- must be reached on EVERY path
   |
   v
AuthorizationFilter -> DispatcherServlet -> JWTAuthenticationController -> 200 OK
No HttpSession is created anywhere in flow 2. That is what "stateless" means in practice: put the request behind a load balancer and any instance can serve it.

expert.content:
WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter: deprecated, then deleted

The class the source material is built on was deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 (February 2022) and removed entirely in Spring Security 6.0, which is what every Spring Boot 3.x application uses. This is not a warning you can suppress - the handout's @SuppressWarnings("deprecation") silences the 5.7 warning but does nothing on 6.x, where the import simply cannot be resolved.

The reason for the removal is worth understanding, because it explains the shape of the replacement. The adapter forced inheritance: to change one thing you subclassed a base class and overrode a protected method, and the base class decided the order in which your overrides ran. You could not have two independent chains, you could not unit-test a rule in isolation, and the configure(HttpSecurity) and configure(AuthenticationManagerBuilder) overrides interacted in ways that were hard to reason about. The component-based model replaces it: you publish beans, Spring composes them, and each bean is an ordinary object you can construct in a test.

Old API (5.6 and earlier)Modern replacement (5.7+ / 6.x)
extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdaptera SecurityFilterChain @Bean
configure(HttpSecurity http)the body of that bean method, returning http.build()
configure(AuthenticationManagerBuilder auth)publish a UserDetailsService / AuthenticationProvider bean
configure(WebSecurity web).ignoring()a WebSecurityCustomizer @Bean, or better, permitAll() in the chain
super.authenticationManagerBean()AuthenticationConfiguration.getAuthenticationManager()
antMatchers(..)requestMatchers(..)
authorizeRequests(..)authorizeHttpRequests(..)
and() chainingthe lambda DSL - each configurer takes a Customizer

Why NoOpPasswordEncoder must never be used

Both source documents configure NoOpPasswordEncoder.getInstance(). The class exists for exactly one purpose - letting a legacy application boot while its stored passwords are migrated - and it has carried @Deprecated since Spring Security 5.0 for that reason. Its encode() returns the input unchanged and its matches() is a plain String.equals. Two independent consequences follow.

Every password sits in the database in plain text. One SQL injection, one leaked backup, one curious DBA, and every account is compromised - and because people reuse passwords, so are their accounts elsewhere.

The comparison is not constant-time. String.equals returns as soon as two characters differ, so the time it takes leaks how many leading characters were correct. Real encoders compare fixed-length hashes and are immune to this.

What to use instead

EncoderGuidance
BCryptPasswordEncoderThe sensible default. Generates its own random salt, stores it inside the 60-character output, and takes a work factor (default 10). Raise it as hardware gets faster; every increment doubles the cost. Silently truncates input at 72 bytes.
Argon2PasswordEncoderWinner of the Password Hashing Competition and the current best choice for new systems. Tunable in memory as well as time, which is what defeats GPU and ASIC attackers - bcrypt is cheap to parallelise on a GPU, Argon2id is not. Needs BouncyCastle on the classpath.
SCryptPasswordEncoderAlso memory-hard; reasonable, but Argon2id is the more current recommendation.
Pbkdf2PasswordEncoderUse when FIPS compliance is required. Not memory-hard, so needs a high iteration count.
MessageDigestPasswordEncoder (MD5/SHA)Never for passwords. A modern GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second; the whole point of a password hash is to be slow.
DelegatingPasswordEncoderWhat PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() returns and what Boot uses by default. Reads a {id} prefix on the stored hash and dispatches to the matching encoder, which is how you migrate encodings without a big-bang password reset.

The filter chain, and why order decides behaviour

Spring Security is not magic applied to your controllers; it is a list of servlet Filter objects with a defined order, wired into the container by a single DelegatingFilterProxy named springSecurityFilterChain. That proxy hands the request to FilterChainProxy, which picks the first matching SecurityFilterChain and runs its filters in order. Everything you configure - CSRF, login, authorization - is a filter placed at a fixed position in that list.

Two positions in the list explain most of the confusing behaviour students hit.

AuthorizationFilter is last. It makes the accept/reject decision, so anything that must establish identity has to run before it. A custom JWT filter registered after it always sees an empty context and every request 401s.

ExceptionTranslationFilter sits just above it. It catches the exceptions the authorization filter throws and turns them into HTTP: AuthenticationException becomes a call to the AuthenticationEntryPoint (a 401 or a redirect to the login page), and AccessDeniedException becomes 403. A filter that throws above ExceptionTranslationFilter is not caught by it, which is why an exception thrown from your JWT filter often reaches the client as a raw 500 rather than a tidy 401.

Authentication and authorization are separate mechanisms

The two words get taught as a pair of definitions, but in Spring Security they are two distinct subsystems with different interfaces, different failure modes and different HTTP status codes. Being precise about which one is failing is most of the skill in debugging a security problem.

AspectDetail
AuthenticationEstablishes who the caller is. Implemented by AuthenticationManager delegating to AuthenticationProviders; produces an Authentication object placed in the SecurityContext. Failure raises AuthenticationException and the entry point returns 401.
AuthorizationDecides what that established identity may do. Implemented by AuthorizationManager against the request's GrantedAuthority set. Failure raises AccessDeniedException and returns 403.
OrderingAuthentication always first. There is nothing to authorize until there is a principal - though an unauthenticated caller is given an anonymousUser principal, which is why getAuthentication() is usually non-null rather than null.
The 403-on-anonymous trapBecause anonymous authentication exists, a missing token can produce 403 rather than 401 on a chain with no configured entry point - exactly what the source material observes mid-exercise. Configure an explicit authenticationEntryPoint to get the correct 401.
ROLE_ prefixhasRole("ADMIN") checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN - the prefix is added for you. hasAuthority("ADMIN") checks for the literal string ADMIN. Mixing the two silently denies access with no error message anywhere.
Roles against authoritiesA role is a coarse label (ADMIN); an authority is a fine-grained permission (order:delete). Both are GrantedAuthority instances - the distinction is convention only, and large systems are better served by permissions.

CSRF: what it defends, and why disabling it is safe only for stateless APIs

Nearly every Spring Security tutorial begins with csrf().disable() and never says why, which produces developers who disable it on session-based applications too. The reasoning matters more than the line of code.

A cross-site request forgery works because the browser attaches ambient credentials - a session cookie, or a saved Basic Auth credential - to a request automatically, based only on the destination origin. It does not care which page caused the request. So a form on evil.example can POST to bank.example/transfer, and the browser will helpfully attach the victim's bank.example session cookie. The server sees a perfectly authenticated request.

The defence is to require a value the attacker's page cannot read: a random CSRF token rendered into your own page and echoed back in the body or a header. The same-origin policy stops evil.example from reading it.

Now apply that to a JWT API. The token lives in localStorage or in memory and is attached by your JavaScript, explicitly, on each request. A cross-site form post carries no Authorization header - the attacker's page cannot add one, and the browser will not add it for them. There is no ambient credential, so there is nothing to forge, and CSRF protection defends against nothing. That - and only that - is what makes disabling it safe.

SituationCSRF setting
Session cookie plus form login, server-rendered pagesLeave it enabled. Disabling it is a live vulnerability.
JWT in the Authorization header, SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESSSafe to disable - no ambient credential exists.
JWT stored in a cookieThe cookie is ambient. You need CSRF protection again, plus SameSite=Strict. Storing a token in a cookie undoes the reason you disabled CSRF.
Single-page app plus session cookieKeep it enabled and use CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() so JavaScript can read the token and send it back as X-XSRF-TOKEN.
HTTP Basic from a browserThe browser caches and resends the credential, so it is ambient too. Keep CSRF enabled.

One further point on where a token is kept: localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS flaw hands the attacker the token. An HttpOnly cookie is immune to XSS theft but reintroduces CSRF. There is no option without a trade-off; the usual answer is a short-lived access token in memory plus a refresh token in an HttpOnly, SameSite cookie.

Session against stateless: what you actually trade

The exercise sets SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS without discussing the cost. Both models are legitimate; they fail in different ways, and the difference that matters most is revocation.

AspectSession (cookie)Stateless (JWT)
Where identity livesServer memory or a session store; the cookie is just a keyInside the signed token, at the client
Per-request costA session store lookupOne HMAC verification, no I/O
Horizontal scalingNeeds sticky sessions or a shared store (Spring Session + Redis)Any instance can verify independently
RevocationImmediate - delete the sessionNot possible without adding server state, which gives back the statelessness
Changing a user's rolesEffective on the next requestEffective only when the token expires
Payload size~32 bytes of cookie500-1000 bytes on every request; large claim sets can exceed header limits
LogoutGenuineClient-side only - the token stays valid until it expires
Main riskSession fixation, cookie theftKey compromise; a stolen token is usable for its full lifetime

That revocation row is the whole argument. A JWT is a bearer credential: whoever holds it is the user, and the server has agreed in advance to accept it until it expires. The standard mitigation is a short-lived access token (5-15 minutes) paired with a long-lived refresh token that is stored server-side and can be revoked. That is a hybrid, not pure statelessness, and admitting so is the honest position.

For a single-instance internal application with no scaling requirement, a plain session is simpler, revocable, and better. Choose JWT when you have several services or several instances that must verify identity without a shared session store.

Failure modes worth recognising on sight

SymptomCause
Every request returns 401 despite a token that decodes correctlyThe JWT filter is registered after AuthorizationFilter, or not registered on the chain that matched. Enable logging.level.org.springframework.security=DEBUG and read the filter list printed at startup.
Postman reports "socket hang up" on POST /tokenfilterChain.doFilter(...) is inside the if (header != null) block, so an unauthenticated request is never forwarded and no response is written. This is the bug in the source material.
403 instead of 401 for a missing tokenAnonymous authentication succeeded and the authorization rule then denied it. Configure an explicit authenticationEntryPoint.
There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id "null"The context holds a DelegatingPasswordEncoder but the stored hash has no {bcrypt} prefix. Either declare a concrete encoder bean or prefix the stored values.
WeakKeyException: The signing key's size is 48 bitsA short HMAC secret such as "secret". HS256 requires 256 bits; generate 32 random bytes and hold them in configuration or a secrets manager.
NoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/DatatypeConverterjjwt 0.9.0 on Java 11 or later. Upgrade to jjwt 0.12.x rather than adding the jaxb-api shim.
Login always fails although the password is demonstrably correctThe password was stored unencoded, or was encoded twice - a @PrePersist hook that encodes plus a service that also encodes. Print the stored value: a bcrypt hash starts with $2a$ and is exactly 60 characters.
Passwords longer than 72 characters all behave as the same passwordBCrypt truncates its input at 72 bytes. Reject over-long passwords, or pre-hash with SHA-512 before encoding.
Authentication works but SecurityContextHolder is empty in a @Async methodThe context is held in a ThreadLocal. Use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or the MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL strategy.
A browser front end gets CORS errors after security is addedThe preflight OPTIONS request has no credentials and is rejected. Configure .cors(...) with real origins - do not "fix" it with cors().disable(), which removes the headers entirely.
Every authenticated request triggers a database SELECTExpected for a stateless API - each request reloads the user. Cache UserDetails briefly, or carry the authorities as claims inside the token and skip the lookup, accepting that role changes then lag until the token expires.
Security rules work in the app but not in @WebMvcTestSlice tests do not import your SecurityFilterChain unless you add @Import(SecurityConfig.class), and they need spring-security-test with @WithMockUser.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why was WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter deprecated, and in which version?Deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 and removed in 6.0. It forced configuration through inheritance, which prevented multiple independent chains, made ordering opaque and made rules hard to test in isolation. The replacement is a component model: publish a SecurityFilterChain bean and let Spring compose it.
Write the modern equivalent of configure(HttpSecurity).A @Bean method taking HttpSecurity, configured with the lambda DSL and returning http.build(); antMatchers becomes requestMatchers, authorizeRequests becomes authorizeHttpRequests, and .and() chaining disappears because each configurer takes a Customizer.
What replaces configure(AuthenticationManagerBuilder)?Nothing is overridden - publish a UserDetailsService and a PasswordEncoder bean and Boot builds a DaoAuthenticationProvider automatically. Where an explicit AuthenticationManager is needed, obtain it from AuthenticationConfiguration.getAuthenticationManager().
Why must NoOpPasswordEncoder never be used?It stores passwords in plain text and compares with String.equals, so any database leak exposes every real password, and the non-constant-time comparison leaks how many leading characters matched. It has been deprecated since Spring Security 5.0 and exists only to let a legacy system boot during migration.
Why BCrypt or Argon2 rather than SHA-256?Password hashes must be deliberately slow and individually salted. SHA-256 is fast by design - billions of guesses per second on a GPU. BCrypt salts automatically and has a tunable work factor; Argon2id is additionally memory-hard, which is what defeats GPU and ASIC attackers.
Why does encoding the same password twice give different hashes, and how does login still work?Each call generates a fresh random salt, which is stored inside the hash string. matches() extracts that salt, re-hashes the supplied password with it, and compares. This is why a login can never be implemented as a SQL WHERE password = ? comparison.
Where in the filter chain must a custom JWT filter go, and why?Before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, and therefore well before AuthorizationFilter. AuthorizationFilter is last and makes the decision, so any filter that establishes identity must have already populated the SecurityContext - register it later and every request 401s despite a valid token.
What does ExceptionTranslationFilter do?It sits directly above AuthorizationFilter and converts security exceptions into HTTP: AuthenticationException invokes the AuthenticationEntryPoint (401 or a login redirect) and AccessDeniedException becomes 403. Exceptions thrown above it in the chain are not translated and surface as 500s.
Authentication or authorization - which fails with 401 and which with 403?Authentication failure gives 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header: identity was not established. Authorization failure gives 403: identity is accepted but the authorities are insufficient. A missing token can wrongly produce 403 when anonymous authentication succeeds and no AuthenticationEntryPoint is configured.
Why is csrf().disable() safe on a JWT API but dangerous on a session app?CSRF exploits ambient credentials the browser attaches automatically, such as a session cookie. A Bearer token is attached explicitly by your own JavaScript and cannot be added by an attacker's page, so there is nothing to forge. With a session cookie the ambient credential exists and disabling CSRF is a live vulnerability - as it is if you store the JWT in a cookie.
What does SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS actually guarantee?Only that Spring Security will neither create nor read an HttpSession, and that the SecurityContext is discarded after each request. Application code calling request.getSession() still creates one, so the API is not as stateless as the setting suggests.
How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?You cannot, without reintroducing server state. The practical answer is a short-lived access token (5-15 minutes) plus a revocable refresh token held server-side; logout deletes the refresh token and the access token simply expires. A blocklist works but trades away the statelessness that motivated JWT.
Is a JWT encrypted?No. Header and payload are base64url-encoded and readable by anyone holding the token; the signature only detects modification. Never place passwords or other confidential data in a claim, and always verify with a key you chose - never with the algorithm the token's own header names.
hasRole("ADMIN") against hasAuthority("ADMIN") - what is the difference?hasRole prepends ROLE_ and therefore checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN, while hasAuthority checks the literal string. Storing "ADMIN" and testing hasRole("ADMIN") denies access silently with nothing logged - one of the most common and least obvious security bugs.

The Problem Stateless Auth Solves

Classic form login stores the logged-in user in an HTTP session. The browser holds a JSESSIONID cookie, and the server holds a map from that id to the user. That works perfectly on one machine and starts falling apart the moment there are two.

SESSION-BASED, scaled to 3 instances

            +----------------+
  login --->|  Instance A    |  session map: { S1 -> "ajay" }
            +----------------+
            +----------------+
  next  --->|  Instance B    |  session map: { }        <- who is S1?
  request   +----------------+                             401. Logged out.
            +----------------+
            |  Instance C    |  session map: { }
            +----------------+

The load balancer sent request 2 to a machine that has never
heard of session S1.

The usual patches each cost something:

PatchWhat it costs
Sticky sessions - the balancer pins a client to one instanceThat instance restarting logs everyone on it out. Deployments become disruptive, and traffic no longer balances evenly.
Session replication - instances copy sessions to each otherNetwork chatter that grows with the square of the instance count, and a cluster that is now stateful.
Shared session store (Spring Session with Redis)Genuinely good, and the honest alternative to tokens. The cost is one more piece of infrastructure that must be highly available - if Redis is down, nobody is logged in.
Stateless token (JWT)The client carries the proof of identity. Any instance can verify it with nothing but a key. The cost is that you can no longer easily revoke it - the whole of the Expert tab circles back to this.

Mobile apps and third-party API clients have no cookie jar to begin with, which is the other reason token auth became the default for REST APIs.

What a JWT Actually Is

A JSON Web Token (RFC 7519) is three Base64URL-encoded strings joined by dots. Not encrypted - encoded. The first two parts are plain JSON that anyone can read; the third is a signature over the first two.

   eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9  .  eyJzdWIiOiJhamF5Iiwicm9sZXMiOlsi... .  qX3nO0kZ1s9dJ7fT2mVbYl8cPqRhE5wA6uKgN3tXsIY
   \_________________________________/     \____________________________/     \_________________________________________/
              HEADER                                  PAYLOAD                                   SIGNATURE
        base64url(JSON)                          base64url(JSON)              HMACSHA256(header + "." + payload, key)

  +-----------------------+   +--------------------------------+   +------------------------------+
  | { "alg": "HS256",     |   | { "sub": "ajay",               |   | opaque bytes - proves the    |
  |   "typ": "JWT" }      |   |   "roles": ["ROLE_USER"],      |   | two parts on the left have   |
  |                       |   |   "iat": 1756900000,           |   | not been altered since the   |
  | which algorithm was   |   |   "exp": 1756900900 }          |   | server signed them.          |
  | used to sign this     |   |                                |   |                              |
  +-----------------------+   | the CLAIMS - readable by       |   | NOT a secret. NOT encryption.|
                              | absolutely anyone              |   +------------------------------+
                              +--------------------------------+

The signature does not hide anything. It proves integrity and authenticity: this token was issued by someone holding the signing key, and nobody has edited it since. Change one character of the payload and the signature no longer matches, so the server rejects it.

The Standard Claims

A claim is one key/value pair in the payload. Some names are reserved by the RFC so that different systems agree on their meaning; the rest are yours.

ClaimMeaning
sub (subject)Who the token is about. Usually the user id or username. This is what your filter turns back into a UserDetails.
iss (issuer)Who minted it. Verify it when more than one system issues tokens you accept.
aud (audience)Who it is intended for. A token for the payments API should be rejected by the reporting API.
exp (expiration)Unix seconds after which the token must be rejected. Not optional in practice - a token without it never dies.
nbf (not before)Unix seconds before which it is not yet valid.
iat (issued at)When it was created. Useful for a token-version or global-logout check.
jti (JWT id)A unique id for this token. The hook a denylist hangs on - see the Expert tab.
Custom claimsAnything you add: roles, tenantId, email. Keep them small and non-secret; every request carries them.

Claims are a cache, not a source of truth. A role baked into a token at 10:00 is still in that token at 10:14 even if you revoked it at 10:05. Short lifetimes are what keep the staleness window small.

Dependencies and the Signing Key

jjwt (Java JWT) is the usual library. Since 0.11 it ships as three artifacts - the API you compile against and two runtime implementations - so that your code depends only on interfaces.

The signing key belongs in configuration, never in the source. HS256 requires at least 256 bits of key material; jjwt refuses anything shorter.

</dependency>

beginner.content:
The Registration Endpoint

Registration writes a user row with a hashed password. Nothing about JWT is involved yet - the token flow only starts at login - but the two endpoints are always built together.

BCryptPasswordEncoder is one-way and salts each hash itself, so two users with the same password get different stored values. The column must be at least 60 characters wide or the hash is truncated and nobody can ever log in.

The Login Endpoint - Issuing the Token

Login is the only place credentials are ever checked. It runs them through the AuthenticationManager, and only if that succeeds does it ask the token service for a token.

Do not hash the password yourself here. The DaoAuthenticationProvider behind the manager loads the user, calls PasswordEncoder.matches(raw, storedHash) and throws BadCredentialsException on a mismatch. Reimplementing that loses the timing-attack protection it already has.

Validating the Token on Every Request

Once the client has a token it sends it on every request in the Authorization header. A filter reads it, verifies the signature and expiry, and puts an Authentication into the SecurityContextHolder so the rest of the chain treats the caller as logged in.

GET /api/orders     Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9....
   |
   v
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| JwtAuthenticationFilter  (extends OncePerRequestFilter)        |
|                                                                |
|  1. header present and starts with "Bearer " ?  -- no --> skip |
|  2. parse + verify signature with the key      -- bad --> skip |
|  3. exp in the future ?                        -- no  --> skip |
|  4. build UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken                  |
|  5. SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...)  |
|                                                                |
|  6. chain.doFilter(request, response)   <-- ALWAYS, every path |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
   |
   v
AuthorizationFilter   context empty -> 401 / 403
   |                  context populated -> check roles
   v
DispatcherServlet -> OrderController -> 200 OK

The filter never rejects anything itself. It either populates the context or leaves it empty; the authorization filter further down decides the outcome. Mixing those two responsibilities is what produces filters that return 403 where a 401 was correct.

OncePerRequestFilter is the right base class because a forward or an ERROR dispatch would otherwise run the filter a second time on the same request.

Wiring It Into the SecurityFilterChain

Three things make the application a stateless token API: the filter is registered before the username/password filter, the session policy is STATELESS, and the login and registration endpoints are open.

The filter is declared as a plain @Bean rather than a @Component on purpose. A Filter bean in the context is picked up by Boot's servlet auto-registration and installed in the container's chain as well, so it runs twice - once outside Spring Security and once inside. Declaring it here keeps it in one chain only.

Role-Based Authorization From the Token's Claims

The authorities in the SecurityContext come from the token's roles claim (or from the database lookup the filter does). Once they are there, both URL rules and method annotations work exactly as they do with any other authentication mechanism.

Spring Security's hasRole("ADMIN") checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN - it prepends the prefix for you. hasAuthority("ADMIN") does not. Storing "ADMIN" and asking for hasRole("ADMIN") is the single most common cause of a 403 that "makes no sense".

expert.content:
Signed, Not Encrypted - the Point Everyone Misses

This is the first thing to get right, because most JWT mistakes descend from it. A standard JWT (a JWS, JSON Web Signature) is signed. The payload is Base64URL, which is an encoding, not a cipher. There is no key involved in reading it.

PropertyDoes a JWS give it to you?
Integrity - nobody edited the claimsYes. That is what the signature is for.
Authenticity - it was issued by the key holderYes.
Confidentiality - nobody can read the claimsNo. Everyone can read them. Always.

So a JWT payload is visible to: the browser's JavaScript, browser devtools, any proxy on the path, your access logs if you ever log a URL containing a token, an APM tool, a screenshot in a bug report, and anyone the user pastes it to. Everything you put in it is public to whoever holds the token.

Never place in a JWT: a password or password hash, a card number, an API key or database credential, a national identity number, medical or salary data, an internal host name or connection string, anything under a data-protection regime.
Do place: a user id, a username, roles or scopes, a tenant id, expiry - identifiers, not secrets.

If the claims genuinely must be hidden, the answer is JWE (JSON Web Encryption), a different structure with five segments rather than three. In most systems the better answer is not to put the secret in the token.

alg=none and Algorithm Confusion

The header carries the algorithm - and the header is written by whoever sends the token. A verifier that trusts it is trusting the attacker.

AttackHow it works
alg=noneThe RFC defines an "unsecured JWT" with "alg":"none" and an empty signature. An attacker takes a real token, rewrites the payload to "roles":["ROLE_ADMIN"], sets the header algorithm to none, drops the signature and sends it. A library that honours the header verifies nothing and accepts it.
RS256 to HS256 confusionThe server verifies RS256 with an RSA public key, which is public by definition. The attacker changes the header to HS256 and signs the forged token with that public key as the HMAC secret. A verifier that picks the algorithm from the header uses the same public key as an HMAC key - and the signature checks out.
Key confusion via jku/jwkThose header parameters name (or embed) the key to verify with. A verifier that fetches the key the token points at lets the attacker supply their own key. Never resolve a verification key from the token.

The rule: pin the expected algorithm and the expected key on the verifier side, and ignore what the header asks for. Current jjwt is safe by default - verifyWith(SecretKey) only accepts the MAC algorithms that key supports, and parseSignedClaims rejects an unsecured token. The vulnerable pattern is code that reads the header first and then chooses.

HS256 or RS256 - Symmetric Against Asymmetric

HS256 (HMAC-SHA256)RS256 / ES256 (RSA / ECDSA)
KeysOne shared secret, used to sign and to verifyA private key signs; the public key verifies
Who can mint tokensAnyone who can verify oneOnly the holder of the private key
Key distributionEvery verifier needs the secret, so every verifier is a place it can leak fromThe public key can be published - typically at a JWKS endpoint
Token size and CPUSmall signature, very fastLarger signature (256 bytes for RSA-2048), slower to sign; ES256 is compact and fast
Key rotationCoordinated - every service must swap at onceIndependent - publish the new public key with a new kid, verifiers pick it up
FitsA single service, or a monolith, that both issues and verifiesAn auth server plus several resource services; anything third parties verify

The decisive question is: how many services need to verify? With HS256 and five microservices, the signing secret is deployed to five places. Any one of them, compromised, can mint an admin token for the whole estate - and you cannot tell from the token which service issued it. With RS256 the private key lives in exactly one process and the other four hold only a public key, which is harmless if it leaks.

The kid header. Rotation needs the verifier to know which key signed a given token. Put a key id in the header, keep a map of active keys, and rotation becomes: publish the new key, start signing with it, and retire the old one once every token signed with it has expired.
codeExamples:
// In practice, once you are asymmetric, let Spring Security fetch the keys.
# application.yml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          # The provider publishes its public keys here. Spring caches them,
          # matches the token's "kid", and picks up rotated keys with no
          # deployment on your side.
          jwk-set-uri: https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com
          audiences: javaschoollab-api

// OUTPUT (behaviour): no filter, no JwtService, no key file. Signature,
// exp, nbf, iss and aud are all validated by the framework, and an
// unknown "kid" triggers one refresh of the JWKS rather than a rejection.

expert.content:
The Revocation Problem

Here is the honest trade of stateless auth. A signed token cannot be un-signed. "Log out" on the client deletes the token from that client; the token itself remains valid until exp. If it was copied - XSS, a shared machine, a proxy log - deleting the client's copy achieves nothing.

10:00  token issued to ajay,  exp = 20:00   (a 10-hour token)
10:05  ajay's laptop is stolen with the token in localStorage
10:06  admin disables the ajay account in the database
10:07  attacker sends the stolen token
       -> signature valid, exp valid, no database is consulted
       -> 200 OK

       The account is disabled. The token still works.
       It keeps working until 20:00.

There is no clever way out: any real revocation requires server-side state, which is the very thing the token was meant to avoid. The engineering choice is how much state, and where.

ApproachHow it trades off
Short-lived access token + refresh tokenThe main answer. Access token 5-15 minutes, refresh token days. Revocation is applied at refresh time, so the worst-case exposure is one access-token lifetime. No per-request state.
Denylist keyed by jtiOn logout or compromise, store the token's jti in Redis with a TTL equal to its remaining lifetime; the filter checks membership. Immediate and precise. Costs one lookup per request, and the auth path now depends on Redis being up.
Token-version claimPut ver in the token and a token_version column on the user. Bump the column to invalidate every token that user holds. One cheap comparison, no extra infrastructure - and it is all-or-nothing per user, which is exactly right for "log out everywhere" and a password change.
Allowlist of issued tokensStore every live token server-side and check each request. Correct, immediate, and you have re-invented sessions with worse ergonomics. If you need this, use Spring Session and a shared store honestly.

What to do in practice: short access tokens plus a stored, revocable refresh token, and a token-version claim for account-wide invalidation. Reach for the jti denylist only when a single-token, immediate kill switch is a stated requirement.

Refresh Tokens, Rotation and Reuse Detection

Splitting the credential in two is what makes short access-token lifetimes tolerable. The access token is a short-lived JWT sent to every endpoint; the refresh token is long-lived, sent only to the refresh endpoint, and - unlike the access token - is stored server-side so it can be revoked.

A refresh token that is itself a self-validating JWT gains you nothing. Its whole purpose is to be revocable, and that requires a row in a table. Store an opaque random string (or its hash), not a JWT.

Rotation: every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the one presented. This bounds the value of a stolen refresh token to a single use.

Reuse detection is what turns rotation into a defence rather than a formality. If an already-used refresh token is presented, exactly one of two things has happened: the legitimate client is retrying after a lost response, or an attacker is replaying a stolen token. You cannot tell which - so you revoke the entire family and force a fresh login.

   client                                            server
     |-- POST /login ------------------------------->|
     |<-- access A1 (15 min) + refresh R1 (7 days) --|   R1 stored, family F
     |                                               |
     |  ... 15 minutes pass, A1 expires ...          |
     |-- POST /refresh  { R1 } --------------------->|   R1 valid & unused
     |<-- access A2 + refresh R2 --------------------|   R1 marked USED, R2 stored
     |                                               |
  ~~ attacker stole R1 earlier and replays it ~~     |
     |-- POST /refresh  { R1 } --------------------->|   R1 already USED
     |<-- 401, and family F is revoked entirely -----|   R2 killed too
     |                                               |
     |  the real user's next refresh with R2 fails,  |
     |  they log in again - and you have a signal    |
     |  that a token was stolen, which is the point. |

Where the Browser Should Keep the Token

There is no option here without a real weakness, and pretending otherwise is how bad advice spreads. Both common answers are vulnerable to something.

localStorage / sessionStoragehttpOnly cookie
Readable by JavaScriptYes - so any XSS on your origin exfiltrates the tokenNo - httpOnly hides it from document.cookie
Sent automatically by the browserNo - your code attaches it, so cross-site requests carry nothingYes - which is precisely what CSRF exploits
Needs CSRF defenceNoYes - SameSite, and a CSRF token for anything not fully same-site
Works cross-origin / for mobile clientsStraightforwardlyAwkward - third-party cookie rules, CORS credentials, no cookie jar on a native client
Survives a tab closelocalStorage yes, sessionStorage noDepends on Max-Age

The actual trade-off: localStorage is exposed to XSS; an httpOnly cookie is exposed to CSRF. Neither is strictly safer - they fail to different attacks. The difference in severity is that XSS is strictly worse when it happens: script running on your origin can read the token, make authenticated requests, and read the responses. CSRF makes a request but cannot read the reply, and SameSite=Strict or Lax defeats most of it at the cost of a browser-compatibility floor.

A defensible position, not a slogan:
• Same-site web app: an httpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie for the refresh token, and the access token in JavaScript memory only (a variable, not localStorage) - it dies with the tab and never lands in storage an XSS payload can read at leisure.
• Cross-origin SPA, mobile app or third-party client: the Authorization header, with a short access-token lifetime.
• Either way: if you have XSS, you have lost. A cookie only means the attacker rides the session from your page instead of stealing the token - Content-Security-Policy and output encoding are the real defence.

Never put a token in a URL. Query strings land in access logs, browser history, and the Referer header sent to every third-party asset on the page.

Expiry, Clock Skew and Other Sharp Edges

IssueWhat happens, and what to do
Clock skewexp and nbf are absolute times compared against the verifier's clock. If the issuing server is 30 seconds ahead, a freshly minted token has an nbf/iat in the verifier's future and is rejected as not-yet-valid - an intermittent 401 that reproduces nowhere. Allow 30-60 seconds of leeway (clockSkewSeconds) and run NTP. Leeway is not a substitute for synchronised clocks.
Seconds, not millisecondsexp, iat and nbf are Unix seconds. Writing System.currentTimeMillis() into exp yields a token expiring in the year 56000 - it never expires, and no library warns you.
No exp at allA token with no expiry is a permanent credential. Most libraries accept it happily. Always set it, and reject tokens that lack it.
Lifetime too long10 hours is common in tutorials and indefensible in production: it is the exact window during which a stolen token works and nothing can stop it. 5-15 minutes for an access token.
Claim bloatEvery claim is sent on every request, base64-expanded by a third. Fifty permissions in a token can push it past a proxy's header limit and produce 431 Request Header Fields Too Large - or a silent truncation.
Logging tokensAn Authorization header in a debug log or an APM trace is a live credential sitting in a system with far broader access than the API. Mask it at the logging layer.
Trusting sub without verifyingReading the subject before the signature check - or with an unsecured parser - is an authentication bypass. Verify first, read second, always in that order.
No aud checkA token minted for the marketing API is accepted by the payments API because both trust the same issuer. Require the audience.

Role-Based Against Permission-Based Authorization

hasRole('ADMIN') is easy to write and ages badly. The role is a label for a bundle of capabilities, and the moment the bundle needs to differ for one customer you end up with ROLE_ADMIN_LITE and a checked-in list of exceptions.

Role-basedPermission-based (scopes/authorities)
The check readshasRole('ADMIN')hasAuthority('order:delete')
Changing what a role can doEdit every endpoint that names the role, and redeployEdit the role-to-permission mapping in data; the endpoints do not change
Reading the code"Only admins" - but what is an admin allowed to do? Nobody can say without grepping.The annotation states the capability the endpoint requires. Self-documenting.
Token sizeTwo or three rolesPotentially dozens of strings - which is the real cost
FitsSmall applications, few and stable rolesMulti-tenant products, anything where customers configure their own roles

The usual arrangement: roles are how permissions are administered; permissions are what the code checks. Roles map to permissions in the database, the token carries the resolved permissions (or the role, with the service resolving it), and every endpoint names a capability.

Neither answers "may this user touch this row". That is an ownership question and no claim in a token can settle it - the token says what you may do, not to what. Check ownership in the service, against the loaded entity.

Do Not Hand-Roll This

Everything above is worth understanding, and in most real projects you should not write it. Spring Security ships an OAuth2 resource server that does token validation properly, and an authorization server or an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito, Entra ID) that does issuance, refresh, rotation, revocation, MFA and key rotation.

ConcernHand-rolled filteroauth2-resource-server
Signature and algorithm pinningYours to get rightBuilt in, safe by default
exp / nbf / iss / aud validationYours, and commonly incompleteConfigured, with skew handling
Key rotationA deploymentJWKS fetched and cached, kid matched automatically
Claim-to-authority mappingHand-writtenJwtAuthenticationConverter
Error responsesWhatever your filter doesRFC 6750 WWW-Authenticate with proper error codes
Opaque-token introspectionNot supportedOne property change
Login, refresh, rotation, MFA, password resetAll yours, foreverThe identity provider's problem

Write the filter when you are learning how this works, or the application is genuinely small and self-contained and adding an identity provider is disproportionate. Use the framework when more than one service verifies tokens, when tokens come from an external provider, or when the system holds anything worth stealing. "We wrote our own JWT filter" is a finding in a security review, not a boast.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is a JWT encrypted?No. A standard JWT is signed, not encrypted - the payload is Base64URL and anyone holding the token can read every claim. The signature guarantees integrity and authenticity only. Encryption needs JWE.
What are the three parts of a JWT?Header (algorithm and type), payload (the claims), and signature over base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload) using the signing key.
What problem does a stateless token solve?Server-side sessions do not survive being spread over N instances without sticky sessions, replication or a shared store. A signed token lets any instance verify identity with only a key.
Which claims matter, and why aud?sub, exp, iat, iss, aud, jti. Without an audience check, a token minted for one API is accepted by every other API that trusts the same issuer.
What is the alg=none attack?The algorithm lives in the attacker-controlled header. Setting it to none and dropping the signature bypasses verification in any library that trusts the header. Pin the expected algorithm and key on the verifier.
What is algorithm confusion (RS256 to HS256)?The attacker rewrites the header to HS256 and signs with the RSA public key as the HMAC secret. A verifier that selects the algorithm from the header then validates a forgery. Never let the token choose its own verification method.
HS256 or RS256?HS256 shares one secret for signing and verifying - fine when a single service does both. RS256 signs with a private key and verifies with a public one, so several services can verify without any of them being able to mint tokens. Asymmetric wins as soon as verification is distributed.
How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?Strictly, you cannot - that is the cost of statelessness. Practical answers: short-lived access tokens with a revocable refresh token, a jti denylist in Redis with a TTL, or a token-version claim compared against a column on the user.
What does logout actually do in a JWT system?It deletes the client's copy and revokes the stored refresh token. The access token itself stays valid until exp, which is why that lifetime must be short.
Why have a refresh token at all?It lets the access token be short-lived without asking the user to log in every fifteen minutes. It is stored server-side, so it is the revocable half of the pair - which is why it should be opaque, not a JWT.
What is refresh token rotation and reuse detection?Each refresh issues a new refresh token and marks the old one used. Presenting a used token means it was replayed, so the whole token family is revoked and the user must log in again - turning a silent theft into a detected one.
localStorage or httpOnly cookie?Neither is safe outright: localStorage is readable by any XSS on your origin; an httpOnly cookie is sent automatically and so is exposed to CSRF (mitigated by SameSite). Name the trade-off - a cross-origin or mobile client points to the header, a same-site web app to a cookie for the refresh token with the access token held in memory.
Why does a valid token sometimes give 401 intermittently?Clock skew. exp and nbf are compared against the verifier's clock, so an issuer running fast produces tokens that are not yet valid elsewhere. Allow 30-60 seconds of leeway and synchronise clocks with NTP.
401 or 403 for a valid token without the right role?403. Authentication succeeded - identity is known - and only authorization failed. 401 is for a missing, expired or invalid token.
Role-based or permission-based authorization?Roles are convenient for administration; permissions (order:delete) are what code should check, because changing what a role may do then becomes data rather than a redeployment. Neither settles row-level ownership - check that in the service against the loaded entity.
Should you write your own JWT filter in production?Usually not. spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server validates signature, algorithm, expiry, issuer and audience, handles JWKS and key rotation, and returns RFC 6750 errors. Hand-rolled filters are where the algorithm and expiry bugs live.
