The Problem: Code That Does Not Belong Where It Sits

Open any real service class and you will find two kinds of code mixed together. There is the code that answers the question the class exists to answer - transfer money, register a student, price an order. And there is the code that is there because the system needs it - logging, timing, security checks, transaction boundaries, retries, auditing.

The second kind is called a cross-cutting concern. It cuts across the class hierarchy: it is not the responsibility of any one class, yet every class needs it. Because inheritance runs vertically and this need runs horizontally, ordinary object-oriented tools cannot capture it. So it gets copy-pasted.

The Fix: Say It Once

Aspect-Oriented Programming lets you write that plumbing once, in its own class, and declare where it should apply. The service goes back to being about orders.

Nothing in OrderService refers to the aspect. That is the whole point - the concern is applied from the outside, so the business class never learns it is being logged.

The Vocabulary

AOP has five terms. They sound abstract until you map them onto the example above, so the table does exactly that.

TermMeaning
AspectThe module holding a cross-cutting concern. LoggingAspect is one - a class annotated @Aspect.
Join PointA point in program execution where an aspect could be applied. In Spring AOP a join point is always a method execution on a Spring bean - nothing else.
PointcutAn expression selecting which join points to advise. execution(* com.jsl.service..*(..)) is a pointcut.
AdviceThe code that runs at a matched join point, and when it runs: before, after, or around.
WeavingThe act of linking aspects into the target. Spring does it at runtime by wrapping the bean in a proxy; AspectJ can do it at compile time.
Target objectThe real, unadvised bean - the actual OrderService instance sitting behind the proxy.

A one-line summary worth memorising: a pointcut selects join points, and advice is what runs there.

Where each advice type fires relative to the method call:
      caller
        |
        v
  +-----------------------------------------------------+
  |  PROXY                                              |
  |                                                     |
  |    @Around  (before proceed)                        |
  |    @Before  ------------------------+               |
  |                                     v               |
  |                          +---------------------+    |
  |                          |  target method      |    |
  |                          |  (the JOIN POINT)   |    |
  |                          +----------+----------+    |
  |                                     |               |
  |             returns normally  <-----+----->  throws |
  |                    |                           |    |
  |            @AfterReturning              @AfterThrowing
  |                    |                           |    |
  |                    +-------------+-------------+    |
  |                                  v                  |
  |    @After   (finally - runs on BOTH paths)          |
  |    @Around  (after proceed - skipped if it threw)   |
  +-----------------------------------------------------+
        |
        v
      caller

Note the asymmetry: @After is a finally block and always runs. The code after proceed() in an @Around is not a finally block - if the target throws, that code is skipped unless you wrote your own try/finally.

Setting It Up

One starter. It pulls in aspectjweaver (Spring AOP borrows AspectJ's annotations and pointcut syntax, though not its weaver) and switches on @EnableAspectJAutoProxy through auto-configuration.

You do not need @EnableAspectJAutoProxy in a Spring Boot application. In a plain Spring application you do.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-aop</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Gradle:
     implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-aop' -->

<!-- WITHOUT this dependency, an @Aspect class still compiles if
     aspectjweaver arrives transitively, and it is still registered as a
     @Component - but no advice ever fires. The class looks correct and
     does nothing, which is the most confusing failure mode there is. -->

# application.properties - useful while learning
logging.level.org.springframework.aop=DEBUG

# Force CGLIB even for beans that implement interfaces.
# Spring Boot already defaults this to true; see the Expert tab for why.
spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true

beginner.content:
Your First Aspect: @Before

Two annotations make a class an aspect, and both are required:

@Aspect - tells Spring this class contains advice.
@Component - tells Spring to create the bean in the first place.

@Aspect alone is a very common mistake. It is an AspectJ annotation, not a Spring stereotype, so it does not cause bean creation. If Spring never instantiates the class, Spring never reads its advice.

Pointcut Expressions, Piece by Piece

The pointcut is where most of the learning is. The commonest designator is execution, and its grammar is:

execution( modifiers?  return-type  declaring-type?.method-name(params)  throws? )
             optional    REQUIRED       optional    REQUIRED   REQUIRED   optional


execution( *  com.jsl.service.OrderService.placeOrder(..) )
           |            |            |          |        |
           |            |            |          |        +-- any arguments
           |            |            |          +----------- this method only
           |            |            +---------------------- this class only
           |            +----------------------------------- this package
           +------------------------------------------------ any return type


Wildcards:
    *      exactly one element   (one package segment, one word, one arg)
    ..     zero or more          (sub-packages, or any argument list)


execution(* com.jsl.service.*.*(..))       every method of every class
                                           DIRECTLY in com.jsl.service

execution(* com.jsl.service..*.*(..))      ... and in every SUB-package too
                          ^^
                          this is the difference: '..' descends

execution(public * *(..))                  every public method, anywhere
execution(* save*(..))                     any method whose name starts "save"
execution(String com.jsl..*.*(..))         only methods returning String
execution(* *..*Service.*(..))             any class named *Service
execution(* com.jsl..*.find*(Long))        find* taking exactly one Long
execution(* com.jsl..*.find*(Long, ..))    find* whose FIRST arg is a Long

Four other designators cover almost everything else:

DesignatorSelects
within(com.jsl.service..*)Any join point inside that package or its sub-packages. Coarser than execution, and cheaper to match.
@annotation(com.jsl.Auditable)Methods carrying that annotation. The most maintainable option - the target opts in explicitly.
@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)Methods of any class carrying that annotation, e.g. every @Service.
bean(*Service)Beans whose name matches. Spring-specific, and useful when you think in beans rather than packages.
args(Long, ..)Calls whose runtime arguments match, and can bind them into the advice.

The Five Advice Types

AnnotationWhen it runs
@BeforeBefore the method. Cannot prevent it running or alter the result; can only throw.
@AfterAfter the method, on every path - like finally. Use it for cleanup that must always happen.
@AfterReturningOnly when the method returned normally. Can read (and with returning= bind) the returned value.
@AfterThrowingOnly when the method threw. Can bind the exception. It does not swallow it - the exception still propagates.
@AroundWraps the call. The most powerful: it can change arguments, skip the call entirely, alter the return value, catch exceptions, or retry.

@Around and Performance Monitoring

@Around is the only advice that receives a ProceedingJoinPoint, and the only one that decides whether the target method runs at all. Calling pjp.proceed() invokes it; not calling it means the method never executes.

The single most common bug in AOP: forgetting to return the result of proceed(). The advice runs, the method runs, and the caller receives null.

expert.content:
Spring AOP is a Proxy, Not a Weaver

This single fact explains every surprise in Spring AOP, so it is worth stating precisely.

AspectJ is a full AOP implementation. It performs bytecode weaving: at compile time or class-load time it rewrites the .class files, physically inserting advice into the method bodies. It can advise constructors, field access, static methods, private methods, and objects you created with new.

Spring AOP does none of that. It creates a proxy - a separate object that implements the same interface or extends the same class, holds a reference to your real bean, and interposes advice on each call it forwards. Your bytecode is untouched.
What the container actually injects:

  @Autowired OrderService orderService;
                  |
                  v
        +---------------------+          +--------------------+
        |  OrderService$$      |  calls  |   OrderService     |
        |  SpringCGLIB$$0      | ------> |   (the TARGET,     |
        |                      |         |    your real bean) |
        |  advice runs HERE    |         |                    |
        +---------------------+          +--------------------+

  Every consequence below follows from this one picture:
  advice runs on the ARROW, not inside the box.

Aspect of the modelConsequence
Advice lives on the proxyOnly calls that go through the proxy are advised.
The proxy is a Spring beanObjects created with new are never advised.
The proxy overrides methodsfinal, private and static methods cannot be advised.
Join points are method executions onlyNo field access, no constructor, no new - unlike AspectJ.

Self-Invocation: The Failure Everyone Hits

If a method of a bean calls another method of the same bean, the call goes through this - the raw target object - not through the proxy. The proxy is never involved, so no advice runs.

This is the exact mechanism behind the most-reported Spring bug on the internet: "@Transactional is not working". It is not broken; the call simply never reached the proxy. The same is true of @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, @Retryable and your own aspects, because they are all the same machinery.

JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB

Spring has two ways to build the proxy, and which one it picks changes what can be advised and what you can inject.

 JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB
Mechanismjava.lang.reflect.Proxy - implements the interfacesGenerates a runtime subclass of the target
RequiresThe bean implements at least one interfaceA non-final class with a usable constructor
Can be injected asThe interface only - never the concrete classThe class or its interfaces
Cannot adviseMethods not on the interfacefinal classes and final methods
Also blockedprivate and static methods, in both

Historically Spring chose JDK proxies when interfaces were present and CGLIB otherwise. Spring Boot sets spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true, so CGLIB is the default regardless of interfaces - specifically to avoid the "cannot inject the concrete type" failure below, which confused people for years.

Advice Ordering with @Order

When several aspects match the same join point the order matters, and the default is undefined. Give each aspect an explicit precedence.

Lower number means higher precedence, and for an @Around the higher-precedence aspect is the outermost wrapper - it runs first on the way in and last on the way out. Think of nested boxes, not a queue.
@Order(1) SecurityAspect     @Order(2) TxAspect      @Order(3) LoggingAspect

  +-- Security in ---------------------------------------+
  |    +-- Tx begin ------------------------------------+ |
  |    |    +-- Log enter -------------------------+    | |
  |    |    |          TARGET METHOD               |    | |
  |    |    +-- Log exit --------------------------+    | |
  |    +-- Tx commit -----------------------------------+ |
  +-- Security out --------------------------------------+

  IN:   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> target
  OUT:  target -> 3 -> 2 -> 1        (reverse - it is a stack)

  Consequence that bites: put logging at @Order(3), inside the
  transaction aspect, and your "method finished" log line is
  written BEFORE the commit. If the commit then fails, the log
  says success and the database says nothing happened.

Within a single aspect class, ordering between advice methods is not controlled by @Order at all. Spring orders by advice type (@Around and @Before first, then @After/@AfterReturning/@AfterThrowing), and beyond that it is unspecified. If two pieces of advice must be ordered relative to each other, put them in separate aspect classes.

The Best Thing to Know: Spring Itself Is Built On This

Students treat AOP as an optional extra. It is not. A large part of Spring's declarative programming model is AOP, and once you see that, a whole class of bugs becomes predictable rather than mysterious.

AnnotationHow it actually works
@TransactionalTransactionInterceptor - an @Around advice that begins a transaction, calls proceed(), then commits or rolls back.
@Cacheable, @CacheEvictCacheInterceptor - around advice that looks in the cache and skips proceed() on a hit.
@AsyncAsyncExecutionInterceptor - around advice that submits proceed() to a TaskExecutor and returns immediately.
@PreAuthorize, @Secured, @RolesAllowedSpring Security method security - around advice evaluating the expression before proceed().
@Retryable (Spring Retry)Around advice calling proceed() in a loop.
@Validated on a beanMethodValidationInterceptor - validates arguments before proceed().
@Timed (Micrometer)Around advice recording a timer - exactly the aspect from the beginner tab.

Because they share one mechanism, they share every limitation: all of them fail silently on self-invocation, on final methods, on private methods, and on objects created with new. Learn the rule once and you have debugged five features.

The Practical Pattern: a Custom @Auditable Annotation

Package-based pointcuts such as execution(* com.jsl.service..*(..)) are a maintenance liability: they silently start advising code that someone adds to that package next year, and reading a service method tells you nothing about what wraps it.

A custom annotation with an @annotation pointcut inverts that. The target opts in visibly, the pointcut is narrow and fast, and the annotation can carry parameters the advice needs. This is how @Transactional and @Cacheable are designed, and it is the pattern to reach for in your own code.

Cost, and Why a Broad Pointcut Is a Bad Idea

A single advised call costs very little - a proxy dispatch and an interceptor chain walk, on the order of tens to hundreds of nanoseconds. The problem is never one call. It is the pointcut that matches a hundred thousand of them.

PointcutProblem
execution(* com..*.*(..))Matches every method of every bean, including repositories, converters and getters. Every bean becomes a proxy; hot loops calling a getter a million times pay the interceptor cost a million times.
execution(public * *(..))The same, with no package limit at all. Spring must evaluate this against every candidate method of every bean at startup.
Logging every argumentArrays.toString(pjp.getArgs()) calls toString() on entities. A lazy JPA collection is initialised by the logging - extra queries, or a LazyInitializationException thrown from the logging, which then breaks a request that was working.
Advice writing to a databaseAn audit insert on every service call doubles your write load and adds its latency to every request.

Guidance
Prefer @annotation - narrowest possible match, explicit opt-in.
Otherwise anchor on a specific package and layer: within(com.jsl.service..*) && execution(public * *(..)).
Put within(...) or @within(...) first in a compound pointcut - they are cheap type-level checks that let AspectJ discard most classes before the expensive execution signature match.
Never advise repositories or entities. Never advise getters.
Guard expensive advice: if (log.isDebugEnabled()) before building any log string.
For real production metrics, use Micrometer's @Timed rather than a hand-rolled aspect - it aggregates into histograms instead of writing a line per call.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a cross-cutting concern?A requirement affecting many modules but belonging to none - logging, security, transactions, caching, auditing. Inheritance cannot express it because it runs across the hierarchy rather than down it.
Define aspect, join point, pointcut and advice.An aspect is the module holding the concern; a join point is a place where advice could run (in Spring AOP, always a method execution); a pointcut is the expression selecting join points; advice is the code that runs there.
How is Spring AOP implemented?By runtime proxies - JDK dynamic proxies or CGLIB subclasses - not by bytecode weaving. Advice runs in the proxy as it forwards the call to the target bean.
Spring AOP vs AspectJ?Spring AOP advises only public method executions on Spring beans and needs no build step. AspectJ weaves bytecode and can advise constructors, fields, static and private methods, and non-Spring objects, at the cost of a compile-time or load-time agent.
Why does @Transactional silently do nothing sometimes?The call did not cross the proxy: self-invocation within the same bean, a final, private or static method, or an object created with new.
What is self-invocation and how do you fix it?One method of a bean calling another through this, bypassing the proxy. Fix by moving the method to a separate bean (preferred), self-injecting with @Lazy, using AopContext.currentProxy(), or switching to AspectJ weaving.
JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB - how does Spring choose?Classically JDK when the bean implements an interface, CGLIB otherwise. Spring Boot sets proxy-target-class=true, so CGLIB is the default either way.
Why can a final method not be advised?CGLIB proxies by generating a subclass and overriding methods; a final method cannot be overridden, so the call reaches the inherited original with no interception - and no warning is issued.
Which advice types exist?@Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing and @Around. Only @Around can prevent the call, change arguments, or alter the return value.
Difference between @After and @AfterReturning?@After is a finally block and runs on both the normal and exceptional paths; @AfterReturning runs only on normal completion and can bind the returned value.
What happens if @Around does not return proceed()'s result?The target method runs but the caller receives null. It compiles cleanly, which makes it the commonest AOP bug.
What does @Order mean for @Around advice?Lower value means higher precedence and an outer position: it runs first entering and last leaving. Ordering between advice inside a single aspect class is not guaranteed - split them into separate aspects.
Which Spring features are built on AOP?@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @Retryable, method-level Spring Security, and method validation - which is why they all share the same proxy limitations.
Why is execution(* com..*.*(..)) a bad pointcut?It proxies and intercepts every method of every bean, including getters and repositories in hot loops. It slows startup, floods the logs, and can break startup on infrastructure beans. Prefer @annotation or a package-anchored pointcut on public methods.
Why is @Aspect alone not enough?@Aspect is an AspectJ annotation and does not create a bean. Without @Component (or an explicit @Bean) Spring never instantiates the class and never reads its advice.

What is Transaction Management?

• Transaction management is the mechanism used to maintain consistency of the user's data.
• With it we can handle errors and faults while the code is running. @Transactional is placed above a method to ensure that the code reverts all its changes if any error or exception occurs while it runs.
• In a Spring Boot application we use @Transactional on the business logic that is data-critical.

Why do we need it?

Suppose you want to store a user together with their policies:

1.  save the USER      -> committed to the database
2.  save POLICY #1     -> committed to the database
3.  save POLICY #2     -> RUNTIME EXCEPTION

Result WITHOUT a transaction:
    user  : saved
    policy: only one of two saved

The user row now exists with incomplete policy data.
What is the use of that user record?

To overcome this issue, transaction management comes into the picture. Either everything is saved, or nothing is.

The two annotations

AnnotationWhere it goes
@EnableTransactionManagementAbove the main class of the Spring Boot application.
@TransactionalOn the service method that must succeed or fail as one unit.

Note: in a Spring Boot application @EnableTransactionManagement is already applied by auto-configuration whenever a DataSource is on the classpath. Adding it explicitly is harmless and makes the intent visible, which is why the walkthrough includes it.

Example - One User Has Many Policies

Business requirement: save one user's details with multiple policies.

Problem statement: design the REST API to save one user with multiple policies.

Steps

expert.content:
The Rule That Catches Everyone: Rollback Only on Unchecked Exceptions

By default, Spring rolls back on RuntimeException and Error - and commits on a checked exception. This surprises almost everyone the first time.

Self-Invocation: Why @Transactional Sometimes Does Nothing

@Transactional works through a proxy. Spring wraps your bean in a proxy that opens a transaction, calls your method, then commits or rolls back. Callers get the proxy, so the transaction starts.

A call from inside the same class does not go through the proxy - it is a plain this.method() call - so the annotation is simply ignored.

EXTERNAL CALL - works
   controller ---> [ PROXY: begin tx ] ---> service.saveAll()
                            |
                            v
                   commit / rollback

INTERNAL CALL - annotation ignored
   service.outer() ---> this.saveAll()      no proxy, no transaction
Silent failureWhy
Calling an annotated method from another method of the same classThe call never leaves the object, so the proxy is bypassed.
@Transactional on a private methodA proxy cannot intercept it. Public only.
@Transactional on a final method or classCGLIB cannot subclass it to create the proxy.
Annotated method called from the constructor or @PostConstructThe proxy does not exist yet.

Propagation and Isolation

@Transactional has two attributes worth knowing beyond rollbackFor.

Propagation answers: what should happen if a transaction is already running?

PropagationBehaviour
REQUIRED (default)Join the existing transaction, or start one if there is none.
REQUIRES_NEWAlways start a new, independent transaction and suspend the outer one. Its rollback does not affect the caller.
SUPPORTSJoin if one exists; run without a transaction otherwise.
MANDATORYJoin, or throw if there is no active transaction.
NEVERThrow if a transaction is active.
NESTEDA savepoint inside the outer transaction - can roll back partially.

Isolation answers: what can this transaction see of other, concurrent ones?

IsolationPrevents
READ_UNCOMMITTEDNothing. Dirty reads are possible.
READ_COMMITTEDDirty reads. The PostgreSQL and Oracle default.
REPEATABLE_READDirty and non-repeatable reads. The MySQL/InnoDB default.
SERIALIZABLEEverything including phantom reads. Slowest.

REQUIRES_NEW has one genuinely common use: writing an audit or log record that must survive even when the business transaction rolls back.

A Simpler Alternative for This Example: Cascade

The walkthrough saves the user, then loops and saves each policy. JPA can do that for you if the association is mapped with a cascade - and then there is only one save() call to make transactional.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does transaction management solve?It makes a multi-step database operation atomic: either every step commits, or every step is rolled back, so the data never ends up half-written.
What are the ACID properties?Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (a commit survives a crash).
Where should @Transactional go?On the service method that represents the whole unit of work. Splitting it across several methods gives several transactions and defeats the purpose.
Do you need @EnableTransactionManagement in Spring Boot?No - auto-configuration enables it when a DataSource is present. Adding it is harmless and documents intent.
Which exceptions roll back by default?Only unchecked ones - RuntimeException and Error. A checked exception commits unless you set rollbackFor.
What happens if you catch the exception inside the method?Nothing escapes, so Spring commits. Rethrow, or call setRollbackOnly() explicitly.
Why does @Transactional not work on an internal method call?It is proxy-based. A this.method() call never passes through the proxy, so no transaction is started. Move the method to another bean.
Can @Transactional go on a private method?No - the proxy cannot intercept private or final methods. It must be public.
What is the default propagation?REQUIRED - join the current transaction, or start one if none exists.
When would you use REQUIRES_NEW?When a step must commit independently of the caller - audit or log records that should survive the business transaction's rollback.
What does readOnly = true do?Skips Hibernate's dirty-checking snapshot and allows routing to a read replica - a real speed-up on query-only methods.
Which @Transactional should you import?org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional - the javax/jakarta one lacks propagation, isolation, readOnly and rollbackFor.
Default isolation level in MySQL?REPEATABLE_READ for InnoDB; READ_COMMITTED in PostgreSQL and Oracle.

Business Requirement

An application is deployed to a production server. A user reports that saving an employee failed. You cannot attach a debugger to production, you cannot reproduce the request, and the stack trace scrolled off somebody's terminal three days ago. The application must therefore record what it did, when, and with what data - so a defect can be diagnosed from the evidence it left behind.

What a Logger Is

A logger keeps a durable, timestamped record of what the application is doing. It is the only view you have into a running production system, and it is the difference between "the save failed" and "the save failed at 09:14:22 in EmployeeServiceImpl with a duplicate-key violation on employees.email".

Facilities you will hear named together:
SLF4J - the API you write against
Logback - the implementation Spring Boot ships with
Log4j2 - an alternative implementation
java.util.logging - the JDK's own, rarely used directly
A log management tool - ELK, Splunk, Loki, CloudWatch - which collects and indexes what the application writes

Steps

1. Create a Spring Boot starter project
2. Add the Maven dependencies to pom.xml
3. Write the logging configuration in application.properties
4. Create the model
5. Create the service interface
6. Create the service implementation
7. Create the repository
8. Create the REST controller
9. Add logger statements to the controller and the service implementation
10. Run the application
11. Send the request from Postman and read the response
12. Check the row in the database
13. Check the log file

Note that no logging dependency is added. spring-boot-starter-web pulls in spring-boot-starter-logging transitively, which brings SLF4J and Logback. That is why the imports in step 9 resolve without touching pom.xml.

Step 3 - Configuration in application.properties

The datasource block is ordinary JPA configuration. The #Log configuration block underneath is what this topic is about.

PropertyPurpose
logging.level.rootThe level applied to every logger with no more specific rule. WARN means INFO and DEBUG are discarded application-wide.
logging.level.<package>Overrides the level for one package or class. Levels are inherited down the package hierarchy, and the longest matching prefix wins.
logging.file.nameWrites to that exact file in addition to the console.
logging.file.pathWrites spring.log into that directory. Use one or the other, not both.
logging.pattern.fileThe Logback layout pattern for the file appender. logging.pattern.console does the same for the console.

Two corrections to the PDF's property block are marked in the code.
codeExamples:
# Step 3 - application.properties

spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/8julyspringbootbatch
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.MySQL8Dialect
# The PDF prints "org.hibernate.dial ect.MySQL8Dialect" - a line-break artefact.
# It must be one unbroken token or Hibernate throws
#   ClassNotFoundException: org.hibernate.dial
# Boot 2.7+ detects the dialect from the JDBC metadata, so this line is optional.

#Log configuration
logging.level.root=WARN
logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG
logging.level.org.hibernate=ERROR
logging.level.com.velocity=INFO
# ^ ADDED. With root=WARN and nothing for com.velocity, the log.info(...)
#   calls written in step 9 are silently discarded and the exercise appears
#   to do nothing. This is the single most common mistake with this setup.

logging.pattern.file=%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n
# The PDF wraps the pattern in double quotes. Properties files do not strip
# quotes, so the quote characters end up printed in every line of the file.
# It also omits the time from %d{yyyy-MM-dd }, leaving every entry dated but
# not timed - useless for ordering events.

logging.file.name=D:/application.log
# Absolute paths on a developer's D: drive do not exist on a Linux server.
# Prefer a relative path or an externally supplied value:
#   logging.file.name=${LOG_DIR:logs}/application.log

Steps 4-7 - Model, Service, Repository

Ordinary layering: entity, service interface, service implementation, Spring Data repository. Nothing here is logging-specific yet; it is the application the log statements will describe.

The entity's id is int, so the repository must be JpaRepository<Employee, Integer> - the second type parameter is the boxed id type. JpaRepository<Employee, Long> compiles but fails at start-up with an identifier-type mismatch.

javax.persistence is correct for Spring Boot 2.x. On Boot 3.x every one of these imports becomes jakarta.persistence; leaving them as javax produces Not a managed type: class com.velocity.model.Employee.

Step 9 - Adding the Logger

Three lines are all it takes: import org.slf4j.Logger, import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory, and declare
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(EmployeeController.class);

Every class gets its own logger, named after itself. That name is what appears in the %logger{36} position of the output, and it is what logging.level.com.velocity=INFO matches against.

The PDF's service implementation imports com.velocity.restcontroller.EmployeeController and never uses it. Remove it - a service must not depend on a controller, and even an unused import in that direction invites someone to add a real one later.

expert.content:
SLF4J Is a Facade, Logback Is the Implementation

SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is an API and nothing else. slf4j-api.jar contains interfaces - Logger, LoggerFactory, Marker - and no code that writes a byte anywhere. At start-up SLF4J binds to exactly one implementation found on the classpath. Spring Boot puts Logback there.

The separation exists because a library cannot dictate the logging framework of every application that uses it. Spring, Hibernate and Jackson all call SLF4J; your application decides whether those calls end in Logback, Log4j2 or nothing. Swapping the implementation is a pom.xml exclusion, not a code change.

LayerResponsibility
SLF4J APIWhat you write against: Logger, LoggerFactory, the level methods, the {} placeholder contract.
Bindinglogback-classic (or log4j-slf4j2-impl) - the adapter that connects the facade to a real engine. Exactly one must be present.
Bridgesjul-to-slf4j, log4j-over-slf4j, jcl-over-slf4j - reroute libraries that call an older API so everything lands in one place with one configuration.
ImplementationLogback: loggers, levels, appenders, encoders, filters, async queues, rolling policies.

Do not import ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger in application code. It compiles and works, and it welds your application to Logback for no benefit.
codeExamples:
<!-- Switching Logback for Log4j2: exclusion plus one starter, no code change -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-log4j2</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Forget the exclusion and you get, at start-up:
     SLF4J: Class path contains multiple SLF4J providers.
     SLF4J: Found provider [ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.LogbackServiceProvider]
     SLF4J: Found provider [org.apache.logging.slf4j.SLF4JServiceProvider]
     SLF4J: Actually provided by [...]
     Whichever the class loader reaches first wins - so which framework
     reads your configuration is decided by jar ordering. -->

expert.content:
Why private static final and Not an Instance Field

private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(EmployeeController.class); is not a stylistic convention; each modifier earns its place.

static - one logger per class, not one per object. An instance field on an entity created a million times per hour means a million getLogger lookups and a million extra references. The logger holds no per-instance state, so there is nothing to gain from duplicating it.
final - the reference cannot be reassigned, so the JIT can treat it as a constant and the level check folds away cheaply.
private - loggers are not inherited API. A protected logger in a base class logs under the base class name from every subclass, so all your subclasses appear in the log as the parent and per-class level configuration stops working.
X.class, not getClass() - getClass() on a Spring bean may return the CGLIB proxy, giving a logger named EmployeeServiceImpl$$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$9f3c1ab. That name changes between runs, so no configuration can target it.

An instance field is not wrong in the sense of failing; it is wasteful, and the getClass() variant actively breaks configuration. Lombok's @Slf4j generates precisely the static final form.

Parameterised Logging

log.debug("Saving employee id={} for city={}", id, city) passes the format string and the arguments separately. Logback checks the level first and only builds the message if the statement will actually be emitted.

Concatenation - log.debug("Saving employee id=" + id + " city=" + city) - inverts that. The JVM evaluates the argument before the call, so the StringBuilder runs, toString() is invoked on every operand, and a String is allocated. Then debug() sees the level is INFO and discards it. In a hot path you have paid for every disabled DEBUG statement in the application, in allocation and in garbage-collection pressure.

SLF4J placeholders use {}, not %s and not printf syntax. Two to three arguments are passed directly; more than that goes through a varargs array, which is why the two-argument overloads exist. A trailing Throwable is special: pass the exception as the last argument with no matching {} and Logback prints the full stack trace.

Where an argument is genuinely expensive to compute - serialising an object, a database call - guard it with if (log.isDebugEnabled()), or pass a Supplier via a fluent API. Do not wrap ordinary parameterised calls in a guard; the placeholder form already handles it.

Levels - and When Each One Is Right

A level is a filter, and filters are only useful if the boundaries mean something consistent. The ordering is TRACE < DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < OFF: setting a logger to INFO emits INFO, WARN and ERROR and discards the rest.

LevelWhen it is right
ERRORThe operation failed and a human needs to act. Include the exception. If it does not warrant an alert, it is not an ERROR - a routine 404 or a validation rejection is not one.
WARNSomething recovered, degraded or is heading for trouble: a retry succeeded on the third attempt, a fallback was used, a deprecated endpoint was called, the connection pool is at 90%.
INFOMilestones in normal operation that you would want in production: application started, order 4417 accepted, scheduled job finished in 812 ms. Low volume, one or two per business operation. This is the default and the level production usually runs at.
DEBUGDetail for diagnosing a problem: branch taken, parameter values, intermediate results. Off in production by default, switchable at runtime when investigating.
TRACEVery fine-grained - loop iterations, wire-level detail. Enabled briefly on one class, never broadly.

The material's logging.level.root=WARN with org.springframework.web=DEBUG is a good instinct badly aimed: it silences your own INFO statements while emitting a large volume of Spring's internal DEBUG. Set root to INFO, your own package to INFO or DEBUG, and turn framework packages down rather than up.

Levels are also changeable without a restart through the Actuator loggers endpoint - the difference between diagnosing a production incident in two minutes and waiting for a redeploy.
codeExamples:
# A sane production baseline
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.velocity=INFO
logging.level.org.springframework=WARN
logging.level.org.hibernate=WARN

# Never in production - these two log every bound parameter, and bound
# parameters include passwords, card numbers and personal data:
# logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
# logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE

# Change a level at runtime with Actuator - no restart, no redeploy
# management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,loggers   (and secure it)

curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.velocity
# {"configuredLevel":"INFO","effectiveLevel":"INFO"}

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.velocity.service \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'
# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# DEBUG output begins immediately for that package only.

# Put it back when you are done:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/com.velocity.service \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"configuredLevel":null}'

expert.content:
logback-spring.xml and Profile-Scoped Appenders

application.properties covers levels, one file and a pattern. Anything beyond that - several appenders, asynchronous logging, JSON encoding, different behaviour per environment - needs a Logback configuration file.

Use logback-spring.xml, not logback.xml. Plain logback.xml is read by Logback directly, before Spring exists, so it cannot see profiles or the Spring Environment. The -spring variant is loaded by Boot's initialiser and unlocks <springProfile> and <springProperty>.

The practical shape: a readable, coloured console appender for dev; a rolling JSON file appender for prod; nothing but console at WARN for test so the build output stays readable. One file, three environments, no code change.

Wrap the production file appender in AsyncAppender. File I/O in the request thread is a real latency cost under load - the async appender hands lines to a background thread through a bounded queue. Set discardingThreshold to 0 so it does not silently drop WARN and ERROR when the queue fills.
codeExamples:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<configuration>

    <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/defaults.xml"/>

    <!-- springProperty reads from the Spring Environment - profiles,
         env vars, config server - which plain logback.xml cannot do -->
    <springProperty scope="context" name="appName"
                    source="spring.application.name" defaultValue="orders-api"/>
    <springProperty scope="context" name="logDir"
                    source="logging.file.path" defaultValue="logs"/>

    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %highlight(%-5level) %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
        <file>${logDir}/${appName}.log</file>
        <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy">
            <fileNamePattern>${logDir}/${appName}.%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.%i.log.gz</fileNamePattern>
            <maxFileSize>100MB</maxFileSize>
            <maxHistory>30</maxHistory>
            <totalSizeCap>10GB</totalSizeCap>
            <cleanHistoryOnStart>true</cleanHistoryOnStart>
        </rollingPolicy>
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level [%X{traceId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <appender name="ASYNC_FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">
        <appender-ref ref="FILE"/>
        <queueSize>8192</queueSize>
        <discardingThreshold>0</discardingThreshold>
        <!-- 0 = never discard. The default 20 silently drops everything
             below WARN once the queue is 80% full - exactly when you
             most need the detail. -->
        <neverBlock>false</neverBlock>
    </appender>

    <springProfile name="dev">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
        </root>
        <logger name="com.velocity" level="DEBUG"/>
    </springProfile>

    <springProfile name="test">
        <root level="WARN">
            <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>

    <springProfile name="prod">
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="ASYNC_FILE"/>
        </root>
        <logger name="org.springframework" level="WARN"/>
        <logger name="org.hibernate" level="WARN"/>
    </springProfile>

</configuration>

# What the rolling policy produces after a month in production
logs/orders-api.log                    <- today, being written
logs/orders-api.2024-07-07.0.log.gz    <- yesterday, first 100MB
logs/orders-api.2024-07-07.1.log.gz    <- yesterday, second 100MB
logs/orders-api.2024-06-08.0.log.gz    <- 30 days back; deleted tomorrow

# maxHistory=30    keep 30 days
# totalSizeCap=10GB  hard ceiling regardless of maxHistory - this is the
#                    setting that stops logs filling the disk and taking
#                    the application down with "No space left on device"

# Without a rolling policy, logging.file.name grows without bound.
# A single 40GB application.log is unreadable, ungreppable and fatal.

expert.content:
MDC and Correlation Ids

Under load, one request's log lines are interleaved with hundreds of others. [http-nio-8080-exec-1] identifies the thread, and threads are reused, so it does not identify a request. Given a user complaint you cannot reconstruct what happened.

MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a thread-local map of key-value pairs that Logback merges into every line the thread writes, through the %X{key} conversion word. Put a correlation id in it at the edge of the request and every line downstream carries it. Grep for one id and you have the complete story of that request, in order.

Two rules make it work in practice. Accept an incoming X-Correlation-Id header if there is one and generate a UUID if not, so the id spans several microservices rather than being reinvented at each hop. And always clear the MDC in a finally block - the value is thread-local, the servlet container pools threads, and a value left behind will reappear stamped on an unrelated user's request. That is both a debugging trap and, if you put a user id in there, a data-leak.

MDC does not cross thread boundaries by itself: @Async, CompletableFuture and reactive pipelines lose it unless you propagate it explicitly. Spring Boot 3.x with Micrometer Tracing does this for you and supplies traceId/spanId automatically.
codeExamples:
# Pattern picks it up with %X{traceId}
# logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level [%X{traceId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n

# OUTPUT - two concurrent requests, cleanly separable
11:42:17.204 [http-nio-8080-exec-1] INFO  [a41f9c2e] c.v.r.EmployeeController - Inside saveEmployee()
11:42:17.206 [http-nio-8080-exec-2] INFO  [7d0b13aa] c.v.r.EmployeeController - Inside saveEmployee()
11:42:17.208 [http-nio-8080-exec-1] INFO  [a41f9c2e] c.v.s.i.EmployeeServiceImpl - Inside saveEmployee()
11:42:17.301 [http-nio-8080-exec-2] ERROR [7d0b13aa] c.v.s.i.EmployeeServiceImpl - Failed to save employee city=Pune
11:42:17.331 [http-nio-8080-exec-1] INFO  [a41f9c2e] c.v.r.EmployeeController - completed, id=1

# grep a41f9c2e application.log  -> the whole successful request
# grep 7d0b13aa application.log  -> the whole failed one, including the trace

expert.content:
Structured JSON Logging

A pattern-formatted line is written for a human reading a terminal. In production nobody reads the terminal - the lines are shipped to Elasticsearch, Splunk or Loki and queried. Parsing them back out with a regular expression is fragile, and it collapses entirely on multi-line stack traces, where each frame arrives as a separate document.

Structured logging emits one JSON object per event, with the timestamp, level, logger, thread, message, MDC entries and stack trace as named fields. The aggregator indexes the fields directly, so you can query level:ERROR AND traceId:a41f9c2e instead of matching text, and a stack trace stays one document.

Two routes. Spring Boot 3.4+ has it built in: set logging.structured.format.console=ecs - Elastic Common Schema, or logstash, or gelf. Earlier versions add logstash-logback-encoder and swap the encoder in logback-spring.xml. Either way, use JSON in prod and the readable pattern in dev; JSON in a development console is unreadable and slows people down.

The complement to structured output is structured arguments: kv("employeeId", id) puts the value in its own indexed field rather than embedding it in the message text.
codeExamples:
<!-- Pre-3.4: logstash-logback-encoder -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>

<!-- logback-spring.xml, prod profile -->
<appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
    <file>${logDir}/${appName}.json</file>
    <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy">
        <fileNamePattern>${logDir}/${appName}.%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.%i.json.gz</fileNamePattern>
        <maxFileSize>100MB</maxFileSize>
        <maxHistory>14</maxHistory>
        <totalSizeCap>10GB</totalSizeCap>
    </rollingPolicy>
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
        <includeMdcKeyName>traceId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <customFields>{"service":"orders-api","env":"prod"}</customFields>
    </encoder>
</appender>

<!-- Spring Boot 3.4+ needs no encoder at all:
     logging.structured.format.console=ecs
     logging.structured.format.file=ecs
     logging.structured.ecs.service.name=orders-api -->

expert.content:
Never Log Passwords, Tokens or PII

Logs are the least protected data store in most systems. They are shipped to a third-party aggregator, retained for months, indexed for full-text search, and readable by every engineer, every on-call rota and every support analyst - none of whom would be granted SELECT on the users table. Anything written to a log should be treated as published.

Never log: passwords (plain or hashed), authentication tokens - JWTs, session ids, API keys, refresh tokens - full card numbers, CVVs, national identifiers, health data, or Authorization and Cookie headers.
Under GDPR, names, email addresses and IP addresses are personal data: logging them creates a retention obligation and a subject-access liability. Log an internal id and join to the database when you actually need the person.

The dangerous leaks are rarely deliberate. log.debug("Request: {}", user) calls toString(), and a Lombok @Data or IDE-generated toString() includes every field including password. logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE prints every bound parameter, which is every value your application ever writes. An exception message from a failed authentication can carry the credential. And a JWT is not encrypted - anyone with the logged token can decode the claims and, until it expires, replay it.

Defend at three points: annotate sensitive fields so toString() and JSON serialisation exclude them; mask at the log call for anything that must appear at all; and add a Logback replacement filter as a backstop for what slips through the first two.
codeExamples:
<!-- Backstop: a Logback replacement filter in the pattern.
     Not a substitute for the two measures above - a safety net for
     what a new joiner logs without thinking. -->
<pattern>
  %d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level [%X{traceId}] %logger{36} -
  %replace(%msg){'(?i)(password|passwd|secret|token|authorization|api[-_]?key)\s*[=:]\s*[^,\s\}]+','$1=****'}%n
</pattern>

<!-- INPUT : User login password=Str0ngP@ss! token=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...
     OUTPUT: User login password=**** token=****

     Also switch these OFF everywhere but a local machine:
       logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
       logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE
       logging.level.org.springframework.web=DEBUG
     The last one logs full request bodies, headers included. -->

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
SLF4J versus Logback?SLF4J is a facade - interfaces only, no output code. Logback is the implementation Spring Boot binds it to. Writing against the facade lets an application swap Logback for Log4j2 through a pom.xml exclusion, with no code change, and lets libraries log without dictating a framework.
What does Spring Boot use by default, and what pulls it in?Logback, via spring-boot-starter-logging, which arrives transitively with spring-boot-starter-web. No logging dependency needs to be declared.
Why private static final Logger?static gives one logger per class rather than one per instance; final lets the JIT treat it as a constant; private stops subclasses inheriting a logger named after the parent, which would break per-class level configuration.
Why X.class rather than getClass()?On a proxied Spring bean getClass() returns the CGLIB subclass, so the logger is named EmployeeServiceImpl$$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$.... That name varies between runs and no logging.level.* property can match it.
Why is string concatenation in a log call wasteful?The argument is evaluated before the call, so the StringBuilder runs and a String is allocated even when the level is disabled and the line is discarded. The {} form checks the level first and formats only if the event will be emitted.
How do you log an exception with its stack trace?Pass the Throwable as the last argument with no matching placeholder: log.error("Failed for id={}", id, ex). log.error("Failed " + ex) prints only toString() and loses the trace.
When is ERROR right rather than WARN?ERROR means the operation failed and a human must act - it should be alertable. WARN means something recovered or degraded: a retry succeeded, a fallback was used, a pool is near capacity. A validation rejection or a 404 is neither.
Can you change a log level without restarting?Yes - POST to the Actuator /actuator/loggers/{name} endpoint with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}. It takes effect immediately for that logger and its children. Secure the endpoint; it is a live control over production output.
logback.xml or logback-spring.xml?logback-spring.xml. Plain logback.xml is read by Logback before Spring initialises, so it cannot see profiles or the Environment. Only the -spring variant supports <springProfile> and <springProperty>.
How do you stop logs filling the disk?A rolling file appender with SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy: maxFileSize for rotation, maxHistory for retention in days, and totalSizeCap as a hard ceiling. Without totalSizeCap, a burst of errors can still fill the volume.
What is MDC and what does it solve?A thread-local map merged into every log line via %X{key}. Putting a correlation id in it at the request boundary makes all lines from one request greppable by that id, which thread names cannot do because threads are pooled and reused.
Why must MDC be cleared in a finally?The value lives on a pooled container thread. Left behind, it is stamped onto the next unrelated request - producing wrong diagnostics and, if it holds a user identifier, leaking one user's data into another's log lines.
Why log JSON in production?Aggregators index named fields rather than parsing text with regular expressions, so queries like level:ERROR AND traceId:x work, and a multi-line stack trace stays a single document instead of fragmenting into one per frame.
What must never be logged?Passwords, tokens and API keys, full card numbers and CVVs, national identifiers, health data, and Authorization/Cookie headers. Under GDPR, names, emails and IP addresses are personal data. Logs are retained for months and read by far more people than the database is.
Where do leaks usually come from?toString() on a request or entity object that includes a password field, org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE printing every bound parameter, and org.springframework.web=DEBUG printing full request bodies. Exclude fields from toString(), mask at the call site, and add a Logback %replace filter as a backstop.
What does AsyncAppender buy, and what is its trap?It moves file I/O off the request thread through a bounded queue. The trap is discardingThreshold, which defaults to 20 and silently drops everything below WARN once the queue is 80% full. Set it to 0 for production.
