Business Requirement

The team ships a Spring Boot service every fortnight. Before each release somebody opens the application, hits the endpoints by hand and reads the console to check the numbers are right. That is slow, it is not repeatable, and nobody re-checks the old features.

Problem Statement: replace the manual "run it and look at the console" check with automated tests that run on every build and fail loudly the moment a method stops behaving.

Unit testing is the level of testing where an individual unit of code - a method, a class, a module - is exercised in isolation to confirm it does exactly what it claims. It is written by developers during the coding phase, not by a QA team afterwards.

JUnit is the free, open-source unit testing framework for Java, originally written by Kent Beck and Erich Gamma and first released in 1997. It is lightweight: a test is an ordinary Java method with an annotation on it.

The manual approach the PDF starts with:
System.out.println("Addition is>>" + result); - a human reads the number and decides.
The automated approach:
assertEquals(30, result); - the machine decides, every single build, forever.

Steps - the first test

StepWhat you do
1File -> New -> Spring Starter Project, name it, finish
2Confirm spring-boot-starter-test is in pom.xml - it is added by default and brings JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ and Hamcrest with it
3Write the production class Example under src/main/java
4Write ExampleTest under src/test/java, in the same package
5Right-click the test class, Run As -> JUnit Test
6Read the JUnit view: green means passed, red means failed

Two rules that trip people up on day one: the test class lives under src/test/java (never src/main/java, or it ships to production), and it mirrors the production package so it can see package-private members.

@Test marks a method as a test case. assertEquals(expected, actual) compares the two - and the order matters, expected first, because that is what the failure message prints.

What a failing test looks like

Deliberately break one assertion so you learn to read the failure. Expect 20 from 3 * 4:

The bar turns red and JUnit prints a ComparisonFailure-style message naming both values. This is why assertEquals(expected, actual) argument order matters - swap them and every failure message you ever read will be back to front, which costs real debugging time.

Lifecycle annotations - stop creating the object in every test

In the version above we wrote new Example() inside both test methods. That is duplication, and in a real test class the setup is far heavier than one constructor call. JUnit 5 gives four hooks:

AnnotationBehaviour
@BeforeAllRuns once, before any test in the class. Must be static (unless the class is @TestInstance(PER_CLASS)). Use for genuinely expensive one-time setup.
@AfterAllRuns once, after every test in the class has finished. Also static. Use to release what @BeforeAll acquired.
@BeforeEachRuns before every test method. Non-static. This is where fresh, per-test state belongs.
@AfterEachRuns after every test method. Non-static. Cleanup that must happen even between tests.

A detail the console output makes obvious: test execution order is not source order. JUnit 5 uses a deterministic but deliberately non-obvious algorithm, so a test that only passes because an earlier test left state behind will fail unpredictably. That is precisely why @BeforeEach exists.

The JUnit 5 assertion family

An assertion validates the expected output against the actual output. All of them are static methods on org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions, so they are normally brought in with a static import.

AssertionChecks
assertEquals / assertNotEqualsValue equality via equals(). For objects this means your entity must implement equals() sensibly, or the comparison falls back to reference identity.
assertTrue / assertFalseA boolean condition.
assertNull / assertNotNullReference is or is not null.
assertSame / assertNotSameReference identity (==), not equals(). Useful when a cache or a singleton is supposed to hand back the very same instance.
assertThrowsThe supplied lambda throws the expected exception type; returns the exception so you can assert on its message.
assertAllGroups several assertions so that all of them are evaluated and every failure is reported, instead of stopping at the first.

JUnit 5's assertions live in the Jupiter API. The dependencies you need are org.junit.jupiter (the programming model) and org.junit.platform (the launcher that actually runs it) - both arrive transitively with spring-boot-starter-test, so in a Boot project you add nothing.

@ParameterizedTest - one method, many inputs

Problem Statement: isPalindrome(String) needs checking against "madam", "katak", "nitin", "level" and a handful of non-palindromes. Writing five near-identical @Test methods is noise.

A @ParameterizedTest runs the same method once per input, and each run is reported as a separate test with its own pass/fail. Note it replaces @Test - you do not put both on the method. Four source annotations feed it:

Source annotationWhere the values come from
@ValueSourceA literal array in the annotation itself - strings, ints, longs, doubles, booleans. One argument per run only.
@CsvSourceInline comma-separated rows, so a run can take several arguments - typically input plus expected result.
@CsvFileSourceThe same, but the rows live in a .csv file on the test classpath. numLinesToSkip = 1 skips the header row.
@MethodSourceA static method that returns a Stream of arguments - the only option when the inputs are objects rather than literals.

Two more annotations worth knowing at this point: @RepeatedTest(5) runs the same method a fixed number of times, and @Disabled skips a test class or method without deleting it (always give it a reason string).

@CsvFileSource - inputs and expected results in a file

Problem Statement: getEvenOddNumber(int) returns "even" or "odd". The test data is a table of input plus expected output, and the analyst who owns the cases would rather edit a spreadsheet than Java source.

Put the file under src/test/resources so it lands on the test classpath, and reference it with a leading slash. Each non-skipped row becomes one run, and each column becomes one method parameter in order.

Testing that an exception is thrown

Problem Statement: convertToInt(String) must reject null and blank input with an IllegalArgumentException. The failure path is behaviour too, and it needs a test just as much as the happy path.

assertThrows takes the expected exception class and a lambda. It fails if nothing is thrown, fails if the wrong type is thrown, and returns the caught exception so you can assert on the message - which is the part most people forget, and it is what stops a test passing for the wrong reason.

Mocking - why the service cannot be tested alone

Problem Statement: UserService.getEmailByUserId(id) delegates to UserDao.findEmailById(id), which hits a database. Test it as it stands and you are testing MySQL, the network, the schema and the data all at once - and the test fails on a laptop with no database running.

Mocking replaces that external dependency with a dummy object you control completely. The purpose is to isolate the code under test so a failure can only mean one thing: the code under test is wrong. 

WITHOUT MOCKING                    WITH MOCKING

  UserServiceTest                    UserServiceTest
        |                                  |
        v                                  v
   UserService                        UserService
        |                                  |
        v                                  v
    UserDaoImpl                     UserDao (mock)
        |                                  |
        v                                  |
     MySQL  <-- must be running       returns whatever
        |                              you told it to
        v
   real rows  <-- must exist

  slow, fragile, needs a DBA        fast, deterministic, offline

Steps - mocking a DAO with Mockito

The source material reaches for PowerMock here. That advice is now out of date and you should not follow it - see the expert section. The modern equivalent, which ships inside spring-boot-starter-test with no extra dependency at all, is Mockito.

StepWhat you do
1Create the Spring Boot starter project
2Confirm spring-boot-starter-test (test scope) is present - it already contains Mockito, so add nothing
3Create the UserDao interface and its UserDaoImpl
4Create UserService, taking UserDao through its constructor
5Create UserServiceTest under src/test/java with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
6Run as JUnit test and read the result

Notice that UserService takes its dependency through a constructor. That single design choice is what makes it testable - a field-injected @Autowired private field with no constructor cannot be given a mock without reflection.

The Mockito test

Three moving parts, in this order every time:
• @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) - the JUnit 5 extension that creates the mocks and verifies them afterwards.
• @Mock - "give me a fake UserDao". Every method on it returns a type-appropriate default (null, 0, false, empty collection) until you say otherwise.
• when(...).thenReturn(...) - stubbing: "when this exact call is made, hand back this value".

The test then asserts on what UserService did with that value. No database was involved at any point.

Application Flow - the full service-layer test

Putting it together on the insurance example from the fourth handout: a Policy entity, a PolicyRepository, and a PolicyServiceImpl that delegates to it. The service is what we are testing; the repository is what we mock. 

    PolicyServiceImplTest
             |
             |  @InjectMocks  -> builds a REAL PolicyServiceImpl
             |                   and pushes the mocks into it
             v
      PolicyServiceImpl                (the unit under test)
             |
             |  @Mock -> PolicyRepository is a FAKE
             v
      PolicyRepository (mock)
             |
             X   no Hibernate, no JDBC, no MySQL, no schema
                 nothing below this line ever runs

@InjectMocks instantiates the class under test and injects every @Mock in the test class into it - by constructor if there is a matching one, otherwise by field, using reflection. That last part is why it works on a class whose @Autowired fields are private with no setter.

The corrected service test

The handout's version of this test carries four separate problems, all of them common in real projects. The corrected file is below with each one called out.

1. JUnit 4 and JUnit 5 mixed in one file. It imports org.junit.Test (JUnit 4) but asserts with org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions (JUnit 5). Under Boot 2.4+ the JUnit 4 engine (Vintage) is not on the classpath, so the methods are silently never executed - the build goes green having run nothing at all.
2. @RunWith(SpringRunner.class) is the JUnit 4 runner. JUnit 5 replaced runners with extensions: @ExtendWith.
3. @SpringBootTest with @Mock is a contradiction. It boots the entire application context - including a real MySQL DataSource that must connect - and then does not use a single bean from it, because @Mock and @InjectMocks are plain Mockito and bypass Spring completely. Delete it and the test runs in milliseconds offline.
4. deletePolicyTest tests nothing. It calls the mock repository directly and then asserts on the mock's own return value. The service is never invoked. It would pass with the service class deleted from the project.

Note on the entity used by these tests

The Policy entity from the handout is used above. Two things about it matter for testing.

First, assertEquals(list, policyList) and assertEquals(policy, savedPolicy) both go through equals(). The handout's Policy does not override equals() and hashCode(), so those comparisons fall back to reference identity - they pass only because the very same object instance is handed back by the mock. Change the service to copy the object and the test breaks for no good reason.

Second, the System.out.println calls scattered through its constructor and setters are debugging left in production code. They will run millions of times in a live application.

expert.content:
JUnit 4 to JUnit 5 - the migration table you will need

Almost every legacy Spring project you inherit is on JUnit 4, and the two versions are not source-compatible. JUnit 5 is not one library but three: JUnit Platform (the engine-hosting launcher that IDEs and Maven talk to), JUnit Jupiter (the new annotations and assertions), and JUnit Vintage (an engine that runs old JUnit 3/4 tests on the new platform).

JUnit 4JUnit 5 (Jupiter)Why it changed
org.junit.Testorg.junit.jupiter.api.TestDifferent package entirely - the imports are the first thing to fix
@Before@BeforeEachThe old names never said whether they ran once or per test
@After@AfterEachSame
@BeforeClass@BeforeAllSame
@AfterClass@AfterAllSame
@Ignore@DisabledPlus richer conditional forms: @EnabledOnOs, @EnabledIfSystemProperty
@RunWith(X.class)@ExtendWith(X.class)A class could carry only ONE runner, which is why you could not combine Spring and Mockito runners. Extensions compose - you can stack as many as you like
@Test(expected = Foo.class)assertThrows(Foo.class, () -> ...)The old form passed if the exception came from ANYWHERE in the method, including the setup lines. assertThrows pins it to one expression and hands the exception back so you can assert on its message
@Test(timeout = 100)assertTimeout / @TimeoutSame reasoning
@Rule, @ClassRuleExtensionsRules and runners were two separate extension mechanisms; Jupiter has one
org.junit.Assertorg.junit.jupiter.api.AssertionsMessage parameter moved to the LAST argument, so it can be a lazily-evaluated Supplier

The failure mode that costs teams a whole afternoon: mix the two in one file and the build stays green while running nothing. A JUnit 4 @Test method in a project without the Vintage engine is not an error - the Jupiter engine simply does not recognise it, reports zero tests, and Maven is perfectly happy. Configure failIfNoTests, or better, keep maven-surefire-plugin current and watch the "Tests run:" count.

@Mock versus @MockBean, and the real cost of @MockBean

Both hand you a Mockito mock. They differ in where that mock lives, and the difference is measured in minutes of CI time.

Aspect@Mock (Mockito)@MockBean (Spring Boot Test)
Packageorg.mockito.Mockorg.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean
Needs a Spring contextNoYes - there is nothing to register the mock into otherwise
What it doesCreates an objectCreates an object AND replaces the matching bean definition in the ApplicationContext
Injected by@InjectMocks, or your own constructor callSpring's normal autowiring, into every collaborator
Reset between testsNew mocks per test methodReset after each test method (Boot does this for you)
Startup costMicrosecondsA fresh application context - seconds

The cost is not the mock, it is what the mock does to the test context cache. Spring caches a loaded ApplicationContext and reuses it across every test class whose configuration key is identical, so a hundred test classes can share one three-second startup. The set of @MockBean declarations is part of that cache key. Two test classes that mock different beans - or the same beans in a different combination - are two different keys, so they get two different contexts, each paying full startup cost.

Rule: use @Mock whenever the test does not need Spring at all - which is nearly every service-layer test.
Use @MockBean only when a context is genuinely being loaded anyway (@WebMvcTest, @SpringBootTest) and something inside it must be replaced.
Keep the set of mocked beans identical across classes where you can - often by hoisting them into a shared abstract base class - so they share one cached context.
On Spring Boot 3.4+, @MockBean is deprecated in favour of @MockitoBean (and @MockitoSpyBean), which is the Spring Framework 6.2 equivalent. The caching behaviour is the same.

verify() and ArgumentCaptor - asserting on interactions, not values

assertEquals checks what came back. Sometimes the interesting behaviour has no return value at all: a void notification method, a delete, an audit write. For those, the only observable evidence is which calls the unit made on its collaborators.

ConstructMeaning
verify(mock).method(arg)Was called exactly once with that argument. Shorthand for times(1).
verify(mock, times(n))Called exactly n times.
verify(mock, never())Never called - the assertion people forget. "We must NOT charge the card when validation fails" is a real requirement.
verify(mock, atLeastOnce() / atMost(n))Loose bounds, for retry logic.
verifyNoMoreInteractions(mock)Nothing beyond what you already verified. Use sparingly - it makes tests brittle against harmless refactoring.
InOrderCalls happened in a specific sequence across one or several mocks.
ArgumentCaptorGrabs the actual object that was passed, so you can assert on its fields afterwards.

ArgumentCaptor earns its keep when the unit constructs the argument itself. If the service builds an AuditEvent internally and hands it to the repository, you cannot write verify(repo).save(expectedEvent) without an equals() on AuditEvent and a way to predict its timestamp. Capture it instead and assert on the fields you actually care about.

A caution on over-use: verify() asserts on implementation. A test that verifies six interactions has to be rewritten every time the method is refactored, even when its behaviour is unchanged. Prefer asserting the outcome; reach for verify() when there is no outcome to assert.

Strict stubs, argument matchers, and the errors they produce

Since Mockito 2, MockitoExtension runs in Strictness.STRICT_STUBS by default. This is a feature, and the two errors it produces are the most-searched Mockito messages in existence.

UnnecessaryStubbingException - you stubbed something the test never called. Almost always it means the arguments do not match what the code actually passes (you stubbed findById(101), the code calls findById(1)), or the stub is left over from a refactoring. Deleting the stub is usually right; lenient() silences it and should be rare.

PotentialStubbingProblem - the mock was called with arguments no stub matches. Under the old lenient default it would have quietly returned null and you would have chased a NullPointerException five frames away.

Argument matchers (any(), eq(), argThat()) have one rule that catches everybody: if you use a matcher for one argument, you must use matchers for all of them. when(repo.find(any(), 5)) throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException; write when(repo.find(any(), eq(5))). And prefer specific matchers to any() - any() makes a stub match calls it was never meant to.

For void methods the when() syntax does not compile at all; use doThrow(...).when(mock).method() or doNothing().

PowerMock: why the handout's advice should not be followed

The source classifies mock frameworks as "stub based" (EasyMock) versus "byte code manipulation based" (PowerMock) and recommends the latter. That taxonomy has not described the landscape for over a decade, and the recommendation is actively harmful on a modern project.

Claim in the sourceReality
EasyMock is "stub based" and cannot mock final or private membersThe final/private limitation is real, but it applied to every mainstream mock framework, Mockito included, because they all worked by generating a subclass - and you cannot subclass a final class or override a private method
PowerMock is byte-code based and therefore preferredPowerMock achieves this with a custom classloader that rewrites bytecode at load time. That is precisely why it breaks: it is coupled to the internals of both JUnit and the JDK, and every JDK upgrade has historically stranded it
Use powermock-module-junit4 and powermock-api-mockito2The artifact name says junit4. It runs through @RunWith(PowerMockRunner.class), which does not exist in JUnit 5. Combined with the handout's Jupiter assertions, the file cannot work as printed. PowerMock has no supported JUnit 5 runner
You need it to mock static methodsMockito 3.4+ has mockStatic() built in. Mockito 5's default mockito-inline maker also mocks final classes and final methods without any extra dependency

Mockito 5 (the default in Spring Boot 3.x) uses the inline mock maker, which instruments classes through the Java agent API rather than by subclassing. Final classes, final methods, static methods and constructors are all mockable out of the box, on modern JDKs, with JUnit 5. There is no remaining reason to add PowerMock to a new project.

The deeper point: needing to mock a static method is nearly always a design signal. LocalDateTime.now() scattered through a service makes it untestable; injecting a java.time.Clock makes it trivially testable and is better production code besides.

What deserves a test, and why getters and setters do not

Coverage percentage is a diagnostic, not a target. Chase 100% and the cheapest way to get there is to test the code that cannot break, which inflates the number while testing nothing.

CodeTest it?
Plain getters and settersNo. They contain no decision, no branch, nothing that a compiler would not already catch. A test asserting setName("x") then getName() equals "x" is asserting that Java field assignment works
Generated code - Lombok, MapStruct, toString(), buildersNo. You would be testing the generator, and its authors already did
Framework wiring - "does this @Service get autowired"No, beyond a single context-loads smoke test for the whole application
Business rules with branches - eligibility, pricing, discounts, state machinesYes, and this is where most of your tests should live
Boundary conditions - null, empty, zero, negative, off-by-one, maximum valuesYes. Most production defects are boundary defects
Error paths - what happens when the dependency throwsYes. This is the code that runs during an incident, and it is nearly always the least-exercised code in the system
Every bug you fixYes - write the failing test first. It proves the diagnosis and pins the fix permanently
Custom repository queries (JPQL, native SQL, derived method names)Yes, but not with a mock - a mocked repository returns whatever you told it and can never catch a broken query. This needs a real database; see the integration testing topic
equals() and hashCode() when hand-writtenYes. Getting the contract wrong silently corrupts every HashMap and HashSet the object touches

The economic test: would this test have caught a defect that actually reached production, and will it still pass after a legitimate refactoring? If the answer to the first is no, it is not earning its maintenance cost. If the answer to the second is no, it is testing implementation rather than behaviour and will be deleted in frustration six months from now.

A useful discipline for judging a suite is mutation testing (PIT on the JVM). It changes your production code - flips a > to >=, returns null instead of a value - and re-runs your tests. Any mutation that survives is a line your suite covers but does not actually check. Line coverage of 90% with a mutation score of 30% is the classic profile of a suite full of getter tests.

Running tests from the command line and in CI

The IDE's "Run As -> JUnit Test" is fine for the loop you are in; the build is what gates the merge. Maven Surefire runs unit tests during the test phase and fails the build on the first failure.

CommandEffect
mvn testCompile and run everything Surefire matches: *Test.java, Test*.java, *Tests.java, *TestCase.java
mvn -Dtest=PolicyServiceImplTest testOne class
mvn -Dtest=PolicyServiceImplTest#savePolicyTest testOne method
mvn -DskipTests packageCompile the tests but do not run them
mvn -Dmaven.test.skip=true packageDo not even compile them - which hides compilation breakage in test code, so avoid it
mvn -DfailIfNoTests=true testFail rather than pass when zero tests ran - the guard against the silent JUnit 4/5 mix-up
mvn verifyRuns Surefire, then Failsafe for *IT.java integration tests, with proper pre/post-integration phases

Keep unit tests in Surefire and integration tests in Failsafe. Surefire failing stops the build immediately; Failsafe defers its failure until after the post-integration-test phase, so containers and servers still get shut down cleanly. A JUnit 5 @Tag gives the same split within one plugin if you prefer.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml: split fast unit tests from slow integration tests -->
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <configuration>
        <excludedGroups>integration</excludedGroups>
        <failIfNoTests>true</failIfNoTests>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
      <executions>
        <execution>
          <goals>
            <goal>integration-test</goal>
            <goal>verify</goal>
          </goals>
        </execution>
      </executions>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

// Tag the slow ones:
@Tag("integration")
@SpringBootTest
class PolicyEndToEndIT { /* ... */ }

// OUTPUT of mvn test (unit tests only):
// [INFO] --- maven-surefire-plugin:3.2.5:test ---
// [INFO] Running com.cybage.PolicyServiceImplTest
// [INFO] Tests run: 5, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, Time elapsed: 0.412 s
// [INFO] Running com.cybage.PremiumCalculatorTest
// [INFO] Tests run: 11, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, Time elapsed: 0.088 s
// [INFO] Results:
// [INFO] Tests run: 16, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
// [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
// [INFO] Total time: 6.1 s

// OUTPUT of a failure - note the exit code, which is what CI reads:
// [ERROR] PolicyServiceImplTest.getPolicyByIdTest:58
//         expected: <103> but was: <104>
// [ERROR] Tests run: 5, Failures: 1, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
// [INFO] BUILD FAILURE
// $ echo $?
// 1

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What replaced @Before and @BeforeClass in JUnit 5?@BeforeEach and @BeforeAll. The names now state explicitly whether the hook runs per test method or once per class, which the JUnit 4 names never did. @BeforeAll must still be static unless the class is annotated @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS).
Why did @RunWith become @ExtendWith?A JUnit 4 class could carry only one @RunWith runner, so you could not combine SpringRunner and MockitoJUnitRunner. JUnit 5 extensions compose - you can stack @ExtendWith declarations freely, and Spring Boot's slice annotations are themselves meta-annotated with @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class).
What is wrong with @Test(expected = Foo.class)?It passes if the exception comes from anywhere in the method, including setup lines that were never meant to throw, and it gives you no handle on the exception object. assertThrows pins the expectation to one expression and returns the exception so you can assert on its message and fields.
What happens if you mix org.junit.Test with JUnit 5 in a Spring Boot 2.4+ project?The Vintage engine is not on the classpath, so the Jupiter engine does not recognise those methods, reports zero tests, and the build passes having executed nothing. Guard against it with failIfNoTests and by watching the "Tests run:" count.
What is the difference between @Mock and @MockBean?@Mock is plain Mockito with no Spring involvement, injected via @InjectMocks or your own constructor call. @MockBean creates a Mockito mock and registers it in the Spring ApplicationContext, replacing the real bean definition everywhere it is autowired - so it requires a context to be loading.
Why is @MockBean expensive?The set of @MockBean declarations forms part of the Spring test context cache key. Any class with a different combination of mocked beans cannot reuse a cached context and pays a full startup. Hoisting a common set of mocks into a shared abstract base class restores the cache hit.
What does @InjectMocks actually do?It instantiates the class under test and pushes every @Mock declared in the test class into it - preferring the biggest matching constructor, then falling back to setter and then field injection by reflection. That reflection fallback is why it works on classes with private @Autowired fields and no constructor.
What is UnnecessaryStubbingException and why does it exist?Strict stubs (the default under MockitoExtension) fail a test that stubs a call the code never makes. It almost always means the stubbed arguments do not match the real ones, which under the old lenient default would have silently returned null and surfaced as a confusing NullPointerException elsewhere.
When would you use ArgumentCaptor instead of asserting on a return value?When the unit constructs the argument internally and passes it to a collaborator - an audit event, a mapped DTO, an email message. You cannot predict the object to match it with eq(), so you capture what was actually passed and assert on the fields that matter.
Why should you not use PowerMock on a new project?It is built on a JUnit 4 runner with no JUnit 5 equivalent, uses a custom classloader coupled to JDK internals, and everything it was needed for - final classes, final and static methods - Mockito 3.4+ and the inline mock maker now do natively with no extra dependency.
How do you test code that calls LocalDateTime.now()?Preferably by not needing to: inject a java.time.Clock and call LocalDate.now(clock), so the test supplies Clock.fixed(). If the call is in code you cannot change, Mockito.mockStatic() in a try-with-resources block works, but it is thread-local and must be closed.
Why is testing getters and setters considered noise?They contain no decision or branch, so no realistic defect can hide in them. Such tests raise line coverage without raising the number of bugs the suite can detect - a gap that mutation testing tools like PIT expose immediately as a high coverage percentage with a low mutation score.
Your service test mocks the repository and passes. What class of bug can it still not catch?Anything below the mock: a broken JPQL or derived query, a wrong column mapping, a missing constraint, a lazy-loading failure. The mock returns whatever it was told to. Queries have to be exercised against a real database, which is what @DataJpaTest and Testcontainers are for.

beginner.content:
Business Requirement

The insurance handout builds a complete Spring Boot application: a Policy entity, a PolicyRepository, a PolicyServiceImpl and a PolicyController exposing /getAll, /save, /get/{id} and /delete/{id} over MySQL. The only test it writes is a service test with a mocked repository. Everything above and below that service is verified by opening Postman and looking at the response by hand.

Problem Statement: the mocked service test passes even when the URL mapping is wrong, the JSON field names are wrong, the derived query does not compile, the column name does not exist and the HTTP status is 500. Those defects live in the wiring, and a mock has nothing to say about wiring.

This topic covers the half of Spring Boot testing that needs a Spring application context. The companion topic, Unit Testing with JUnit 5 & Mockito, covers the half that does not - plain JUnit assertions, Mockito @Mock/@InjectMocks, and testing PolicyServiceImpl in isolation. The boundary between them is exactly this: does Spring have to start?

Unit test: you construct the object yourself (or Mockito does). No ApplicationContext. Milliseconds.
Slice test: Spring starts, but only the auto-configuration for one layer. Hundreds of milliseconds to a second or two.
Integration test: Spring starts the whole application, often with a real HTTP port and a real database. Seconds.

The application under test

Everything below is tested against the handout's own application, with its errors corrected. Three of them matter before a single test can run.

1. CrudRepository<Policy, Serializable> - the second type parameter is the ID type, and Policy's @Id is an Integer. Written as Serializable the repository still starts, but findById and deleteById accept any object at all and fail at runtime instead of at compile time.
2. public Policy findById(Integer Id); declared in the repository clashes with the inherited Optional<Policy> findById(ID). Same erasure, different return type - that is neither an override nor an overload, and javac rejects it.
3. javax.persistence.* is correct for Spring Boot 2.x. Boot 3.x moved to Jakarta EE 9+, where the package is jakarta.persistence.* - the javax classes are not deprecated there, they are simply absent from the classpath.

Test slices - loading one layer instead of the application

Spring Boot ships a family of test slice annotations. Each one turns on a fixed subset of auto-configuration and turns everything else off, so the context that starts contains only what that layer needs.

Slice annotationWhat it brings up
@WebMvcTestThe MVC infrastructure: @Controller/@RestController, @ControllerAdvice, WebMvcConfigurer, Jackson converters, Filter beans, Spring Security's filter chain, and an auto-configured MockMvc. No @Service, no @Repository, no DataSource.
@DataJpaTestSpring Data JPA repositories, EntityManager, TestEntityManager, an embedded database, and transaction management. No controllers, no services.
@JdbcTestThe same idea one layer lower: JdbcTemplate and a DataSource, no JPA.
@DataMongoTest / @DataRedisTestThe equivalent slices for those stores.
@JsonTestJackson/Gson configuration only, with JacksonTester. For asserting that an entity serialises to the exact JSON the API contract promises.
@RestClientTestRestTemplateBuilder plus MockRestServiceServer, for testing a client of somebody else's API.
@SpringBootTestNot a slice. The whole context, exactly as the application starts it, optionally on a real port.

A slice finds its configuration by walking up from the test class's package until it meets a @SpringBootConfiguration - normally your @SpringBootApplication class. That is why the test package must mirror the main package: move the test outside that tree and the context fails to start with "Unable to find a @SpringBootConfiguration".
codeExamples:
SLICE MAP - what starts, and what you must supply yourself

   @SpringBootTest                        @WebMvcTest(PolicyController.class)
   +---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
   | DispatcherServlet         |          | DispatcherServlet         |
   | PolicyController          |          | PolicyController          |
   | PolicyServiceImpl  (real) |          | PolicyService   @MockBean |  <- you supply
   | PolicyRepository   (real) |          |         X  not loaded     |
   | DataSource -> MySQL       |          |         X  not loaded     |
   | Hibernate SessionFactory  |          |         X  not loaded     |
   | 180 beans, ~4.0 s         |          | 30 beans, ~1.1 s          |
   +---------------------------+          +---------------------------+

   @DataJpaTest                           plain @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension)
   +---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
   |        X  no web layer    |          |        X  nothing         |
   |        X  no services     |          | PolicyServiceImpl  (real) |
   | PolicyRepository   (real) |          | PolicyRepository   @Mock  |
   | EntityManager             |          |                           |
   | H2 in-memory DataSource   |          | no Spring at all          |
   | 45 beans, ~1.4 s          |          | ~0.02 s                   |
   +---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
                                          (covered in the unit-testing topic)

beginner.content:
Steps - testing the controller with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc

MockMvc dispatches a request straight into the DispatcherServlet. There is no socket, no Tomcat, no port and no serialisation over the wire - but everything the framework does after the request arrives is real: handler mapping, path variable binding, message conversion, validation, exception handling and the status code.

StepWhat you do
1Annotate the test @WebMvcTest(PolicyController.class) - naming the controller keeps the slice to one controller instead of all of them
2@Autowired MockMvc mockMvc - the slice auto-configures it for you
3@MockBean PolicyService policyService - the service is not in the slice, so without this the context fails to start
4Stub the service with when(...).thenReturn(...) exactly as in a unit test
5mockMvc.perform(get(...)) then chain .andExpect(...) matchers
6Add .andDo(print()) while you are writing the test - it dumps the whole request and response

The failure you will hit first is the one worth understanding: omit the @MockBean and you get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException before any test runs. That is the slice working as designed - it is telling you that the controller's dependency is deliberately outside the boundary.

What MockMvc can assert

The chain reads like the HTTP conversation itself. Everything on the left of the table is a static import from MockMvcResultMatchers.

MatcherChecks
status().isOk() / isCreated() / isNotFound() / isBadRequest()The response status code. There are named methods for the whole range, plus status().is(418).
content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)The Content-Type header the converter chose.
content().json(expectedJson)Whole-body comparison that ignores field order and, by default, tolerates extra fields. Far less brittle than content().string(...).
jsonPath("$.name").value("Rajaram")One field, addressed by JSONPath. $[0] indexes an array, $..email searches recursively.
jsonPath("$.password").doesNotExist()A field is absent - the assertion that stops you leaking a hash into a response body.
header().string("Location", "...")A response header.
view().name(...) / model().attribute(...)For a classic MVC controller returning a template name rather than JSON.
andReturn()Ends the chain and hands back the MvcResult, so you can deserialise the body and assert on a real object.

Two request-builder details that catch people out. get("/api/policies/{id}", 3) uses a URI template, so the value is encoded properly - do not build the path by string concatenation. And a POST without .contentType(...) produces 415 Unsupported Media Type, not a helpful message, because no HttpMessageConverter volunteers to read it.

Steps - testing the repository with @DataJpaTest

Problem Statement: PolicyRepository needs a finder by policy number and one by status. Derived query methods are parsed from the method name at context startup, and a JPQL @Query is parsed at startup too. Neither is checked by the compiler, so a typo is a runtime failure - and a mocked repository will never find it.

@DataJpaTest gives you the persistence layer and nothing else. Three of its behaviours define how the test feels:

BehaviourEffect
Embedded database substitutionAny DataSource you configured is replaced by an in-memory one (H2, HSQLDB or Derby, whichever is on the classpath). Your MySQL settings in application.properties are ignored.
Transactional and rolled backEvery test method runs in a transaction that is rolled back at the end. Tests cannot pollute each other, and no cleanup code is needed.
TestEntityManagerA test-facing wrapper over EntityManager with persistAndFlush, find and clear. Use it to set up rows without going through the repository you are trying to test.

The flush() and clear() pair is the part beginners miss. Inside one transaction the persistence context is a cache: save() then findById() can hand you back the very same Java object without ever touching the database, so a broken column mapping goes undetected. flush() forces the INSERT to be issued and clear() empties the cache, so the subsequent read is a genuine SELECT.

Steps - the full integration test with @SpringBootTest

@SpringBootTest starts the real context. Its webEnvironment attribute decides whether a servlet container starts with it, and that choice determines which client you use.

webEnvironmentWhat happens
MOCK (the default)A mock servlet environment, no port is bound. Combine with @AutoConfigureMockMvc to get a MockMvc that runs through the whole context - controller, real service, real repository.
RANDOM_PORTA real embedded Tomcat on a free port, injected into the test with @LocalServerPort. Requests go over a real TCP socket. This is the only mode that exercises the HTTP stack, connectors, filters ordering and real serialisation.
DEFINED_PORTA real container on the configured port. Avoid it - parallel builds and a developer's running application collide on it.
NONEContext only, no web environment. For batch jobs and scheduled components.

With RANDOM_PORT you inject a TestRestTemplate - a fault-tolerant wrapper over RestTemplate that does not throw on 4xx or 5xx, so you can assert on an error status instead of catching an exception. On a reactive stack, or on any Boot 3 project, WebTestClient is the better choice: fluent, non-blocking, and usable against either a real port or a mock environment.

Test configuration and test data

An integration test must not talk to the developer's MySQL instance, and it must start from a known set of rows. Spring Boot gives several mechanisms; the useful thing is knowing which one wins.

MechanismPurpose
src/test/resources/application.propertiesReplaces the main one entirely for tests on the test classpath. Blunt, but it is where show-sql and log levels belong.
application-test.properties + @ActiveProfiles("test")The usual arrangement: a profile-specific file layered over the defaults, activated per test class.
@TestPropertySource(properties = {...})Highest precedence, declared inline on the class. Ideal for one or two overrides - but note it changes the context cache key.
@DynamicPropertySourceA static method that registers properties computed at runtime, which is how a container's randomly-assigned port and JDBC URL reach the context.
@Sql("/data/policies.sql")Runs a SQL script before (or, with executionPhase, after) the test method. Precise, readable seed data.
src/test/resources/data.sql + schema.sqlRun automatically against an embedded database at startup. Convenient, but shared by every test in the context.
@Transactional on the test classWraps each test method in a transaction that is rolled back - what @DataJpaTest does for you. On a RANDOM_PORT test it does not work, because the server handles the request on a different thread with its own transaction.

That last row is a genuine trap. Developers add @Transactional to a RANDOM_PORT integration test expecting automatic cleanup, the rows persist, and the next test fails on stale data. Over a real socket the only options are an explicit cleanup step, a fresh database per class, or a container that is thrown away.

Application Flow - which test sees which defect

The point of having three levels is that each one can see a class of defect the others cannot.

DefectCaught by
Wrong arithmetic or a wrong branch in the serviceThe Mockito unit test - fastest, and the right place for it
Wrong URL path, wrong HTTP verb, wrong status code@WebMvcTest
JSON field named differently from the API contract@WebMvcTest or @JsonTest
Exception not mapped to a status by @ControllerAdvice@WebMvcTest
Typo in a derived query method name, broken JPQL@DataJpaTest - it fails at context startup
Column name in @Column does not exist in the schema@DataJpaTest against a real schema, or a Testcontainers test
Missing @Transactional causing a lazy-loading failure@SpringBootTest with a real request thread
Two beans of the same type, ambiguous injectionAny test that loads the full context - including the generated contextLoads() smoke test
Filter ordering, CORS, security rules@SpringBootTest with RANDOM_PORT, or @WebMvcTest with security auto-configuration on
codeExamples:
REQUEST PATH, AND WHERE EACH TEST CUTS IT

  HTTP client
      |
      |  <=== TestRestTemplate / WebTestClient enter here  (RANDOM_PORT)
      v
  Tomcat connector  ................. only a real port exercises this
      |
      v
  Servlet filters / Spring Security
      |
      |  <=== MockMvc enters here    (@WebMvcTest, @AutoConfigureMockMvc)
      v
  DispatcherServlet
      |
      +-- HandlerMapping        : is the URL right?
      +-- Argument resolvers    : does @PathVariable bind?
      +-- HttpMessageConverter  : does the JSON deserialise?
      v
  PolicyController
      |
      |  <=== the unit test enters here, calling the object directly
      v
  PolicyServiceImpl                      business rules live here
      |
      |  <=== a mock cuts the chain here (unit test)
      v
  PolicyRepository (Spring Data proxy)
      |
      |  <=== @DataJpaTest covers from here down
      v
  Hibernate  ->  JDBC  ->  H2 / Testcontainers MySQL / real MySQL


  A test is worth writing when it is the CHEAPEST level that can see
  the defect you are trying to prevent. Anything higher is slower and
  more brittle for no additional information.

expert.content:
@Mock versus @MockBean, and the price of dirtying the cache

The unit-testing topic argues for @Mock on the grounds that a service test needs no context at all. Here the question is different: you are already loading a context, so what does adding a @MockBean cost?

Aspect@Mock (Mockito)@MockBean / @MockitoBean (Spring)
Packageorg.mockito.Mockorg.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean
Requires a contextNoYes - there is nothing to register into otherwise
MechanismCreates an objectCreates an object, then replaces the bean definition in the BeanFactory before refresh
Reaches collaboratorsOnly via @InjectMocks or your own constructor callEverywhere Spring would have injected the real bean
Effect on the context cacheNoneBecomes part of the cache key - a different mock set is a different context
CostMicrosecondsPotentially a full context startup, per test class

The mock itself is cheap. What is expensive is that a set of bean overrides makes the context unique. Spring's MergedContextConfiguration - the cache key - includes the ContextCustomizer that @MockBean contributes, and that customiser carries the definitions being overridden. Two classes that mock different beans therefore cannot share a context, and each pays a cold start. This is the single largest avoidable cost in most Spring test suites.

On Spring Framework 6.2 / Boot 3.4, @MockBean and @SpyBean are deprecated in favour of @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean, part of a general bean-override mechanism that also includes @TestBean (replace a bean with a real object from a static factory method). The caching consequence is unchanged.
@SpyBean wraps the real bean so unstubbed calls still execute. Useful for a legacy component you want to observe rather than replace, and for verifying that a real collaborator was called - but note it forces Spring to create the real bean first, with all its dependencies.

How the test context cache actually works, and what invalidates it

TestContextManager keeps a static, JVM-wide, LRU map from a context key to a fully refreshed ApplicationContext. Every test class computes its key; a hit reuses the context, a miss builds a new one. Understanding what goes into that key is the difference between a two-minute suite and a twenty-minute one.

Key componentContributed by
locations / classes@ContextConfiguration, @SpringBootTest(classes = ...), and the discovered @SpringBootConfiguration
context initializersApplicationContextInitializer classes named on the test
active profiles@ActiveProfiles - and the set is order-sensitive unless sorted
property source locations and inlined properties@TestPropertySource, and @SpringBootTest(properties = ...)
context customizers@MockBean/@MockitoBean sets, @DynamicPropertySource methods, the web environment, @AutoConfigure* annotations, excluded auto-configuration
context loader and parent contextRarely varied in practice

Everything else is fair game for sharing. Two @WebMvcTest classes for different controllers still produce different keys, because the controller list is a customizer - which is why @WebMvcTest without arguments (all controllers) can, counter-intuitively, be faster across a large suite than many single-controller slices.

@DirtiesContext is the explicit invalidation: it closes the context and evicts it after the class (or method, with methodMode). It is occasionally necessary - a test that mutates a singleton's state, shuts down a scheduler, or changes a static registry - but it is very often used as a blunt fix for test pollution that would be better fixed at its cause. Every @DirtiesContext costs one startup for the class that carries it and one for the next class that wanted that context.

The cache holds 32 contexts by default (spring.test.context.cache.maxSize). Exceed it and you get LRU thrashing: contexts are evicted and rebuilt in a cycle, which looks exactly like a slow machine and is in fact a configuration problem.

@WebMvcTest versus @SpringBootTest - the real cost, and the real coverage

The usual claim is that slices are "faster". That is true but imprecise; the interesting part is what each one stops testing.

Question@WebMvcTest@SpringBootTest
Beans createdWeb infrastructure plus the named controllers - typically 25-40Every bean the application defines - hundreds
Auto-configuration appliedA fixed allow-list from spring.factories: Jackson, MVC, validation, security, error handlingAll of it, including JPA, the connection pool, caching, messaging, metrics, scheduling
DataSourceNone. A repository that is @MockBean-ed still needs no database, and one that is not causes a startup failureReal. It will connect, and CI needs that database to exist
Typical startup~1 s cold, then cached across classes with the same key3-8 s cold on a medium application
What only it can catchNothing the full test cannot; it is a subsetBean wiring conflicts, missing configuration properties, transaction boundaries, real query execution, filter ordering, startup failures
What it wrongly reports greenAnything below the mocked serviceLittle - which is also why its failures are harder to localise

The subtlety about failure localisation matters more than the seconds. A @WebMvcTest failure points at one controller. A @SpringBootTest failure could be the controller, the service, the mapping, the schema, the profile, or a bean that failed to construct - and you read a two-hundred-line stack trace to find out. Fast tests are not only fast to run, they are fast to diagnose.

Two operational notes. @WebMvcTest loads Spring Security's filter chain if Spring Security is on the classpath, so every request without credentials comes back 401 and your tests fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the controller - use @WithMockUser, or turn the filters off deliberately. And do not annotate a test with both @SpringBootTest and a slice annotation: they configure the context in incompatible ways and Boot rejects the combination.

@DataJpaTest: rollback by default, and the database it silently swaps in

Two behaviours of @DataJpaTest are frequently misunderstood, and both change what the test actually proves.

Rollback by default. @DataJpaTest is meta-annotated @Transactional, and the Spring TestContext framework rolls back a test-managed transaction when the method ends. Nothing is ever committed. Three consequences follow:
• Tests are isolated for free and need no cleanup.
• The persistence context lives for the whole method, so an entity you save() is still managed - a subsequent findById() may return it from the first-level cache without issuing a SELECT. Call flush() and clear() when you want to prove the round trip.
• Because there is always an open transaction, lazy associations resolve happily in the test and then throw LazyInitializationException in production, where the session closed at the end of the service call. A @DataJpaTest can never catch that defect.

@Rollback(false) or @Commit turns the rollback off, but then you own the cleanup.

Automatic embedded-database substitution. @DataJpaTest implies @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.ANY). Whatever DataSource your configuration defines is discarded and an in-memory one is substituted. This is why the test runs on a laptop with no MySQL - and why it can pass against SQL your production database would reject.

H2 pretendsMySQL disagrees
Identifier quoting and case handling are forgivingTable name case matters on Linux; a name that works on a developer's Windows machine can fail in production
Reserved words differA column called rank or groups is fine in one and a syntax error in the other
No native SQL functions in commonAny @Query(nativeQuery = true) using GROUP_CONCAT, JSON_EXTRACT or ON DUPLICATE KEY cannot be tested against H2 at all
Default isolation, locking and deadlock behaviourRow locking, gap locks and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE semantics are genuinely different
Type coercion and truncationMySQL's strict mode, zero dates and implicit conversions have no H2 equivalent

MODE=MySQL narrows some of this and closes none of it. If the query matters, test it against the real engine - which is what Testcontainers is for.

Testcontainers - testing against the database you actually deploy on

The honest answer to "H2 is not MySQL" is to run MySQL. Testcontainers starts a real database in a Docker container for the duration of the build, hands the test its randomly-assigned port, and throws it away afterwards. The container is disposable, so tests can commit freely and each class can start from a known state.

ConcernHow Testcontainers handles it
Port conflictsThe container binds a random host port; the test reads it back at runtime
Leftover containersA companion "Ryuk" container reaps everything when the JVM exits, including after a crash
Startup timingWait strategies block until the database is genuinely accepting connections, not merely until the process started
Startup costReal - several seconds. Mitigate with the singleton-container pattern or @Testcontainers(disabledWithoutDocker = true) plus reuse
CINeeds a Docker daemon on the agent. That requirement is the main reason teams hesitate, and it is usually a one-line change

On Spring Boot 3.1+ the wiring became a single annotation. @ServiceConnection on a container bean tells Boot to derive spring.datasource.url, username and password from that container automatically - no @DynamicPropertySource, no property names to get wrong. It works for MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ and Elasticsearch containers alike. Boot 3.1 also added @ServiceConnection's development-time counterpart, so spring-boot-testcontainers can start the same containers when you run the application locally.

A word on scope: this is not a replacement for slice tests. Keep the fast pyramid - unit tests for logic, @WebMvcTest for the web contract - and use Testcontainers for the queries and the schema, where a fake database gives a false answer.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
  <artifactId>mysql</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
  <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>


// ---- Spring Boot 3.1+ : @ServiceConnection ----
package com.cybage.genworth.insurance.repository;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.jdbc.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.testcontainers.containers.MySQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class PolicyRepositoryMySqlTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                       // Boot 3.1+ does the wiring
    static MySQLContainer<?> mysql = new MySQLContainer<>("mysql:8.0.36");

    @Autowired private PolicyRepository repository;

    @Test
    void nativeQueryRunsOnRealMySql() {
        assertNotNull(repository.summariseByStatus());
    }
}
// Note "static": a static @Container starts once for the class. A
// non-static one restarts for EVERY test method, which is the usual
// cause of "why is my Testcontainers suite so slow".


// ---- Before 3.1, or for a property @ServiceConnection does not cover ----
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class PolicyRepositoryLegacyWiringTest {

    @Container
    static MySQLContainer<?> mysql = new MySQLContainer<>("mysql:8.0.36")
            .withDatabaseName("project")
            .withUsername("root")
            .withPassword("root");

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void datasourceProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.datasource.url",      mysql::getJdbcUrl);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.username", mysql::getUsername);
        registry.add("spring.datasource.password", mysql::getPassword);
        // Suppliers, not values - they are called after the container starts.
    }
}


// ---- Singleton container: ONE database for the whole build ----
abstract class AbstractContainerTest {

    static final MySQLContainer<?> MYSQL =
            new MySQLContainer<>("mysql:8.0.36").withReuse(true);

    static { MYSQL.start(); }     // started once per JVM, never stopped;
                                  // Ryuk cleans up at exit

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("spring.datasource.url", MYSQL::getJdbcUrl);
        r.add("spring.datasource.username", MYSQL::getUsername);
        r.add("spring.datasource.password", MYSQL::getPassword);
    }
}

// OUTPUT:
// Creating container for image: mysql:8.0.36
// Container mysql:8.0.36 is starting: 3f9c1e...
// Container mysql:8.0.36 started in PT8.412S
// Started PolicyRepositoryMySqlTest in 11.204 seconds
// ...
// Container mysql:8.0.36 started in PT0.031S   <- reused by later classes
//
// FAILURE when Docker is absent:
// java.lang.IllegalStateException: Could not find a valid Docker
// environment. Please see logs and check configuration.
// Guard it: @Testcontainers(disabledWithoutDocker = true) skips instead
// of failing, which keeps the suite runnable on a machine without Docker.

expert.content:
MockMvc: standaloneSetup versus webAppContextSetup, and its limits

MockMvc can be built two ways, and the choice decides how much of Spring MVC is real.

AspectstandaloneSetup(controller)webAppContextSetup(context)
Spring contextNone. You hand it an instance you constructed yourselfThe loaded WebApplicationContext - what @WebMvcTest and @AutoConfigureMockMvc use
StartupMillisecondsContext startup, then cached
@ControllerAdviceNot applied unless you register it explicitlyApplied - it is a bean
Filters, Spring SecurityNot applied unless added by handApplied
Message converters, validation, formattersA minimal default set, not your customised configurationExactly your configuration
What it provesThe controller method's own logic and its annotationsThe application's real web behaviour

The trap with standaloneSetup is that it is quietly more permissive. Your custom ObjectMapper with snake-case naming is not there, your @ControllerAdvice is not there, your argument resolver is not there - so the test asserts on behaviour the deployed application does not have. It is a legitimate tool for a controller with no framework interaction, and a source of false confidence everywhere else. Prefer @WebMvcTest.

What MockMvc cannot test at all, whichever way it is built: it never opens a socket. There is no connector, no HTTP parsing, no chunked transfer, no TLS, no real timeout, no client. Boot 3.2 added MockMvcTester (an AssertJ-flavoured API over the same engine) and WebTestClient can now bind to a MockMvc setup too - but none of that changes the boundary. For anything at the wire level you need RANDOM_PORT.

What deserves an integration test, and what does not

Every integration test is a permanent cost: seconds on every build, a database dependency in CI, and a failure that takes longer to diagnose. It earns that cost only when it can see something no cheaper test can.

ScenarioWhich level, and why
Premium calculation, eligibility rules, discount bands, state transitionsUnit. Pure logic with branches. An integration test here is slower, harder to read, and finds nothing extra.
Does the endpoint return 404 rather than 500 for a missing policy@WebMvcTest. The status code is produced by framework machinery a unit test never runs.
Does the response JSON match the published API contract@WebMvcTest or @JsonTest. Field renames are a classic silent break for consumers.
Does findByStatusAndPremiumAmountGreaterThan actually parse and return the right rows@DataJpaTest, ideally on Testcontainers. A mock cannot fail here, and that is the problem.
Does a native query with vendor-specific SQL workTestcontainers. H2 cannot answer the question.
Does the context start at all with production-like configurationOne @SpringBootTest smoke test. The generated contextLoads() is not a formality - it catches missing properties, ambiguous beans and cyclic dependencies.
The two or three journeys the business would notice if broken: create a policy, pay, retrieve it@SpringBootTest end to end. Few, named after the business flow, not after a class.
Every CRUD permutation of every entity, end to endNo. This is how a suite reaches forty minutes while catching nothing the layer tests missed.
Third-party payment gateway behaviourNot in your build. Mock the client for your tests; verify the contract separately with WireMock or a consumer-driven contract test.

A workable ratio: roughly 70% unit, 20% slice, 10% full integration - not as a target to hit, but as a shape to notice you have inverted.
The diagnostic question: if this test fails, will it tell me where the defect is? A failing unit test names a method. A failing end-to-end test names a journey and leaves the search to you.
The ice-cream cone - many end-to-end tests, few unit tests - is the common failure shape. It is slow, flaky, and its failures teach nothing, so people start re-running the build instead of reading it. That is the moment a suite stops being an asset.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the practical difference between @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest?@WebMvcTest applies a fixed allow-list of web auto-configuration and creates only the MVC infrastructure plus the named controllers - typically 25-40 beans, about a second, and no DataSource. @SpringBootTest builds the entire context including JPA, the connection pool and every @Service, which takes several seconds and needs the database to exist. The slice is also far easier to diagnose: its failure points at one controller.
Why is @MockBean described as expensive when the mock itself is cheap?The set of bean overrides becomes part of the Spring test context cache key, through the ContextCustomizer that @MockBean contributes. A class with a different combination of mocked beans cannot reuse a cached context and pays a full startup. Hoisting a common set of mocks into a shared abstract base class restores the cache hit.
What goes into the test context cache key?The configuration classes or locations, context initializers, active profiles, property source locations and inlined properties, the context loader, the parent context, and all context customizers - which is where @MockBean sets, @DynamicPropertySource, the web environment and the @AutoConfigure* annotations land. Anything that differs in one of those produces a separate context.
When is @DirtiesContext justified, and what does it cost?When a test genuinely mutates shared state that would corrupt later tests - shutting down a scheduler, changing a static registry, mutating a singleton's internal state. It closes and evicts the context, so it costs one startup for that class and another for the next class that wanted it. Used as a blanket fix for test pollution it is usually treating the symptom.
Does @DataJpaTest commit anything?No. It is meta-annotated @Transactional and the TestContext framework rolls back at the end of each method, so tests are isolated with no cleanup code. @Rollback(false) or @Commit turns that off, at which point cleanup becomes your responsibility.
Which database does @DataJpaTest use, and how do you stop it?It implies @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.ANY), which discards your configured DataSource and substitutes an embedded one - H2, HSQLDB or Derby, whichever is on the classpath. @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) keeps the configured DataSource, which is how you point a @DataJpaTest at a Testcontainers instance.
Why is passing a @DataJpaTest against H2 not proof that a query works on MySQL?Reserved words, identifier case sensitivity, native SQL functions such as GROUP_CONCAT and JSON_EXTRACT, ON DUPLICATE KEY, strict-mode type coercion, and locking and isolation behaviour all differ. MODE=MySQL narrows the gap and does not close it. Anything vendor-specific has to run against the real engine.
What class of bug can a @DataJpaTest never catch?A LazyInitializationException. The test method runs inside an open transaction for its whole duration, so lazy associations always resolve; in production the session closes when the service call returns. Only a test that goes through the web layer end to end reproduces it.
What does Testcontainers give you that an embedded database does not, and what does it cost?The real database engine, the real SQL dialect, real locking and real constraints, in a disposable container with a random port that is reaped automatically. It costs several seconds of container startup and requires a Docker daemon on the CI agent - mitigated by static @Container fields, the singleton-container pattern and withReuse(true).
What does @ServiceConnection do?On Spring Boot 3.1+, placing it on a Testcontainers container bean makes Boot derive the connection properties - JDBC URL, username, password, or the equivalent for Mongo, Redis, Kafka and others - from the running container automatically, replacing the hand-written @DynamicPropertySource block and the chance of misspelling a property name.
MockMvc standaloneSetup or webAppContextSetup - which and why?webAppContextSetup, which is what @WebMvcTest configures, because it uses the real context: your @ControllerAdvice, filters, security chain, message converters and formatters. standaloneSetup constructs the controller yourself with a minimal default MVC configuration, so it is fast but quietly more permissive than production, and tests written against it can assert behaviour the deployed application does not have.
When do you need @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) rather than MockMvc?When the thing under test lives below the DispatcherServlet: the servlet container itself, connectors, TLS, real timeouts, chunked encoding, or a real HTTP client's behaviour. MockMvc never opens a socket, so nothing at the wire level is exercised by it.
Why does @Transactional not clean up after a RANDOM_PORT integration test?The server handles the request on its own thread, in its own transaction, which commits. The test thread's transaction is a separate one and rolling it back takes nothing with it. Over a real socket you need explicit cleanup, a fresh schema per class, or a disposable Testcontainers database.

Unit Test vs Integration Test

Testing a Spring Boot application happens at two very different levels:

1. Unit Test

• Tests one class in isolation - for example, just a service class.
• Any dependency the class needs is faked (mocked) so no real database, no real Spring context, no real network call happens.
• Very fast, because nothing heavy is loaded.

2. Integration Test

• Tests the whole wired application (or a large slice of it) - Spring actually creates the beans, wires them together, and everything runs as it would in production.
• Slower, because the Spring context has to start up.
• Used to check that all the pieces work correctly together, not just individually.

Unit TestIntegration Test
ScopeOne classMultiple classes / full app
Spring context loaded?NoYes (fully or partially)
SpeedVery fastSlower
DependenciesMockedReal (or close to real)

A Basic JUnit 5 Test (No Spring Involved)

This is the simplest possible test - a plain service class with no Spring annotations at all, tested with plain JUnit 5.
• @Test marks a method as a test case.
• assertEquals(expected, actual) checks that the value produced matches what we expect.

What @SpringBootTest Does

@SpringBootTest tells Spring to load the full application context - all your @Component, @Service, @Repository, configuration classes etc. get created and wired together, just like when the real app starts.
This makes it an integration test - you are testing the real wiring, not a fake version of it. It is slower than a plain unit test because the whole context has to boot up.

Mocking a Dependency with Mockito

Sometimes we want to test a class in isolation but it depends on something else (like a repository). Instead of using the real dependency, we create a mock - a fake object we fully control.
• @Mock creates the fake object.
• when(...).thenReturn(...) tells the mock what to return when a method is called on it.

expert.content:
Test Slice Annotations - Loading Only What You Need

A full @SpringBootTest boots the entire application context - every controller, every service, every repository, every auto-configuration. For a large app that can take several seconds per test class, which adds up fast across hundreds of tests.

Spring Boot provides test slice annotations that load only the beans relevant to one layer, keeping the rest of the context out entirely:
• @WebMvcTest - loads only the web layer (controllers, @ControllerAdvice, converters, filters) - services and repositories are NOT loaded, so you must mock them.
• @DataJpaTest - loads only the JPA/repository layer (an embedded in-memory database by default) - controllers and services are NOT loaded.

AnnotationWhat it loadsWhat it skipsTypical use
@SpringBootTestEntire application contextNothing - everything is realFull end-to-end integration test
@WebMvcTestMVC infra: controllers, filters, converters, @ControllerAdvice@Service, @Repository beans (must mock with @MockBean)Testing controller request/response behavior
@DataJpaTestJPA repositories + embedded DB (e.g. H2) + entity managerControllers, services, web layerTesting repository queries

@SpringBootTest         (slowest - loads everything)
   |
   +-- Controllers
   +-- Services
   +-- Repositories
   +-- Full DB config
   +-- All auto-configuration

@WebMvcTest              (fast - web layer only)
   |
   +-- Controllers        <-- loaded
   +-- Services            X  must @MockBean
   +-- Repositories        X  not loaded

@DataJpaTest              (fast - persistence layer only)
   |
   +-- Repositories       <-- loaded
   +-- Embedded DB (H2)   <-- loaded
   +-- Controllers          X  not loaded
   +-- Services             X  not loaded

Because slices load a much smaller subset of beans, the context startup is dramatically faster, which matters a lot when you have hundreds of test classes running in CI.

Testing REST Controllers with MockMvc

MockMvc lets you send a fake HTTP request into the Spring MVC layer (no real server, no real port) and assert on the resulting status code and JSON body. It is typically combined with @WebMvcTest for a fast, focused controller test.

@MockBean vs Plain Mockito @Mock

Both create a fake object that you can program with when(...).thenReturn(...), but they operate at different levels:

• @Mock (Mockito) - creates a plain fake object with no Spring involvement at all. Used in pure unit tests where there is no application context to worry about.
• @MockBean (Spring Boot Test) - creates a Mockito mock and registers it in the Spring application context, replacing the real bean of that type. Any other bean that gets the real one autowired will instead receive this mock. Requires a Spring context to already be loading (e.g. inside @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest).

@Mock@MockBean
Spring context required?NoYes
Registered as a Spring bean?NoYes - replaces the real bean
Typical usagePure unit tests (@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class))Slice tests (@WebMvcTest) or full @SpringBootTest
SpeedFastest - no contextSlower - context still loads (minus the real bean)

In-Memory H2 Database vs Mocking the Repository

When testing code that talks to a repository, there are two common strategies, each with real tradeoffs:

1. In-memory database (e.g. H2) with @DataJpaTest - a real (but temporary, in-memory) relational database is started, real SQL runs, real JPA/Hibernate mapping happens.
2. Mocking the repository entirely - no database at all, the repository interface is faked and told what to return.

AspectH2 In-Memory DB (@DataJpaTest)Mocked Repository (@Mock / @MockBean)
What it actually verifiesReal SQL/JPQL queries, entity mappings, constraintsOnly that your service code calls the repository correctly
SpeedSlower (DB starts, schema created)Very fast (no DB at all)
Catches broken queries?YesNo - the mock returns whatever you told it to
Catches wrong service logic?YesYes
Best used forTesting the repository layer itselfTesting service/controller layers in isolation

Rule of thumb: use H2 with @DataJpaTest to verify your custom queries actually work; mock the repository when testing a service so a broken query in an unrelated method can't make an unrelated test fail.

Test Lifecycle Annotations

JUnit 5 gives hooks to run setup/teardown code around your tests:
• @BeforeEach - runs before every test method (fresh state each time).
• @AfterEach - runs after every test method (cleanup).
• @BeforeAll - runs once, before any test in the class (must be static) - good for expensive one-time setup.
• @AfterAll - runs once, after all tests finish (must be static).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?A unit test checks one class in isolation with dependencies mocked; an integration test loads real, wired components (often via a Spring context) to check they work together correctly.
What does @SpringBootTest do?It loads the complete Spring application context, giving you a real integration test environment identical to how the app runs in production.
Why use @WebMvcTest instead of @SpringBootTest for a controller?@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, so the test starts much faster and stays focused on controller behavior; service/repository beans must be supplied as @MockBean.
What does @DataJpaTest configure by default?An embedded in-memory database (e.g. H2), the JPA repositories, and the entity manager - without loading controllers or services.
What is MockMvc used for?Simulating HTTP requests against Spring MVC controllers without starting a real HTTP server, then asserting on status code and response body.
What is the key difference between @Mock and @MockBean?@Mock is a plain Mockito fake with no Spring involvement; @MockBean creates a mock AND registers it in the Spring ApplicationContext, replacing the real bean everywhere it's autowired.
When would you prefer testing against a real H2 database over mocking the repository?When you need to verify that a custom query (JPQL/derived query method) is actually correct - a mock can't catch a broken query since it just returns whatever you configured.
What is the difference between @BeforeEach and @BeforeAll?@BeforeEach runs before every single test method (fresh state each time); @BeforeAll runs once before all tests in the class and must be static, typically used for expensive shared setup.
Why are test slices generally faster than @SpringBootTest?They load only the beans relevant to one layer instead of the entire application context, so far fewer beans need to be created and wired at startup.
Can @MockBean be used without any test slice or @SpringBootTest?No - @MockBean needs an active Spring test context to register the mock into; without one loading, there is no ApplicationContext to inject the fake bean into.
