What is the Actuator?

The Actuator is used to manage and monitor all the information about a running application.

Why do we use it?

Suppose you have a server in the UK, and that server runs one Spring Boot application:

        SERVER - UK
   +--------------------+
   |    APPLICATION     |   <--- deployed here, you are somewhere else
   +--------------------+

From where you sit, you want to know:

• How many beans has the application loaded?
• What does the heap look like?
• How many threads are running?
• What are the URL mapping details?
• Is the application healthy?

You cannot open a debugger on a production machine in another country. The Actuator answers all of these over HTTP, in detail, with no code of your own.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project
2. Add the Maven dependency to pom.xml
3. Create the REST controller
4. Run the application
5. Check the console
6. Go to a browser or Postman and enter the URL

Steps 1 and 2 - Project and Dependencies

File -> New -> Spring Starter Project, click Next, select the dependencies, then Next and Finish.

Three dependencies are used here: the actuator itself, spring-web for the test endpoint, and devtools for automatic restarts during development.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Step 6 - Hitting the Endpoints

Open a browser or Postman and enter the URL. Both work identically for GET endpoints.

Note 1 - by default only the /health endpoint is exposed over HTTP. That is why the console said "Exposing 1 endpoint(s)".

URLResponse
http://localhost:8080/actuatorTestSpring boot actuator test details - your own endpoint
http://localhost:8080/actuatorA discovery document listing the exposed endpoints - only health, so far
http://localhost:8080/actuator/health{"status":"UP"}

Note 2 - Exposing More Endpoints

Only one endpoint is available by default. To see URL mappings, the number of bean classes loaded and everything else, add one line to application.properties:

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*

Restart the application. The console now reports a much larger endpoint count, and /actuator lists them all.

EndpointWhat it shows
/actuator/healthApplication health status - UP or DOWN.
/actuator/beansEvery bean the container loaded. Use it to check whether ActuatorController is really there.
/actuator/mappingsEvery URL mapping - both your endpoints appear here.
/actuator/conditionsThe auto-configuration report: which configurations matched, which did not, and why.
/actuator/envThe environment - server port and every other property.
/actuator/heapdumpDownloads a heap dump file automatically.
/actuator/metricsJVM, CPU and HTTP metrics.
/actuator/loggersLog levels, readable and changeable at runtime.

Excluding Endpoints

Include everything, then take back the ones you do not want. To exclude beans:

management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=beans

Restart, and the console reports 12 endpoints instead of 13. Multiple endpoints can be excluded with a comma-separated list:

management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=beans,metrics

Restart again - the console now shows 11 endpoints, and /actuator no longer lists beans or metrics. Exclude always wins over include.

The shutdown endpoint

shutdown is disabled by default - not merely unexposed, but switched off - because it stops the application. Enable it explicitly:

management.endpoint.shutdown.enabled=true

Restart and check /actuator - shutdown is now listed. Note it accepts POST only, so a browser cannot trigger it; use Postman.
codeExamples:
# application.properties - the full set used above
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=beans,metrics
management.endpoint.shutdown.enabled=true

expert.content:
Never Ship include=* to Production

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* is the right line for the tutorial and a serious mistake on a public port. Consider what it publishes to anyone who can reach the application:

EndpointWhat an attacker learns
/actuator/envEvery property, including database URLs and often credentials.
/actuator/heapdumpA full memory image - passwords, tokens and customer data in plain text.
/actuator/beansYour entire class and package structure.
/actuator/mappingsEvery URL, including the ones not in your public documentation.
/actuator/configpropsConfiguration values with their sources.
/actuator/shutdownA one-request denial of service.

Three defences, in order of importance:

DefenceHow
Expose only what you needinclude=health,info,metrics,prometheus - name them; never use *.
Move actuator to its own portmanagement.server.port=9001, reachable only inside the network and never through the public load balancer.
Require authenticationWith spring-boot-starter-security, protect EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint() and require a role.
codeExamples:
# application-prod.properties - a sane production setup
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus
management.server.port=9001
management.server.address=127.0.0.1
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized

expert.content:
enabled vs exposed - Two Different Switches

The shutdown endpoint needed management.endpoint.shutdown.enabled=true and inclusion in the exposure list. That is not redundancy; they are two separate gates and knowing which one is closed saves a lot of guessing.

PropertyControls
management.endpoint.<id>.enabledWhether the endpoint bean exists at all. All are true by default except shutdown.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.includeWhether an enabled endpoint is reachable over HTTP. Only health by default.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.excludeRemoves an endpoint from the include set. Exclude always wins.
management.endpoints.web.base-pathChanges /actuator to something else - a cheap obscurity measure, not security.

So a 404 on /actuator/beans has two possible causes: the endpoint is disabled, or it is enabled but not exposed. Check the exposure list first - it is nearly always that.

Health Indicators, and Why /health Is Not Just "UP"

{"status":"UP"} is the summary. Underneath, Spring Boot runs a HealthIndicator for every piece of infrastructure it detected: db, diskSpace, redis, mail, rabbit. The overall status is the worst of them - one DOWN indicator makes the whole endpoint DOWN and returns HTTP 503.

That is the contract a load balancer or Kubernetes probe relies on: 200 means "send me traffic", 503 means "take me out of rotation".
codeExamples:
# show the individual indicators, not just the summary
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

# Kubernetes-friendly probes - separate liveness from readiness
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
# GET /actuator/health/liveness   -> is the process alive? restart if not
# GET /actuator/health/readiness  -> can it serve traffic? remove from LB if not

expert.content:
Metrics, and Where the Numbers Go

/actuator/metrics is backed by Micrometer, a vendor-neutral facade for metrics - roughly what SLF4J is for logging. Add the registry for your monitoring system and the same instrumentation is exported to it, unchanged.

DependencyExports to
micrometer-registry-prometheusPrometheus, scraped from /actuator/prometheus
micrometer-registry-datadogDatadog
micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2AWS CloudWatch

Reading a metric by hand is fine for a spot check; the point of the endpoint is that a monitoring system scrapes it every few seconds and alerts on it.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the Spring Boot Actuator?A starter that exposes ready-made HTTP endpoints for managing and monitoring a running application - health, metrics, beans, mappings, environment and more.
Which dependency do you add?spring-boot-starter-actuator.
Which endpoint is exposed by default?Only /actuator/health over HTTP.
How do you expose all endpoints?management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* - fine in development, dangerous in production.
Difference between "enabled" and "exposed"?enabled controls whether the endpoint bean exists; exposure controls whether it is reachable over HTTP. shutdown is the one endpoint disabled by default.
How do you exclude endpoints?management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=beans,metrics. Exclude always beats include.
Which HTTP method does /actuator/shutdown accept?POST only - a browser GET returns 405.
Why is exposing /actuator/env and /actuator/heapdump dangerous?env leaks configuration including credentials; a heap dump is a full memory image containing passwords, tokens and customer data.
How do you secure the actuator endpoints?Expose only what you need, move them to a separate internal port with management.server.port, and protect EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint() with Spring Security.
What determines the overall health status?The worst status among all HealthIndicators. Any DOWN component makes the endpoint DOWN and returns HTTP 503.
How do you add your own health check?Implement HealthIndicator and register it as a bean; the bean name minus "HealthIndicator" becomes the component key.
What library backs /actuator/metrics?Micrometer - a vendor-neutral metrics facade that exports the same instrumentation to Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch and others.
Which endpoint tells you why an auto-configuration did or did not apply?/actuator/conditions.

What are Microservices?

Microservices is an architectural style in which the application is designed as a collection of services.

Why do we use it?

Before microservice architecture, most of the IT industry used monolithic architecture.

What is monolithic architecture?

It is a single application in which all the functionality is available.

Take makemytrip.com as an example - flights, hotels, trains, buses and payments all inside one deployable unit, talking to one database.

                 MONOLITHIC ARCHITECTURE

              +--------------------------+
              |    User Interface (UI)   |
              +--------------------------+
                           |
              +--------------------------+
              |                          |
              |   Flight    Hotel        |
              |   Train     Bus          |      ONE application
              |   Payment   Booking      |
              |                          |
              +--------------------------+
                           |
                    +-------------+
                    |  DATABASE   |          ONE database
                    +-------------+

Disadvantages of the monolith

• Maintenance is high - everything is tangled together.
• Single point of failure - one bad module can take the whole application down.
• Redeploy the whole application - a one-line fix in Hotels means redeploying Flights, Trains and Payments too.

Microservice Architecture

• Each functionality is separated into a different project.
• Each project has its own database.
• There is only one user interface.

                  MICROSERVICE ARCHITECTURE

              +--------------------------+
              |    User Interface (UI)   |
              +--------------------------+
                |     |     |     |     |
        +-------+     |     |     |     +-------+
        |             |     |     |             |
   +---------+  +---------+ | +---------+  +---------+
   | Flight  |  | Hotel   | | | Train   |  | Payment |
   | Service |  | Service | | | Service |  | Service |
   +---------+  +---------+ | +---------+  +---------+
        |            |      |      |            |
     +----+       +----+  +----+ +----+      +----+
     | DB |       | DB |  | DB | | DB |      | DB |
     +----+       +----+  +----+ +----+      +----+

Advantages

• Maintenance is easy - each service is small enough to understand.
• High availability - if Hotels goes down, Flights keeps serving.
• Faster development - separate teams work in parallel without blocking each other.
• Application deployment is fast - deploy only the service that changed.

Note: one microservice means one RESTful web service.

Key Points

PointDetail
One project per serviceCreate a separate Spring Boot project for every microservice.
One server per serviceEach application runs independently in its own Tomcat instance, on its own port.
CommunicationFor microservices to talk to each other we use Spring Cloud with a Eureka Server.
Eureka ServerA discovery server - the directory of which services exist and where they are.
RegistrationEvery microservice must register itself on the Eureka Server to be discoverable.
Client roleEach microservice is a client of the Eureka Server.

                +--------------------------+
                |      EUREKA SERVER       |
                |   (Discovery Server)     |
                |    port 8761             |
                +--------------------------+
                    ^        ^        ^
          register  |        |        |  register
                    |        |        |
             +----------+ +--------+ +---------+
             | Flight   | | Hotel  | | Payment |
             | :8081    | | :8082  | | :8083   |
             +----------+ +--------+ +---------+
                  Eureka clients

First Microservice Example

The smallest possible microservice: a Spring Boot project with one REST endpoint, running on its own port.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project
2. Add the Maven dependency to pom.xml
3. Set the port in application.properties
4. Create the REST controller
5. Run the Spring Boot application
6. Open Postman

Step 1: File => New => Spring Starter Project, enter the project name MicroServiceExample, then Next and Finish.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml : just the web starter for now -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

# Step 3 - application.properties
server.port=8082

# Every microservice gets its OWN port, because each one runs in
# its own Tomcat instance on the same machine during development.

expert.content:
Microservices Are a Trade, Not an Upgrade

The advantages list is real and it is only half the picture. Splitting one process into twenty replaces in-process method calls with network calls, and everything that was previously guaranteed becomes something you must handle.

In a monolithIn microservices
A method call always succeeds or throwsA network call can time out, half-succeed, or succeed slowly
One database transaction spans everythingNo distributed transaction - you need sagas and compensating actions
A stack trace covers the whole requestA request spans services; you need correlation ids and distributed tracing
One deploymentTwenty pipelines, twenty version numbers, and compatibility between them
Refactoring across modules is an IDE actionA change spanning services needs coordinated releases
Run it locally by pressing RunRun twenty services, or build good stubs

The widely-held advice is "monolith first". Build a well-modularised monolith, learn where the real boundaries are, and extract services once you have evidence - a module that needs to scale differently, or a team that needs to release independently. Splitting on day one means guessing the boundaries, and the wrong boundary is far more expensive to fix once it is a network call.

The honest criterion: microservices solve an organisational problem - letting many teams deploy without coordinating. If you have one team, you are paying the cost and not collecting the benefit.

"Each Project Has Its Own Database" Is the Hard Part

That one line in the key points carries most of the difficulty in the entire architecture, and it is the rule people break first.

Once Flights and Payments own separate databases, a query that used to be a JOIN is no longer possible:

MONOLITH - one query
    select b.*, u.name, p.status
    from booking b
    join user u    on b.user_id = u.id
    join payment p on p.booking_id = b.id

MICROSERVICES - three services, three databases
    GET /bookings/42          -> Booking service
    GET /users/7              -> User service
    GET /payments?booking=42  -> Payment service
    ... then join the results in application code.
ProblemUsual answer
Cross-service queriesAPI composition, or a read model built from events (CQRS)
Cross-service transactionsThe Saga pattern - a sequence of local transactions plus compensating actions
Duplicated reference dataEach service keeps its own copy, kept fresh by events, and accepts eventual consistency
Reporting across everythingA separate data warehouse fed from all services

The anti-pattern to avoid is the shared database: several services reading and writing the same tables. It looks like microservices on the deployment diagram and behaves like a monolith - nobody can change a column without breaking someone else, and the independent deployability you paid for is gone. This is called a distributed monolith, and it has the costs of both styles and the benefits of neither.

What a Real Microservice Platform Needs

Eureka is one piece. A production setup needs several more, and each exists to solve a problem the monolith never had.

ConcernComponentProblem it solves
Service discoveryEureka, Consul, Kubernetes DNSInstances come and go; hard-coded hosts break
API gatewaySpring Cloud GatewayOne public entry point for auth, routing, rate limiting
Load balancingSpring Cloud LoadBalancerSpreading calls across instances of a service
Central configurationSpring Cloud Config, Kubernetes ConfigMapsTwenty services should not each own a copy of the settings
ResilienceResilience4jCircuit breakers, retries, timeouts, bulkheads
Distributed tracingMicrometer Tracing + Zipkin/JaegerFollowing one request across eight services
Centralised loggingELK, LokiLogs scattered across many containers
Async messagingKafka, RabbitMQRemoving synchronous coupling between services

The circuit breaker is the one to understand first. Without it, a slow downstream service exhausts the caller's thread pool, which makes the caller slow, which exhausts its caller - a cascading failure that takes down the platform from one broken service.
codeExamples:
# The breaker's states, and what the settings mean
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.policyService:
  sliding-window-size: 10
  failure-rate-threshold: 50          # 5 of 10 failing -> OPEN
  wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s    # reject instantly for 30s
  permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3

resilience4j.timelimiter.instances.policyService:
  timeout-duration: 2s

# CLOSED     -> calls pass through, failures counted
# OPEN       -> calls fail immediately, no network attempt at all
# HALF_OPEN  -> a few trial calls; success closes it, failure reopens
#
# The point of OPEN is that failing in 1ms protects your thread pool.
# Waiting 30 seconds for a dead service is what kills the caller.

expert.content:
How Big Is a Microservice?

"One microservice means one RESTful web service" is a fine starting definition and is not a sizing rule. Two failure modes sit either side of the right answer.

Too small (nanoservices)Too large (distributed monolith)
A service per entity or per endpointServices that must be released together
Every operation is a chain of network hopsShared database tables
More infrastructure than business logicA change to one always needs a change to another
Latency dominated by serialisationAll the cost of distribution, none of the independence

The useful sizing heuristics:

• A service should map to a business capability - "payments", "policy administration" - not to a database table.
• A service should be owned by one team, and a team should be able to release it without asking anyone.
• A service should be able to be rewritten in a few weeks if it had to be.
• If two services always change together, they are one service.

Domain-Driven Design gives the formal version: a service should align with a bounded context - a region of the domain where the terms have one consistent meaning. "Customer" means different things to Sales and to Support, and that difference is exactly where the boundary belongs.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are microservices?An architectural style where one application is built as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each owning its own data.
What is a monolithic architecture?A single application containing all functionality, deployed as one unit against one database.
What are the disadvantages of a monolith?High maintenance, a single point of failure, and having to redeploy everything for any change.
What are the advantages of microservices?Easier maintenance, high availability, faster parallel development, and deploying only the service that changed.
Why does each service need its own database?A shared database couples services at the schema, so nobody can change a column independently - you get a distributed monolith.
What is a distributed monolith?Services that must be deployed together or share a database - all the cost of distribution with none of the independence.
How do you query across services?API composition (call each service and combine), or a read model built from events. There is no cross-service JOIN.
How do you handle transactions across services?The Saga pattern - a chain of local transactions with explicit compensating actions. There is no distributed rollback.
What is a service registry and why is one needed?A directory of running instances - Eureka, Consul, Kubernetes DNS. Instances change address as they scale and restart, so hard-coded hosts break.
What is a circuit breaker?A component that stops calling a failing service after a failure threshold, failing fast instead of hanging - preventing cascading failure.
How do you debug a request spanning several services?Distributed tracing with a correlation id propagated across calls, collected by Zipkin or Jaeger.
When should you NOT use microservices?With a small team, an unclear domain, or no operational maturity. Start with a modular monolith and extract services once boundaries are proven.
How do you decide service boundaries?By business capability and bounded context, and by team ownership. If two services always change together, they should be one.

Calling One Microservice From Another

Two independent services, each with its own database and its own port. The User service needs policy details that only the Policy service owns - so it makes an HTTP call.

   CLIENT
     |
     |  GET /getUser/1
     v
+---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
|   UserMicroService        |          |   PolicyMicroService      |
|   port 8282               |          |   port 8181               |
|                           |          |                           |
|  UserController           |          |  PolicyController         |
|  UserServiceImpl  --------|--------->|  GET /getPolicy/{id}      |
|      | WebClient          |   HTTP   |          |                |
|  UserRepository           |          |  PolicyRepository         |
+---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
     |                                            |
  +------+                                    +--------+
  | user |                                    | policy |
  +------+                                    +--------+

Response: ResponseDto { user: {...}, policy: {...} }

The User service composes a single response out of its own data plus data fetched over the network. That composition is the pattern - a monolith would have done it with a JOIN.

Part 1 - The Policy Microservice (the callee)

An ordinary REST service. It has no idea anyone will call it from another service.

Steps

1. Create the project   2. Add dependencies   3. Model class   4. Service   5. Service implementation
6. Repository   7. REST controller   8. application.properties   9. Run   10. Postman
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>

    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>

    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
<!-- com.mysql:mysql-connector-j is the current coordinate.
     The old mysql:mysql-connector-java is deprecated. -->

#MySQL

spring.datasource.username=root

beginner.content:
Part 2 - The User Microservice (the caller)

Same structure, plus two additions: the WebFlux dependency (which brings WebClient) and a set of DTO classes for the composed response.

ClassPurpose
User (entity)This service's own table.
UserDtoThe user fields that go into the response.
PolicyDtoThe shape of what the Policy service returns - a local copy, not a shared class.
ResponseDtoThe combined answer: a user plus a policy.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - the extra dependency that provides WebClient -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- Adding webflux alongside spring-boot-starter-web does NOT turn
     the application reactive. Boot detects both and keeps the
     servlet stack; webflux is here only for the WebClient type. -->

beginner.content:
Step 10 - Declare the WebClient Bean

WebClient is not auto-configured as a bean, only its builder is. Without this bean the application fails at startup with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type WebClient.

Steps 5 to 8 - The Service That Makes the Call

This is the heart of the topic. webClient.get().uri(...).retrieve().bodyToMono(PolicyDto.class).block() performs an HTTP GET against the other service and deserialises the JSON into PolicyDto.

CallMeaning
.get()The HTTP method.
.uri(...)The target URL.
.retrieve()Send the request and prepare to read the body.
.bodyToMono(PolicyDto.class)Deserialise the body into one object, asynchronously.
.block()Wait for it. Turns the async result back into a plain value.
codeExamples:
# Step 9 - application.properties
server.port=8282

#MySQL
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/bootdepth?autoReconnect=true&useSSL=false
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

beginner.content:
Step 12 - Running Both and Testing

Both services must be running: Policy on 8181, User on 8282.

expert.content:
Hard-Coded URLs Defeat the Point

"http://localhost:8181/getPolicy/" works on one laptop and nowhere else. It breaks the moment the Policy service moves host, changes port, or scales to more than one instance - and with several instances running, every call still goes to the same one.

ApproachWhat it fixes
Externalised propertyThe URL is configurable per environment. Still one fixed instance.
@LoadBalanced + EurekaCall by service name; discovery resolves it and round-robins across instances.
OpenFeignThe same, expressed as an interface - the least code at the call site.
codeExamples:
# Step 1 - at minimum, get it out of the code
# application.properties
services.policy.base-url=http://localhost:8181

# application-prod.properties
services.policy.base-url=http://policy-service.internal:8181

expert.content:
A Network Call Has Failure Modes a Method Call Does Not

The bare .block() above has no timeout. If the Policy service accepts the connection and then hangs, the calling thread waits indefinitely. Under load, every Tomcat worker ends up parked on that call and the User service stops responding to everything - including requests that never needed a policy.

That is a cascading failure, and it is the single most important thing to get right.

ProtectionWhat it prevents
Connect timeoutWaiting forever for an unreachable host.
Response timeoutWaiting forever for a hung service.
Retry (idempotent calls only)A single transient blip failing the request.
Circuit breakerHammering a service that is already down, and exhausting your own threads.
FallbackA total failure when a degraded answer would do.

.block() Is Fine Here, and Fatal in a Reactive Application

block() converts an asynchronous Mono back into a plain value by waiting. On the servlet stack - which this application uses, because spring-boot-starter-web is present - each request already owns a thread, so blocking it is normal.

In a genuinely reactive application it is a serious bug: blocking one of the few event-loop threads stalls every other request that thread was serving. Reactor detects it and throws.

block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported
in thread reactor-http-nio-3
StackIs block() acceptable?
Servlet (spring-boot-starter-web)Yes - the thread is yours to block.
Reactive (webflux only)No - return the Mono and let the framework subscribe.

The bigger win from not blocking is parallelism. Fetching three services sequentially costs the sum of their latencies; fetching them concurrently costs the maximum.

WebClient vs RestTemplate vs RestClient

Three HTTP clients exist in the Spring ecosystem, and which one to reach for has changed.

ClientStatusAPI style
RestTemplateIn maintenance mode since Spring 5 - not deprecated, but no new featuresBlocking, template methods
WebClientCurrent; needs spring-webfluxFluent, non-blocking, block() available
RestClientNew in Spring 6.1 / Boot 3.2WebClient's fluent API, synchronous, no webflux dependency

RestClient is the natural choice for a servlet application on Boot 3.2+: the same readable chained API as WebClient, without pulling in the reactive stack just to call .block() on everything.

Synchronous Calls Couple Services Back Together

Every synchronous call adds a runtime dependency. If User calls Policy, then User's availability is capped by Policy's - and a chain of four services multiplies the risk.

Each service is up 99.9% of the time.

Chain of 4 synchronous calls:
    0.999 ^ 4  =  99.6%   ->  roughly 35 hours of downtime a year,
                              caused entirely by composition.
QuestionBetter approach
The caller needs an answer nowSynchronous HTTP - but with timeouts, a circuit breaker and a fallback.
The caller only needs to tell someonePublish an event to Kafka or RabbitMQ. The callee can be down; the message waits.
The data changes rarelyCache it locally, or keep a replica updated by events.
The chain is more than two deepReconsider the boundaries - services that always call each other may be one service.

The general rule: use synchronous calls for queries, and events for state changes. An event-driven write path removes the availability coupling entirely, at the price of eventual consistency.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do microservices communicate?Synchronously over HTTP with WebClient, RestClient, RestTemplate or Feign, or asynchronously through a broker such as Kafka or RabbitMQ.
Which dependency provides WebClient?spring-boot-starter-webflux. Adding it beside spring-boot-starter-web does not make the app reactive.
Why must you declare a WebClient bean?Spring Boot auto-configures only WebClient.Builder. Injecting WebClient without a bean fails with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
What does .block() do, and when is it wrong?Waits for the Mono and returns the value. Fine on the servlet stack; on a reactive stack it stalls an event-loop thread and Reactor throws.
Why not hard-code the other service's URL?It breaks when the host or port changes and cannot load-balance across instances. Externalise it, or resolve it by service name through discovery.
What does @LoadBalanced do?Lets the client resolve http://SERVICE-NAME/... via the registry and round-robin across the instances.
What is the danger of a call with no timeout?A hung callee parks the calling thread. Under load every worker ends up blocked and the caller stops serving all requests - a cascading failure.
What does a circuit breaker add on top of a timeout?After enough failures it stops attempting the call at all, failing in microseconds and leaving the thread pool free.
Which calls are safe to retry?Idempotent ones - GET, PUT, DELETE. Retrying a POST can duplicate the effect.
How do you call three services without adding up their latency?Issue them concurrently and combine with Mono.zip, so the cost is the slowest call rather than the sum.
Why define a local PolicyDto instead of sharing the Policy class?A shared class couples the services at compile time, so they can no longer be released independently.
WebClient vs RestClient?Both have the same fluent API; RestClient (Spring 6.1+) is synchronous and needs no webflux dependency, which suits a servlet application.
Why do synchronous chains reduce availability?Availability multiplies: four services at 99.9% compose to 99.6%. Events break that coupling at the cost of eventual consistency.

beginner.content:
RestClient

This topic is being written and will be published shortly.

In the meantime, the surrounding module already covers the ground it sits on - work through the topics either side of it and come back once this one is live.

Service Registry

This topic is being written and will be published shortly.

In the meantime, the surrounding module already covers the ground it sits on - work through the topics either side of it and come back once this one is live.

Registering a Microservice on a Eureka Server

Also called: Spring Cloud Netflix Eureka based Service Registry.

There are two applications to build, and they are different projects:

ApplicationRolePort
Eureka ServerThe registry itself - the directory of services.8761
Eureka ClientAn ordinary microservice that registers itself with the server.8083

        +----------------------------------+
        |        EUREKA SERVER             |
        |   @EnableEurekaServer            |
        |   http://localhost:8761          |
        +----------------------------------+
                      ^
                      |  1. register  ("I am PRODUCTTESTSERVICE at :8083")
                      |  2. heartbeat every 30s
                      |
        +----------------------------------+
        |   PRODUCTTESTSERVICE             |
        |   @EnableEurekaClient            |
        |   http://localhost:8083          |
        +----------------------------------+

8761 is the conventional Eureka port - the default every Spring Cloud example and default configuration expects.

Part 1 - The Eureka Client (the microservice)

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project
2. Add the Maven dependencies to pom.xml
3. Write @EnableEurekaClient on the main class
4. Write the code into application.properties
5. Design the REST controller
6. Run as a Spring Boot application
7. Open Postman (request and response)

In the Spring Starter wizard, select Eureka Discovery Client, Spring Web and Spring Boot Actuator.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- Note the artifactId has hyphens throughout:
     spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client
     "netflixeureka-client" is a typo and will not resolve. -->

<!-- Spring Cloud versions are managed by a BOM, not set per
     dependency. The BOM version must match your Boot version. -->
<properties>
    <spring-cloud.version>2022.0.4</spring-cloud.version>
</properties>

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-cloud.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- Boot 3.1 -> Spring Cloud 2022.0.x
     Boot 3.2 -> Spring Cloud 2023.0.x
     Boot 2.7 -> Spring Cloud 2021.0.x
     A mismatched pair fails at startup with NoSuchMethodError. -->

beginner.content:
Steps 4 and 5 - Configuration and Controller

spring.application.name is the single most important property here: it becomes the service id under which the service appears in the registry, and the name other services use to call it.
codeExamples:
# Step 4 - application.properties
spring.application.name=producttestservice
server.port=8083

# Where the registry is. This is the default, so it can be omitted
# while everything runs on one machine - but be explicit.
eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone=http://localhost:8761/eureka/

# The registry displays the name in UPPERCASE, so this service
# appears as PRODUCTTESTSERVICE.

beginner.content:
Part 2 - The Eureka Server

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project
2. Add the Maven dependency to pom.xml
3. Write @EnableEurekaServer on the main class
4. Write the code into application.properties
5. Run as a Spring Boot application
6. Open the browser

This is a separate project from the client - a different folder, a different pom.xml, a different main class.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml : the SERVER artifact, not the client -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- With the spring-cloud-dependencies BOM imported as above, no
     <version> is needed here - and should not be given, or you can
     pair a Spring Cloud release with an incompatible Boot version. -->

# Step 4 - application.properties
server.port=8761

# A standalone server must not try to register with itself,
# or to fetch a registry from a peer that does not exist.
eureka.client.register-with-eureka=false
eureka.client.fetch-registry=false

# Omitting fetch-registry=false leaves the console repeating
#   Cannot execute request on any known server
# every 30 seconds. Both properties belong together.

beginner.content:
Putting It Together

Start the server first, then the client.

OrderApplicationURL
1Eureka Serverhttp://localhost:8761/
2producttestservicehttp://localhost:8083/product/list

The client's console shows the registration:

expert.content:
How Registration Actually Works

Registration is not a one-off announcement. It is a lease that must be continually renewed, which is what makes the registry reflect reality.

CLIENT                                    EUREKA SERVER
   |                                            |
   |-- POST /eureka/apps/PRODUCTTESTSERVICE --->|   register
   |<-- 204 No Content --------------------------|   lease granted (90s)
   |                                            |
   |-- PUT  .../instanceId  (every 30s) ------->|   heartbeat - renew lease
   |<-- 200 OK ----------------------------------|
   |                                            |
   |-- GET  /eureka/apps    (every 30s) -------->|   fetch the registry
   |<-- the full service list -------------------|   cached locally
   |                                            |
   |-- DELETE .../instanceId ------------------->|   graceful shutdown
   |<-- 200 OK ----------------------------------|   removed immediately
PropertyDefaultMeaning
eureka.instance.lease-renewal-interval-in-seconds30How often the client sends a heartbeat.
eureka.instance.lease-expiration-duration-in-seconds90How long the server waits before evicting a silent instance.
eureka.client.registry-fetch-interval-seconds30How often clients refresh their local copy of the registry.

Those defaults mean a crashed instance can stay in the registry for up to 90 seconds, and callers can hold a stale copy for another 30. Callers must therefore tolerate calling a dead instance - which is why a circuit breaker and retry are not optional extras here.
codeExamples:
# Faster detection for development - at the cost of more traffic
eureka.instance.lease-renewal-interval-in-seconds=5
eureka.instance.lease-expiration-duration-in-seconds=15
eureka.client.registry-fetch-interval-seconds=5

# Now a dead instance disappears within ~15 seconds instead of 90.
# Do not push these too low in production: every client heartbeating
# every second against one registry is a lot of load.

# A stable instance id, so restarts do not create duplicate entries
eureka.instance.instance-id=${spring.application.name}:${server.port}

# On a cloud platform, register the IP rather than the hostname -
# container hostnames are rarely resolvable by other containers
eureka.instance.prefer-ip-address=true

# Let Eureka report health from Actuator, so a service with a broken
# database is marked DOWN instead of UP
eureka.client.healthcheck.enabled=true
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

expert.content:
Self-Preservation Mode - the Red Banner

Stop a client and the dashboard often shows:

EMERGENCY! EUREKA MAY BE INCORRECTLY CLAIMING INSTANCES ARE UP WHEN
THEY'RE NOT. RENEWALS ARE LESSER THAN THRESHOLD AND HENCE THE
INSTANCES ARE NOT BEING EXPIRED JUST TO BE SAFE.

This is a deliberate design decision, not a fault. Eureka expects a certain number of heartbeats per minute. If renewals drop below 85% of that, it concludes that the network is more likely broken than every service dying at once, and stops evicting anything.

The reasoning: wrongly removing healthy services during a network partition is far worse than briefly keeping dead ones. A stale entry causes one failed call the caller can retry; an empty registry takes down the whole platform.

This is Eureka choosing AP over CP in CAP terms - availability over consistency.

SettingEffect
eureka.server.enable-self-preservation=falseAlways evict on missed heartbeats. Fine in development; risky in production.
eureka.server.renewal-percent-thresholdDefault 0.85 - the fraction of expected renewals below which preservation kicks in.
eureka.server.eviction-interval-timer-in-msDefault 60000 - how often the eviction task runs.

With one or two services in development the threshold is trivially crossed, which is why the banner appears constantly on a laptop and rarely in a real cluster.
codeExamples:
# Development - see instances disappear promptly
eureka.server.enable-self-preservation=false
eureka.server.eviction-interval-timer-in-ms=5000

# Production - leave self-preservation ON (the default).
# A network blip should not empty your service registry.

expert.content:
A Single Registry Is a Single Point of Failure

One Eureka server on port 8761 is exactly the problem microservices set out to avoid: if it dies, no new instance can register and no client can discover anything.

Eureka servers are designed to peer with each other. Each registers with the others and replicates its registry, so any one can serve the whole picture.
codeExamples:
# peer1 - application-peer1.properties
spring.application.name=eureka-server
server.port=8761
eureka.instance.hostname=peer1
eureka.client.register-with-eureka=true
eureka.client.fetch-registry=true
eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone=http://peer2:8762/eureka/

# peer2 - application-peer2.properties
spring.application.name=eureka-server
server.port=8762
eureka.instance.hostname=peer2
eureka.client.register-with-eureka=true
eureka.client.fetch-registry=true
eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone=http://peer1:8761/eureka/

# Note register-with-eureka and fetch-registry are now TRUE - the
# opposite of the standalone setup, because each peer is a client
# of the other.

# Clients list every peer, so losing one changes nothing
eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone=http://peer1:8761/eureka/,http://peer2:8762/eureka/

# Run them:
#   java -jar eureka-server.jar --spring.profiles.active=peer1
#   java -jar eureka-server.jar --spring.profiles.active=peer2
#
# OUTPUT: each dashboard shows the other as a registered replica,
# and both list every service. Kill peer1 and clients fail over
# to peer2 with no configuration change.

expert.content:
Discovery Is Only Useful If Something Uses It

Registration on its own changes nothing - the client still answers its own endpoints exactly as before. The payoff comes when a caller looks a service up by name instead of by host and port.

ApproachWhat it gives you
Hard-coded URLNothing. Breaks when the port or host changes, and cannot load-balance.
DiscoveryClientThe raw instance list. Useful for tooling; verbose for everyday calls.
@LoadBalanced RestTemplate / WebClientCall http://SERVICE-NAME/path; the client resolves and round-robins across instances.
Spring Cloud OpenFeignA declarative interface - the least code, and the usual choice.

Is Eureka Still the Right Choice?

Worth knowing, because the answer has changed.

ComponentStatus
Eureka Server / ClientStill maintained in Spring Cloud - the only Netflix OSS piece that survived.
Ribbon (client load balancing)Removed. Replaced by Spring Cloud LoadBalancer.
Hystrix (circuit breaker)Removed. Replaced by Resilience4j.
Zuul (gateway)Removed. Replaced by Spring Cloud Gateway.
@EnableEurekaClientOptional since 2020, removed in Spring Cloud 2022.0.

On Kubernetes you usually do not need Eureka at all. A Kubernetes Service gives every workload a stable DNS name and load-balances across healthy pods, using liveness and readiness probes that the platform already runs. Running Eureka on top duplicates that with something you have to operate yourself.

Use Eureka whenUse platform discovery when
Deploying to VMs or bare metalRunning on Kubernetes
You want client-side load balancing you controlServer-side balancing via a Service is enough
The stack is already Spring Cloud NetflixStarting fresh - use the platform's own mechanism
codeExamples:
# On Kubernetes, this replaces the entire registry:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: producttestservice
spec:
  selector:
    app: producttestservice
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8083

# Any pod can now call:
#   http://producttestservice/product/list
# Kubernetes resolves the DNS name and load-balances across the
# healthy pods. No Eureka server to run, patch or monitor.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Eureka?A service registry - a discovery server where microservices register themselves so others can find them by name rather than by host and port.
Why is a registry needed?Instances start, stop and move as they scale, so hard-coded addresses break. The registry is the live directory.
Which annotations set up each side?@EnableEurekaServer on the registry; @EnableEurekaClient on a service - though that one is optional now and removed in Spring Cloud 2022.0.
What port does Eureka use by convention?8761.
Why set register-with-eureka and fetch-registry to false on the server?A standalone server would otherwise try to register with itself and fetch a registry from a peer that does not exist, logging errors every 30 seconds.
Which property becomes the service id?spring.application.name - shown uppercased in the dashboard and used by callers.
How does the server know a service is alive?Heartbeats - by default every 30 seconds, with a 90-second lease expiry.
How long can a dead instance stay registered?Up to 90 seconds, plus up to 30 more in a client's cached copy - so callers must tolerate calling a dead instance.
What is self-preservation mode?When renewals fall below 85% of expected, Eureka stops evicting instances, assuming a network problem rather than mass failure. It favours availability over consistency.
How do you make Eureka highly available?Run several peer-aware servers that register with each other and replicate the registry; clients list all peers.
What does @LoadBalanced do?Lets a RestTemplate or WebClient resolve http://SERVICE-NAME/... through discovery and round-robin across instances.
Do you need Eureka on Kubernetes?Usually not - a Kubernetes Service provides stable DNS and load balancing using the platform's own health probes.
Which Netflix components were replaced?Ribbon by Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Hystrix by Resilience4j, Zuul by Spring Cloud Gateway. Eureka is the one that remains.

topics.name: API Gateway with Spring Cloud Gateway

beginner.content:
The Problem: Clients Talking to Twenty Services

Once an application is split into services, every one of them has its own host and port. Without a gateway, the browser or mobile app has to know all of them.

WITHOUT A GATEWAY

   +-----------+
   |  Browser  |----- http://user-svc:8282/users/1 ------> [ User    :8282 ]
   |           |----- http://policy-svc:8181/policies/1 -> [ Policy  :8181 ]
   |           |----- http://claim-svc:8383/claims/1 ----> [ Claim   :8383 ]
   |           |----- http://pay-svc:8484/payments/1 ----> [ Payment :8484 ]
   +-----------+

   The client knows every address.
   Every service implements its own auth, CORS and rate limiting.
   Every service is exposed to the public internet.

Three separate problems come out of that picture:

ProblemWhy it hurts
The client knows every addressMoving, renaming or splitting a service breaks every deployed mobile app.
Cross-cutting concerns are duplicatedAuthentication, CORS, rate limiting and request logging get written four times, four slightly different ways - and the weakest copy is the one an attacker uses.
Everything is publicly reachableAn internal-only service is one firewall mistake away from being on the internet.

An API gateway is one service that sits in front of the others. The client talks only to it; it decides which service each request belongs to.

With a Gateway

WITH A GATEWAY

   +-----------+          +--------------------------+
   |  Browser  |--------->|   SPRING CLOUD GATEWAY   |
   +-----------+   one    |        port 9090         |
                  address |                          |
                          |  authenticate            |
                          |  rate limit              |
                          |  CORS                    |
                          |  log / trace             |
                          |  route by path           |
                          +--------------------------+
                             |      |      |      |
              /users/**  ----+      |      |      +---- /payments/**
                                    |      |
                        /policies/**+      +/claims/**
                             |      |      |      |
                             v      v      v      v
                       [ User ] [Policy] [Claim] [Payment]
                        :8282    :8181    :8383    :8484
                          (not exposed to the internet)

Gateway responsibilityWhat it means
RoutingMatch an incoming request and forward it to the right service.
PredicatesThe conditions that decide whether a route matches - path, method, header, host, time.
FiltersCode that runs before or after forwarding - add a header, strip a path prefix, check a token, count requests.
Single entry pointOne TLS certificate, one public address, one place to apply security policy.
Protocol and shape adaptationThe public API does not have to mirror the internal service layout.

Creating the Gateway Project

The gateway is its own Spring Boot application - a separate project, exactly like the Eureka server was.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project
2. Add spring-cloud-starter-gateway (and the Spring Cloud BOM)
3. Define routes in application.yml
4. Run it
5. Call the gateway instead of the service

There is one dependency rule that matters more than any other here, and it catches everyone once: do not add spring-boot-starter-web. The gateway runs on WebFlux and Netty, and the two starters cannot coexist.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-gateway</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- The Spring Cloud BOM, as for every Spring Cloud project -->
<properties>
    <spring-cloud.version>2023.0.3</spring-cloud.version>
</properties>

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-cloud.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- DO NOT ALSO ADD spring-boot-starter-web.
     Startup fails immediately with:

     ***************************
     APPLICATION FAILED TO START
     ***************************
     Description:
     Spring MVC found on classpath, which is incompatible with
     Spring Cloud Gateway.
     Action:
     Please remove spring-boot-starter-web dependency.        -->

beginner.content:
Step 3 - Routes in YAML

A route has four parts: an id, a uri to forward to, a list of predicates that decide whether it matches, and an optional list of filters that modify the request or response.

YAML is the usual format here because the route list is deeply nested; the same thing in .properties is unreadable.

Route elementPurpose
idA unique name. Appears in logs and metrics.
uriWhere to forward: http://host:port, or lb://SERVICE-NAME to resolve through discovery.
predicatesAll must match for the route to be chosen. Routes are evaluated in order.
filtersApplied to this route only, in the order written.
codeExamples:
# Step 3 - application.yml
server:
  port: 9090

spring:
  application:
    name: api-gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:

        - id: user-service
          uri: http://localhost:8282
          predicates:
            - Path=/users/**

        - id: policy-service
          uri: http://localhost:8181
          predicates:
            - Path=/policies/**

        - id: claim-service
          uri: http://localhost:8383
          predicates:
            - Path=/claims/**

# GET http://localhost:9090/users/1
#   -> forwarded to http://localhost:8282/users/1
# GET http://localhost:9090/policies/1
#   -> forwarded to http://localhost:8181/policies/1
#
# The path is passed through UNCHANGED by default. If the downstream
# service expects /getPolicy/1 rather than /policies/1, you need a
# rewrite filter - see below.

# The common predicates
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: examples
          uri: http://localhost:8181
          predicates:
            - Path=/policies/{id}              # path, with a variable
            - Method=GET,POST                  # HTTP method
            - Header=X-Tenant, acme-.*         # header name + regex
            - Query=version, v2                # query parameter
            - Host=**.example.com              # Host header
            - Cookie=session, [A-Za-z0-9]+     # cookie name + regex
            - After=2026-01-01T00:00:00+00:00[Asia/Kolkata]
            - RemoteAddr=192.168.1.0/24        # client CIDR

# ALL predicates on a route must match. To express OR, write two
# routes with the same uri.
#
# Routes are matched in DECLARATION ORDER, and the first match wins.
# A route with Path=/** placed first will swallow everything below it -
# this is the most common "my route is being ignored" cause.

# Filters - the everyday ones
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: policy-service
          uri: http://localhost:8181
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/policies/**
          filters:
            - StripPrefix=2                    # /api/policies/1 -> /1
            - AddRequestHeader=X-Source, gateway
            - AddResponseHeader=X-Gateway, api-gateway
            - RewritePath=/api/policies/(?<id>.*), /getPolicy/${id}

      # Filters applied to EVERY route
      default-filters:
        - AddResponseHeader=X-Powered-By, velocity-gateway
        - DedupeResponseHeader=Access-Control-Allow-Origin

# Note the ${id} inside RewritePath is a regex group reference read by
# the gateway, NOT a Spring property placeholder. In a .properties file
# it must be escaped as $\{id} or Spring tries to resolve a property
# called "id" and fails at startup.

beginner.content:
Steps 4 and 5 - Running It

Start the downstream services first, then the gateway. Everything is then called through port 9090.
codeExamples:
# Turn on route logging while you are learning - it is the fastest
# way to see WHY a request matched or did not match.
logging:
  level:
    org.springframework.cloud.gateway: DEBUG
    reactor.netty.http.client: DEBUG

# CONSOLE:
# Route matched: policy-service
# Mapping [Exchange: GET http://localhost:9090/policies/1]
#     to Route{id='policy-service',
#              uri=http://localhost:8181,
#              order=0,
#              predicate=Paths: [/policies/**], match trailing slash: true}

# When NOTHING matches, the gateway returns 404 with an empty body and
# logs nothing by default - which is why this logger is worth enabling.

beginner.content:
The Java RouteLocator DSL

The same routes can be built in Java instead of YAML. Use it when a route needs logic YAML cannot express - a value computed at startup, a conditional route, or a custom filter you wrote yourself.

YAMLJava DSL
Changeable without recompiling; refreshable from a Config ServerFixed at build time
Readable by people who are not Java developersType-checked, and IDE-completable
The default for ordinary path routingThe choice when filters need real code

The two can be mixed - routes from both sources are merged.

Integrating With Eureka - lb:// Routing

uri: http://localhost:8181 has the same problem hard-coded URLs always have: one fixed instance, on one machine. Adding the Eureka client to the gateway lets a route name a service instead of an address.

SchemeMeaning
http://localhost:8181Exactly this host and port. No load balancing.
lb://POLICYSERVICEResolve the name through discovery and load-balance across every UP instance.
forward:/fallbackHandle it inside the gateway itself, rather than forwarding.

The lb scheme requires Spring Cloud LoadBalancer on the classpath - the Eureka client starter brings it in. Without it, the request fails with UnsupportedOperationException or a 503.
codeExamples:
<!-- Add discovery to the gateway -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- This also brings spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer, which is
     what makes lb:// work. -->

# application.yml - routes by service name
server:
  port: 9090

spring:
  application:
    name: api-gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: user-service
          uri: lb://USERSERVICE            # spring.application.name
          predicates:
            - Path=/users/**

        - id: policy-service
          uri: lb://POLICYSERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/policies/**

eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://localhost:8761/eureka/

# The gateway is itself a Eureka client - it registers, and it fetches
# the registry so it can resolve lb:// names.
#
# Start a second Policy instance on 8182 and the gateway begins
# alternating between them with no configuration change at all.

# Automatic routes from the registry - no route list at all
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      discovery:
        locator:
          enabled: true
          lower-case-service-id: true

# Every registered service instantly gets a route:
#   http://localhost:9090/policyservice/getPolicy/1
#          -> POLICYSERVICE /getPolicy/1
#
# Convenient in development. Avoid it in production: it publishes
# EVERY registered service - including internal-only ones - on the
# public gateway, and the URL structure is dictated by internal
# service names you may later want to change.

expert.content:
The Gateway Is Reactive, and That Governs Everything

Spring Cloud Gateway is built on Spring WebFlux running on Netty. It does not use Tomcat, it does not use a thread per request, and it is not a servlet application. Two consequences follow, and both bite in practice.

1. It cannot be mixed with spring-boot-starter-web. This is not a warning; the application refuses to start.

***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

Spring MVC found on classpath, which is incompatible with Spring
Cloud Gateway.

Action:

Please set spring.main.web-application-type=reactive or remove
spring-boot-starter-web dependency.

The suggested web-application-type=reactive makes it boot, but it is the wrong fix: Spring MVC is still on the classpath, and anything that auto-configures for MVC will misbehave. Remove the dependency. It usually arrives transitively - mvn dependency:tree finds who pulled it in.

2. Blocking code in a filter destroys throughput. Netty serves all traffic on a small event loop - typically one thread per CPU core. A blocking call on one of those threads stalls every other connection that thread is multiplexing.

Global Filters, Route Filters, and Order

Two kinds of filter exist, and the difference is scope.

KindScopeHow it is written
GlobalFilterEvery route, alwaysA @Bean implementing GlobalFilter
GatewayFilterThe route it is attached toNamed in the route's filters: list, or produced by a GatewayFilterFactory
default-filtersEvery route, but expressed as route filtersYAML - useful when a route filter should apply everywhere

Filters are not "before" handlers. Each filter wraps the rest of the chain, so code before chain.filter(exchange) runs on the way in and code appended to the returned Mono runs on the way out - in reverse order.

REQUEST                                              RESPONSE

  |  filter A  (order -100)  pre                          ^
  v                                                       |  A post
  |  filter B  (order 0)     pre                          ^
  v                                                       |  B post
  |  filter C  (order 1000)  pre                          ^
  v                                                       |  C post
  +------------> NettyRoutingFilter (order MAX) ----------+
                 the actual call downstream

Lower order value = earlier on the request, LATER on the response.

Ordering ruleDetail
Implement Ordered, or annotate @OrderThe only reliable way to place a GlobalFilter. Bean declaration order is not a contract.
Route filters run in written orderWithin a route's filters: list, top to bottom.
Authentication must run earlyBefore rate limiting keyed on user identity, and before anything that logs the body.
You cannot change response headers after the body is committedNetty streams the response; mutate headers in beforeCommit, not in then(...).

Security at the Edge - and Why It Must Not Be the Only Check

Validating a JWT once at the gateway is attractive: one place to configure, one place to rotate keys, and downstream services stay simple. It is also the design that produces the classic breach.

THE TRUSTING-GATEWAY DESIGN

   internet --> [ GATEWAY ]  validates JWT
                    |        adds  X-User-Id: 42
                    v
              [ Policy service ]  trusts X-User-Id blindly


THE PROBLEM - anything already inside the network skips the gateway:

   compromised pod ------------------------> [ Policy service ]
   curl -H "X-User-Id: 1" policy-svc:8181/policies/all
                                             ...and is served.

   Also skips it: a misconfigured Kubernetes Service, a debug port
   left open, a developer's port-forward, an SSRF in any other
   service, and the service's own actuator endpoints.

The gateway is a coarse first filter, not the security boundary. The principle is defence in depth: the edge does what only the edge can do, and each service still enforces what only it knows.

Belongs at the gatewayBelongs in each service
Rejecting requests with no token at allRe-validating the token signature and expiry
Coarse rate limiting and IP blockingAuthorisation: may this user read this policy?
TLS termination, CORS, request size limitsOwnership checks against its own data
Attaching a correlation idAudit logging of what was actually accessed

The cost of re-validating a JWT in each service is a signature check against a cached JWKS - microseconds. That is a very cheap insurance premium.

Also strip inbound copies of your own trusted headers. If the gateway sets X-User-Id, it must first remove any X-User-Id the client sent, or a client can simply supply its own.
codeExamples:
# Gateway as an OAuth2 resource server
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/realms/velocity
# Note: on the gateway this configures the REACTIVE security filter
# chain. Copying a servlet SecurityFilterChain configuration from an
# MVC service will not apply - the types are
# ServerHttpSecurity / SecurityWebFilterChain, not HttpSecurity.

expert.content:
Rate Limiting, and Why the Key Resolver Decides Everything

The built-in RequestRateLimiter filter uses Redis and a token bucket algorithm, executed as an atomic Lua script so several gateway instances share one counter.

ParameterMeaning
replenishRateTokens added per second - the sustained rate allowed.
burstCapacityBucket size - the largest instantaneous burst. Set equal to replenishRate to forbid bursts.
requestedTokensTokens one request costs. Charge an expensive endpoint more.
KeyResolverWhat identifies "one caller". This is the decision that matters.

Redis is not an optional detail - the limit must be shared. With three gateway instances and a per-instance in-memory counter, a "100 per second" limit is really 300 per second, and the effective limit changes every time you scale.

The key resolver is where rate limiting is usually got wrong:

KeyConsequence
Client IPEveryone behind one corporate NAT or mobile carrier shares a bucket, so one office locks out a whole customer. Behind a load balancer, getRemoteAddress() returns the balancer's IP - one bucket for the entire internet - unless X-Forwarded-For is honoured, which a client can forge if it is not sanitised at the edge.
Authenticated user idThe fair choice for authenticated traffic - but it is null on login and signup, exactly the endpoints most worth protecting.
API key / tenantRight for machine-to-machine traffic; lets you sell tiers.
A constantOne global bucket - a denial-of-service on yourself, since one abusive client starves everyone.

The practical answer is several limiters at different keys: a generous per-IP limit on unauthenticated paths, a tighter per-user limit once identity is known.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- REACTIVE Redis. The blocking starter would block the event loop
     and the RequestRateLimiter filter would not find its bean:
     "No qualifying bean of type ReactiveStringRedisTemplate" -->

spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: policy-service
          uri: lb://POLICYSERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/policies/**
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10      # 10 req/sec sustained
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20      # short bursts to 20
                redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1
                key-resolver: "#{@userKeyResolver}"       # SpEL bean reference

# RESPONSE when the bucket is empty:
#   HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
#   X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
#   X-RateLimit-Burst-Capacity: 20
#   X-RateLimit-Replenish-Rate: 10
#
# If Redis is DOWN the filter denies every request - the gateway fails
# CLOSED. Decide deliberately whether that is what you want; for a
# public read API, failing open is often better than a total outage.

expert.content:
CORS at the Edge

With a gateway there is exactly one origin the browser talks to, so CORS is configured once - at the gateway - and removed from every downstream service.

Leaving @CrossOrigin in the services as well is the usual cause of the duplicate-header failure:

The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header contains multiple values
'https://app.example.com, https://app.example.com', but only one
is allowed.

Both the gateway and the service added the header, and the browser rejects the response. Either strip it downstream with DedupeResponseHeader, or - better - delete the CORS configuration from the services.

SettingGuidance
allowedOriginsList them explicitly. "*" on a credentialed API is a real vulnerability, and the browser rejects it outright with allowCredentials: true.
allowedOriginPatternsUse for wildcard subdomains (https://*.example.com) where a literal list is impractical.
allowCredentialsOnly if the browser sends cookies. A bearer token in a header does not need it.
maxAgeCache the preflight. Without it, every non-simple request costs an extra OPTIONS round trip.
Preflight and securityThe OPTIONS preflight carries no credentials - so an authenticated gateway must permit it, or every cross-origin call fails before it starts.
codeExamples:
# Global CORS at the gateway
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      globalcors:
        add-to-simple-url-handler-mapping: true   # needed for OPTIONS preflight
        cors-configurations:
          '[/**]':
            allowedOrigins:
              - https://app.example.com
              - https://admin.example.com
            allowedMethods: [GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS]
            allowedHeaders: [Authorization, Content-Type, X-Request-Id]
            exposedHeaders: [X-Request-Id, X-RateLimit-Remaining]
            allowCredentials: true
            maxAge: 3600

      default-filters:
        # Drop any duplicate the downstream service adds
        - DedupeResponseHeader=Access-Control-Allow-Origin Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, RETAIN_FIRST

# add-to-simple-url-handler-mapping is easy to miss. Without it the
# preflight OPTIONS request is routed downstream instead of being
# answered by the gateway, and the browser reports a CORS failure that
# looks like the origin list is wrong when it is not.

expert.content:
Resilience at the Gateway, and Netflix Zuul

The gateway is a single point through which everything passes, which makes it both the best place to apply a circuit breaker and the worst place to have one misconfigured.

The CircuitBreaker filter wraps a route in Resilience4j and can forward to a fallback route inside the gateway when the breaker is open.

Gateway-level protectionEffect
CircuitBreaker filterStops forwarding to a failing service; serves a fallback instead of a 504.
Retry filterRetries on chosen statuses and methods. Restrict it to idempotent methods.
RequestSize filterRejects oversized bodies at the edge with 413, before they reach a service.
Response timeoutPer route or global; without it a hung service holds gateway connections open.

A breaker at the gateway is coarse: it opens for a whole route, so one broken endpoint can trip every endpoint of that service. Per-dependency breakers inside each service are finer-grained. Use both - the gateway breaker exists to stop the gateway itself becoming the bottleneck.

Zuul

Netflix Zuul 1 is dead and Spring Cloud Gateway replaced it. Worth knowing why, because it is a standard interview question.

Zuul 1Spring Cloud Gateway
Blocking, servlet, thread-per-requestNon-blocking, WebFlux on Netty
A slow backend exhausts the thread poolSlow backends hold a connection, not a thread
No first-class WebSocket supportWebSocket and Server-Sent Events supported
Netflix OSS, in maintenance; removed from Spring CloudActively developed by the Spring team
@EnableZuulProxy, zuul.routes.*spring.cloud.gateway.routes, predicates and filters

Zuul 2 was rewritten to be non-blocking, but arrived after Spring had already built Gateway; Spring Cloud never adopted it. If you meet @EnableZuulProxy in an existing codebase, it is a migration target.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-circuitbreaker-reactor-resilience4j</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- REACTOR variant. The plain
     spring-cloud-starter-circuitbreaker-resilience4j is the blocking
     one and is the wrong dependency for the gateway. -->

spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      httpclient:
        connect-timeout: 2000            # milliseconds
        response-timeout: 5s
      routes:
        - id: policy-service
          uri: lb://POLICYSERVICE
          predicates:
            - Path=/policies/**
          filters:
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args:
                name: policyBreaker
                fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/policies
            - name: Retry
              args:
                retries: 2
                methods: GET                       # idempotent only
                statuses: BAD_GATEWAY,SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
                backoff:
                  firstBackoff: 100ms
                  maxBackoff: 1s
                  factor: 2
                  basedOnPreviousValue: false
            - name: RequestSize
              args:
                maxSize: 1MB

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      policyBreaker:
        sliding-window-size: 20
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 20s
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      policyBreaker:
        timeout-duration: 4s
# The TimeLimiter must be SHORTER than httpclient.response-timeout,
# or the breaker never sees a timeout - the HTTP client fails first
# and the breaker records a different error than you configured for.

expert.content:
Operating a Gateway

Everything now depends on one application, so it needs more care than the services behind it.

ConcernWhat to do
It is a single point of failureRun at least two instances behind a load balancer. The gateway is stateless, so this is straightforward - keep it that way by putting rate-limit state in Redis, not memory.
Business logic creeps inResist it. A gateway that transforms payloads and calls three services becomes a distributed monolith's control centre and must be redeployed for every change.
Route configuration driftBack it with a Config Server and refresh with POST /actuator/gateway/refresh rather than restarting.
Debugging routesGET /actuator/gateway/routes returns the resolved route table - the fastest way to see what the gateway actually believes.
Header size and hop countEach hop adds headers. Netty's default 8KB header limit is reachable with a large JWT plus tracing headers; the symptom is a bare 431 or a truncated request.
ObservabilityGenerate the correlation id here if the client did not send one; every downstream log line should carry it.
codeExamples:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,gateway,metrics,prometheus
  endpoint:
    gateway:
      access: unrestricted        # Boot 3.4+; was "enabled: true" before

# GET /actuator/gateway/routes
[
  {
    "route_id": "policy-service",
    "uri": "lb://POLICYSERVICE",
    "order": 0,
    "predicate": "Paths: [/policies/**], match trailing slash: true",
    "filters": [
      "[[CircuitBreaker name = 'policyBreaker', fallback = '/fallback/policies']]",
      "[[StripPrefix parts = 1]]"
    ]
  }
]

# POST /actuator/gateway/refresh
# Reloads routes from the current configuration without a restart.
#
# These endpoints expose your entire internal topology. Never expose
# the actuator port publicly - bind it to a separate management port
# and firewall it.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is an API gateway and why use one?A single entry point in front of the services. It gives clients one address, keeps internal services off the public network, and puts cross-cutting concerns - auth, CORS, rate limiting, logging - in one place instead of in every service.
What are the parts of a Gateway route?An id, a uri to forward to, predicates that decide whether it matches, and filters that modify the request or response.
What is the difference between a predicate and a filter?A predicate decides whether a route handles the request; a filter changes what is sent or returned.
Why can't spring-boot-starter-web be on the gateway's classpath?Gateway is built on WebFlux and Netty. Spring MVC on the classpath fails startup with "Spring MVC found on classpath, which is incompatible with Spring Cloud Gateway". Remove the dependency rather than forcing web-application-type=reactive.
Why is blocking code in a filter a serious problem?Netty serves all traffic on a few event-loop threads. Blocking one stalls every connection it multiplexes, capping throughput regardless of hardware. Use a reactive client, or offload to Schedulers.boundedElastic().
Global filter versus route filter?A GlobalFilter bean applies to every route; a GatewayFilter applies only to the route that names it. default-filters applies a route filter to all routes.
How is filter order determined?By the Ordered interface or @Order for global filters, and by declaration order within a route. Lower order runs earlier on the request and later on the response, because each filter wraps the rest of the chain.
What does lb://SERVICE-NAME do?Resolves the name through service discovery and load-balances across every UP instance, instead of pinning one host and port. It needs Spring Cloud LoadBalancer on the classpath.
Is authenticating at the gateway enough?No. Anything already inside the network can call a service directly and bypass it. Each service must still validate the token and enforce its own authorisation - defence in depth.
What must you do with trusted headers the gateway sets?Strip the client's copy first. If the gateway sets X-User-Id without removing an inbound one, a client can supply its own and impersonate any user.
Why does the rate limiter need Redis?The limit must be shared across gateway instances. A per-instance in-memory counter multiplies the effective limit by the number of instances and changes whenever you scale.
Why does the KeyResolver choice matter?Keying on IP puts everyone behind one NAT in a single bucket and returns the load balancer's address unless X-Forwarded-For is honoured and sanitised; keying on user id is null on login and signup. Usually you need both, at different limits.
Why configure CORS only at the gateway?The browser talks to one origin. Leaving @CrossOrigin downstream too produces duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, which the browser rejects.
What replaced Netflix Zuul, and why?Spring Cloud Gateway. Zuul 1 was blocking and thread-per-request, so a slow backend exhausted its thread pool; Gateway is non-blocking on Netty, supports WebSockets, and is actively developed by the Spring team.
