beginner.content:
Step 5 - the model class

A plain Java object, one field per CSV column. Spring Batch does not require it to be a JPA entity - the writer in this project is a JdbcBatchItemWriter and works on named SQL parameters, not on Hibernate. The @Entity annotation below is present only so that ddl-auto=update creates the destination table for you.

The no-argument constructor is mandatory. BeanWrapperFieldSetMapper instantiates the target type reflectively and then calls setters. Without a default constructor the reader fails on the first line.

Step 7 - BatchConfig: reader, writer, Step, Job

This is the whole application. Read it in four parts.

BeanWhat it does
FlatFileItemReader<User>Reads the file one line at a time. setResource points it at the CSV; setLinesToSkip(1) skips the header row; setLineMapper tells it how to turn a line of text into a User.
DefaultLineMapperThe two-stage mapper. A LineTokenizer splits the raw line into a FieldSet, then a FieldSetMapper turns that FieldSet into an object.
DelimitedLineTokenizerSplits on a delimiter (comma by default). setNames(...) gives each column a name - these names must match the property names of the target class, not the CSV header text.
BeanWrapperFieldSetMapperCreates an instance of the target type and calls the setter matching each column name. Type conversion from String to long happens here.
JdbcBatchItemWriter<User>Executes one SQL statement for the whole chunk using JDBC batching. BeanPropertyItemSqlParameterSourceProvider binds the named parameters :id, :name and so on from the bean's properties.

The version question you will hit immediately. The classroom code injects JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory. Those two classes were deprecated in Spring Batch 4.3 and removed in Spring Batch 5, which is what Spring Boot 3 ships. Both versions are shown below, because you will meet both.

Steps 8 and 9 - run it and check the database

There is no controller and no Postman request in this project. Spring Boot's JobLauncherApplicationRunner finds every Job bean in the context and runs it automatically once the application context is ready. The web starter is only there so the process stays alive; a pure batch application does not need it.

Run it a second time and watch what happens. That is the single most instructive moment in this whole exercise, and it is covered in the expert section.
codeExamples:
# Two properties worth knowing before you run anything

# 1. Stop the job from firing on every application startup. Useful when the
#    job should be triggered by a REST endpoint or a scheduler instead.
#    Spring Boot 2.x:
spring.batch.job.enabled=false
#    Spring Boot 3.x removed that flag. You now name the jobs to run, and
#    "none" means run nothing:
spring.batch.job.name=none

# 2. If you have several Job beans, Boot 2.x runs ALL of them unless you set
#    spring.batch.job.names=importUserJob. Boot 3.x uses the singular
#    spring.batch.job.name and accepts one job.

expert.content:
The model underneath the annotations

Spring Batch is small once you see the shape. A Job is a container of Steps. A chunk-oriented Step is a loop driven by three interfaces. Everything else - listeners, skip policies, partitioning - hangs off that loop.

                            JobLauncher.run(job, jobParameters)
                                        |
                                        v
        +-------------------------------------------------------------+
        |  JobInstance  = job name + IDENTIFYING job parameters        |
        |     |                                                       |
        |     +--> JobExecution #1   FAILED                            |
        |     +--> JobExecution #2   COMPLETED   (a restart)           |
        +-------------------------------------------------------------+
                                        |
                                        v
        +-------------------------------------------------------------+
        |  JOB "USER-IMPORT-JOB"                                      |
        |                                                             |
        |   +---------------+     +---------------+                   |
        |   |  STEP  load   |---->|  STEP  report |  (on COMPLETED)   |
        |   +---------------+     +---------------+                   |
        +---------|---------------------------------------------------+
                  |
                  v
   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  CHUNK-ORIENTED STEP,  commit-interval = 10                         |
   |                                                                     |
   |   begin transaction                                                 |
   |     repeat 10 times:                                                |
   |         item  = reader.read()          <-- one item                 |
   |         out   = processor.process(item) <-- one item, may be null   |
   |         accumulate out into a List                                  |
   |     writer.write(chunk of <=10)         <-- the WHOLE list at once  |
   |     jobRepository.update(stepExecution) <-- read/write counts, ctx  |
   |   commit transaction                                                |
   |                                                                     |
   |   ...until reader.read() returns null                               |
   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+
                  |
                  v
        JobRepository  ->  BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE
                           BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION       (+_PARAMS, _CONTEXT)
                           BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION      (+_CONTEXT)

ConceptWhat it really is
JobA definition, not a run. It is a bean, created once at startup, and it is shared across every execution. Anything you store in a Job bean field is shared state - a frequent source of bugs.
JobInstanceThe logical run: job name plus the identifying job parameters. "The import for 2026-09-03" is one JobInstance, whether it took one attempt or four.
JobExecutionOne physical attempt at a JobInstance. It has a start time, an end time, a BatchStatus and an ExitStatus. A JobInstance can have many JobExecutions; only one may be COMPLETED.
Step / StepExecutionSame distinction one level down. The StepExecution carries the counters - readCount, writeCount, filterCount, skipCount, commitCount, rollbackCount - and the ExecutionContext that makes restart possible.
ExecutionContextA serialised map of key/value pairs persisted with each execution. A restartable reader writes its position here (FlatFileItemReader stores userItemReader.read.count), which is why the reader must have a name.
ItemStreamThe interface that gives a reader or writer open(), update() and close() callbacks around the Step. It is how the ExecutionContext gets written. Custom readers that skip it are not restartable.

Chunk-oriented processing: what commit-interval really controls

.chunk(10, txManager) looks like a batch size. It is a transaction boundary, and calling it the commit-interval - the name Spring Batch actually uses - makes the consequences obvious.

Every chunk is one database transaction. Ten reads, ten processes, one write, one StepExecution update, one commit. If anything in that window throws and no skip policy applies, the whole chunk rolls back - all ten items, not the one that failed.

Commit-intervalConsequence
1One transaction per item. Maximum restart precision - a failure loses nothing. Also maximum overhead: a commit per row makes a large load an order of magnitude slower.
10 - 1000The usable range. JDBC batching amortises the network round trips and the commit cost across the chunk.
50000Long-running transactions, a bloated undo/redo log, lock contention with online traffic, and up to 50,000 items of work discarded on a single failure. It also holds 50,000 objects in memory.

The restart-granularity point, stated precisely. The JobRepository is updated inside the same transaction as the chunk write. So the framework's record of "how far did we get" advances one chunk at a time. On restart, the Step resumes at the last committed chunk boundary - never mid-chunk. With a commit-interval of 1000, a crash at item 4,999 restarts at item 4,000 and re-reads 999 items you had already processed. That is not a bug; it is the price of the commit-interval you chose.

commit-interval = 1000, input of 10,000 items, crash while processing #4,999

  items 1-1000     [chunk 1]  COMMIT   read.count = 1000  persisted
  items 1001-2000  [chunk 2]  COMMIT   read.count = 2000  persisted
  items 2001-3000  [chunk 3]  COMMIT   read.count = 3000  persisted
  items 3001-4000  [chunk 4]  COMMIT   read.count = 4000  persisted
  items 4001-4999  [chunk 5]  X CRASH  ------ ROLLBACK ------
                                       read.count stays at 4000

  RESTART:  reader.open(executionContext) sees read.count=4000
            and skips forward 4000 lines. Processing resumes at 4001.
            Items 4001-4999 are processed a SECOND time.

  The writer must therefore be idempotent, or those 999 rows
  become duplicate keys. This is the same lesson as at-least-once
  delivery in a message broker.

Where the transaction actually lives. The transaction manager is the Step's, not the writer's. In Spring Batch 5 you pass it explicitly to chunk(size, txManager), which was a deliberate change - in Batch 4 it was picked up implicitly and people did not notice they were committing against the wrong DataSource. If the JobRepository and the business data live in different databases, they are two independent transactions and can disagree after a crash.

The JobRepository: six tables that do all the real work

Everything Spring Batch knows about a run lives in the metadata schema. The DDL ships inside spring-batch-core.jar as org/springframework/batch/core/schema-mysql.sql (one per vendor), and spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=always is what runs it.

TableWhat it holds
BATCH_JOB_INSTANCEOne row per logical run. Columns: JOB_INSTANCE_ID, JOB_NAME, JOB_KEY. The JOB_KEY is an MD5 hash of the identifying job parameters, and (JOB_NAME, JOB_KEY) carries a UNIQUE constraint. That constraint is the entire duplicate-run mechanism.
BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMSThe parameters of one execution, with an IDENTIFYING flag per parameter. Only identifying parameters feed the JOB_KEY.
BATCH_JOB_EXECUTIONOne row per attempt: CREATE_TIME, START_TIME, END_TIME, STATUS, EXIT_CODE, EXIT_MESSAGE (the stack trace), LAST_UPDATED. Many rows may point at one JobInstance.
BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_CONTEXTThe serialised job-level ExecutionContext, as JSON since Batch 4.
BATCH_STEP_EXECUTIONOne row per step attempt, and the most useful table for diagnosis: READ_COUNT, FILTER_COUNT, WRITE_COUNT, READ_SKIP_COUNT, PROCESS_SKIP_COUNT, WRITE_SKIP_COUNT, COMMIT_COUNT, ROLLBACK_COUNT, STATUS, EXIT_MESSAGE.
BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION_CONTEXTThe step-level ExecutionContext - where the reader's position is stored. This is what a restart reads to know where to resume.

Why a JobInstance cannot run twice

Run the classroom job, then run it again with no parameters, and you get:

org.springframework.batch.core.repository.JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException:
A job instance already exists and is complete for parameters={}. If you want to run this job again, change the parameters.

This is not a defect. Spring Batch's contract is that a JobInstance may complete exactly once. The identity of a JobInstance is job name plus identifying parameters, so an empty parameter set means every run is the same logical run. Once it is COMPLETED, re-running it would mean re-doing finished work - exactly the accident the framework exists to prevent. The rule is enforced by the unique index on (JOB_NAME, JOB_KEY), not by application code.

Three ways forward, in increasing order of correctness:

ApproachEffect
RunIdIncrementerAdds a run.id parameter and increments it on each launch, so every launch is a new JobInstance. Convenient for demos and for jobs that are genuinely idempotent. It also means you can never restart a failed run - the incrementer has moved on.
A meaningful parameterPass the thing that actually distinguishes the run: the input file name, the business date, the batch id. importUserJob(inputFile=users-2026-09-03.csv) is one JobInstance, and re-launching it after a failure restarts it rather than creating a new one. This is what production jobs do.
Non-identifying parametersnew JobParametersBuilder().addString("debug", "true", false) - the false marks it non-identifying, so it is recorded but excluded from the JOB_KEY. Use it for anything that changes behaviour but not identity.

The trap with RunIdIncrementer is that it silently converts "restart the failed load" into "run the whole load again from the start", because the new run.id creates a fresh JobInstance with an empty ExecutionContext. If your job must be restartable, do not use it.

Restartability, skip and retry

Three distinct mechanisms that students routinely conflate. They answer three different questions.

MechanismThe question it answers
Restart"The process died. Can I pick up where it stopped instead of starting over?" - decided by the JobRepository and the ExecutionContext.
Skip"This particular item is bad. Can the job carry on without it?" - decided by a skip policy, per item.
Retry"That failure was transient. Can I try the same item again in a moment?" - decided by a retry policy, per item, within the same execution.

Restart, precisely

• A restart only occurs when the JobInstance already exists and its last JobExecution is FAILED or STOPPED. Same job name, same identifying parameters.
• A Step whose previous execution COMPLETED is skipped on restart, unless it is marked allowStartIfComplete(true). This is the point of splitting a job into steps: a five-step job that failed in step four restarts at step four.
• preventRestart() on the JobBuilder forbids restart entirely, and any attempt throws JobRestartException. Use it when a partial re-run would be worse than a full one.
• startLimit(n) on a Step caps how many times that Step may be attempted across restarts - a guard against a job that fails, restarts, fails, forever.

Restart requires a restartable reader. FlatFileItemReader, JdbcCursorItemReader and JpaPagingItemReader implement ItemStream and persist their position. A reader you wrote yourself, or one wrapping a stream you cannot rewind, does not - and a "restart" then silently reprocesses everything from the beginning. Also note the whole mechanism depends on the reader's name: the ExecutionContext key is <name>.read.count, so an unnamed reader in a multi-reader step will collide. saveState(false) disables the mechanism deliberately - which is required for readers used in a multi-threaded step.

Skip and retry together

The two interact in a way worth stating: retry happens first. An exception listed in both retry() and skip() is retried up to the retry limit, and only if it still fails is it considered for skipping. Also, on a skip during the write phase, Spring Batch rolls back the chunk and replays it item by item with a commit-interval of 1 to identify which item was at fault - so a chunk containing one bad row costs you a rollback plus N single-item transactions. A high skip limit on a dirty file is a performance cliff, not just a tolerance setting.

Listeners: where to put the cross-cutting work

Every phase of a Job has a listener interface. They exist so that logging, metrics, notification and cleanup do not end up inside the processor.

ListenerWhen it fires and what it is for
JobExecutionListenerbeforeJob runs once before any step; afterJob runs once after the last step whether the job succeeded or failed. This is where you send the completion e-mail, publish the duration metric, or archive the input file. Check jobExecution.getStatus() - afterJob on a FAILED job is the normal case, not an exception.
StepExecutionListenerbeforeStep receives the StepExecution, which is how you pull values out of the job ExecutionContext into step-scoped state. afterStep returns an ExitStatus - and returning a custom one is how you drive conditional flow between steps.
ChunkListenerbeforeChunk, afterChunk, afterChunkError. Useful for progress logging every N items without touching the processor. afterChunkError fires after the rollback.
ItemReadListener / ItemProcessListener / ItemWriteListenerPer-item hooks, each with a before, after and onError callback. Cheap to add, expensive to abuse - they run once per item.
SkipListenerCalled when an item is skipped. The only place the skipped item is still available. Not optional in production.
RetryListenerWraps each retry attempt. Useful for counting retries as a metric rather than reading them out of logs.

Passing data between steps. The job ExecutionContext is the supported channel, and the idiom is: afterStep promotes a value into it (or use ExecutionContextPromotionListener), and a later step's beforeStep reads it. Do not use a field on a @Configuration class - the Job bean is a singleton shared across executions, and in a partitioned or multi-threaded step that field is a race condition.

Scaling: multi-threaded steps and partitioning

A single-threaded chunk loop is limited by whichever of read, process and write is slowest. Spring Batch offers several ways out, and choosing the wrong one produces corrupted output rather than an error.

StrategyHow it works, and what it costs
Multi-threaded stepOne reader, one writer, N threads pulling chunks from the same reader concurrently. Set with .taskExecutor(...). Simple to switch on and easy to get wrong: the reader and writer must be thread-safe, and restart state is lost.
PartitioningA Partitioner splits the input into N logical partitions, each with its own ExecutionContext. Each partition runs the same step definition as a separate StepExecution with its own reader, writer and transaction. This is the recommended approach.
Parallel steps (split)Different, independent steps run at the same time via .split(taskExecutor). Use when two unrelated loads can proceed concurrently - not for scaling one load.
Remote chunking / remote partitioningWorkers on other JVMs, coordinated over a messaging middleware. Remote chunking sends items over the wire (heavy); remote partitioning sends only partition metadata (light). Reach for these only when one machine is genuinely the ceiling.

Why a non-thread-safe reader breaks a multi-threaded step

This is the question interviewers use to find out whether you have actually run one.

In a multi-threaded step there is one reader instance and N threads calling read() on it. FlatFileItemReader, JdbcCursorItemReader and the paging readers keep their position in a mutable field. Two threads entering read() at once interleave the read of that counter and its increment, so the same line is returned twice, or a line is never returned at all, or the underlying BufferedReader is left mid-line and the parse fails. 

MULTI-THREADED STEP - one shared reader, four threads

              +----------------------------+
              |  FlatFileItemReader        |
              |  currentItemCount = 41     |   <-- MUTABLE, NOT SYNCHRONIZED
              +----------------------------+
                  ^      ^      ^      ^
              T1  |  T2  |  T3  |  T4  |
                  read() read() read() read()

  T1 reads count 41 ......... T2 reads count 41
  T1 increments to 42 ....... T2 increments to 42
  -> row 42 is read TWICE and row 43 is never read at all.

  Symptoms: duplicate rows in the destination, a row count lower than the
  file's line count, or a FlatFileParseException on a half-consumed line.
  No exception says "your reader is not thread safe".


PARTITIONED STEP - N StepExecutions, each with its OWN reader

  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  Partitioner: split the input into 4 ranges                   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
        |            |            |            |
   partition0   partition1   partition2   partition3
   ctx{1-2500}  ctx{2501-  } ctx{5001-  } ctx{7501-  }
        |            |            |            |
   StepExecution StepExecution StepExecution StepExecution
   own reader    own reader    own reader    own reader
   own writer    own writer    own writer    own writer
   own tx        own tx        own tx        own tx
        |            |            |            |
        +------------+-----+------+------------+
                           v
              all COMPLETED -> master step COMPLETED
              each partition restarts INDEPENDENTLY

Fixes for a multi-threaded step, in order of preference: use partitioning instead; or use a reader that is genuinely thread-safe (JdbcPagingItemReader with a stable sort is safe because each page is an independent query); or wrap the reader in SynchronizedItemStreamReader, which serialises read() and makes the reader the bottleneck again - it only helps when processing, not reading, is the expensive part. In every case you must call saveState(false), because the persisted read count is meaningless when threads interleave, and a restart based on it would silently skip data.

Spring Batch 5 and Spring Boot 3: what changed

This is the most common source of "the code in the notes does not compile". Spring Boot 3 ships Spring Batch 5, and Batch 5 made breaking changes deliberately.

ChangeDetail
JobBuilderFactory removedJobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory were deprecated in 4.3 and deleted in 5.0. Use new JobBuilder(name, jobRepository) and new StepBuilder(name, jobRepository). The factories existed to hide the JobRepository; hiding it turned out to be the problem, because people did not realise which repository or transaction manager they were using.
chunk() takes a transaction manager.chunk(10) became .chunk(10, transactionManager), and .tasklet(t) became .tasklet(t, transactionManager). Same reason: the implicit lookup was a source of silent misconfiguration when more than one DataSource was present.
@EnableBatchProcessing is no longer neededWith Boot 3, BatchAutoConfiguration provides the JobRepository, JobLauncher, JobExplorer and JobOperator. Adding @EnableBatchProcessing (or defining a DefaultBatchConfiguration subclass) disables that auto-configuration - the opposite of what most people expect from adding an annotation.
javax to jakartajavax.persistence to jakarta.persistence, javax.sql.DataSource is unchanged (it is in the JDK). Batch 5 also moved to JSR-352's jakarta namespace.
Metadata schema changesBATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS was restructured: the four typed columns (DATE_VAL, LONG_VAL, DOUBLE_VAL, STRING_VAL) collapsed into PARAMETER_TYPE plus PARAMETER_VALUE, and timestamps moved from TIMESTAMP to DATETIME(6). An in-place upgrade needs a migration script; it is not a drop-in.
Property renamesspring.batch.initialize-schema to spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema. spring.batch.job.enabled was removed - use spring.batch.job.name=none. spring.batch.job.names (plural) became spring.batch.job.name (singular).
ObservabilityBatch 5 instruments jobs and steps with Micrometer Observation, so spring.batch.job.active, spring.batch.job and spring.batch.step timers appear in Actuator without extra code.
Java 17 baselineBatch 5 requires Java 17 and Spring Framework 6.

Operational things the classroom project does not cover

ConcernWhat to do about it
initialize-schema=always in productionSet it to never and apply the schema-<vendor>.sql DDL through Flyway or Liquibase like any other migration. Letting the application create its own tables at startup means the application needs DDL privileges it should not have.
Two instances launching the same jobThe JobRepository is the lock. The second instance gets JobExecutionAlreadyRunningException because the unique (JOB_NAME, JOB_KEY) row is already STARTED - provided both share the same metadata database. Two instances with their own H2 databases have no such protection.
A job left STARTED after a JVM killIt is not running, but the repository still says STARTED, so a relaunch fails. There is no automatic recovery. Use JobOperator / JobExplorer to mark it ABANDONED, or JobRepository.update() the status to FAILED, before restarting.
Secrets in job parametersJob parameters are written verbatim to BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS and echoed in the launch log line. Never pass a password or token as a job parameter.
Growing metadata tablesNothing prunes them. A job running every five minutes writes over 100,000 BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION rows a year, plus context blobs. Schedule a purge with the correct delete order (contexts, then params, then step executions, then job executions, then instances).
Memory during a large loadA cursor reader holds one JDBC connection open for the whole step; a paging reader issues one query per page and is safer for long jobs. JpaPagingItemReader additionally needs the persistence context cleared, or the first-level cache grows with every row read.
Testingspring-batch-test gives you JobLauncherTestUtils.launchJob(params) and launchStep("step1"), so a step can be tested in isolation. Assert on the counters, not just on BatchStatus.COMPLETED.
codeExamples:
-- Recovering a job stuck in STARTED after the JVM was killed.
-- Symptom on relaunch:
--   org.springframework.batch.core.repository.JobExecutionAlreadyRunning
--   Exception: A job execution for this job is already running: JobInstance:
--   id=17, version=0, Job=[USER-IMPORT-JOB]

SELECT JOB_EXECUTION_ID, JOB_INSTANCE_ID, STATUS, START_TIME, END_TIME, LAST_UPDATED
FROM BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION WHERE STATUS = 'STARTED';
-- | 34 | 17 | STARTED | 2026-09-03 01:00:02 | NULL | 2026-09-03 01:04:47 |
-- END_TIME NULL with LAST_UPDATED hours ago = the JVM died.

-- Preferred: do it through the API so versions and step rows stay consistent.
--   jobOperator.stop(34);  then  jobOperator.abandon(34);
-- Only if the API cannot reach it, and only with the job definitely not
-- running anywhere:
UPDATE BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION SET STATUS = 'FAILED', END_TIME = NOW()
 WHERE JOB_EXECUTION_ID = 34 AND STATUS = 'STARTED';
UPDATE BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION SET STATUS = 'FAILED', EXIT_CODE = 'FAILED',
       END_TIME = NOW()
 WHERE JOB_EXECUTION_ID = 34;
-- The instance can now be restarted.

# Production-shaped configuration
spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=never
spring.batch.job.name=none

# Metadata schema managed as a migration, not by the application.
spring.flyway.enabled=true
spring.flyway.locations=classpath:db/migration
# V1__batch_schema.sql is a copy of
#   org/springframework/batch/core/schema-mysql.sql from spring-batch-core.jar

# Separate the metadata from the business data if they live in different
# databases - and understand that they are then two transactions. A crash
# between the business commit and the metadata commit leaves the repository
# believing less was done than actually was, and the restart reprocesses it.
# Idempotent writers are the answer, not distributed transactions.

# Actuator: Batch 5 publishes these automatically.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics,prometheus
# spring.batch.job.active     - gauge, jobs currently running
# spring.batch.job            - timer, duration by name and status
# spring.batch.step           - timer, duration by step name and status
# spring.batch.item.read/process/write - timers per item

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between a JobInstance and a JobExecution?A JobInstance is the logical run, identified by the job name plus its identifying job parameters. A JobExecution is one physical attempt at that instance. A JobInstance may have many executions - one per attempt - but only one of them may be COMPLETED.
Why does re-running a job with the same parameters throw JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException?Because the JobInstance identity is job name plus identifying parameters, and BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE has a unique index on (JOB_NAME, JOB_KEY) where JOB_KEY is a hash of those parameters. A completed instance may not complete twice - that would mean redoing finished work. Change a parameter, or add an incrementer.
What does RunIdIncrementer do, and what is wrong with it?It adds an incrementing run.id parameter so every launch is a new JobInstance and the exception never fires. The cost is that you also lose restart: a new instance starts with an empty ExecutionContext, so a failed run is re-run from the beginning rather than resumed. Prefer a meaningful identifying parameter such as the business date or file name.
What does the chunk size actually control?The commit interval. Each chunk is one transaction: N reads, N processes, one write of the whole chunk, one JobRepository update, one commit. It is a throughput/restart-granularity trade-off, not just a buffer size.
Where does a restarted step resume?At the last committed chunk boundary, never mid-chunk, because the reader's position is written to the step ExecutionContext inside the same transaction as the chunk. With a chunk size of 1000, a crash at item 4,999 resumes at 4,001 and reprocesses 999 items - which is why the writer must be idempotent.
Which tables does the JobRepository use?BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE, BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION, BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS, BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_CONTEXT, BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION and BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION_CONTEXT. The step execution table carries the read, write, filter, skip, commit and rollback counts; the step context table carries the reader position that makes restart work.
What is the difference between skip and retry?Skip discards a bad item and continues - the data is at fault. Retry attempts the same item again - the operation is at fault, typically a deadlock or a timeout. Retry is evaluated first; an exception configured for both is retried to the limit and only then considered for skipping.
What happens when an exception is skipped during the write phase?The chunk transaction rolls back and Spring Batch replays the chunk one item at a time to identify the offending item, then skips it. That makes a dirty input expensive - a chunk of 1000 with one bad row costs a rollback plus 1000 single-item transactions.
What does returning null from an ItemProcessor mean?The item is filtered - it is not passed to the writer and filterCount increments. It is not an error and does not affect the job status. Skipping on error is a separate mechanism configured with a skip policy.
When do JobExecutionListener and StepExecutionListener fire?beforeJob/afterJob wrap the whole job; afterJob runs on failure too, so it must branch on getStatus(). beforeStep/afterStep wrap one step, and afterStep can return a custom ExitStatus that drives conditional flow to the next step.
Why does a multi-threaded step break with a FlatFileItemReader?There is one reader shared by all threads, and its position counter is a mutable unsynchronised field. Concurrent read() calls interleave the read and the increment, so items are returned twice or missed entirely, with no exception. Fix it with partitioning, a thread-safe paging reader, or SynchronizedItemStreamReader plus saveState(false).
How does partitioning differ from a multi-threaded step?Partitioning creates N separate StepExecutions, each with its own reader, writer, transaction and ExecutionContext, driven by a Partitioner that splits the input. Nothing is shared, so it is safe and each partition restarts independently. A multi-threaded step shares one reader and writer across threads and is not restartable.
What changed in Spring Batch 5?JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory were removed in favour of new JobBuilder(name, jobRepository) and new StepBuilder(name, jobRepository); chunk() and tasklet() now take an explicit transaction manager; @EnableBatchProcessing is no longer required with Boot 3 and actively disables the auto-configuration if you add it; the metadata schema and several properties changed; Java 17 is the baseline.
Why does the first run fail with "Table BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE doesn't exist"?The metadata tables are not created automatically against a real database. Either set spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=always for development, or - in production - apply schema-<vendor>.sql from spring-batch-core.jar through Flyway or Liquibase and leave the setting at never.

Working with Multiple Images

Business requirement: save multiple images into the database.

The parameter becomes an array, and the controller loops. Everything else is the same.

File Download - Fetching an Image from the Database

Business requirement: fetch a single image from the database.
Problem statement: design the REST API to download or fetch an image from the database.

The repository gains one derived finder, and the controller returns the entity.

expert.content:
Returning JSON Is Not a Download

The download endpoint returns the entity, so the bytes arrive base64-encoded inside a JSON object. A browser cannot render that, an <img> tag cannot point at it, and the payload is a third larger than the file.

A real download sets the content type and streams the raw bytes.

HeaderEffect
Content-Type: image/jpegThe browser renders it instead of showing text.
Content-Disposition: inlineDisplay in the page.
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="x.jpg"Trigger a Save-As dialog.
Content-LengthLets the browser show a progress bar.

Storing Files in the Database Is Usually the Wrong Choice

@Lob byte[] works and is the simplest thing to demonstrate. At any real scale it becomes the bottleneck.

ProblemWhy
Backups explodeA 200 GB media library makes every database dump 200 GB. Restores go from minutes to hours.
Memory pressurebyte[] loads the entire file into the JVM heap. Twenty 50 MB uploads at once is 1 GB of heap.
Accidental fetchesfindAll() on the images table drags every blob into memory - and @Lob is eager by default.
No CDNEvery image request hits your application and your database. Object storage serves them from the edge.
Replication lagLarge blobs slow down replication for every other table.

The usual pattern: put the file in object storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) or on disk, and store only the metadata and the key in the database.

Validating an Upload Properly

Checking getContentType() is a start and is not a security control - the content type is supplied by the client and can say anything.

CheckWhy
Size limits in propertiesRejected by Spring before your code runs, so a huge upload never reaches the heap.
Extension allow-listNever a deny-list - you will forget one.
Magic bytesThe real format. A .jpg that starts with MZ is a Windows executable.
Generated filenameBlocks path traversal and collisions.
Serve from a separate domainA stored HTML/SVG file cannot then run scripts against your session.

The two size properties do different jobs: max-file-size caps one file, max-request-size caps the whole multipart request. Ten 10 MB files pass the first check and fail the second - which is exactly what you want.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which type represents an uploaded file in Spring?MultipartFile - it exposes the bytes, original filename, size and content type.
Which annotation binds it?@RequestParam("file"), with the request sent as multipart/form-data, not JSON.
How do you accept several files?Declare the parameter as MultipartFile[] or List<MultipartFile> and repeat the same form key per file.
What does @Lob do?Maps a byte[] or long String to a large-object column - LONGBLOB or LONGTEXT in MySQL.
Difference between max-file-size and max-request-size?The first caps one file; the second caps the whole multipart request, so many small files can still be rejected together.
Why is returning the entity a poor download endpoint?The bytes arrive base64-encoded inside JSON - about 33% larger, and unusable by a browser or an img tag. Return the raw bytes with the right Content-Type.
Which header triggers a Save-As dialog?Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="...". inline displays it in the page instead.
Why is storing files in the database usually a bad idea?Backups balloon, every fetch loads the file into the heap, and you cannot put a CDN in front of it. Store metadata in the DB and the bytes in object storage.
Is checking getContentType() enough validation?No - it is supplied by the client. Verify the magic bytes and use an extension allow-list.
Why must you never use the client's filename directly?Path traversal: ../../etc/passwd writes outside the upload directory. Generate a name and verify the resolved path stays under the root.
Why does "image/jpeg".equals(contentType) beat the other order?getContentType() can return null, and contentType.equals(...) then throws a NullPointerException.
What status code fits an oversized upload?413 Payload Too Large - handle MaxUploadSizeExceededException in a @RestControllerAdvice.

Reading CSV Data - Uploading a CSV into MySQL

Business requirement: read data from a CSV file and store it in the MySQL database.
Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch the data from a CSV file and store it into MySQL.

Steps

1. Create the project   2. Add dependencies   3. Model class   4. Service   5. Service implementation
6. Repository   7. REST controller   8. CommonUtil   9. ResponseMessage   10. application.properties
11. Run   12. Postman   13. Check the database   14. Application flow

The one new dependency is Apache Commons CSV, which handles the parsing.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml : the CSV library, on top of the usual three -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
    <version>8.0.33</version>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
    <artifactId>commons-csv</artifactId>
    <version>1.8</version>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
Step 8 - CommonUtil: Parsing the CSV

This class does the real work. CSVFormat.DEFAULT.withFirstRecordAsHeader() tells Commons CSV that row one holds column names, so each following row can be read by name rather than by position.

SettingEffect
withFirstRecordAsHeader()Row 1 becomes the header; record.get("name") works.
withIgnoreHeaderCase()Name, NAME and name all match.
withTrim()Strips surrounding whitespace from every value.

Steps 4 to 7 and 9 - Service, Repository, Controller

saveAll() writes the whole parsed list in one call.

Writing CSV Data - Exporting the Database to a CSV

Business requirement: fetch employee data from the database and write it into a CSV file.
Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch the data from the database and write it into a CSV file.

The direction reverses: CSVPrinter instead of CSVParser, and the response streams a file back.

expert.content:
Two Silent Failures in the Export Path

Both produce a file with no error message, which makes them harder to find than a crash.

MistakeSymptom
Not closing/flushing the CSVPrinterThe PrintWriter buffer is never drained, so toByteArray() returns nothing. An empty CSV downloads successfully.
No withHeader(...)The file has data but no column names. Re-importing it treats row 1 as data, or fails on Integer.parseInt("id").

The round trip is the test worth running: export, then import the exported file. If it does not survive that, one of the two is wrong.

CSV Is Harder Than split(",")

This is why Commons CSV exists rather than a loop over String.split. Real files contain all of the following, and a naive split mangles every one of them.

CaseWhat it looks like
Comma inside a value1,"Patil, Ambaji",pune - one field, not two.
Quote inside a value1,"He said ""hi""",pune - a doubled quote is one literal quote.
Newline inside a valueA quoted field spanning two physical lines.
Empty vs missing1,,pune is an empty string; a short row is a missing column.
UTF-8 BOMExcel writes EF BB BF first, so the first header reads ﻿id and lookups by "id" fail.
Leading =, +, -, @Excel executes it as a formula - CSV injection.

QuoteMode.MINIMAL handles the first four automatically when writing: it quotes a field only when it contains a delimiter, a quote or a newline.

Importing Large Files Without Running Out of Memory

csvParser.getRecords() loads every row into a List, and saveAll() then holds every entity in the persistence context. A 500 MB CSV will exhaust the heap.

TechniqueEffect
Iterate the parser instead of getRecords()Streams row by row; only one record is in memory.
Batch inserts + flush() + clear()Bounds the persistence context.
hibernate.jdbc.batch_sizeGroups inserts into one round trip instead of one per row.
Collect errors, do not abortA bad row on line 4,000 should not discard 3,999 good ones - report them all.
codeExamples:
# Batch the inserts - without this, saveAll() sends one INSERT per row
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates=true

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which library parses CSV here, and why not split(",")?Apache Commons CSV. Split breaks on commas inside quoted values, escaped quotes and embedded newlines.
What does withFirstRecordAsHeader() do?Treats row 1 as column names so records can be read by name - record.get("city") - instead of by index.
Why does the exported CSV sometimes come out empty?The CSVPrinter was never flushed or closed, so the PrintWriter buffer never reached the ByteArrayOutputStream. Use try-with-resources.
Which header makes the browser download the file?Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=..., with Content-Type: text/csv.
Why should the import be @Transactional?Otherwise a failure part-way through leaves the file half-imported, with earlier rows already committed.
What does QuoteMode.MINIMAL mean?Quote a field only when it contains the delimiter, a quote character or a newline.
What is CSV injection?A value starting with =, +, - or @ that Excel executes as a formula when the export is opened. Prefix it with an apostrophe.
Why does a CSV saved by Excel break header lookups?Excel writes a UTF-8 BOM, so the first column name becomes ﻿id. Strip it with a BOMInputStream.
How do you import a very large CSV safely?Iterate the parser rather than calling getRecords(), and flush/clear the EntityManager every N rows.
How do you speed up bulk inserts?Set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size so inserts are grouped into one round trip instead of one statement per row.
Should one bad row abort the whole import?Usually not - collect per-row errors and report them, so 4,998 good rows are not discarded because of two bad ones.

beginner.content:
Writing Excel Data - Exporting from MySQL into an Excel File

Business requirement: you have employee data stored in the database and want to fetch it and save it into an Excel file.

Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch the employee data from the database and store it into an Excel file.

Table structure

   EMPLOYEE TABLE
 +--------------+
 | id      (PK) |
 | name         |
 | city         |
 +--------------+

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project   2. Add Maven dependencies   3. Create the model class
4. Create the service   5. Create the service implementation   6. Create the repository
7. Create the REST controller   8. application.properties   9. Run   10. Postman   11. Check the output

The new dependency is Apache POI - the Java library for reading and writing Microsoft Office formats.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-java</artifactId>
    <version>8.0.33</version>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.poi</groupId>
    <artifactId>poi</artifactId>
    <version>4.1.2</version>
</dependency>

beginner.content:
The Apache POI Object Model

Four types, nested inside each other. Once the hierarchy is clear the code reads naturally.

TypeRepresents
WorkbookThe whole file - the .xls or .xlsx document.
SheetOne tab inside the workbook.
RowOne row of that sheet, indexed from 0.
CellOne cell in that row, indexed from 0.

Two implementations, two file formats:

Class prefixFormat
HSSF - HSSFWorkbookThe old binary .xls (Excel 97-2003). Limited to 65,536 rows.
XSSF - XSSFWorkbookThe modern .xlsx. Over a million rows. Needs the poi-ooxml dependency.

The walkthrough uses HSSFWorkbook, which is why the download is named employee.xls.

Steps 4 to 6 - Service, Implementation, Repository

The service builds the workbook and writes it straight into the response's output stream.

Step 7 - The REST Controller

Two headers turn a plain HTTP response into a file download.

HeaderPurpose
Content-Type: application/octet-streamTells the browser these are raw bytes, not text to render.
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=employee.xlsTriggers the Save-As dialog and names the file.
codeExamples:
# Step 8 - application.properties
server.port=8181

#MySQL
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/test?autoReconnect=true&useSSL=false
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.MySQL8Dialect

expert.content:
poi Alone Only Gives You .xls

The dependency list has org.apache.poi:poi, which contains the HSSF classes and produces the 1997-era binary format. That format has hard limits people still hit:

Limit.xls (HSSF).xlsx (XSSF)
Rows per sheet65,5361,048,576
Columns per sheet25616,384
Dependencypoipoi-ooxml
Correct MIME typeapplication/vnd.ms-excelapplication/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet

Export 70,000 employees to HSSF and POI throws IllegalArgumentException: Invalid row number (65536) part-way through - after the response headers have already been sent, so the browser saves a truncated, corrupt file.

application/octet-stream works because it means "unknown binary", but the specific MIME type lets the operating system pick Excel to open it.
codeExamples:
<!-- For .xlsx, poi-ooxml (it pulls in poi transitively) -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.poi</groupId>
    <artifactId>poi-ooxml</artifactId>
    <version>5.2.5</version>
</dependency>

expert.content:
Large Exports: SXSSFWorkbook and Streaming the Query

Two independent memory problems sit in this endpoint, and both bite at the same scale.

ProblemFix
findAll() loads every row as a managed entityStream the results, or page through them
HSSFWorkbook/XSSFWorkbook hold the whole sheet in memorySXSSFWorkbook - keeps a sliding window of rows and flushes the rest to a temp file

With 500,000 employees the naive version needs gigabytes; the streaming version stays flat at a few hundred megabytes.

One caveat: SXSSFWorkbook writes rows to disk as it goes, so you must call dispose() to delete the temp files - otherwise the server's temp directory fills up.

Errors After the First Byte Cannot Be Reported

Writing directly into HttpServletResponse is efficient and has one sharp edge: once any byte has been written, the status code and headers are already sent. A failure after that point cannot become a 500 - the client just receives a truncated file.

response.setContentType(...)          headers queued
response.setHeader(...)               headers queued
workbook.write(outputStream)          FIRST BYTE -> headers committed
    |
    v
  exception here
    |
    v
Spring tries to send a 500 error page and cannot:
    java.lang.IllegalStateException: Cannot call sendError() after
    the response has been committed
The browser saves a corrupt .xls with HTTP 200.

For anything that can plausibly fail, build the workbook in memory first, then write it - so a failure still becomes a proper error response.

Formatting: Types, Widths and a Frozen Header

setCellValue() is overloaded, and which overload runs decides whether Excel sees a number or a string. Passing everything as a String is the usual reason a spreadsheet cannot be sorted or summed.

CallCell type in Excel
setCellValue(long) / (double)Numeric - sortable, summable
setCellValue(String)Text - "10" sorts before "9"
setCellValue(boolean)Boolean
setCellValue(Date) + a date styleDate. Without the style it shows as a serial number like 45183.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which library writes Excel files from Java?Apache POI.
What are the four core POI types?Workbook, Sheet, Row and Cell - each nested inside the one before it.
Difference between HSSF, XSSF and SXSSF?HSSF writes the old binary .xls; XSSF writes .xlsx; SXSSF writes .xlsx with a sliding in-memory window for very large files.
What is the row limit of a .xls file?65,536. Exceeding it throws IllegalArgumentException: Invalid row number. .xlsx allows 1,048,576.
Which dependency do you need for .xlsx?poi-ooxml - poi alone only provides HSSF.
Which headers turn a response into a file download?Content-Type (the MIME type) and Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=....
Why must dispose() be called on SXSSFWorkbook?It flushes rows to temporary files; without dispose() those files are never deleted.
Why can't you return a 500 after writing to the output stream?The first byte commits the response, so headers and status are already sent - sendError() then throws IllegalStateException and the client gets a truncated file.
How do you avoid that?Build the workbook into a ByteArrayOutputStream first and return it as a ResponseEntity<byte[]>.
Why do numbers sort wrongly in an export?They were written with the String overload of setCellValue, so Excel treats them as text.
Why does a date show as 45183?Excel stores dates as serial numbers; the cell needs a CellStyle with a date format applied.
When should you avoid autoSizeColumn?On large exports - it measures every cell in the column. Set fixed widths instead.

Writing PDF Data - Exporting from the Database into a PDF

Business requirement: you have employee data stored in the database and want to fetch it and save it into a PDF file.

Problem statement: design the REST API to fetch the data from the database and write it into a PDF file.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project   2. Add Maven dependencies   3. Create the model class
4. Create the service   5. Create the service implementation   6. Create the repository
7. Create the REST controller   8. Create PDFUtils   9. application.properties
10. Run   11. Postman   12. Check the output

The new dependency is iText 7, a Java library for generating PDFs.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

<dependency>

</dependency>
<!-- itext7-core is an aggregate POM, so <type>pom</type> is required.
     Without it Maven looks for a non-existent itext7-core-7.0.4.jar. -->

beginner.content:
The iText 7 Object Model

Four types, layered from the file outwards.

TypeRepresents
PdfWriterWhere the bytes go - an output stream or a file.
PdfDocumentThe low-level PDF document wrapped around that writer.
DocumentThe high-level layout API - you add paragraphs and tables to this.
Table / Cell / ParagraphThe content elements themselves.

OutputStream
     |
     v
 PdfWriter  ------>  PdfDocument  ------>  Document
                                              |
                                              +--> Paragraph  ("Employee Details")
                                              +--> Table
                                                     +--> Cell  ("id")
                                                     +--> Cell  ("name")
                                                     +--> Cell  ("city")

Steps 4 to 6 - Service, Implementation, Repository

The service does one thing: fetch the rows. The PDF building lives in its own utility class.

Step 8 - PDFUtils: Building the Document

new Table(new float[] { 20f, 50f, 30f }) creates three columns with those relative widths - so the name column is two and a half times the width of the id column.

new Cell(1, 3) creates a cell spanning 1 row and 3 columns - the merged title bar across the top of the table.

Step 7 - The REST Controller

Same two headers as any other download, with the PDF media type.
codeExamples:
# Step 9 - application.properties
server.port=8181

#MySQL
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/test?autoReconnect=true&useSSL=false
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

expert.content:
Swallowing the Exception Produces a Corrupt PDF

The original wraps the document building in try { ... } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); }. Two things go wrong with that.

ProblemConsequence
document.close() is inside the tryIf anything throws before it, the PDF is never finalised - no trailer, no cross-reference table. The file downloads and will not open.
The exception is only printedThe caller has no idea it failed, so the response still says 200 OK.

A PDF is only a valid PDF once it has been closed. close() belongs in a finally block or a try-with-resources.

iText Licensing - the Thing to Check Before You Ship

This matters more than any API detail here.

VersionLicence
iText 2.1.7 and earlierLGPL/MPL - permissive, but ancient and unmaintained.
iText 5 and iText 7AGPL, or a paid commercial licence.

AGPL is copyleft that extends over a network: if users interact with your application over HTTP - which is exactly what this endpoint does - you must release your entire application's source under the AGPL, or buy a commercial licence from the vendor.

For a closed-source commercial product this is a real cost, and it surprises teams late. Permissively-licensed alternatives:

LibraryLicenceNotes
Apache PDFBoxApache 2.0Lower-level; you position text yourself.
OpenPDFLGPL/MPLA fork of the last LGPL iText - closest drop-in.
Flying SaucerLGPLRenders XHTML + CSS to PDF; good with a Thymeleaf template.
JasperReportsLGPLFull reporting engine with a visual designer.
codeExamples:
<!-- OpenPDF - the closest permissive substitute -->
<dependency>
