expert.content:
Large Reports: Repeating Headers and Page Breaks

A table with 5,000 rows spills across a hundred pages. By default the header row appears only on page one, so every page after that is unlabelled columns.

MethodEffect
table.addHeaderCell(...)Marks a cell as part of the header - repeated on every page.
table.addFooterCell(...)Same for a footer row.
setSkipFirstHeader(true)Omit the header on the first page when a title already covers it.
document.add(new AreaBreak())Force a page break.
setLargeTable(true)Flush rows to the output as they are added, instead of holding the whole table in memory.

Non-Latin Text Needs an Embedded Font

The built-in PDF fonts cover Latin-1 only. Hindi, Marathi, Chinese or even a plain rupee sign renders as blanks or boxes - silently, with no exception.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which library generates the PDF here?iText 7, via the itext7-core aggregate POM.
What are the four main iText 7 types?PdfWriter (where bytes go), PdfDocument (the document), Document (the layout API), and elements like Table, Cell and Paragraph.
Why does <type>pom</type> matter for itext7-core?It is an aggregate POM, not a jar. Without it Maven fails looking for a jar that does not exist.
Why must document.close() always run?Closing writes the PDF trailer and cross-reference table. Skip it and the file is structurally invalid and will not open.
What does new Cell(1, 3) do?Creates a cell spanning 1 row and 3 columns - a merged title bar.
What do the floats in new Table(new float[]{20f, 50f, 30f}) mean?Relative column widths, so the middle column is 2.5x the first.
What is the licensing catch with iText 5 and 7?AGPL or a paid commercial licence. AGPL triggers over a network, so a web app serving PDFs must open-source its whole codebase or buy a licence.
Which permissive alternatives exist?Apache PDFBox (Apache 2.0), OpenPDF (LGPL/MPL), Flying Saucer for HTML-to-PDF, JasperReports.
How do you repeat a table header on every page?Use addHeaderCell() instead of addCell() for the header row.
How do you keep a huge report from exhausting memory?Create the table with largeTable = true, add it to the document first, then flush() periodically and complete() at the end.
Why does Hindi or a rupee sign come out blank?The built-in fonts are Latin-1 only. Embed a Unicode TTF with PdfEncodings.IDENTITY_H.
Why build the PDF in memory rather than streaming to the response?Once a byte is written the response is committed, so a later failure cannot become a 500 - the client saves a corrupt file instead.

beginner.content:
Sending Mail from a Spring Boot Application

Business requirement: an application often has to notify a user by email - a registration confirmation, a password reset link, an invoice, a nightly report. Rather than talking to an SMTP server by hand, Spring Boot gives you a configured mail client and you supply the message.

Problem statement: design a REST endpoint that accepts an email address and sends a message to it through Gmail's SMTP server.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project   2. Add spring-boot-starter-mail   3. Configure SMTP in application.properties
4. Model class   5. Mail service   6. REST controller   7. Run   8. Call it from Postman
9. Check the mailbox   10. Generate a Google App Password   11. Add email validation   12. Send an attachment

The starter pulls in Jakarta Mail (formerly JavaMail) and, more importantly, auto-configures a JavaMailSender bean from the spring.mail.* properties. That bean is the single thing you inject; you never open a socket or build a Session yourself.
codeExamples:
<!-- Step 2 - pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-mail</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Only spring-boot-starter-mail creates the JavaMailSender bean.
     Without it the application starts, but injecting JavaMailSender fails with:
     // OUTPUT:
     // Parameter 0 of constructor in com.velocity.service.MailService required
     // a bean of type 'org.springframework.mail.javamail.JavaMailSender'
     // that could not be found. -->

beginner.content:
Step 3 - application.properties

Every one of these keys is read by Spring Boot's MailSenderAutoConfiguration. Anything under spring.mail.properties.* is passed straight through to Jakarta Mail as a session property.

PropertyPurpose
spring.mail.hostThe SMTP server. smtp.gmail.com for Gmail.
spring.mail.port587 for STARTTLS, 465 for implicit SSL/TLS.
spring.mail.usernameThe account the mail is sent from.
spring.mail.passwordA Google App Password, never the account password.
...mail.smtp.authAuthenticate before sending; without it Gmail rejects the connection.
...mail.smtp.starttls.enableUpgrade the plain connection on port 587 to TLS.
...mail.smtp.connectiontimeoutCap how long a dead SMTP server can hold your request thread.

Correction to the source material. The PDF sets socketFactory.port=465, socketFactory.class=javax.net.ssl.SSLSocketFactory and socketFactory.fallback=false, and it says two-step verification "should not be enabled". Both are out of date. The socketFactory keys are a legacy JavaMail idiom superseded by mail.smtp.ssl.enable, and since May 2022 Google has removed the "less secure app" switch entirely: two-step verification must be on, because that is the only way to obtain an App Password. The steps later in the PDF that turn 2FA back off and paste the App Password into the account password field would leave you with no working credential at all.
codeExamples:
# Step 3 - application.properties  (port 587, STARTTLS - the current recommendation)
spring.mail.host=smtp.gmail.com
spring.mail.port=587
spring.mail.username=javaindustryexperience@gmail.com
spring.mail.password=${MAIL_APP_PASSWORD}

spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.auth=true
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.starttls.enable=true
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.starttls.required=true

# Never let a hung SMTP server pin a Tomcat thread for ever.
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.connectiontimeout=5000
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.timeout=5000
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.writetimeout=5000

server.port=8083

# Alternative: implicit SSL on 465, the port the PDF uses.
spring.mail.host=smtp.gmail.com
spring.mail.port=465
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.auth=true
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.ssl.enable=true

# The PDF's older equivalent - still works, but no longer the idiomatic form:
# spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.socketFactory.port=465
# spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.socketFactory.class=javax.net.ssl.SSLSocketFactory
# spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.socketFactory.fallback=false

beginner.content:
Step 4 - The model class

A plain holder for the recipient address.

Correction to the source material. The PDF declares the class as Users but every import and injection point refers to User, so the code as printed does not compile. It also annotates the model @Component and injects it into the controller with @Autowired. That makes the recipient address a singleton shared by every HTTP request - two users hitting the endpoint at the same moment can overwrite each other's address and the mail goes to the wrong person. A request-scoped value belongs in a local variable or a @RequestBody DTO, never in a singleton bean.

Step 5 - The mail service

SimpleMailMessage is the easy path: a to, a subject and a plain-text body. javaMailSender.send(...) opens the SMTP connection, authenticates, transfers the message and closes.

Note the constructor injection. Spring can autowire a single constructor without @Autowired since 4.3, and constructor injection makes the dependency final and the class testable without a container.

Step 6 - The REST controller

The endpoint takes the address as a query parameter and delegates to the service. MailException is the root of Spring's mail hierarchy and is unchecked, so catching it is a choice rather than an obligation.

Correction to the source material. The PDF catches MailException, prints it and still returns "Your mail has been sent successfully". The caller is told the mail went out when it did not. Return an accurate status - and note the URL in the PDF says port 8080 while application.properties sets server.port=8083, which is why the request appears to hang for students copying it verbatim.

Steps 7 to 9 - Run, call, and check the mailbox

Start the application, then send the request from Postman.

Request   Method: GET
URL: http://localhost:8083/sendmailapp?email=velocityjavapune@gmail.com
Params: key email, value velocityjavapune@gmail.com

Response   200 OK   Your mail has been sent successfully

The mail arrives in the recipient's inbox with the subject and body set in the service. The first time it is often filed as spam, because a message sent from a personal Gmail account through SMTP has no DKIM alignment with any sending domain.

Steps 10 to 21 - Getting a Google App Password

Gmail stopped accepting account passwords over SMTP in May 2022. An App Password is a 16-character credential tied to one application; it can be revoked on its own without changing your real password, and it does not grant access to the account's web session.

Go to https://myaccount.google.com/apppasswords
2-Step Verification must be ON - App Passwords do not exist without it
Pick an app and a device name, then Generate
Copy the 16-character value and Done - it is shown once and never again
Put it in spring.mail.password, ideally via an environment variable

Correction to the source material. Steps 16 to 19 of the PDF instruct you to turn 2-Step Verification back off and then paste the App Password into the Google account's password-change form. Do neither. Turning off 2FA revokes every App Password immediately, and pasting it as your account password replaces the credential you actually use to sign in. Leave 2FA on and leave the account password alone; the App Password is used only in application.properties.
codeExamples:
# Keep the credential OUT of the repository.
# Committed SMTP credentials are found by automated scanners within minutes
# and the account is then used to send spam until the provider suspends it.

# application.properties - reads from the environment, with no default:
spring.mail.password=${MAIL_APP_PASSWORD}

# Supply it at run time:
#   Linux/macOS :  export MAIL_APP_PASSWORD='abcd efgh ijkl mnop'
#   Windows     :  set MAIL_APP_PASSWORD=abcd efgh ijkl mnop
#   IDE         :  Run Configuration -> Environment tab
#   Container   :  a Kubernetes Secret mounted as an env var

# OUTPUT if the variable is missing:
// Could not resolve placeholder 'MAIL_APP_PASSWORD' in value "${MAIL_APP_PASSWORD}"
// - which is the correct behaviour. The application refuses to start rather
//   than silently trying to authenticate with an empty password.

beginner.content:
Email validation

Sending to a malformed address means a wasted SMTP round trip and an exception. Bean Validation rejects it before the service is reached.

StepWhat it does
Add spring-boot-starter-validationPuts Hibernate Validator on the classpath.
@Validated on the classNeeded for constraints on method parameters; @Valid alone only covers request bodies.
@Email on the parameterChecks the address is syntactically valid.

What @Email does not do: it checks syntax only. It cannot tell you the mailbox exists, that the domain has an MX record, or that the address is not a typo like gmial.com. For that you need a verification email with a one-time link - which is why almost every real signup flow has one.

Email with an attachment

SimpleMailMessage cannot carry a file. An attachment needs a MimeMessage, and MimeMessageHelper is the wrapper that saves you from building MIME parts by hand.

The second constructor argument is the important one: new MimeMessageHelper(mimeMessage, true) switches the message to multipart mode. Without that true, addAttachment throws IllegalStateException: Not in multipart mode.

Correction to the source material. The PDF's catch block is empty apart from a // Handle exception comment. A silently swallowed MessagingException means the caller gets "Email with attachment sent successfully!" for a mail that never left the process. Rethrow it wrapped, or return a failure status.

Application flow

 Postman
    |  GET /sendmailapp?email=...
    v
 UserController.sendingMail()
    |  builds a User with the address
    v
 MailService.sendMail(user)
    |  SimpleMailMessage: from / to / subject / text
    v
 JavaMailSender.send(message)          <- the auto-configured bean
    |
    |  opens a socket to smtp.gmail.com:587
    |  EHLO -> STARTTLS -> TLS handshake
    |  AUTH LOGIN  (username + App Password)
    |  MAIL FROM / RCPT TO / DATA
    |  250 2.0.0 OK   <- accepted for delivery
    v
 Gmail queues and delivers it
    |
    v
 Controller returns 200 "Your mail has been sent successfully"
Note what "250 OK" actually means: Gmail has accepted the message, not delivered it. A later bounce - unknown mailbox, full inbox, spam rejection at the receiving end - arrives asynchronously and your code never sees it.

expert.content:
JavaMailSender, MimeMessage and MimeMessageHelper

Three types with distinct roles, and interviewers reliably ask you to separate them.

TypeResponsibility
MailSenderThe narrow interface. Sends SimpleMailMessage only - no HTML, no attachments, no encoding control.
JavaMailSenderExtends it with createMimeMessage() and send(MimeMessage). This is what the starter auto-configures, as a JavaMailSenderImpl.
MimeMessageThe Jakarta Mail message itself. Assembling multipart bodies on it directly is verbose and easy to get wrong.
MimeMessageHelperA thin builder over MimeMessage: setTo, setText(body, isHtml), addAttachment, addInline, encoding.
MimeMessagePreparatorA callback form - sender.send(mimeMessage -> {...}) - that lets Spring own creation and exception translation.

addAttachment vs addInline. addAttachment produces a downloadable file. addInline registers a Content-ID so the HTML body can reference it with <img src="cid:logo">. Order matters: call setText before addInline, or the inline part is not linked and the image renders broken.

Plain text, HTML and multipart/alternative

An HTML-only mail is a mistake in production. Text-only clients, screen readers and some spam filters see an empty body, and a body that is HTML with no plain-text alternative measurably raises the spam score.

The correct shape is multipart/alternative: the same content twice, plain first and HTML second. Clients render the last part they understand.

FormWhen to use
SimpleMailMessageInternal alerts, cron output, anything a human will not look at closely.
setText(html, true)Quick HTML mail. Acceptable internally, weak for customer mail.
setText(plain, html)The production choice. One call, produces multipart/alternative.

Why an App Password or OAuth2 - and never a committed credential

Basic authentication over SMTP hands the server your account password in plain text inside a TLS tunnel. Whoever holds that string holds the whole account. Google closed this off in May 2022 by removing the "less secure apps" toggle.

CredentialRisk profile
Account passwordRejected by Gmail since 2022. Would grant full account access if it worked.
App Password16 characters, SMTP/IMAP only, revocable individually. Requires 2FA to exist. Still a long-lived static secret.
OAuth2 / XOAUTH2Short-lived access token from a refresh token, scoped to gmail.send. Revocable server-side, no password anywhere. The correct choice for a real service.
Transactional API (SES, SendGrid, Postmark)An API key rather than SMTP, plus bounce and complaint webhooks, DKIM signing and deliverability reporting.

Never commit SMTP credentials. Git history is permanent: deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it, and a repository that is public even briefly is scraped within minutes. A stolen sending credential is used for phishing, which gets the domain blacklisted long before anyone notices. Keep secrets in environment variables, Spring Cloud Config with encryption, Vault, or the platform's secret manager - and if one leaks, rotate it, because you cannot un-publish it.

Why Gmail SMTP is not a production mail channel. Free Gmail caps you at roughly 500 recipients a day and will lock the account for bursts. It also rewrites the From header to the authenticated account, so your carefully set sender address is discarded, and it gives you no bounce feed. Any real system uses a transactional provider with SPF, DKIM and DMARC aligned to its own domain.

Sending asynchronously - do not block the HTTP thread

An SMTP round trip takes 300 ms on a good day and 30 seconds when the provider is degraded. Sending inline means a Tomcat request thread is held for that entire time. With the default pool of 200 threads, a slow mail server takes the whole application down while the database sits idle.

@Async moves the send onto a separate executor and returns the HTTP response immediately.

@Async only works through a proxy. Calling an @Async method from another method of the same class runs it on the caller's thread - the invocation never leaves the object, so the proxy is bypassed. Put the async method on a different bean.
Never rely on the default executor. Without an explicit TaskExecutor bean, Boot 2.1+ supplies a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with an unbounded queue - a mail outage silently grows the queue until the heap is exhausted.
An @Async void method swallows exceptions. Return CompletableFuture, or register an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, or the failure is logged nowhere useful.

Why a mail failure must not roll back the business transaction

Consider registration: save the user, then send a welcome mail. If the send happens inside the transaction and SMTP is down, the exception propagates and the INSERT is rolled back. The user filled in the form, got a 500, and has no account - because a notification server was unavailable. That is the wrong trade: the account is the durable business fact and the mail is a courtesy.

The inverse failure is just as real. Send inside the transaction and let the transaction roll back afterwards for some other reason, and you have emailed the user about something that never happened - "your order is confirmed" for an order that does not exist. Mail cannot be un-sent.

The fix is to make the send happen strictly after a successful commit, and to isolate its failure. Spring's @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) does exactly this. For anything that must not be lost, write the message to an outbox table in the same transaction and have a scheduled worker drain it - the transactional outbox pattern.

Retries, timeouts and knowing what is worth retrying

SMTP failures split cleanly along the protocol's own reply codes, and retrying the wrong class of error wastes work and damages your sender reputation.

FailureRetry?
4xx - temporary (421 too many connections, 451 try again)Yes, with exponential backoff and jitter.
Connection refused / read timeoutYes - the server may simply be restarting.
5xx - permanent (550 no such mailbox, 553 bad address)No. Retrying a bad address forever looks like an attack to the receiving server.
535 authentication failedNo - the credential is wrong or revoked. Alert a human.

Timeouts are not optional. Jakarta Mail defaults to no timeout at all. A dead SMTP server holds the socket - and the thread - indefinitely. Always set mail.smtp.connectiontimeout, mail.smtp.timeout and mail.smtp.writetimeout.

Beyond retries, a circuit breaker stops you hammering a provider that is clearly down: after N consecutive failures the breaker opens, sends fail fast into the outbox, and a probe request tests recovery.

Templating the body with Thymeleaf

String-concatenated HTML in a service class is unmaintainable and unsafe. A name containing <script> is injected straight into the body; a designer cannot touch the layout without a redeploy; and translations are impossible.

Thymeleaf renders a template to a string, which then becomes the mail body. Two details matter for mail specifically:

Use TemplateEngine.process(name, context) - not a Spring MVC view resolver. There is no HTTP response to write to.
Thymeleaf escapes by default with th:text, so user-supplied values cannot inject markup. th:utext disables that - use it only on content you generated.
Email clients ignore most CSS. Inline styles and table layout are still the norm; Outlook renders with the Word engine.
Every link must be absolute. There is no base URL in an inbox, so /reset resolves to nothing.
codeExamples:
// src/main/resources/templates/mail/welcome.html

Welcome

Your enrolment for Course is confirmed.

Activate

date

expert.content:
Testing mail without sending any

Hitting a real SMTP server from a test is slow, flaky, rate-limited, and eventually mails a real person. Two approaches cover almost everything.

ApproachWhat it verifies
GreenMail (in-process SMTP)End to end: the message really left the sender and can be read back - headers, body, parts, attachments.
@MockBean JavaMailSenderThat the service called send, and with what. Fast, but proves nothing about MIME correctness.
MailHog / Mailpit in DockerManual and QA use - a fake SMTP server with a web inbox for eyeballing rendering.

Deliverability, and what actually determines whether the mail is read

The code is the easy part. Whether the message lands in the inbox or in spam is decided by DNS records you publish for the sending domain.

MechanismWhat it asserts
SPFA TXT record listing which servers may send for the domain.
DKIMA cryptographic signature over the headers and body, verified against a public key in DNS.
DMARCA policy saying what to do when SPF and DKIM fail to align, plus a reporting address.
List-UnsubscribeA one-click unsubscribe header. Since 2024 Gmail and Yahoo require it for bulk senders.
Bounce handlingRepeatedly mailing dead addresses raises your complaint rate and gets you throttled.

Legal constraints are real. Marketing mail under GDPR needs a lawful basis and a working unsubscribe; CAN-SPAM requires a physical postal address and honouring opt-outs within ten days. Transactional mail - password resets, receipts - is treated differently, which is precisely why you must not smuggle marketing content into a transactional message.

What to monitor. Sends attempted, sends failed by exception type, queue depth on the mail executor, outbox age of the oldest unsent row, and provider-reported bounce and complaint rates. A silently growing outbox is the failure mode that goes unnoticed longest.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Which bean does spring-boot-starter-mail auto-configure, and from what?A JavaMailSenderImpl as JavaMailSender, built by MailSenderAutoConfiguration from the spring.mail.* properties. It backs off if you define your own.
When must you use MimeMessage rather than SimpleMailMessage?For HTML bodies, attachments, inline images, explicit character encoding, or custom headers. SimpleMailMessage handles plain text only.
What does the boolean in new MimeMessageHelper(msg, true) do?Switches the message to multipart mode. Without it addAttachment throws IllegalStateException: Not in multipart mode.
Why can you not use your Gmail account password?Google removed "less secure app access" in May 2022. SMTP now requires an App Password (which needs 2FA enabled) or OAuth2 XOAUTH2; the account password returns 535-5.7.8.
Why should a mail failure not roll back the business transaction?The durable fact - the registration, the order - matters more than the notification. Rolling it back because SMTP is down loses real data. Publish an AFTER_COMMIT event, or use a transactional outbox.
What breaks if you send mail inside the transaction and it later rolls back?You have told the user something happened that did not. Mail cannot be recalled, so the send must be strictly after commit.
Why does @Async sometimes do nothing?Self-invocation. Calling the annotated method from another method of the same bean bypasses the proxy, so it runs on the caller's thread. Move it to a separate bean, and ensure @EnableAsync is present.
What is wrong with the default async executor for mail?Its queue is unbounded, so a mail outage grows the queue until the heap is exhausted. Define a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with a fixed queueCapacity and a rejection policy.
Which SMTP failures are worth retrying?4xx temporary codes and connection or read timeouts, with exponential backoff and jitter. Never retry 5xx permanent codes such as 550, or 535 authentication failures.
Why set mail.smtp.timeout?Jakarta Mail has no default timeout. A hung SMTP server holds the socket and the thread indefinitely, which exhausts the Tomcat pool and takes down endpoints unrelated to mail.
How do you render the body with Thymeleaf?Inject TemplateEngine and call process(templateName, context) to get a String, then pass it to helper.setText(plain, html). Do not go through a Spring MVC view resolver.
Why send both plain text and HTML?It produces multipart/alternative. Text-only clients and screen readers get readable content, and HTML with no plain alternative raises the spam score.
How do you test mail without a real server?GreenMail as an in-process SMTP server, with @DynamicPropertySource pointing spring.mail.port at its random port, then assert on the received MimeMessage. A @MockBean JavaMailSender only proves the call was made.
What stops the mail landing in the inbox even when the code is correct?Missing SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for the sending domain, HTML-only bodies, no List-Unsubscribe header on bulk mail, and a poor sender reputation from unhandled bounces.

Sending an OTP by SMS from a Spring Boot Application

Business requirement: before you trust that a phone number belongs to the person using it, you send a short numeric code to that number and ask them to type it back. Registration, password reset, payment confirmation and "log in with your mobile" all rest on the same mechanism - a one-time password, or OTP.

Problem statement: expose one endpoint that generates an OTP and sends it to a mobile number through an SMS gateway, and a second endpoint that verifies the code the user types back.

Pre-requisite: an account on Twilio, which is the SMS gateway used here. Twilio gives you three things - an Account SID (effectively the username), an Auth Token (the password) and a purchased sender number that messages are sent from. Your application never speaks to a mobile network; it makes an HTTPS call to Twilio, and Twilio hands the message to the carrier.

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project   2. Add the Maven dependencies   3. Create the SMS DTO
4. Create the REST controller   5. Run   6. Call it from Postman   7. Create WebSocketConfig
8. Create SMSService   9. Back to the controller   10. Run   11. Postman again
12. Create VerifyOtpController   13. Create the TempOtp DTO   14. Create StoreOtp
15. Verify from Postman   16. Replace the static store with server-side OtpService

The material builds the flow twice on purpose. The first pass hard-codes the expected OTP so you can see the request and response shapes; the second pass introduces a real server-side store with an expiry. Read the second version as the intended answer - the first is scaffolding.

Step 2 - Maven dependencies

Four dependencies matter: spring-boot-starter-web for the REST endpoints, the Twilio Java SDK for the gateway call, spring-boot-starter-websocket for the live status feed the material pushes to a browser, and Guava for the expiring cache that holds the OTP.

Correction to the source material. The PDF pins spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf to 2.3.3.RELEASE and Guava to 19.0. Never pin a version on a starter that the Spring Boot parent POM already manages - you get two different Spring versions on the classpath and a NoSuchMethodError at runtime that is painful to diagnose. Guava 19.0 dates from 2015; use a current release. The Twilio SDK at 7.1.0 is likewise several major versions behind, and the modern SDK has a different builder API.

</dependency>

<dependency>

<!-- The PDF also adds thymeleaf pinned to 2.3.3.RELEASE. Doing that on a

     Remove the <version> tag and let the parent decide. -->

beginner.content:
Steps 3 and 4 - The DTO and the first controller

SMS is a plain request body holding the destination number. The first version of the controller does nothing but print it, which is enough to confirm that JSON binding works before any gateway is involved.

Correction to the source material. The DTO is declared package com.dto; but the controller imports com.model.SMS. That does not compile. Keep the package consistent - one package name for one class. A phone number should also be validated on the way in: Twilio requires E.164 format (a leading +, the country code, then the national number, digits only). Anything else is rejected by the API with a 400 after you have already paid for the round trip.

Step 7 - WebSocketConfig

The material pushes a live status line - "SMS has been sent" - to a browser page over STOMP over WebSocket, so a dashboard can watch sends happen without polling.

ElementPurpose
@EnableWebSocketMessageBrokerTurns on STOMP message handling backed by a message broker.
WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurerThe callback interface where you declare the broker and the endpoints.
enableSimpleBroker("/lesson")An in-memory broker. Anything published to a destination starting /lesson is fanned out to every client subscribed to it.
setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app")Messages sent by a client to /app/... are routed to @MessageMapping methods rather than straight to the broker.
registerStompEndpointsThe URL the browser opens the WebSocket handshake against - here /gs-guide-websocket.
.withSockJS()A fallback transport for clients or proxies that cannot hold a WebSocket open.

Note on the simple broker. enableSimpleBroker keeps subscriptions in the heap of one JVM. Run two instances behind a load balancer and a client connected to instance A never sees a message published on instance B. Production uses a real broker relay - RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ - via enableStompBrokerRelay.

Step 8 - SMSService and the Twilio call

Twilio.init(sid, token) installs the credentials into a static holder; Message.creator(to, from, body).create() then makes the HTTPS POST to Twilio's REST API and returns a Message with an SID and a status.

The credentials in the PDF are hard-coded in the class, and one pair is a real-looking live Account SID and Auth Token.
Committing a Twilio Auth Token is a direct financial loss, not a theoretical one. Public repositories are scanned continuously; a leaked token is used within minutes to pump traffic to premium-rate numbers that the attacker earns a share of, and the bill lands on you.
Put the SID, token and sender number in application.properties read from environment variables, and keep the properties file's real values out of Git.

Correction to the source material. The generator is (int)(Math.random() * (max - min + 1) + min). Math.random() is backed by java.util.Random, a 48-bit linear congruential generator whose entire internal state can be recovered from two consecutive outputs. An attacker who has ever received one OTP from your system can compute the next one. Use SecureRandom. This is covered in full in the expert section.
codeExamples:
# application.properties - nothing secret is written here literally
twilio.account-sid=${TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID}
twilio.auth-token=${TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN}
twilio.from-number=${TWILIO_FROM_NUMBER}

server.port=8080

# Supply them at run time:
#   Linux/macOS :  export TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN='...'
#   Windows     :  set TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN=...
#   IDE         :  Run Configuration -> Environment tab
#   Container   :  a Kubernetes Secret mounted as an env var
#
# OUTPUT if the variable is absent - and this is the correct behaviour:
# Could not resolve placeholder 'TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN' in value "${TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN}"
# The application refuses to start rather than calling Twilio unauthenticated.

beginner.content:
Step 9 - The controller, now with the send and the WebSocket feed

The controller calls the service and publishes a status line to /lesson/sms so a connected dashboard sees the result. A second endpoint receives Twilio's delivery callback.

Correction to the source material. Two problems here.

First, the method returns void, so the caller gets 200 OK with an empty body whether the send worked or not - and when it throws, throw e produces a raw 500 with a stack trace. Return a proper ResponseEntity.

Second, the broadcast contains the full phone number. enableSimpleBroker fans a message out to every client subscribed to that destination, with no per-user filtering, and the endpoint has no authentication. Anyone who can open the WebSocket sees every number your system texts. Publish to a user-scoped destination, or publish only a non-identifying event.

Steps 12 to 15 - Verifying the code, the first (broken) version

The material's first verification controller compares the submitted code against the literal 1234, then replaces that with a StoreOtp class holding a static int. Both are placeholders that must not survive into anything real.

Comparing against a hard-coded 1234 means every user's OTP is 1234. There is nothing to verify.
private static int otp in StoreOtp is one field for the whole JVM. Two users requesting a code at the same time overwrite each other, and the second user's code verifies the first user's session. It is a data race and an authentication bypass in one line.
@Controller instead of @RestController makes return "Correct OTP" a view name. Spring then tries to resolve a template called Correct OTP and the response is a 500 or a 404, not the string.
No expiry, no attempt limit, no single-use invalidation. The code stays valid for ever and can be guessed at any rate the network allows.

Correction to the source material. The VerifyOtpController in step 13 also carries a stray import org.apache.http.annotation.Contract; that nothing uses, and TempOtp is first declared with only an otp field while the later version calls tempOtp.getPhoneNo() - the field and its accessor have to be added or that call does not compile.

Server-side verification with OtpService

The second half of the material replaces the static field with a Guava LoadingCache keyed by phone number, with expireAfterWrite. That is the right shape: an OTP is a short-lived value that must expire on its own even if nobody ever verifies it.

MethodResponsibility
generateOTP(key)Produce a six-digit code and store it against the phone number.
getOTP(key)Read the stored code back, or nothing if it expired.
clearOTP(key)Invalidate the entry so the code cannot be reused.
expireAfterWriteThe entry disappears N minutes after it was written, regardless of reads.

Correction to the source material - and this one is an authentication bypass. The PDF's getOTP is:

try { return otpCache.get(key); } catch (Exception e) { return 0; }

The CacheLoader.load returns null, so for a key with no OTP Guava throws InvalidCacheLoadException, which is caught, and the method returns 0. The controller then compares tempOtp.getOtp() == 0 against an int field that defaults to 0 when the JSON omits it. Posting {"phoneNo":"+91...","otp":0} - or omitting otp entirely - verifies successfully for any number that has no pending code. Use a Cache rather than a LoadingCache, return Optional, and never let "absent" collapse into a value a caller can submit.

Application flow

 SEND
 ----
 Postman  POST /mobileNo  {"phoneNumber":"+919876543210"}
    |
    v
 SMSController.smsSubmit()          @Valid checks E.164 shape
    |
    v
 SmsService.sendOtp(number)
    |
    +--> OtpService.generateAndStore()
    |        SecureRandom -> "418203"
    |        cache.put("+919876543210", hash("418203"))   TTL 5 min
    |
    +--> Twilio  Message.creator(to, from, body).create()
    |        HTTPS POST api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/.../Messages.json
    |        <- 201 Created  {"sid":"SM3f1a...","status":"queued"}
    |
    +--> SimpMessagingTemplate -> /lesson/sms  "code sent to *******210"
    v
 202 Accepted "If that number is valid, a code has been sent."
                                             carrier delivers the SMS
 VERIFY
 ------
 Postman  POST /otp  {"phoneNo":"+919876543210","otp":"418203"}
    |
    v
 VerifyOtpController.verifyOtp()
    |
    +--> attempt counter for this number: 1 of 5
    +--> OtpService.peek()  -> hash present, not expired
    +--> constant-time compare of hash(submitted) with stored hash
    |
    +--> match: cache.invalidate(number)      <- single use
    v
 200 OK "Correct OTP"      |  401 "Incorrect OTP" on mismatch, expiry
                           |       or attempt limit reached
The two endpoints are independent HTTP requests. Nothing links them except the phone number used as the cache key - which is exactly why the key must be the number and never a static field.

expert.content:
Never store the OTP in plain text

An OTP is a credential. For the few minutes it is alive it grants exactly the same authority as a password - it proves possession of the phone and, in most flows, completes a login or authorises a payment. Treat it as a password: store only a hash.

The PDF holds the code as an int in a Guava cache. Every place that value passes through becomes a place it can leak - a heap dump taken for an unrelated memory investigation, an APM agent capturing local variables, a toString() on the cache in a debug log, or a support engineer with read access to a Redis instance. The PDF also prints it: System.out.println("number>>>>>>" + number) puts every live OTP into the application log, where log shipping copies it to a search index that a far wider group can read.

ChoiceGuidance
AlgorithmA fast hash is correct here, not BCrypt. The input space is only 106, so slow hashing buys little; the protection comes from expiry and attempt limits. HMAC-SHA-256 with a server-side pepper is the practical choice.
Why HMAC and not bare SHA-256A bare hash of six digits is trivially reversed by a rainbow table of a million entries. Keyed with a secret the attacker does not have, that table cannot be built.
What binds into the hashThe phone number and the purpose ("login", "payment"), so a code issued for one action cannot be replayed against another.
Never log itNot at DEBUG, not in an exception message, not in a Twilio error body you echo back.

SecureRandom, and why java.util.Random is a vulnerability

java.util.Random and Math.random() implement a linear congruential generator with a 48-bit seed. It is fast and statistically even, which is why it passes casual inspection - and it is completely predictable, which is why it must never generate a credential.

The state update is seed = (seed * 0x5DEECE66D + 0xB) mod 2^48. Each nextInt reveals the top 32 bits of the new seed. Two consecutive outputs leave only 216 possibilities for the missing low bits - 65,536 candidates, brute-forced in milliseconds. Recover the seed and you can compute every OTP the service will ever issue, for every user.

The attack is concrete. Register two accounts you control, receive two OTPs, recover the seed, then predict the code sent to someone else's phone. No interception is required at all.
SecureRandom draws from the operating system's CSPRNG - /dev/urandom on Linux, CryptGenRandom on Windows - and its outputs reveal nothing about future ones.
Construct it once and share it. It is thread-safe. A new SecureRandom() per request forces reseeding and shows up as contention under load.
Do not use SecureRandom.getInstance("SHA1PRNG") with an explicit setSeed. Seeding it yourself replaces the OS entropy with whatever you supplied, which is usually System.currentTimeMillis() and therefore guessable.

Also fix the range. 100000 + random.nextInt(900000) yields 900,000 values, not a million: no code ever starts with a zero. That is a 10% reduction in the key space given away for nothing. Generate nextInt(1_000_000) and zero-pad, which requires the code to be a String - another reason the PDF's int field is wrong.

Expiry, single use, and attempt limiting

A six-digit OTP has one million possible values. That sounds like a lot until you notice that unlimited guessing needs on average 500,000 attempts, and a script doing 200 requests a second gets there in about forty minutes. The entropy of the code is not what protects it - the attempt limit is.

ControlWhy it is required
Short expiryFive minutes is the usual figure. It bounds the window for an intercepted or shoulder-surfed code, and it caps how long a brute-force run has. The PDF's ten minutes doubles that window.
Single useInvalidate on the first successful verification. Without it a code recovered from a screenshot, a notification preview or a shared phone stays valid for the rest of its TTL.
Invalidate on failure tooAfter N wrong guesses, delete the code - do not merely reject the request. Otherwise the attacker keeps guessing against a target that is still there.
Attempt limitingFive attempts per issued code. With five guesses out of a million the success probability is 1 in 200,000 per code - now genuinely infeasible.
Cap resendsOtherwise the attacker requests a fresh code after every five failures and the per-code limit means nothing. Limit issuance per number per hour.
Atomic counterRead-check-increment must be atomic, or a burst of concurrent requests all read "attempt 4" and all proceed.

Uniform failure responses. Wrong code, expired code, no code outstanding and attempt limit exceeded must return the same status and the same body. A distinct "code expired" message tells the attacker their timing was wrong rather than their guess, and a distinct "no OTP for this number" turns the endpoint into a user-enumeration oracle.

Rate limiting: SMS pumping is a financial attack, not an inconvenience

The /mobileNo endpoint spends real money on every call. Left unlimited it is not a denial-of-service risk so much as a revenue channel for the attacker.

SMS pumping, also called toll fraud or artificially inflated traffic, works like this. Fraudsters control blocks of premium-rate mobile numbers, or have a revenue-share arrangement with a small carrier. They script your public OTP endpoint to send tens of thousands of messages to those ranges. Each message costs you between a few cents and several dollars depending on destination; the carrier pays a share of that back to the fraudster. Nobody ever reads the messages. Real companies have lost seven-figure sums in a weekend this way, and it is the single most common way an unprotected OTP endpoint turns into a bill.

LimitWhat it stops
Per phone number3 sends per hour, 10 per day. Stops repeated targeting of one victim and caps the resend loop that defeats attempt limiting.
Per IP address10 sends per hour. Stops one script walking a range of numbers - the per-number limit alone does nothing against that.
Per country / prefixA daily cap per destination country, and an allow-list if you only serve a few. Pumping targets expensive, obscure ranges.
Global spend capA hard ceiling on messages per hour across the whole service, with an alert. This is the last line and it is what actually stops the bleeding at 3 a.m.
Cooldown between sends60 seconds before a resend to the same number, enforced server-side, not by a disabled button.
CAPTCHA or proof of workApplied after the first send from an IP, or on any anomaly. Cheap for a real user, expensive at scale.

Both dimensions are needed. Per-number limiting alone lets one host text a million distinct numbers. Per-IP limiting alone lets a botnet hit one number from ten thousand hosts. Neither is a substitute for the other, and the global cap catches the case where the attacker is distributed enough to slip under both.

Constant-time comparison

String.equals and == on the stored value both short-circuit on the first differing byte. The time a comparison takes therefore depends on how many leading characters matched, and that difference is measurable.

Against a six-digit code the attack is a digit-at-a-time search: guess the first digit ten times, keep the one that took marginally longer, move to the second. That converts a 106 search into roughly 60 measurements. In practice network jitter buries a single measurement, so the attacker averages over many samples - which is exactly what a script does well, and why the defence is cheap enough to just always apply.

MessageDigest.isEqual is the standard answer in Java: it compares the full length regardless of where the first mismatch occurs. Compare the hashes, not the codes, which also removes the length side-channel because every hash is the same length.

Comparing hashes with MessageDigest.isEqual is safe.
Comparing plaintext OTPs with equals leaks a timing signal and means you stored plaintext.
Arrays.equals(byte[], byte[]) is not constant time - it returns early.
An attempt limit of five is itself a strong mitigation, because a timing attack needs thousands of samples. Constant-time comparison is defence in depth, and the same discipline applies to API keys and session tokens where no attempt limit exists.

Why SMS is the weakest second factor

This is the question that separates someone who has implemented OTP from someone who understands it. SMS OTP is better than nothing and much better than a password alone, but it is the weakest of the mainstream second factors, and knowing why tells you when it is acceptable.

WeaknessHow it works
SIM swapThe attacker social-engineers or bribes a carrier employee into porting the victim's number to a SIM they control. Every SMS then arrives on the attacker's phone. No technical flaw in your code is involved and nothing you do server-side prevents it.
SS7 interceptionThe signalling network that routes messages between carriers has effectively no authentication between operators. Anyone with SS7 access - obtainable from small carriers worldwide - can reroute or copy messages for an arbitrary number.
Not end-to-end encryptedThe message is plaintext at the carrier and at every intermediary aggregator. Your SMS provider's staff can read every code you send.
Lock-screen previewsThe code is legible on a locked phone by default, so physical proximity is enough.
MalwareAn Android app with SMS read permission forwards codes silently. Whole malware families exist for exactly this.
Phishing relayA convincing fake login page asks for the code and replays it to the real site within its five-minute window. Any shared-secret OTP, including TOTP, falls to this.
Delivery is unreliableRoaming, carrier filtering and aggregator outages lose messages. Users abandon signup, and support gets the call.

NIST deprecated it. Special Publication 800-63B flagged SMS as a restricted authenticator: implementers must assess the risk of the channel, warn users, and offer an alternative. It has not been banned, but it is no longer recommended for anything of consequence.

FactorAssessment
SMS OTPWeakest. Vulnerable to SIM swap, SS7 and phishing. Costs money per message and invites pumping fraud.
TOTP (authenticator app, RFC 6238)Stronger and free. The shared secret never leaves the device after enrolment, so there is no channel to intercept. Still phishable in real time.
Push approvalGood usability, resists interception. Vulnerable to notification fatigue - users approve prompts reflexively - so use number matching.
WebAuthn / passkeysThe strongest. The credential is a private key bound to the site's origin, so a phishing site cannot elicit a usable response. Phishing-resistant by construction; this is what regulated systems are moving to.

Where SMS OTP still earns its place: proving that a phone number is reachable and belongs to the person supplying it - the actual requirement in this material. As number verification it is the right tool. As a login second factor for a bank it is not.

Keeping the provider credentials out of the repository

The PDF hard-codes an Account SID and an Auth Token as private final String fields, with a second commented-out pair below them. Once that is committed, the token is public for the life of the repository.

Deleting the line later does not help. Git keeps every revision. git log -p recovers it, and so does every clone anyone has already taken.
Scanners find it in minutes. Automated crawlers watch public push events continuously and specifically match Twilio SID patterns - AC followed by 32 hex characters is unmistakable.
The consequence is a bill. A stolen Twilio token is used to pump premium traffic, and the charges are yours until you notice.
Rotation is the only remedy. If a token has ever been committed, regenerate it in the Twilio console. History rewriting with git filter-repo does not un-publish anything.

MechanismGuidance
Environment variablesThe minimum. @Value("${twilio.auth-token}") resolving to ${TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN}, with no default so a missing value fails startup.
.gitignoreIgnore application-local.properties and commit a .example file with empty values, so a new developer sees which keys exist without seeing any secret.
Secret managerVault, AWS Secrets Manager or a Kubernetes Secret with a CSI driver. Gives you rotation and an audit trail of who read what.
API Keys instead of the Auth TokenTwilio API Keys are per-application, individually revocable credentials. Revoking one does not break every other integration, unlike the account Auth Token.
Pre-commit scanninggitleaks or trufflehog as a hook and in CI. It catches the mistake before the push, which is the only point at which it is still cheap.
Least privilegeScope the key to messaging. A key that can also read message bodies or manage sub-accounts turns a leak into a much larger incident.

Sending asynchronously, and not rolling back the business transaction

An HTTPS call to Twilio takes 200 ms when everything is healthy and thirty seconds when it is not. The PDF sends inline, on the Tomcat request thread. With the default pool of 200 threads, a degraded SMS provider consumes every thread and takes down endpoints that have nothing to do with SMS.

@Async moves the send onto a bounded executor and returns immediately. That is also the honest response shape: you cannot know at request time whether the message was delivered, only that it was accepted for sending. Return 202 Accepted.

Store the OTP before the send, synchronously. If the send is async but the store is too, a fast user typing the code from a fast SMS can verify before the record exists.
@Async works only through the proxy. Calling an @Async method from another method of the same bean runs it on the caller's thread - the call never leaves the object.
Bound the queue. Boot's default executor has an unbounded queue: a provider outage grows it until the heap is exhausted. Set queueCapacity and a rejection policy.
An @Async void method swallows exceptions. Return CompletableFuture or register an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler.

The transaction boundary

Consider registration: save the user, then text a verification code. If the send sits inside the transaction and Twilio is down, the exception propagates and the INSERT is rolled back. The user filled in the form, saw a 500, and has no account - because an SMS gateway was unavailable. That is the wrong trade. The account is the durable business fact; the message is a step in a flow that can be retried.

The inverse is just as real. Send inside the transaction, let it roll back afterwards for an unrelated reason, and you have texted a code for an account that does not exist - or worse, "your payment of 25,000 is confirmed" for a payment that was rolled back. An SMS cannot be recalled.

@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) makes the send happen strictly after a successful commit and isolates its failure. For messages that must not be lost, write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction and drain it from a scheduled worker - the transactional outbox pattern.

Where the OTP lives, and what else breaks in production

The Guava cache is in the heap of one JVM. That is fine for the classroom and wrong the moment there are two instances.

ConcernReality
In-memory cache and horizontal scalingA load balancer sends the send to instance A and the verify to instance B. Instance B has no record and every verification fails intermittently - a bug that looks random and is very hard to reproduce locally.
Restarts and deploymentsEvery outstanding OTP is lost on restart. A rolling deploy during business hours breaks verification for anyone mid-flow.
Unbounded growthCacheBuilder without maximumSize is a memory leak an attacker can drive by sending requests for a million distinct numbers.
Redis as the storeSET key hash EX 300 NX gives expiry, atomicity and sharing across instances in one command. INCR gives you an atomic attempt counter. This is the standard production answer.
Twilio VerifyTwilio's own Verify API generates, stores, expires and rate-limits the code server-side. You never see the OTP at all, which removes most of this topic's failure modes. Worth naming in an interview.
Delivery statusstatus=queued from create() means Twilio accepted it, not that it arrived. Real delivery comes back later on the status callback webhook - validate X-Twilio-Signature before trusting it.
AuditingLog every issue and verify with the masked number, source IP, purpose and outcome - never the code itself. This is what an incident investigation actually needs.
TestingTwilio publishes magic test credentials and numbers that exercise each error path without sending anything. In unit tests, mock the client and inject a fixed SecureRandom; never call a live gateway from CI.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why must an OTP never be stored in plain text?It is a credential with the same authority as a password for its lifetime. Store an HMAC-SHA-256 keyed with a server-side pepper, so a heap dump, a leaked cache or a debug log yields nothing usable. A bare SHA-256 is insufficient - a rainbow table of a million six-digit codes is trivial to build.
What is wrong with java.util.Random or Math.random() for an OTP?It is a 48-bit linear congruential generator. Two consecutive outputs narrow the seed to 216 candidates, which is brute-forced in milliseconds; from there every future OTP is predictable. Use SecureRandom, constructed once and shared.
What is wrong with 100000 + random.nextInt(900000) beyond the PRNG?It generates 900,000 values, not a million - no code can start with zero. Use nextInt(1_000_000) and zero-pad to six characters, which requires the OTP to be a String.
Why is a six-digit code safe at all, given only a million possibilities?Because of the attempt limit, not the entropy. Five attempts per code gives a 1-in-200,000 success probability. With unlimited guessing an attacker succeeds in under an hour.
Why must the OTP be invalidated after a failed-attempt limit, not just rejected?Rejecting leaves the code alive for the rest of its TTL, so the attacker keeps guessing. Delete the record, and cap resends per number as well, or a fresh code after every five failures defeats the limit entirely.
What is SMS pumping and how do you defend against it?Fraudsters script your send endpoint to text premium-rate numbers they earn revenue share on; the messages are never read and you pay for every one. Defend with rate limits per phone number and per IP, per-country caps, a global hourly send ceiling with alerting, a resend cooldown, and CAPTCHA on anomalies.
Why is per-number rate limiting alone not enough?It stops repeated targeting of one victim but not one script walking a million distinct numbers. Per-IP limiting stops that but not a botnet hitting one number. Both are needed, plus a global cap for distributed traffic that slips under each.
Why compare OTP hashes in constant time?String.equals returns on the first differing byte, so response time leaks how many leading characters matched, turning a 106 search into about 60 averaged measurements. Use MessageDigest.isEqual. Arrays.equals is not constant time.
Why is SMS the weakest second factor?SIM swap moves the number to the attacker with no flaw in your code; SS7 has no inter-carrier authentication, so messages can be rerouted; the text is plaintext at every intermediary; lock-screen previews and SMS-reading malware expose it. NIST SP 800-63B restricts it. TOTP is stronger, and WebAuthn/passkeys are phishing-resistant by construction.
What is the recovery-path mistake with strong factors?Protecting an account with a passkey but allowing an SMS code to reset it makes the account only as strong as SMS. An attacker always takes the weakest route.
Where do the Twilio Account SID and Auth Token belong?In environment variables or a secret manager, read through @Value or @ConfigurationProperties with no default so a missing value fails startup. Never in source - a committed token is scanned and used within minutes, deleting the line does not remove it from history, and the only remedy is rotation. Prefer a revocable API Key over the account Auth Token.
Why should the send be asynchronous?The gateway call takes 200 ms healthy and 30 s degraded. Sending inline pins Tomcat threads and a slow provider takes down unrelated endpoints. Use @Async with a bounded executor and return 202 Accepted - you cannot know delivery at request time anyway. Store the OTP synchronously first, or verification can race the store.
Why must an SMS failure not roll back the business transaction?The registration or order is the durable fact; the message is a retryable step. Rolling back because a third-party gateway is down loses real data. Equally, sending inside a transaction that later rolls back tells the user something happened that did not - and an SMS cannot be recalled. Use @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT), or a transactional outbox when the message must not be lost.
What breaks when the OTP lives in an in-memory cache?With more than one instance the send lands on A and the verify on B, so verification fails intermittently; a restart drops every outstanding code; and an unbounded cache is a memory leak an attacker can drive. Use Redis with SET ... EX and INCR for an atomic shared attempt counter.

beginner.content:
Push Notifications

This topic is being written and will be published shortly.

In the meantime, the surrounding module already covers the ground it sits on - work through the topics either side of it and come back once this one is live.

What is Swagger?

• Swagger is used for documenting the API, and you can write or edit that documentation.
• Swagger 2 is an open-source project used to generate REST API documents for RESTful web services.
• It provides a user interface to access your RESTful web services through the web browser.

Why do we use Swagger?

Suppose you have an API with several fields - first name, last name, city, mobile number - and in future you want to add more fields and make further changes to the service. Updating a document manually every time is a big and tedious task, and the document drifts out of date the moment someone forgets.

Swagger reads the code itself, so the documentation cannot fall behind the API.

Steps

1-8. Build the usual project: model, service, implementation, repository, REST controller, application.properties
9. Add the Swagger Maven dependencies
10. Add @EnableSwagger2 and a Docket bean to the main class
11. Annotate the controller methods with descriptions
12. Run the application
13. Open the browser at the Swagger URL
14. Try the endpoints from the UI

Step 9 - Add the Swagger Dependencies

Springfox provides both the generator and the web UI.
codeExamples:
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.springfox</groupId>
    <artifactId>springfox-swagger2</artifactId>
    <version>2.9.2</version>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.springfox</groupId>
    <artifactId>springfox-swagger-ui</artifactId>
    <version>2.9.2</version>
</dependency>
<!-- springfox-swagger2 scans the controllers and produces the
     OpenAPI JSON; springfox-swagger-ui serves the HTML page
     that renders it. -->

# Step 8 - application.properties
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/8julyspringbootbatch
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.dialect=org.hibernate.dialect.MySQL8Dialect

beginner.content:
Step 10 - Enable Swagger in the Main Class

Two things go here: the @EnableSwagger2 annotation, and a Docket bean that tells Swagger which endpoints to document.

PiecePurpose
@EnableSwagger2Switches on Springfox's auto-configuration.
DocketThe configuration object - which paths and which controllers to include.
RequestHandlerSelectors.any()Scan every controller.
PathSelectors.any()Include every path.

Step 11 - Document the Controller Methods

The annotations turn a bare endpoint list into readable documentation.

AnnotationPurpose
@ApiOperationA one-line description of what the method does.
@ApiResponses / @ApiResponseThe status codes the endpoint can return, with a message for each.
@ApiOn the class - names and describes the whole controller group.
@ApiParamDescribes a single parameter.

Steps 12 to 14 - Open the UI and Try It

Run the application, then open the browser at:

http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html

The page lists every endpoint with its method, path and description. For each one:

1. Click the endpoint to expand it.
2. Click Try it out.
3. Fill in the parameters or the request body.
4. Click Execute.
5. The response body, status code and headers appear below - and the console shows the SQL.

URLWhat it serves
/swagger-ui.htmlThe interactive HTML page (Springfox 2.x).
/v2/api-docsThe raw OpenAPI JSON the page is built from.

expert.content:
Springfox Is Dead - Use springdoc-openapi

This is the most important practical point about the walkthrough. Springfox 2.9.2 dates from 2018 and the project is abandoned - its last release was 3.0.0 in 2020.

Springfox on...Result
Spring Boot 2.0-2.5Works.
Spring Boot 2.6+Fails at startup - Failed to start bean 'documentationPluginsBootstrapper', caused by the change from ant-path-matcher to PathPatternParser.
Spring Boot 3.xDoes not work at all - Springfox uses javax.*, Boot 3 uses jakarta.*.

The replacement is springdoc-openapi: actively maintained, supports OpenAPI 3, and needs no @EnableSwagger2 and no Docket bean at all.
codeExamples:
# The Springfox failure on Boot 2.6+, in full:
org.springframework.context.ApplicationContextException:
  Failed to start bean 'documentationPluginsBootstrapper';
  nested exception is java.lang.NullPointerException

# The documented workaround is to revert the path matching strategy:
spring.mvc.pathmatch.matching-strategy=ant_path_matcher
# It works, and it means opting out of a Spring improvement to keep
# an unmaintained library alive. Migrate instead.

<!-- springdoc for Spring Boot 3.x -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
    <version>2.5.0</version>
</dependency>

<!-- springdoc for Spring Boot 2.x -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-ui</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

expert.content:
The JSON Document Is the Real Product

The browser page is the part people notice. The /v3/api-docs JSON is the part that pays for itself, because it is a machine-readable contract other tools consume.

ConsumerWhat it does with the spec
openapi-generatorGenerates a typed client in Java, TypeScript, Python, Go...
Postman / InsomniaImports the whole API as a ready-made collection.
API gatewaysConfigure routing, rate limits and validation from it.
Contract testsFail the build when a response stops matching the schema.
Spectral / lintersEnforce naming and versioning rules across teams.
Diff toolsDetect breaking changes between two versions in CI.
codeExamples:
# Generate a TypeScript client for the frontend team
npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate \
    -i http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs \
    -g typescript-axios \
    -o ./frontend/src/api

# The frontend now calls:
#   const employee = await employeeApi.getEmployeeById(1);
# fully typed, and it stops compiling the moment the API changes
# incompatibly.

<!-- Catch breaking API changes in CI, before release -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <phase>integration-test</phase>
            <goals><goal>generate</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
    <configuration>
        <apiDocsUrl>http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs</apiDocsUrl>
        <outputFileName>openapi.json</outputFileName>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

# Commit openapi.json, then in CI:
#   openapi-diff released/openapi.json target/openapi.json --fail-on-incompatible
# OUTPUT:
#   [BREAKING] GET /api/employees/{id}: response property 'city' removed

expert.content:
Never Expose Swagger UI in Production Unprotected

The UI publishes every endpoint, every parameter, every model field - and lets anyone who can reach it execute those endpoints. On a public server that is a self-service map of your attack surface.

ApproachTrade-off
Disable it in prodSimplest and safest. Docs still available in dev and test.
Serve it on the management portReachable inside the network only.
Require authenticationKeeps it available to your own team.
Publish the JSON to a portalThe right answer for a genuinely public API - docs without a live "Execute" button.
codeExamples:
# application-prod.properties - switch it off entirely
springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false
springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false

# application-dev.properties - on, and tidy
springdoc.api-docs.enabled=true
springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=true
springdoc.swagger-ui.path=/swagger-ui.html
springdoc.swagger-ui.operationsSorter=method
springdoc.swagger-ui.tagsSorter=alpha
springdoc.packagesToScan=com.velocity.restcontroller

expert.content:
Good Documentation Comes From Good DTOs

Swagger documents whatever types your controller signatures use. Point it at JPA entities and the generated schema inherits every problem the entity has.

Entity in the signatureWhat Swagger publishes
Every column, including internal onespasswordHash, deleted, audit fields - all documented as part of your public contract.
Bidirectional associationsRecursive schemas that render as an unusable nested blob.
Database namingColumn names become the documented API field names.
No validation metadataNothing tells the reader which fields are required or what their limits are.

DTOs annotated with Bean Validation solve the last row for free: springdoc reads @NotBlank, @Size and @Min and puts the constraints straight into the schema.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Swagger used for?Generating REST API documentation from the code, plus a browser UI for trying the endpoints live.
Why generate docs instead of writing them?Hand-written docs drift out of date the first time someone forgets to update them; generated docs cannot.
Which two Springfox dependencies are needed?springfox-swagger2 generates the spec; springfox-swagger-ui serves the HTML page.
What does the Docket bean do?Configures which controllers and paths are documented, and carries the API title, version and description.
What is the difference between the UI page and /v2/api-docs?The page is HTML for humans; the JSON is the machine-readable OpenAPI spec that tools consume.
Why should you not use Springfox in a new project?It is abandoned - it breaks on Spring Boot 2.6+ and does not work on Boot 3 at all because of the javax-to-jakarta move.
What replaces it?springdoc-openapi, which needs no @EnableSwagger2 and no Docket bean.
What are the springdoc URLs?/swagger-ui.html for the page and /v3/api-docs for the OpenAPI 3 JSON.
What does @ApiOperation do?Adds a description to one endpoint. In springdoc it is @Operation.
What can you do with the OpenAPI JSON?Generate typed clients, import into Postman, configure gateways, run contract tests, and diff versions to catch breaking changes in CI.
Why is Swagger UI risky in production?It publishes every endpoint and model and lets anyone execute them. Disable it in prod, or put it behind authentication or an internal port.
Why document DTOs rather than entities?Entities leak internal columns, produce recursive schemas from bidirectional associations, and tie the documented contract to the database schema.

Measure First

Almost every performance problem in a Spring Boot application is one of a small number of causes, and almost every failed optimisation effort starts by guessing which one.

The rule: do not optimise anything you have not measured. A change that makes the code uglier and the application no faster is a pure loss - and "I think this loop is slow" is wrong far more often than it is right.

Where the time actually goes

In a typical CRUD service, ranked by how often each is the real culprit:

CauseTypical symptom
N+1 queriesOne endpoint issues hundreds of SELECTs. By far the most common.
Missing database indexOne query is slow and gets slower as the table grows.
Unpaginated collection endpointFine in dev, times out in production.
Connection pool exhaustionRequests queue and time out while the CPU sits idle.
Synchronous external call with no timeoutOne slow dependency stalls every thread.
Serialising too much dataLarge JSON payloads; high CPU in Jackson.
Actual slow Java codeRare. Usually the last thing to look at.

Notice that six of the seven are I/O or data-volume problems, not CPU problems. That is why "make the Java faster" is usually the wrong instinct.

Step 1 - Turn On the SQL Log

The single highest-value diagnostic in a JPA application. Most performance bugs are visible the moment you can see the queries.

Step 2 - Page Every Collection Endpoint

An endpoint that returns "all" of something is a bug waiting for the table to grow. It is fine with the 12 rows in your dev database and fatal with the 2 million in production - it loads every row into the heap, serialises every one to JSON, and holds a database connection throughout.

Step 3 - Index What You Filter On

A query with no usable index makes the database read every row in the table. That is invisible at 1,000 rows and catastrophic at 10 million.
codeExamples:
-- The query your derived method generates
select * from employee where email = 'ajay@gmail.com';

-- Without an index:
EXPLAIN select * from employee where email = 'ajay@gmail.com';
+------+-------------+----------+------+---------+----------+
| type | key         | rows     | Extra                     |
+------+-------------+----------+------+---------+----------+
| ALL  | NULL        | 9847221  | Using where               |
+------+-------------+----------+------+---------+----------+
-- type=ALL and rows=9.8M means a FULL TABLE SCAN.

-- With an index:
CREATE INDEX idx_employee_email ON employee(email);

+------+-------------------+------+---------------------------+
| type | key               | rows | Extra                     |
+------+-------------------+------+---------------------------+
| ref  | idx_employee_email|    1 | Using index condition     |
+------+-------------------+------+---------------------------+
-- type=ref and rows=1. Milliseconds instead of seconds.

expert.content:
Connection Pool Sizing - Smaller Is Usually Faster

The instinct when an application is slow under load is to raise the pool size. It is normally the wrong move, and often makes things worse.

A database can only do so much concurrent work; it is bounded by cores and disk. Beyond that point, extra connections do not add throughput - they add context switching and lock contention, so every query gets slower while the total stays flat.

HikariCP's own guidance:

    connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)

  An 8-core server with SSDs:  (8 * 2) + 1  =  17

That is the pool size for the WHOLE application, and it is far
smaller than most people expect. HikariCP's default is 10.
SymptomLikely cause
Requests queue, database CPU is lowPool too small, or connections held too long
Requests slow, database CPU is highPool too large, or missing indexes
Connection is not available, request timed outPool exhausted - usually a leak, or a long transaction

Note the second row carefully. When several application instances each hold a pool, what matters is the total across all of them: ten instances with a pool of 50 is 500 connections at the database, which will collapse it.
codeExamples:
# Sensible starting configuration
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=15
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=3000    # fail fast, do not hang
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000       # under the DB's wait_timeout
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000

expert.content:
Read the Numbers, Not the Vibes

Actuator plus Micrometer already expose everything needed to find a bottleneck. The metrics worth watching, and what each tells you:

MetricWhat it reveals
http.server.requestsLatency and count per endpoint and status. Start here - it says which endpoint is slow.
hikaricp.connections.pendingThreads waiting for a connection. Above zero means the pool is a bottleneck.
hikaricp.connections.usageHow long connections are held. Long holds are the leak signal.
jvm.memory.used by areaHeap growth and whether it returns after GC.
jvm.gc.pauseGC pause time. Long or frequent pauses point at allocation pressure.
executor.queuedBacklog on your @Async or scheduling pools.

Percentiles matter more than averages: a mean of 80ms hides a p99 of 4 seconds, and the p99 is what users complain about.
codeExamples:
# Publish percentiles, not just a mean
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles.http.server.requests=0.5,0.95,0.99
management.metrics.distribution.slo.http.server.requests=100ms,500ms,1s

expert.content:
Do Less Work: Projections, Caching, and Not Calling At All

The fastest query is the one you never run. In rough order of effect:

TechniqueEffect
Fetch fewer columnsA projection that selects 3 of 40 columns moves a fraction of the data and skips entity construction entirely.
Fetch fewer rowsPagination, and filtering in SQL rather than in Java.
Fetch fewer timesCaching, and batching N calls into one.
Do it laterMove non-essential work off the request thread with @Async or a queue.

The last one is underused. A signup request does not need to wait for a welcome email to be delivered; it needs to wait for the user row to be committed.

JVM and Startup

Two areas people reach for early and that matter less than the database - with one important exception in containers.

SettingWhy
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75In a container, always. A JVM that ignores the cgroup limit sizes its heap from the host's RAM and gets OOMKilled (exit 137).
G1GCThe default since Java 9 and the right choice for almost everything.
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryErrorCosts nothing, and is the difference between diagnosing an OOM and guessing.
Lazy initialisationFaster startup, at the cost of moving configuration errors to the first request. Dev only.

Startup time rarely matters for a long-running service and matters enormously for autoscaling and for serverless, where a cold start is user-visible latency.
codeExamples:
# Container-aware memory. NOT -Xmx, which hard-codes a number that
# becomes wrong the moment the container limit changes.
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heapdump.hprof \
     -jar app.jar

# With a 1Gi container limit, the heap is capped near 768Mi and the
# rest is left for metaspace, thread stacks and native memory.
# Without it, the JVM may size the heap from the HOST's 64Gi and be
# killed the moment it grows.

# Finding what is slow at startup
java -jar app.jar --debug
# Prints the auto-configuration report.

# Or measure it directly:
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=startup
# GET /actuator/startup
# [
#   { "startupStep": { "name": "spring.beans.instantiate",
#                      "tags": [{"key":"beanName","value":"entityManagerFactory"}] },
#     "duration": "PT2.14S" }
# ]
# One bean taking 2.1 seconds is now visible rather than suspected.

expert.content:
Load Testing: the Only Way to Know

Everything above is diagnosis on a running system. To find the limit before production does, you have to generate load.

Test typeQuestion it answers
Load testDoes it meet its latency target at expected traffic?
Stress testWhere does it break, and how? Gracefully, or by falling over?
Soak testDoes it degrade over hours? Memory leaks and connection leaks only appear here.
Spike testDoes it survive a sudden 10x, and does it recover afterwards?

Test against production-like data volumes. A load test on a 100-row table proves nothing about the missing index that will bite at 10 million - the database will keep the whole thing in memory and every query will look fast.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the first thing you do about a slow endpoint?Measure it. Look at http.server.requests percentiles, then the SQL log or Hibernate statistics - never guess.
What is the most common performance bug in a JPA application?The N+1 select problem - one query for a list plus one per row for an association.
How do you detect N+1?Enable hibernate.generate_statistics and count statements per request; 101 queries for 100 rows is the signature.
How do you fix it?join fetch, @EntityGraph, a DTO projection, or @BatchSize.
Why is a bigger connection pool often slower?The database is bounded by cores and disk; extra connections add contention and context switching without adding throughput.
How do you size a pool?Roughly (cores * 2) + spindles, counted across all application instances - ten instances of 50 is 500 connections at the database.
Why should an HTTP call not sit inside a transaction?It holds a database connection for the duration of the network call, capping throughput and exhausting the pool.
Why does a composite index on (city, status) not help a query on status alone?Composite indexes are usable left-to-right only - the leftmost prefix rule.
Why are percentiles better than averages?A mean hides the tail; a 133ms mean can conceal a 4-second p99, and the p99 is what users experience.
Why use MaxRAMPercentage rather than -Xmx in a container?It sizes the heap from the container limit. A JVM sizing from host RAM overshoots and gets OOMKilled with exit code 137.
How do you get slow non-essential work off the request path?@Async with @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT), or publish to a queue.
Why must load tests use production-like data volumes?A missing index is invisible on a small table - the database caches it entirely and every query looks fast.
When do you profile the Java code?Last, after ruling out query count, indexes, pooling and external calls. CPU-bound Java is rarely the bottleneck in a CRUD service.
