What is a Spring Boot Executable JAR?

The Spring Boot executable jar contains the class files together with all the libraries the application needs to run and perform the task it was built for.

Why do we use it?

The user does not have to maintain the dependencies. They just execute it.

TRADITIONAL WAR                     SPRING BOOT FAT JAR

 install Tomcat                      java -jar app.jar
 configure it                              |
 copy app.war to webapps/                  v
 restart Tomcat                       it just runs
      |
      v
  application runs

Steps

1. Create the Spring Boot project   2. Add Maven dependencies   3. Create the REST controller
4. Run the application   5. Open Postman and hit the request   6. Create the executable jar
7. Generate a Build Success   8. Execute the jar at the command prompt

expert.content:
What Is Actually Inside the Fat JAR

A normal jar cannot contain other jars - the standard class loader will not read a jar nested inside a jar. Spring Boot solves this with its own layout and its own loader.

app.jar
 |
 +-- META-INF/
 |     MANIFEST.MF
 |         Main-Class:       org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher
 |         Start-Class:      com.velocity.DemoApplication
 |
 +-- org/springframework/boot/loader/     <- the launcher, unpacked
 |     JarLauncher.class
 |     LaunchedURLClassLoader.class
 |
 +-- BOOT-INF/
       classes/        <- YOUR compiled code and resources
       lib/            <- every dependency, as nested jars
             spring-web-6.0.9.jar
             tomcat-embed-core-10.1.8.jar
             ...
Manifest entryMeaning
Main-ClassJarLauncher - what java -jar actually starts.
Start-ClassYour @SpringBootApplication class, which JarLauncher calls once its class loader is ready.

So java -jar starts Spring Boot's launcher, which installs a class loader able to read the nested jars in BOOT-INF/lib, and only then hands control to your main method.
codeExamples:
# Read the manifest of a built jar
unzip -p app.jar META-INF/MANIFEST.MF

Manifest-Version: 1.0
Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher
Start-Class: com.velocity.SpringBootExecutableJarDemoApplication
Spring-Boot-Version: 3.1.0
Spring-Boot-Classes: BOOT-INF/classes/
Spring-Boot-Lib: BOOT-INF/lib/

# The most common failure, and what it means
$ java -jar target/app.jar
no main manifest attribute, in target/app.jar

# Cause: spring-boot-maven-plugin is missing from pom.xml, so the
# repackage step never ran and the jar has no Main-Class.
# Fix: add the plugin and rebuild.

# A second one:
$ java -jar app.jar
Error: Unable to access jarfile app.jar
# Cause: wrong directory, or the version in the filename changed.
# ls target/*.jar to see the real name.

expert.content:
WAR When You Need It, and How to Build Both

The fat jar is the default and there are still places that require a WAR - an existing corporate Tomcat, a WebLogic or WebSphere estate, an ops team that owns the container.

Two changes are needed, and forgetting the second one is the classic mistake: the WAR deploys, and every URL returns 404, because DispatcherServlet was never registered by the external container.
codeExamples:
<!-- 1. Change the packaging -->
<packaging>war</packaging>

<!-- 2. Mark the embedded Tomcat "provided" so it is NOT bundled -
        the external container supplies its own -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

expert.content:
Layered JARs Make Docker Builds Fast

Copying a 50 MB fat jar into a Docker image means every code change - even a one-character fix - invalidates the layer holding all your dependencies. Spring Boot 2.3+ can split the jar into layers that change at different rates.

LayerChanges
dependenciesRarely - only when pom.xml changes
spring-boot-loaderAlmost never
snapshot-dependenciesOccasionally
applicationEvery build - and it is the smallest

Docker caches unchanged layers, so a code-only change rebuilds and pushes a few hundred kilobytes instead of fifty megabytes.
codeExamples:
<!-- Enable layering (default from Boot 2.4) -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <layers>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </layers>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

# Inspect and extract the layers
java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar list
# dependencies
# spring-boot-loader
# snapshot-dependencies
# application

java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract

# A multi-stage Dockerfile using them
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/*.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
# Ordered least- to most-frequently changed
COPY --from=builder /app/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/application/ ./
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher"]

# OUTPUT: a code-only change rebuilds the last COPY layer only.
# Push size drops from ~50 MB to ~300 KB.

# Or skip the Dockerfile entirely - the plugin can build the image:
#   mvn spring-boot:build-image

expert.content:
Running It as a Real Service

java -jar in a terminal stops when the terminal closes. Production needs the application supervised, restarted on failure, and started at boot. On Linux that is systemd.
codeExamples:
# /etc/systemd/system/employee-app.service
[Unit]
Description=Employee Service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=appuser
WorkingDirectory=/opt/employee-app
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -Xms256m -Xmx512m -jar /opt/employee-app/app.jar
Environment="SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod"
Environment="DB_PASSWORD=..."
SuccessExitStatus=143
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# Manage it
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable employee-app     # start on boot
sudo systemctl start employee-app
sudo systemctl status employee-app
sudo journalctl -u employee-app -f     # follow the logs

# SuccessExitStatus=143 matters: 143 is 128+15 (SIGTERM), which is
# a NORMAL shutdown. Without it systemd treats every graceful stop
# as a crash and keeps restarting.

# Graceful shutdown - let in-flight requests finish
# application.properties
server.shutdown=graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s

# OUTPUT on SIGTERM:
# Commencing graceful shutdown. Waiting for active requests to complete
# Graceful shutdown complete
# Without it, active requests are cut off mid-response.

# And never run as root:
#   User=appuser
# A compromised application should not own the machine.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a Spring Boot executable jar?A self-contained "fat jar" holding your classes, every dependency, and an embedded servlet container, runnable with java -jar.
Which plugin creates it?spring-boot-maven-plugin, through its repackage goal.
What does "no main manifest attribute" mean?The repackage step never ran - usually the plugin is missing from pom.xml - so the jar has no Main-Class.
What is the Main-Class in a Boot jar?org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher. Your own class is recorded separately as Start-Class.
Why is a custom launcher needed?The standard class loader cannot read a jar nested inside a jar, so Boot ships LaunchedURLClassLoader to load BOOT-INF/lib.
Where does your code live inside the jar?BOOT-INF/classes/; dependencies are in BOOT-INF/lib/.
Difference between mvn package and mvn install?package builds the jar into target/; install also copies it into the local ~/.m2 repository.
How do you change the port without rebuilding?java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090.
What is needed to build a deployable WAR?<packaging>war</packaging>, embedded Tomcat scoped provided, and the main class extending SpringBootServletInitializer.
What happens if you skip SpringBootServletInitializer?The WAR deploys but every URL returns 404 - the external container never registers the DispatcherServlet.
What are layered jars for?Splitting the jar so Docker caches dependencies separately from application code, cutting rebuild and push size dramatically.
Why does a systemd unit need SuccessExitStatus=143?143 is 128+SIGTERM, a normal shutdown. Without it every graceful stop looks like a crash and triggers a restart loop.

Business Requirement

An application that runs correctly on the developer's machine must run identically on a tester's machine, on UAT, on production, and on the client's laptop - without anyone installing Java, MySQL, Tomcat or Kafka by hand.

Problem Statement

Consider an application whose environment is Java 1.8, MySQL 5.6, Tomcat 9.0 and Kafka 3.1. A new developer joins with Java 11, MySQL 6.1, Tomcat 8.5 and no Kafka at all. The same source code will not start on that machine. The setup, not the code, is the obstacle.

The classroom material lists four scenarios that all reduce to the same complaint:
Scenario 1 - Team member 1 is on Windows with Oracle 7 and Java 8; team member 2 is on Mac with Oracle 8 and Java 11. "It works on my machine" is true and useless.
Scenario 2 - Test, UAT and Production are three separate servers. Each one has to be provisioned manually with the right Java version, the right database, the right message broker.
Scenario 3 - The client wants to run the application. The client is not technical. Java, Angular and the database still have to be installed before anything happens.
Scenario 4 - The client has many machines. Six months later they ask for three or four more. Every one of them is a fresh manual install, and there is no guarantee the result behaves the same.

Handing over a URL does not help either. Without the runtime installed underneath it, there is nothing for the URL to reach.

First Attempt - Virtualisation

The older answer was to run several operating systems on one physical machine through a hypervisor. Each guest OS carries its own kernel, its own Java, its own MySQL.

That solves portability but costs dearly: every virtual machine boots a complete operating system, so memory and CPU are consumed by four copies of an OS before any application code runs. Start-up is measured in minutes.

  VIRTUAL MACHINES                      CONTAINERS
  +---------+---------+                 +---------+---------+
  |  App A  |  App B  |                 |  App A  |  App B  |
  +---------+---------+                 +---------+---------+
  | Bins/Libs|Bins/Libs|                | Bins/Libs|Bins/Libs|
  +---------+---------+                 +---------+---------+
  | Guest OS| Guest OS|  <-- heavy      |   Container Engine |
  +---------+---------+                 +-------------------+
  |     Hypervisor    |                 |    Host OS Kernel |
  +-------------------+                 +-------------------+
  |     Host OS       |                 |     Hardware      |
  +-------------------+                 +-------------------+
  |     Hardware      |
  +-------------------+
  Boots in minutes, GBs           Starts in ms/seconds, MBs

Containerisation

A container is a package that holds the application together with the libraries, dependencies and runtime it needs, and runs as an isolated process on the host operating system. There is no guest OS inside it - it shares the host kernel.

TermMeaning
DockerfileA text file of instructions describing how to assemble the image - the infrastructure recipe.
Docker imageThe immutable, read-only artefact produced by docker build. It contains the runtime, the libraries and your jar.
Docker containerA running instance of an image, with a thin writable layer on top. Many containers can run from one image.
Docker Hub / registryThe remote store images are pushed to and pulled from.
Docker Engine / daemonThe background service that actually builds images and runs containers.

  Dockerfile  --docker build-->  Image  --docker run-->  Container
       ^                           |                          |
       |                    docker push                docker logs / exec
   you write it                    v
                              Docker Hub  --docker pull--> any machine
The payoff is the point of the whole exercise: setting up an environment drops from about a week of manual installation to five or ten minutes of docker pull and docker run.

Installing Docker Desktop on Windows

1. Go to https://hub.docker.com/ and register an account.
2. Fill in the details, click Sign Up, then verify the email address that arrives in your mailbox.
3. Download Docker Desktop Installer.exe for Windows and run it, allowing it to make changes to the device.
4. Accept the licence terms, then let the installer finish and restart the machine.
5. Docker needs a Linux kernel. In Windows search, open Turn Windows features on or off and tick Windows Hypervisor Platform and Windows Subsystem for Linux.
6. Restart, then confirm WSL from a command prompt.

On Windows, containers do not run on the Windows kernel. WSL 2 supplies a real Linux kernel, and Docker Desktop runs the engine inside it. That is why the WSL feature is not optional.

beginner.content:
Dockerising a Spring Boot Application - Steps

1. Create a Spring Starter Project, packaging Jar, type Maven.
2. Add the Spring Web dependency.
3. Write a REST controller with one endpoint.
4. Set <finalName> in pom.xml so the jar has a predictable name.
5. Run mvn clean package from the project folder to produce the jar in target/.
6. Create a Dockerfile at the project root.
7. docker build -t springbootwithdocker .
8. docker run -p 8080:8080 springbootwithdocker
9. Hit the endpoint in the browser.

finalName matters more than it looks. Without it Maven produces my-app-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar, and the version number changes with every release - which would mean editing the Dockerfile on every release. Fixing the name keeps the Dockerfile stable.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<build>
    <finalName>springbootwithdocker</finalName>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

<!-- NOTE: the PDF sets <finalName>my_first_docker_app</finalName> in one step
     and then the Dockerfile copies target/springbootwithdocker.jar.
     Those two names MUST match, otherwise the build fails with:
       ERROR: "/target/springbootwithdocker.jar": not found
     Pick one name and use it in both places. -->

# Step 5 - build the jar first. Docker does NOT compile your code.
D:\\workspace\\springbootwithdocker> mvn clean package

# OUTPUT (tail):
# [INFO] --- spring-boot-maven-plugin:3.2.0:repackage (repackage) @ springbootwithdocker ---
# [INFO] Replacing main artifact with repackaged archive
# [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
# [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
# [INFO] Total time:  18.442 s
#
# target/springbootwithdocker.jar   (about 19 MB, fat jar)

beginner.content:
The Dockerfile

Create a file named exactly Dockerfile - no extension, capital D - at the project root, beside pom.xml.

InstructionWhat it does
FROMNames the base image the build starts from. Every image begins with a FROM.
EXPOSEDocuments the port the application listens on. It does not publish it - -p on docker run does that.
COPYCopies a file from the build context into the image.
ADDLike COPY but also unpacks local archives and fetches URLs. Prefer COPY unless you need those.
ENTRYPOINTThe executable the container runs. In exec form (a JSON array) it becomes PID 1 directly, with no shell in between.

The PDF uses ADD. Use COPY instead: ADD's extra behaviour - silently extracting a tar, downloading a URL - is a surprise you do not want in a build.
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile - as printed in the PDF
FROM openjdk:8
EXPOSE 8080
ADD target/springbootwithdocker.jar springbootwithdocker.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","springbootwithdocker.jar"]

# Dockerfile - the same thing written the way you would ship it
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# COPY, not ADD - no hidden archive extraction or URL fetching
COPY target/springbootwithdocker.jar app.jar

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

# Why the change from openjdk:8?
#  - The "openjdk" image is deprecated and no longer updated on Docker Hub.
#  - A JRE image is roughly half the size of a JDK image; nothing at runtime compiles.
#  - Exec form ["java","-jar",...] makes the JVM PID 1, so "docker stop" delivers
#    SIGTERM to the JVM and Spring's shutdown hooks actually run.
#    Shell form (ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar) puts /bin/sh at PID 1, the signal
#    never reaches Java, and the container is killed after a 10 second timeout.

no such file or directory: DockerfileThe file was saved as Dockerfile.txt by Notepad, or the prompt is in the wrong folder.
bind: address already in useHost port 8080 is taken. Use -p 9090:8080.
Container starts then exits immediatelyRead docker logs <id>. Usually the application failed to connect to a database that is not in the container.
Communications link failure to MySQLlocalhost inside a container is the container itself, not your machine. See the compose section.

expert.content:
Layers, the Build Cache, and Why COPY Order Decides Your Build Time

Every instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer - a read-only filesystem diff, content-addressed by a hash of the instruction plus the files it touched. On a rebuild, Docker walks the instructions in order and reuses a cached layer as long as the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. The moment one layer misses, every layer after it is rebuilt, regardless of whether its own inputs changed.

That single rule drives the whole design. Order instructions from least likely to change to most likely to change. Dependencies change monthly; your source changes every few minutes. Copying pom.xml and resolving dependencies before copying src/ means a code-only edit reuses the dependency layer and skips a full Maven download.

Layered Jars

A Spring Boot fat jar is a single 40 MB file, so a one-line code change rewrites all 40 MB as a new layer and pushes all 40 MB to the registry. Since Boot 2.3 the jar can be layered: java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract splits it into dependencies, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies and application. Copy each into its own layer and only the last one - a few hundred kilobytes of your own classes - changes between builds.

Boot 3.x replaces the jarmode name: use -Djarmode=tools extract --layers --destination extracted. Both forms are shown below.
codeExamples:
# WRONG ORDER - every source edit re-downloads the internet
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY . .                      # <-- any file change busts this layer
RUN mvn -q clean package      # <-- so this always re-resolves dependencies
# Rebuild after changing one .java file: ~3 minutes

# RIGHT ORDER - dependencies cached separately from source
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline    # cached until pom.xml changes
COPY src ./src                      # only this layer busts on a code edit
RUN mvn -B -DskipTests clean package
# Rebuild after changing one .java file: ~15 seconds

# Layered jar - inspect what Boot produced
java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/app.jar list
# OUTPUT:
# dependencies
# spring-boot-loader
# snapshot-dependencies
# application

java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/app.jar extract --destination extracted
# creates extracted/dependencies/, extracted/spring-boot-loader/,
#         extracted/snapshot-dependencies/, extracted/application/

# Spring Boot 3.3+ syntax (layertools is deprecated there):
# java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

# pom.xml - layers are on by default in Boot 2.4+, but be explicit
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <layers>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </layers>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

expert.content:
Multi-Stage Builds

A build needs Maven, a JDK, a .m2 cache and your sources. A running container needs a JRE and one jar. Shipping the first set as the runtime image gives you an 800 MB image containing a compiler, a build tool and your complete source code - all of it attack surface and all of it pointless in production.

A multi-stage build uses one FROM per stage and copies only the finished artefacts forward with COPY --from. Everything left behind in the builder stage is discarded. The result is typically 180-250 MB instead of 800 MB, with no build tooling and no source inside it.

Combine multi-stage with layered jars and you get both: a small final image and fast incremental pushes.
codeExamples:
# ---------- Stage 1: build ----------
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B -DskipTests clean package
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/app.jar extract --destination extracted

# ---------- Stage 2: runtime ----------
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app

RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S spring -G spring

# Layers copied most-stable first, so a code change only invalidates the last COPY
COPY --from=builder --chown=spring:spring /build/extracted/dependencies/          ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=spring:spring /build/extracted/spring-boot-loader/    ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=spring:spring /build/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=spring:spring /build/extracted/application/           ./

USER spring:spring
EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
# Boot 2.x uses org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher (no ".launch")

# OUTPUT of docker images after this build:
# REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       SIZE
# orders-api   1.4.0     3a91c8de2f10   198MB     <-- vs 812MB single-stage

expert.content:
Never Run as Root

By default a container process runs as uid 0. Container isolation is namespaces and cgroups, not a virtual machine boundary; root inside the container is the same uid 0 the host kernel sees. A container escape - or simply a bind-mounted host directory - then gives an attacker root-level reach outside the container.

Create an unprivileged user in the Dockerfile and switch to it with USER before ENTRYPOINT. Put the USER instruction last, after every RUN that needs to install packages, and make sure the files the application reads are --chowned to that user.

Two consequences to plan for: a non-root process cannot bind ports below 1024 - which is fine, because Spring Boot's default 8080 is above that and the host mapping -p 80:8080 handles the rest - and it cannot write to /. Run with --read-only plus a tmpfs for /tmp where you can, and pass --cap-drop ALL to strip Linux capabilities the JVM never uses.
codeExamples:
# Alpine base
RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S spring -G spring
USER spring:spring

# Debian/Ubuntu base
RUN groupadd -r spring && useradd -r -g spring spring
USER spring:spring

# Verify it took effect:
docker run --rm orders-api:1.4.0 id
# OUTPUT: uid=100(spring) gid=101(spring) groups=101(spring)

# If it did NOT:
# OUTPUT: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)   <-- fix the Dockerfile

# Runtime hardening on the run command
docker run -d \
  --name orders-api \
  --user 1000:1000 \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \
  --memory 1g --cpus 2 \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  orders-api:1.4.0

# Common failure if you forget the tmpfs:
# java.io.IOException: No space left on device
#   at java.base/java.io.UnixFileSystem.createFileExclusively
# Tomcat needs a writable /tmp for its work directory.

expert.content:
The JVM Inside a Container

Before Java 10, the JVM read /proc/meminfo and /proc/cpuinfo - which report the host, not the cgroup limit. A container capped at 512 MB on a 64 GB host would see 64 GB, set a default max heap of 16 GB, allocate freely, and be killed by the kernel OOM killer with exit code 137 and no Java stack trace at all. Modern JVMs (8u191+, 10+) are container-aware: UseContainerSupport is on by default and the JVM reads the cgroup limits instead.

Given that, do not set -Xmx. A fixed number is a guess against an unknown container size: too high and the kernel kills you, too low and you waste the memory the orchestrator reserved. Set MaxRAMPercentage instead and the heap scales with whatever limit the container is given - 75% is a reasonable figure, leaving headroom for metaspace, thread stacks, code cache and direct buffers, all of which live outside the heap and all of which count towards the cgroup limit.

Note the trap in the defaults: for containers under about 256 MB the JVM applies MinRAMPercentage (50%), not MaxRAMPercentage. And exit code 137 means SIGKILL from the OOM killer - a Java OutOfMemoryError would have produced a stack trace and a different exit code.
codeExamples:
# Prove the JVM sees the cgroup limit, not the host
docker run --rm -m 512m eclipse-temurin:17-jre \
  java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MaxHeapSize|UseContainerSupport"
# OUTPUT:
#   size_t MaxHeapSize = 134217728    {product} {ergonomic}   <-- 128MB = 25% of 512MB
#   bool UseContainerSupport = true   {product} {default}

# Now with MaxRAMPercentage
docker run --rm -m 512m eclipse-temurin:17-jre \
  java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize
# OUTPUT:
#   size_t MaxHeapSize = 402653184    {product} {ergonomic}   <-- 384MB = 75% of 512MB

# Dockerfile - let the flag come from the environment so ops can tune it
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
               -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp"

ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "exec java $JAVA_OPTS -jar /app/app.jar"]
# "exec" matters: without it, sh stays PID 1 and swallows SIGTERM.
# If you need no shell expansion at all, prefer the pure exec form:
# ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

# The failure mode this prevents
docker run -m 512m -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Xmx2g" orders-api:1.4.0
# ... application starts, serves traffic, then:
docker ps -a
# CONTAINER ID   IMAGE              STATUS
# 7d3e1a90bb52   orders-api:1.4.0   Exited (137) 4 minutes ago
#
# 137 = 128 + 9 = SIGKILL. The kernel OOM killer, not the JVM.
# There is NO OutOfMemoryError in the logs - the process was shot, not unwound.
docker inspect 7d3e1a90bb52 --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# OUTPUT: true

expert.content:
.dockerignore

docker build . tars the entire context directory and sends it to the daemon before the first instruction runs. A Maven project with target/, .git/ and an IDE folder can be hundreds of megabytes, and you will see the build sit on transferring context for seconds before doing anything.

Size is the smaller problem. The real one is secrets and cache invalidation. A COPY . . with no ignore file copies .git (your full history, including any credential ever committed), .env files, and local application-local.properties straight into the image where docker history will happily show them. It also means a change to README.md or a Git operation invalidates the COPY layer and rebuilds everything below it.

The file lives beside the Dockerfile, uses the same syntax as .gitignore, and ! re-includes.
codeExamples:
# .dockerignore  (project root, next to Dockerfile)
.git
.gitignore
.github
target/
!target/*.jar          # keep the built jar if the Dockerfile copies it directly
build/
.idea/
*.iml
.vscode/
.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.jar
**/*.log
**/.env
**/application-local.properties
**/application-secrets.yml
Dockerfile
docker-compose*.yml
README.md
*.md

# Effect on a typical project:
# without .dockerignore:  => transferring context: 264.71MB   6.2s
# with    .dockerignore:  => transferring context:  19.34MB   0.3s

expert.content:
Tagging - Why :latest Is Not a Version

latest is not a special tag. It is the default string Docker fills in when you omit one, and it points at whatever was pushed last. It carries no ordering, no guarantee, and no meaning.

Deploying myapp:latest means a rollback is impossible - there is no earlier tag to go back to - and two nodes pulling the same "version" minutes apart can end up running different code. The image also gets cached: a node that already has latest locally may never pull the new one unless the pull policy forces it.

Tag with something immutable. The strongest form is the digest, myapp@sha256:..., which addresses exact content and cannot be moved. Practically, tag with the semantic version plus the git commit SHA, and push latest as an additional convenience tag for developers only.

Pin your base images too. FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre silently changes underneath you; FROM eclipse-temurin:17.0.9_9-jre-alpine does not.
codeExamples:
# In CI - one build, several names, all pointing at the same image id
VERSION=1.4.0
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)      # e.g. 9f3c1ab

docker build -t orders-api:${VERSION} .
docker tag orders-api:${VERSION} registry.example.com/orders-api:${VERSION}
docker tag orders-api:${VERSION} registry.example.com/orders-api:${VERSION}-${SHA}
docker tag orders-api:${VERSION} registry.example.com/orders-api:latest

docker push --all-tags registry.example.com/orders-api

# Production deploys the immutable one:
#   registry.example.com/orders-api:1.4.0-9f3c1ab
# or, strongest, by digest:
#   registry.example.com/orders-api@sha256:6c1f...e42b

# Find the digest after a push
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' orders-api:1.4.0
# OUTPUT:
# registry.example.com/orders-api@sha256:6c1f9a0d3b77e2c5a1f8b0c4d9e7a2b31c5f8e42b...

# Compare pull policies:
docker run myapp:latest          # uses the local copy if one exists - may be stale
docker run --pull=always myapp:latest
# Kubernetes: imagePullPolicy defaults to Always for :latest and
# IfNotPresent for any other tag - another reason not to deploy :latest.

expert.content:
docker compose - App plus MySQL

Two facts break every first attempt at this. First, localhost inside a container is that container. The application cannot reach MySQL at jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/...; on a compose network it reaches it at the service name, jdbc:mysql://mysql-db:3306/.... Second, depends_on is not what most people think it is.

Why depends_on Is Not Enough

Plain depends_on only orders container start. Compose starts the MySQL container, sees it running, and immediately starts the application - while mysqld is still initialising its data directory, which on a first run takes 20-40 seconds. Spring Boot's HikariCP tries to open a pool, fails, and the application exits before MySQL is ready to accept a single connection.

The fix is a healthcheck on the database plus depends_on: condition: service_healthy. Compose then waits for the healthcheck to pass, not merely for the process to exist. This is a container-level analogue of the same lesson everywhere in distributed systems: "started" and "ready" are different states.

Even with that, keep the application resilient - restart: on-failure and a sensible Hikari initialization-fail-timeout, because a database can also go away after start-up.
codeExamples:
# docker-compose.yml
services:

  mysql-db:
    image: mysql:8.0.35
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}
      MYSQL_DATABASE: employeedb
    volumes:
      - mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql        # named volume - data survives "down"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "localhost", "-p${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 40s                  # grace window for first-run initialisation
    networks: [appnet]

  orders-api:
    image: registry.example.com/orders-api:1.4.0-9f3c1ab
    depends_on:
      mysql-db:
        condition: service_healthy       # <-- the part that actually waits
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      # "mysql-db" is the SERVICE NAME, resolved by Docker's embedded DNS.
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:mysql://mysql-db:3306/employeedb?useSSL=false&allowPublicKeyRetrieval=true
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: root
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    restart: on-failure
    networks: [appnet]

volumes:
  mysql-data:

networks:
  appnet:

# The failure you get WITHOUT a healthcheck
docker compose up
# orders-api  | com.mysql.cj.jdbc.exceptions.CommunicationsException:
# orders-api  |   Communications link failure
# orders-api  | Caused by: java.net.ConnectException: Connection refused
# orders-api  | HikariPool-1 - Exception during pool initialization.
# orders-api  | APPLICATION FAILED TO START
# orders-api exited with code 1
#
# WITH the healthcheck:
docker compose up
# [+] Running 3/3
#  Network app_appnet     Created
#  Container mysql-db     Healthy      <-- compose waited here, ~34s
#  Container orders-api   Started
# orders-api | HikariPool-1 - Start completed.
# orders-api | Started OrdersApiApplication in 3.109 seconds

docker compose ps
# NAME         IMAGE                 STATUS                   PORTS
# mysql-db     mysql:8.0.35          Up 2 minutes (healthy)   3306/tcp
# orders-api   orders-api:1.4.0      Up 1 minute              0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp

# The credentials come from a .env file beside the compose file,
# which is in .gitignore and .dockerignore. NEVER hardcode them here.
# .env
MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=change-me-in-a-secrets-manager

# Note MySQL is deliberately NOT published with "ports:" - it is reachable
# on the appnet network by the application and by nothing else on the host.
# Add "ports: [3306:3306]" only for local debugging, never in production.

docker compose down       # stops and removes containers, KEEPS the volume
docker compose down -v    # also deletes the volume - your data is gone

expert.content:
Buildpacks - No Dockerfile at All

Spring Boot ships spring-boot:build-image, which uses Cloud Native Buildpacks (Paketo by default) to produce an OCI image straight from the Maven or Gradle build. There is no Dockerfile to write, review or keep current.

The buildpack detects the Java version from your pom.xml, picks a maintained base image, applies the layered-jar split automatically, sets a non-root user, and installs a memory calculator that sizes the heap, metaspace and thread stacks from the container's memory limit at start-up rather than at build time. Everything the previous sections told you to do by hand, done as a policy you inherit.

ApproachWhen it suits
BuildpacksStandard Spring Boot services, many of them, where consistency and free security patching of the base image matter more than control. Rebuild to pick up a patched base with no code change.
DockerfileYou need native OS packages, a specific hardened or distroless base, an unusual entrypoint, or your platform team mandates an approved base image.

Note the daemon requirement: build-image talks to the local Docker daemon by default, which is awkward in some CI runners. Paketo also builds native GraalVM images through the same goal when spring-boot-starter-parent's native profile is active.
codeExamples:
# No Dockerfile anywhere in the project
mvn spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=orders-api:1.4.0

# OUTPUT (abridged):
# [INFO] Building image 'docker.io/library/orders-api:1.4.0'
# [INFO]  > Pulling builder image 'paketobuildpacks/builder-jammy-base:latest'
# [INFO]  > Executing lifecycle version v0.17.0
# [INFO]  > Running detector
# [INFO]     paketo-buildpacks/ca-certificates
# [INFO]     paketo-buildpacks/bellsoft-liberica
# [INFO]     paketo-buildpacks/executable-jar
# [INFO]     paketo-buildpacks/spring-boot
# [INFO]  > Running builder
# [INFO]     Adding layer 'paketo-buildpacks/bellsoft-liberica:jre'
# [INFO]     Spring Boot Layers: dependencies, spring-boot-loader,
# [INFO]                         snapshot-dependencies, application
# [INFO]  > Saving docker.io/library/orders-api:1.4.0
# [INFO] Successfully built image 'docker.io/library/orders-api:1.4.0'
# [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS  Total time: 01:12 min

<!-- pom.xml - pin the image name and push straight to a registry -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <image>
            <name>registry.example.com/orders-api:${project.version}</name>
            <publish>true</publish>
            <env>
                <BP_JVM_VERSION>17</BP_JVM_VERSION>
            </env>
        </image>
        <docker>
            <publishRegistry>
                <username>${env.REGISTRY_USER}</username>
                <password>${env.REGISTRY_TOKEN}</password>
            </publishRegistry>
        </docker>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

# What the buildpack gives you for free - inspect the running container
docker run --rm -m 1g orders-api:1.4.0
# OUTPUT:
# Setting Active Processor Count to 8
# Calculated JVM Memory Configuration: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=10M
#   -Xmx636003K -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=88652K -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=240M -Xss1M
#   (Total Memory: 1G, Thread Count: 250, Loaded Class Count: 12983)
# ... the memory calculator sized the heap AT START-UP from the cgroup limit.

docker inspect orders-api:1.4.0 --format '{{.Config.User}}'
# OUTPUT: 1000:1000        <-- non-root, without you writing a USER line

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Container versus virtual machine?A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS with its own kernel. A container is an isolated process on the host kernel using namespaces and cgroups. Containers start in milliseconds and cost megabytes; VMs take minutes and gigabytes, but give a stronger isolation boundary.
Image versus container?The image is the immutable, read-only stack of layers produced by docker build. A container is a running instance of it with a thin writable layer on top. One image, many containers.
Why does COPY order change build time?Each instruction is a cached layer keyed on its inputs. A cache miss invalidates that layer and every layer below it. Copying pom.xml and resolving dependencies before copying src keeps the dependency layer cached across code edits.
What is a layered jar and why use it?Boot 2.3+ splits the fat jar into dependencies, loader, snapshot-dependencies and application. Copied as separate image layers, a code change rewrites only the small application layer instead of the whole 40 MB jar, so pushes and pulls are far cheaper.
What does a multi-stage build achieve?The builder stage holds Maven, the JDK and your source; only the finished artefacts are copied forward with COPY --from. The final image has no compiler, no build tool and no source code - typically 200 MB instead of 800 MB, with much less attack surface.
Why not run the container as root?Root in the container is uid 0 on the host kernel; the boundary is namespaces, not a hypervisor. Any escape or bind-mount then has host-level privilege. Create a user, USER before ENTRYPOINT, and drop capabilities at run time.
Why avoid -Xmx in a container?It is a fixed guess against a limit set elsewhere. Too high and the kernel OOM-kills the container (exit 137, no Java stack trace); too low and reserved memory is wasted. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 scales with whatever limit the container gets.
What is JVM container awareness?From 8u191/Java 10, UseContainerSupport makes the JVM read cgroup memory and CPU limits instead of /proc/meminfo. Older JVMs saw the whole host and sized the heap catastrophically wrong.
What does exit code 137 mean?128 + 9 = SIGKILL, almost always the kernel OOM killer. Check docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'. It is not a Java OutOfMemoryError - that unwinds and logs a stack trace.
What does .dockerignore do?Excludes paths from the build context. It cuts transfer time, stops .git, .env and local property files being baked into the image, and prevents unrelated file changes from invalidating a COPY layer.
Why not deploy :latest?It is a mutable pointer to the most recent push, with no ordering guarantee. Rollback is impossible, two nodes can run different code under the same name, and caching makes it unpredictable. Tag with version plus commit SHA, or pin by digest.
ADD versus COPY?Both copy files in. ADD additionally extracts local tar archives and fetches remote URLs - implicit behaviour that surprises readers of the Dockerfile. Use COPY unless you specifically need the extraction.
ENTRYPOINT exec form versus shell form?Exec form (a JSON array) runs the binary as PID 1, so docker stop delivers SIGTERM to the JVM and Spring's shutdown hooks run. Shell form puts /bin/sh at PID 1, the signal never reaches Java, and the container is killed after the timeout.
Why is depends_on not enough?It only orders container start-up. MySQL's first-run initialisation takes tens of seconds after the container is "running", so the application starts, fails to open its pool and exits. Add a healthcheck to the database and condition: service_healthy to the dependant.
Why can't the app reach MySQL on localhost?Inside a container localhost is that container's own network namespace. On a compose network, reach the database by service name - jdbc:mysql://mysql-db:3306/... - which Docker's embedded DNS resolves.
When would you use buildpacks over a Dockerfile?mvn spring-boot:build-image gives a maintained base, automatic layering, a non-root user and a start-up memory calculator with no Dockerfile to maintain - ideal for many similar services. Write a Dockerfile when you need OS packages, a specific hardened or distroless base, or an approved corporate base image.

cheatNotes: @SpringBootApplication - Combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan
@EnableAutoConfiguration - Auto-configures beans based on classpath dependencies
Spring Boot Starters - Curated dependency bundles (spring-boot-starter-web, -data-jpa, etc.)
Embedded server - Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow bundled in the JAR, no external deployment needed
spring-boot-maven-plugin - Packages app as an executable fat/uber JAR
application.properties/application.yml - Externalized configuration file
@Value - Injects a single property value into a field
@ConfigurationProperties - Binds a group of properties to a POJO
@Profile - Activates beans/config only for a specific environment (dev/test/prod)
spring.profiles.active - Property to select the active profile
@RestController - @Controller + @ResponseBody combined for REST APIs
@Service - Marks a class as the service/business logic layer
@Repository - Marks a class as the data access layer, enables exception translation
@Component - Generic stereotype for a Spring-managed bean
@Autowired - Injects a bean dependency by type
@Qualifier - Resolves ambiguity when multiple beans of same type exist
@Bean - Declares a bean manually inside a @Configuration class
IoC container - Spring manages object creation and dependency wiring
Dependency Injection - Constructor, setter, or field injection of collaborators
Spring Data JPA - Repository abstraction (JpaRepository) that auto-implements CRUD
CrudRepository/JpaRepository - Built-in interfaces for common DB operations
@Query - Custom JPQL/native query on a repository method
Spring Boot Actuator - Exposes health, metrics, and monitoring endpoints
/actuator/health - Endpoint reporting application health status
@ExceptionHandler - Handles exceptions thrown within a specific controller
@ControllerAdvice - Centralizes exception handling across all controllers
@ResponseStatus - Maps an exception to a specific HTTP status code
REST API design - Use nouns for resources, HTTP verbs for actions, proper status codes
@RequestMapping/@GetMapping/@PostMapping - Map HTTP requests to handler methods
@PathVariable/@RequestParam/@RequestBody - Bind request data to method arguments
Spring Security - Handles authentication and authorization for the app
JWT - Token-based stateless authentication commonly used with Spring Boot APIs
CORS - Cross-Origin config needed when frontend and backend run on different origins
@SpringBootTest - Loads full application context for integration testing
@WebMvcTest - Loads only the web layer for controller unit testing
MockMvc - Simulates HTTP requests in tests without starting a real server
Spring Boot DevTools - Enables automatic restart and live reload during development
Logging - Built-in support via SLF4J/Logback, configurable in application.properties
Externalized config precedence - Command-line args > env vars > application.properties
Spring Boot CLI - Command-line tool to quickly prototype Spring apps
Spring Boot origin - Built by the Pivotal team in 2014; brings RAD to Spring
Five-layer architecture - Client, API/Controller, Service, DAO, Database
Client layer - Presentation logic: JSP, HTML, Angular, React
API layer - RESTful web services, @RestController
Service layer - Business logic; interfaces plus implementations
DAO layer - Persistence logic; translates business objects to and from rows
Layer rule - A layer calls only the layer directly below it
DTO - API-shaped class so a JPA entity never leaves the service layer
spring.main.lazy-initialization - Faster boot, but config errors move to the first request
Startup sequence - main, run(), stop watch, environment, banner, IoC container, refresh, runners
Stop watch - Produces the "Started App in N seconds" line
refreshContext() - Loads bean definitions, runs auto-config, starts Tomcat, builds singletons
banner.txt - Custom startup banner; spring.main.banner-mode=off disables it
CommandLineRunner - run(String... args), fires after the context is refreshed
ApplicationRunner - run(ApplicationArguments args), same timing, parsed arguments
Runner exception - Startup fails; the context closes and the JVM exits non-zero
Property source order - Command line > system properties > env vars > properties file
JSON - JavaScript Object Notation; media type application/json
JSON types - String, Number, Object, Array, Boolean, Null
JSON rules - Key/value pairs, comma separated, {} for objects, [] for arrays
JSON strictness - Double quotes only, no trailing comma, no comments, no leading-dot numbers
Jackson - Default JSON library, arrives with spring-boot-starter-web
@JsonIgnore - Keeps a field out of the JSON entirely
@JsonProperty - Maps a Java field to a differently named JSON key
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) - Accept unknown keys instead of failing
REST - REpresentational State Transfer; an architectural style, not a protocol
REST constraints - Client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered, code on demand
Stateless - No server-side session, which is what lets the API scale horizontally
HTTP verbs - GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes
Idempotent - GET, PUT and DELETE; POST is not
URL design - Noun in the URL, verb in the HTTP method: GET /api/students/10
201 Created - Correct status for a successful POST, with a Location header
204 No Content - Correct status for a successful DELETE
@ResponseStatus - Maps an exception or handler to a specific HTTP status code
Postman - Tool for sending requests with any method, headers and body
HandlerInterceptor - Runs before and after a controller handles a request
preHandle() - Before the controller; returning false stops the chain
postHandle() - After the controller, before the response; skipped if the handler threw
afterCompletion() - After request and response; runs even on failure, so cleanup goes here
addInterceptors() - WebMvcConfigurer method that registers interceptors, once at startup
Filter vs Interceptor - A filter is servlet-level and sees every request; an interceptor knows the handler method
addPathPatterns/excludePathPatterns - Restrict an interceptor to certain URLs
Actuator - Ready-made HTTP endpoints for monitoring and managing a running application
Default exposure - Only /actuator/health is exposed over HTTP
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* - Exposes every endpoint; never in production
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude - Removes endpoints; exclude always beats include
/actuator/beans - Every bean the container loaded
/actuator/mappings - Every URL mapping in the application
/actuator/env - All properties; leaks credentials, so keep it internal
/actuator/conditions - Why each auto-configuration did or did not apply
/actuator/heapdump - Downloads a full memory image; treat as highly sensitive
/actuator/shutdown - Disabled by default; POST only
enabled vs exposed - enabled creates the endpoint bean; exposure makes it reachable over HTTP
management.server.port - Moves actuator to a separate internal port
HealthIndicator - Custom health check; overall status is the worst component
Micrometer - Vendor-neutral metrics facade behind /actuator/metrics
